I don't think there has been a situation in the past where you have had institutional doping on such a scale. We believe the Russian NPC is either unwilling or unable to uphold the IPC anti-doping code, which aligns with the World Anti-Doping Agency code, so that is what they have to respond to."

The report published last week by Canadian law professor Richard McLaren accused Russia of running a state-sponsored doping programme from 2011 to 2015. The IPC responded after McLaren provided names of athletes connected to 35 "disappearing positive samples" from the Moscow laboratory referenced in the report. Additionally, 19 samples suspected of tampering during the 2014 Sochi Paralympic Winter Games have been sent for further testing.

Russia will have up to 21 days to appeal any IPC ruling. The Rio Paralympics are set to begin on 7 September.

Following its entry into administration in October, the team has secured a personal investment from Stephen Fitzpatrick, CEO of energy company Ovo, BBC Sport reports. Former Sainsbury’s chief Justin King has been named interim chairman. While King is not providing financial support, he will oversee the team’s business operations. He expressed confidence that Manor has "the right people, the right values and sheer hard work" to compete "at the highest level."

Fitzpatrick’s investment is independent of Ovo. He stated, "I have a lifelong passion for F1 and can't wait for the season ahead." Manor Marussia confirmed that English driver Will Stevens will race for the team, with a second driver expected to be announced soon.

The team’s new car, a modified version of the 2014 model, must pass Formula 1’s mandatory crash tests before the Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne, scheduled for March 13-15. These tests are set to take place this week.

Graeme Lowdon, who has remained with the team through its previous incarnations as Manor, Virgin, and Marussia, continues as president and sporting director. Reflecting on recent challenges, he said, "It has been a challenging period for all of us but we've come through it and now we just want to go racing again." He added, "With formidable new business leadership in Stephen Fitzpatrick and the board presence of Justin King, we are now in a great place ahead of the new season. This is a fantastic and very rewarding moment for all those involved with the team."

Rangi Chase, the 31-year-old half-back, has signed with Widnes for the remainder of the season after being informed he was not included in Castleford Tigers' plans for the rest of 2017. The former England playmaker was dropped for three games in March following an "internal investigation" at Castleford. Chase leaves the league-leading Tigers to join Widnes, who currently sit at the bottom of the table with just two wins from 13 matches.

Widnes coach Betts spoke about the signing on BBC Radio Merseyside, stating, "It is a great signing for us and I'm excited we've managed to pick up someone of Rangi's quality to come into the side. I know he's excited about playing as he wants to be playing regularly—he wants to start games and play 80 minutes." He added, "He comes here with a clean slate and wants to go again. He's up for the challenge, aware that we've got our backs against the wall and understands the situation. He's ready for the fight, which is really exciting."

The Bulford Kiwi, a 130-meter-tall (420 ft) chalk figure on Bulford Hill near Stonehenge, was created by New Zealand troops stationed nearby. Acting on Historic England’s recommendation, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport has officially designated it as a scheduled monument. New Zealand soldiers played a pivotal role in the Battle of Messines, fought in Belgium in June 1917.

Another monument related to the same battle, located at Cannock Chase in Staffordshire, has also received protected status. This site includes the Terrain Model of Messines, a scale replica of the battlefield constructed by German prisoners of war using soil, concrete, bricks, and pebbles. Once a popular attraction after the war, the model fell into neglect and was lost until its recent excavation. It has since been reburied to protect it from damage and erosion.

Roger Bowdler of Historic England said, “These two monuments pay tribute to the bravery of New Zealand’s fighting forces in the First World War and we are delighted that they are now being protected for the future.” He noted that the Bulford Kiwi was carved into the chalk by Kiwi soldiers at the end of the war to commemorate their presence in England and their achievements on the front. Bowdler added, “The taking of the Messines ridge was one of the war’s most stirring attacks, and this model lay-out remains as testimony to the planning which made possible the victory.” He stressed that these memorials connect us to the past and the events that shaped the nation, and that after 100 years, it is fitting to honor New Zealand’s courage.

Sir Jerry Mateparae, New Zealand High Commissioner to the UK, said, “It’s fantastic to see Historic England protecting two very significant sites of huge importance for New Zealand.” He highlighted the enduring ties formed a century ago between New Zealanders and UK communities where troops trained, calling it moving to see these sites preserved for future generations.

On-loan striker Holman marked his home debut by opening the scoring with a precise half-volley, then doubled his tally with a 12-yard finish. Danny Wright responded with a brace of his own, heading in from James Rowe's corner before adding a second goal from six yards in the second half. Despite a consolation goal from Alex Wall, the Robins secured their seventh victory in eight National League fixtures.

Cheltenham Town sits second in the league standings, trailing Forest Green Rovers by one point, while Bromley has dropped to 14th place after managing just one win in their last 11 matches. Speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire, Cheltenham manager Gary Johnson said, "It's the best we've played for a little while. We've still been getting the results, but I enjoyed the way we played today – we created lots of chances. I was really pleased with our performance and hopefully our supporters can go home nice and happy. Our passing had a bit of an end product to it without going long. All in all, the boys have put it together."

Marco Reus, 27, who missed the 2014 World Cup and has recently struggled with injuries, was left out of the squad. Nevertheless, coach Joachim Low included midfielder Bastian Schweinsteiger, 31, despite his absence from play since a knee injury sustained in March with the national team. Also omitted were Bayer Leverkusen’s Julian Brandt, Karim Bellarabi, and Hoffenheim’s Sebastian Rudy.

Speaking about Reus’s exclusion, which coincided with his birthday, Low said, “The medical staff could not give a clear prognosis for Marco. He has significant injury problems, and they were doubtful about his ability to endure the coming weeks and such a demanding tournament. It is a bitter decision, and bitter for Marco.”

The squad features Liverpool’s Emre Can, Arsenal’s Mesut Ozil, and former Arsenal forward Lukas Podolski, now with Turkish club Galatasaray, as the reigning world champions pursue their first European Championship since 1996.

The full squad is as follows:

Goalkeepers: Manuel Neuer (Bayern Munich), Bernd Leno (Bayer Leverkusen), Marc-Andre ter Stegen (Barcelona)

Defenders: Jerome Boateng (Bayern Munich), Emre Can (Liverpool), Jonas Hector (Cologne), Benedikt Hoewedes (Schalke 04), Mats Hummels (Borussia Dortmund), Shkodran Mustafi (Valencia), Antonio Ruediger (Roma)

Midfielders: Julian Draxler (VfL Wolfsburg), Sami Khedira (Juventus), Joshua Kimmich (Bayern Munich), Toni Kroos (Real Madrid), Thomas Muller (Bayern Munich), Mesut Ozil (Arsenal), Lukas Podolski (Galatasaray), Andre Schurrle (VfL Wolfsburg), Bastian Schweinsteiger (Manchester United), Julian Weigl (Borussia Dortmund)

Forwards: Mario Gomez (Besiktas), Mario Goetze (Bayern Munich), Leroy Sane (Schalke 04)

FIFA president Sepp Blatter stands accused by prosecutors of making a "disloyal payment" of $2 million (£1.6 million) to Michel Platini. Platini has cooperated with investigators, asserting he provided information only as a witness. Both men deny any wrongdoing.

Platini plans to run for FIFA president after Blatter’s resignation. When questioned about criminal charges against him, Platini responded, "Absolutely not. I was heard last week by the Swiss authorities only as a person providing information and I cooperated fully." Swiss Attorney General Michael Lauber challenged this, stating, "We didn't interview Mr Platini as a witness, that's not true. We investigated against him in between as a witness and an accused person." Lauber also indicated he is prepared to search UEFA headquarters as part of the ongoing investigation.

The case revolves around a 2011 payment to Platini, charged to FIFA, for work he completed nearly a decade earlier. The timing—just two months before UEFA endorsed Blatter’s 2011 presidential campaign—has raised questions. Platini said he was informed at the outset that FIFA could not pay him the full amount due to its "financial situation." Yet FIFA’s records reveal a revenue surplus of about $83 million (£55 million) from 1999 to 2002, when Platini served as a technical adviser.

This year, FIFA has been rocked by separate corruption probes from US and Swiss authorities. Blatter is also suspected of signing a contract considered "unfavourable to FIFA." Although he is expected to step down next year, Blatter insists he will remain in office amid the ongoing criminal proceedings.

South African Caster Semenya was the fastest qualifier for Saturday’s final, posting a time of 1:57.67. “Caster Semenya is one of the contenders,” said Maria Mutola, the 2000 Olympic 800m champion, in an interview with BBC Africa. She added, “Pamela Jelimo from Kenya and the Russians are also very capable. I’m looking forward to a good final.”

At 39, Mutola set the benchmark in women’s 800m running before retiring in 2008, having won three world titles and Olympic gold in Sydney. Semenya, who took the 800m title at the 2009 World Championships, invited her “idol” Mutola to coach her late last year, aiming for Olympic gold.

The 21-year-old Semenya looked composed in the semi-finals, accelerating down the back straight to take the lead and finish two metres ahead of her competitors. Mutola, now in London to help fine-tune Semenya’s preparations, said, “In 800m you need to run a fast race and also win a tactical slow race. You need to combine both—if the race is slow, you can still win, and if it’s fast, even better. In the final, they’ll have to run under two minutes.”

Since arriving, Mutola has concentrated on coaching Semenya. “I know she has to do well, so I’m just enjoying being a coach for the first time,” she said.

Semenya made global headlines after the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) requested a gender test following her world title win. Questions arose due to her muscular physique, running style, and rapid improvement. Although suspended by the IAAF for 11 months, she was cleared to compete again in July 2010. Despite a back problem, she won silver at last year’s World Championships in Daegu.

Lawsuits reported by the Associated Press allege significant safety failures by SXSW organizers. Since March, Rashad Charjuan Owens has faced murder charges after his car breached a barrier at the music, film, and interactive festival, killing four people. The crash took place outside the Mohawk venue and injured 23 others.

Among the wrongful death claims is one from the family of Steven Craenmehr, a Dutch music executive who was struck while cycling. His widow and mother assert that SXSW organizers did not provide sufficient pedestrian traffic safeguards during the event, which hosts thousands of bands across venues in Austin. The lawsuit contends, "A festival organiser or traffic design consultant of ordinary intelligence would have anticipated the danger."

SXSW’s legal team responded, saying: "What happened on Red River was a terrible tragedy, caused by Rashad Owen's utter disregard of human life. Our hearts continue to ache for those injured and the families of those who lost their lives. We look forward to his prosecution for his awful crimes."

Authorities report that Owens drove his grey Honda Civic through a barricade after an officer on a drink-drive patrol attempted to stop him. Police confirmed his blood alcohol level was .114, exceeding Texas’ legal limit of .08.

A safety report published in September warned that alcohol consumption and overcrowded venues during SXSW had brought Austin to a "critical point where public safety could be compromised" without reforms. Organizers dismissed the report as incomplete, saying it failed to address underlying causes.

SXSW is widely regarded as one of the world’s premier platforms for emerging music talent.

Mills and Clark upgraded their London silver to gold in the women's 470 event at the Rio Olympics. Four-time world champion Giles Scott, who won Finn gold in Rio 2016, was nominated for the men's award, but it went to Argentina's Santiago Lange. Clark, 37, who retired after Rio, said, "I've got the gold medal that was the childhood dream and the goal we set." Mills, 28, commented, "Our six years together have been focused on building our team and making it as strong as possible. London was a rushed Olympics with just 18 months to prepare, and it felt hastily assembled. In Rio, we had four years to get it right, and our team has been central to that. To finish like this means everything." For advice on starting sailing, see our special guide. Media playback is not supported on this device.

Kruse, ranked 10th in the world, secured the foil title by defeating Italy’s Alessio Foconi 15-8 in the final. The 33-year-old was attacked soon after arriving in Shanghai last week. “The adrenaline that went through my body was unbelievable,” Kruse said, noting he will move up to world number five. “When I came to fence, I was ready to fight.”

Following a fourth-place finish at the 2016 Rio Olympics, Kruse bypassed the qualifying rounds in Shanghai and won his opening match against German Benjamin Kleibrink. He then overcame American Nick Itkin, Hong Kong’s world number seven Cheung Ka-long, Italian Lorenzo Nista, and France’s world number six Erwann le Pechoux to set up the final with Foconi.

Looking back on Rio, Kruse reflected, “Maybe coming fourth in Rio was the best thing to happen to me,” after narrowly missing Great Britain’s first Olympic fencing medal in 52 years. “Had I got a medal then perhaps I wouldn’t have had the motivation to carry on.”

Manchester United manager David Moyes has made 20-year-old Varela his first signing. The defender, who trialed at Old Trafford last season, has appeared once for Penarol and holds nine caps for Uruguay's Under-20 team. Upon signing a five-year contract, Varela expressed his enthusiasm: "I'm very pleased to be a part of this club, one of the best in the world. As everyone in the world knows, this is a huge club that has won everything and I really hope that continues."

Varela is currently participating in the Under-20 World Championships in Turkey, which run from 21 June to 13 July. Last week, Penarol head coach Jorge Da Silva, reportedly resigned since, said the young player had earned the move. "This is what he deserves. It is a shame to see him go but you can't deny him the opportunity to join a club like this," Da Silva stated.

In the previous season, Rafael was Manchester United’s primary right-back, with Phil Jones and Chris Smalling also featuring in that role.

Twelve men were charged with waging war against the nation, conspiracy, and murder, while one was acquitted. The serial bombings on 11 July 2006 resulted in 189 deaths and over 800 injuries. Islamic militants allegedly supported by Pakistan were held responsible, though Pakistan denies these claims.

The attacks took place during the evening rush hour on Mumbai’s suburban train network, which transports more than eight million commuters daily. Seven bombs, concealed in pressure cookers inside bags, detonated within 15 minutes across locations including Matunga, Khar, Mahim, Jogeshwari, Borivali, and Mira Road. Most explosions occurred on moving trains, with two at stations. The bombs appeared to target first-class compartments as passengers returned from the city’s financial district.

The trial spanned eight years and concluded in August last year, examining over 200 witnesses. Prosecutors allege the attack was orchestrated by Pakistan’s intelligence agency ISI and carried out by Lashkar-e-Taiba operatives, with assistance from the banned Indian group Students’ Islamic Movement of India. Pakistan rejects these accusations, citing a lack of evidence.

Sentencing is scheduled for Monday after Judge Yatin D. Shinde hears arguments from both prosecution and defense. Those convicted face either the death penalty or life imprisonment. Public prosecutor Raja Thakre told reporters, “Justice has been done for the people of Mumbai. I will ask for the strictest punishment when I argue for their sentences.”

Reporting by Menaka Rao

Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker has proclaimed August 13 as "Purple Hearts for Healing" Day to honor an unnamed girl who survived being stabbed 19 times by two classmates. The girl's family thanked the governor for recognizing "our little hero." The attackers told police their assault was carried out in "dedication" to Slenderman, a fictional character from the website Creepypasta.

The family has been raising funds to cover the girl's medical expenses, with several Wisconsin businesses organizing fundraisers to support the cause. "The compassion and love expressed to our family by the people of Wisconsin [and from people around the world] has greatly assisted our family in this healing process," they said. They added, "The prayers, cards, hearts, notes, financial support, and now this heartfelt proclamation truly demonstrate that through this tragedy there is so much goodness in the world."

Twelve-year-olds Morgan Geyser and Anissa Weier have been charged as adults with attempted murder and face up to 60 years in prison. Authorities have determined that one of the accused is mentally unfit to stand trial.

In his proclamation, Governor Walker encouraged the public to wear purple in the girl's honor. "This little girl is overcoming a terrible ordeal," he said. "Her strength and determination are an inspiration, and on behalf of Wisconsin, I wish her well as she continues her journey to recovery."

According to police, the girls initially planned to stab their classmate during a sleepover but postponed the attack until the following morning, carrying it out in a nearby park. After their arrest, they told investigators about their belief in the paranormal figure Slenderman and their intent to become his "proxies" by committing the stabbing as a demonstration of loyalty.

The victim was found by a cyclist after crawling out of the woods with stab wounds to her arms, legs, and torso. Medical professionals noted that the knife narrowly missed a major artery near her heart.

Healthcare improvements in the north of the county are being explored, including the possible removal of consultant-led services from West Cumberland Hospital in Whitehaven. Stephen Eames, chief executive of North Cumbria University Hospitals NHS Trust, stated that Whitehaven lacks the necessary "infrastructure" to maintain these services. Midwives have voiced safety concerns, warning that moving consultant-led maternity care to Carlisle Cumberland Infirmary could put mothers and babies at risk of death if services are withdrawn from Whitehaven.

Speaking to BBC Cumbria, Eames said the options under consideration will probably lead to changes in maternity services, with consultant expertise concentrated in a single location. He added that while all involved would prefer consultant-led services at both sites, the challenge involves not only maternity but also other supporting clinical services. Despite some progress in recruiting for children’s services, Eames said it is not viable to develop the infrastructure required for two separate consultant-led units.

Midwives in Whitehaven have raised alarms about the risks for mothers facing unexpected complications who might require a potentially hazardous 40-mile (64km) transfer to Carlisle. Earlier this month, Bernadette Bowness cautioned, "We're going to become a third world area because of our inaccessibility to a consultant-led unit. If ladies have to be transferred, mothers may die, babies may die. If babies have foetal distress, what with the transfer time they may end up brain damaged."

A public consultation will begin next month to collect feedback on the trust’s future service plans. The organisation has been under special measures since 2014, after Care Quality Commission inspectors determined it was failing to provide an adequately high standard of care in several areas.

After discussions with the PSNI, off-licences in the area will close from 16:00 to 21:00 GMT on 17 March, following disturbances during the 2016 St Patrick's Day holiday. The PSNI said the measure aims "to help keep people safe."

Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University have advised students to avoid traveling to the area or to act responsibly if they do. Both universities have cancelled classes on Wednesday 15 March and Thursday 16 March, designating these as "reading days," and will be closed on 17 March.

Colin Neill, chief executive of Hospitality Ulster, praised the voluntary closure by off-licences, expressing sympathy for residents affected by repeated unacceptable behaviour on St Patrick's Day and commending local off-sales for their cooperation. He urged supermarkets to follow suit by halting alcohol deliveries to the Holylands area on 16 and 17 March, highlighting the "fuelling of drink" as a significant factor.

Ray Farley of the Holyland Regeneration Association cautiously welcomed the move as a "welcome first step," suggesting that a half-day closure this year could pave the way for a full-day closure in future years, stressing that "it's drink that's the problem, and the fuelling of drink."

A wooden beach hut located in Abersoch on the Llŷn Peninsula in Gwynedd measures 13ft by 9ft and lacks both electricity and water. Overnight stays are prohibited. The hut sold for a price similar to that of a two-bedroom house in nearby Llanbedrog or a seven-bedroom terraced house in Tywyn, across Cardigan Bay.

Tony Webber, auction surveyor at Beresford Adams Countrywide Auctions, described the sale as "certainly the highest price ever achieved for a beach hut in Abersoch." He added, "It's quite incredible. We had two very determined bidders, both from the Cheshire area, bidding separately. They were very determined to buy it."

The auctioneers mentioned the hut "is in need of some TLC" but includes part of the beach in front of it, extending into the sea. The previous record for beach huts on Abersoch sands stood at £70,000 in 2008.

Earlier this year, signs marking the Clifton Village residents' parking zone were installed, with some fixed to railings that are Grade II* listed. This led to complaints that the signs were damaging the character of the conservation area. The council explained that it used railings where possible to limit the number of posts on the pavement and said it "met regularly" with English Heritage to discuss listed building work and relevant legislation.

The council also noted that when signs were put up in the Kingsdown conservation area, it had been advised that as long as the work did not result in "significant or permanent changes to a building, which would alter its character," it was considered acceptable. Nevertheless, a letter from English Heritage, obtained by the BBC, raised concerns about the "potential cumulative impact" of signs in West Mall and Caledonia Place, both of which include listed buildings.

The letter indicated that, taken together, such work might fall under Section 7 of the Planning and Listed Buildings and Conservation Act 1990. It recommended applying for listed building consent "to allow for a careful consideration of the impact of the works on the special interest of the terrace, of the number of signs and the consideration of alternative locations."

English Heritage has designated numbers 1 to 31 Caledonia Place, along with their attached basement railings, as Grade II* listed due to their "special architectural or historic interest."

The Midlands club remains at the bottom of the Premier League, 10 points adrift of safety, having made no signings in the January transfer window. Reports indicate that Garde may reassess his future in the summer, though the French coach stated, "I'm speaking only about the game. I have nothing else to say. It's not the time to answer this question."

In the match, Villa’s penalty appeal against West Ham was rejected, and Jordan Ayew was sent off after just 17 minutes. West Ham opened the scoring through Michail Antonio—a goal Garde suggested might have been offside—before Cheikhou Kouyate added a second for the Upton Park side.

Garde said, "I'm not going to speak any more about the incident; it's a major one in the game, but I don't have to explain my feelings, and you can guess Jordan's feelings. Whatever happens in the dressing room is private. But I'm not sure it was the only incident that turned the game. Of course, I think we should have had a penalty."

He added, "I'm not a lucky or unlucky man, but I don't like to hear it's because we are at the bottom. The rules in football are there for everybody."

Dane County District Attorney Ishmael Ozanne has concluded that police officer Matt Kenny acted within the law when he shot 19-year-old Tony Robinson Jr., who was unarmed and of mixed race. The shooting occurred on March 6 inside a Madison apartment and ignited protests at the state capitol amid nationwide tensions over police use of force.

Following Ozanne’s Tuesday announcement, additional protesters gathered in Madison carrying "Black lives matter" signs. Robinson’s mother, Andrea Irwin, addressed supporters outside Grace Episcopal Church, pledging to continue the "fight."

Ozanne detailed that Officer Kenny was responding to an emergency call about a man obstructing traffic and allegedly involved in an assault when he encountered Robinson. Autopsy reports indicated Robinson had multiple illicit drugs in his system that night. Friends who made several 911 calls described Robinson as "acting crazy," attempting to choke one of them, attacking people on the sidewalk, and running in front of cars.

Officer Kenny drew his firearm before entering the apartment building where Robinson was located. He said Robinson attacked him at the top of the stairs, and fearing he would be pushed down and lose his gun, Kenny fired seven shots.

Robinson’s family and many protesters in Wisconsin continue to assert that he was a victim of police brutality. Ozanne acknowledged, "My decision won't bring him back, it will not end the racial disparities that exist in the justice system." He added, "It is not based on emotion, rather the facts as they have been investigated and reported to me, guided by the rule of law."

Thousands of furry insects with wingspans reaching up to 16 cm (6 in) disrupted a semi-final match at Darul Makmur Stadium last week. In addition, over 800 sightings were reported in neighboring Singapore last month, sparking lively online discussions. The Lyssa Zampa tropical moth, also called the Laos brown butterfly, is native to Southeast Asia.

Biology lecturer N. Sivasothi acknowledged that while the current moth sightings appear "unprecedented," they are not a new occurrence. He explained that the moths exist in smaller numbers during other parts of the year and typically emerge annually between April and August.

Ecologist Anuj Jain pointed out that moths navigate by light, which often draws them into urban environments. He added that their search for new, uneaten host plants attracts them toward city lights.

Experts stressed that although individuals with asthma might be sensitive to the hairs on the moths’ wings, these nocturnal insects do not pose significant health risks. Lena Chan, Director of the National Biodiversity Centre at Singapore’s National Parks Board, stated, "The moths are harmless and the public has nothing to be afraid of." She also noted that the moths do not cause allergies or diseases and play a vital role as pollinators.

Many Malaysians and Singaporeans took to social media to share photos and experiences of the moths. While some welcomed their presence, others remained cautious. Chinese astrologer Cindy Wu remarked, "In China, moths are viewed as symbols of death as they represent the souls of deceased loved ones. It is therefore considered a serious taboo to kill moths or disturb them."

Hywel Dda University Health Board has put forward a proposal to reduce the daily operating hours of the paediatric ambulatory care unit (PACU) at Withybush Hospital by four hours, citing a shortage of consultant paediatricians. The full health board is scheduled to review the proposal at a meeting on 24 November.

At present, the PACU provides care for children experiencing sudden pain, high temperatures, sickness, infections, and those requiring dressings, blood tests, x-rays, or scans. If the change is approved, the unit’s hours would shift from 10:00–22:00 GMT to 10:00–18:00 GMT. Children needing assessment after 18:00 would be referred or transported by ambulance to Glangwili Hospital in Carmarthen.

The health board explained that the temporary reduction is due to "longstanding difficulties in recruiting paediatric consultants across the UK," compounded by the retirement of a Pembrokeshire paediatric consultant and the maternity leave of another. It cautioned that failing to act would present a "risk."

Additionally, there is a recommendation to merge the on-call rota with the one in Carmarthenshire. This would enable on-call paediatric consultants to provide remote advice during out-of-hours emergencies at Withybush Hospital.

Steve Moore, chief executive of the health board, said: "It is our duty to be realistic about the availability of our consultants and to plan care around this so that it is safe, consistent and to avoid public confusion. Otherwise, we risk the event of having insufficient staff and having to close the unit in an unplanned and uncoordinated way, risking patient safety and public confidence." He added that recruitment efforts remain ongoing.

Moores, who earned a silver medal in this event at London 2012, was considered a strong medal prospect but finished fifth in his heat. "I'm not too disappointed because I haven't been training backstroke. It's all about the breaststroke," he explained. The 22-year-old will now direct his efforts toward the breaststroke.

In athletics, Kyron Duke secured fifth place in the F41 shot put final, while Olivia Breen progressed to the T38 100m final after placing fourth in her heat.

In table tennis, world number one Rob Davies edged past Switzerland’s Silvio Keller 3-2 in his opening class 1 qualifier and is set to face Italy’s Andrea Borgato on Friday. Davies commented, "Hopefully I can play better in my next match and be a bit more clinical." Meanwhile, his teammate Sara Head was defeated 3-0 by Sweden’s Anna-Carin Ahlquist in her opening women’s singles class 3 match.

In wheelchair basketball, Clare Griffiths featured as Great Britain’s women fell 43-36 to Canada, while Phil Pratt and the men’s team claimed a 93-31 victory over Algeria. Owen Burke did not advance to the men’s R1-10m Air Rifle Standing final.

On Friday, seven Welsh athletes will compete on the second day of the Games. Para-rower Rachel Morris, who previously won hand cycling gold in Beijing and bronze in London 2012, will begin her campaign in the Arms Only Sculls. On the track, Jordan Howe, regarded as an outside medal contender in the T35 100m, will start his heats.

On Wednesday, Mrs. Foster announced her intention to deepen her understanding of those who value the Irish language, saying she wants to "listen to and engage with those from the Gaelic Irish background, those without the party political background." Mr. Ó Muilleoir welcomed the initiative, expressing hope the meeting would take place soon. He described it as "a positive move," adding that any effort to promote dialogue and understanding is beneficial.

Negotiations among Stormont’s parties to form an executive have been paused until after Easter. Nearly six weeks after the assembly election, no agreement has been reached. Sinn Féin continues to prioritize securing a commitment to enact an Irish Language Act in the talks.

In February, Arlene Foster stated that the DUP would never support an Irish Language Act. However, she has since indicated a willingness to meet with "people who genuinely love the Irish language and don't want to use it as a political weapon." Mr. Ó Muilleoir expressed hope she would listen closely to Irish speakers, who remain "united and firm on the need for an Irish Language Act." He said, "Arlene will find when she meets the Irish language community that they're a very broad church, people with all political views and none," adding, "They’re united behind the belief that Irish is a shared treasure of our people. It’s a gift Irish speakers want to share with everyone, including unionists who have yet to fully appreciate the language’s importance."

He also cautioned that it is "too early" to assess the DUP’s position on the Irish Language Act but believes the meeting will benefit both Mrs. Foster and the Irish language community.

Meanwhile, the Irish language group Pobal confirmed it would "gladly accept" Mrs. Foster’s invitation and has already reached out to arrange a meeting.

At 26, Christie completed the race in 42.565 seconds, finishing ahead of Canadian Jamie Macdonald and Dutch skater Yara van Kerkhof. The Nottingham-based Scot has been training alongside men and emphasizing "learning to lose" to boost her medal prospects.

During the Sochi 2014 Games, Christie faced three controversial disqualifications but went on to claim World Cup and European titles last season. Reflecting on her return to Calgary, she said, "It's been great to be back here. I haven't had the most straightforward competition with a few falls on Friday and Saturday. My coaches and support team worked with me and my equipment overnight, and the adjustments paid off."

On Friday, Christie was also part of the GB ladies relay team that set a new British record in the 3,000m event. The quartet—Christie, captain Charlotte Gilmartin, Kathryn Thomson, and Samantha Morrison—finished in four minutes 13.719 seconds, breaking the previous record of four minutes 14.57 seconds.

Borja, 23, has completed a move to Swansea from Atletico Madrid for a club-record £15 million, following Fernando Llorente’s transfer from Sevilla. Born in Madrid and a product of Atletico’s academy, Borja spent the past five seasons on loan from Vicente Calderon, netting 18 La Liga goals last season with Eibar.

Reflecting on his Atletico spell, Borja acknowledged, “Of course there's a bit of frustration I didn't play much at Atletico. I grew up there, went through the ranks and wish I'd had more of an opportunity in the first team.” Despite interest from other La Liga and Premier League sides, he was drawn to Swansea’s approach. “Swansea showed the most interest, they seemed to want me more than anyone else,” he said. “It's a great club who have a lot of confidence in their players and I really want to make a good impression here.”

On Swansea’s tactical setup, Borja explained, “We can adapt and play with two strikers or just one, whatever the boss asks from us.” He will, however, miss the season opener against Burnley.

Speaking about Llorente, 31, Borja commented, “We don't know each other personally but I've been told he's a really good guy. I'm sure we'll both work together well and do whatever's best for the team.” While Llorente was part of Spain’s 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012-winning squads, Borja has yet to receive a senior national team call-up. He hopes to follow in the footsteps of former Swansea striker Michu, who earned a Spain cap after a strong season with the club. “Michu did a great job at Swansea which eventually earned him a place in Spain's squad. If only I could score as many goals as he did, helping the team in every possible way, for the good of Swansea, but also to put myself in the frame for national selection too,” Borja said.

The hashtag #penuriecarburantdansunfilm, which translates to "fuel shortage in a film," surged to the top of France’s Twitter trends on Tuesday, generating over 5,000 tweets. A strike opposing new labour laws is disrupting all eight of the country’s oil refineries, causing roughly 20% of petrol stations to run dry or face low fuel supplies.

On social media, users referenced films like Total Recall—released in 1990 and 2012—while noting that Total is also the name of a French multinational oil company. Many creatively tweaked movie titles to reflect the fuel shortage: Pulp Fiction became Pump Friction, The Full Monty was renamed The Fuel Monty, and Mad Max: Fury Road turned into Mad Max: Fury Bicycle Lane.

Vin Diesel and his Fast and Furious franchise attracted particular attention, inspiring playful titles such as Last and Furious, Pas Fast Mais Furious (Not Fast But Furious), Immobile and Furious, and Fuel Furious. Other films received similar treatment, including 8 Mile, starring US rapper Eminem, which was changed to 0 Mile and 8 Miles a Pied (8 Miles on Foot).

American director Stanley Kubrick’s films also featured in the wordplay, with Fuel Metal Jacket referencing his 1987 movie Full Metal Jacket. The French title of Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, 2001, l’Odyssee de l’espace, was highlighted as well; “Espace” is also the name of a minivan produced by French automaker Renault.

Photos of people filling jerrycans at petrol stations inspired further puns, such as Tom and Jerrycan, Jerrycan Beauty, and Catch Me If You Jerrycan. Nicolas Winding Refn’s 2011 film Drive was also renamed Walk and Drive Pas by social media users.

Read more about France’s controversial new labour laws.

While checking on construction at his new home, Campbell Baird heard meowing coming from inside the walls and found a trapped cat named Francee. "I couldn't believe it at first," Mr. Baird said. He used a drill, chisel, and hammer to free the cat, then shared a video of the rescue on Facebook to help find her owner. The video has been shared more than 700 times, and Francee has since been reunited with her owner, appearing shaken but unharmed.

Mr. Baird explained that Francee became stuck in a small cavity after apparently climbing a ladder to the first floor. "The only way in would have been from above, so she must've climbed up and then got stuck down in between the wall," he said. "It's fortunate I came up to the house or the cat would not have been found." He added, "It was a small cavity space in the wall. I pulled some insulation out and used tools to free her."

"I'm just happy I was able to get the cat back home and everything worked out OK," Mr. Baird said. Laughing, he added, "My phone hasn't stopped since I posted the video. But all I wanted was to find the cat's owner, and I'm glad I could do that."

The report called for splitting the combined roles of head of the legal system and president of the States. Political expert Dr. Adrian Lee observed that this dual role is unique to the islands, where the judge also participates in lawmaking—unlike any other democratic jurisdiction.

Authored by the Carswell Committee, the report recommended that Jersey's Bailiff step down as president of the States of Jersey and be replaced by an elected speaker. Lord Carswell remarked, "There are various international constitutional documents, which rather frown on the idea of judges having anything to do with the legislator." He also pointed to a practical concern, noting that the Bailiff has devoted increasing time to States-related duties in recent years.

Dr. Lee, a former politics professor at Plymouth University, added that as the two islands build their international profiles, it is vital for their legal and political systems to be clearly understood externally. He highlighted current confusion over who represents the island—whether it is the chief minister, the Lieutenant Governor, the Bailiff, or all three.

A spokesperson for Guernsey's Policy Council said it would closely monitor developments in Jersey. Meanwhile, the Guernsey States Assembly and Constitution Committee intends to review the report at a meeting scheduled for next week.

Attention on the dual role of both bailiffs intensified after Sark decided in October to split the position of seneschal—who acted as both chief judge and president of Chief Pleas—following outside pressure.

One person was injured in a crash near the national stadium on Saturday night amid heavy rain. Police announced on Monday that both drivers involved were unemployed and in their 20s. This information sparked online speculation about their identities, with a Weibo user asking, “What are their names? Who are their fathers?” according to AFP. Another user quipped, “Socialism is so good that it allows unemployed people to drive supercars.”

Photos released Monday showed the lime green Lamborghini with its front nearly torn off, while the red Ferrari had lost a door and sustained damage along its side and rear. The tunnel where the collision occurred also suffered damage, including a torn section of wall and bent guardrails. Workers were seen clearing debris from the roadway.

The cause of the crash remains unclear as police continue their investigation. Local media reported the tunnel is frequently used for drag racing. Many online observers noted the incident coincided with the Shanghai Grand Prix and the premiere of the latest Fast and Furious film, a franchise known for fast cars and expensive wrecks.

Lisa Doughty, 47, who has been diagnosed with mesothelioma, attended Haggerston Girls' School in Hackney, east London, during the 1980s. She recalled that the music desks were frequently coated in dust, which she believes may have contained asbestos fibers. Spending considerable time each week rehearsing plays in the music room, she described sitting on the desks and regularly wiping away white dust. The room’s entrance featured two heavy doors that often slammed shut, causing the room to shake. Given the school’s poor condition, she suggested the dust might have fallen from the ceiling when the doors closed.

Ms. Doughty expressed concern that the music room could have been the source of her cancer and warned that others might also have been affected. She sought to raise awareness and encouraged former pupils or teachers with similar experiences to come forward.

Her legal team at Slater and Gordon discovered that asbestos ceiling tiles were present during her time at the school and are considering further legal action. A Hackney Council spokesperson said asbestos was historically common in both public and private buildings due to its fire-retardant qualities. The council added that, like other buildings of similar age, Haggerston School has undergone regular condition assessments, asbestos surveys, and removal work. However, it has not received a formal claim and cannot begin an investigation until one is lodged.

Edmund Young, an asbestos-related disease specialist at Slater and Gordon, noted that although mesothelioma has traditionally affected industrial workers, an increasing number of former pupils and teachers exposed to asbestos at school are now coming forward.

Chris Henry, 29, has become the latest player to extend his commitment to Ulster, joining Ruan Pienaar, Nick Williams, and Robbie Diack, who recently signed contract extensions. "I am delighted to have committed to Ulster for the long term," Henry said, praising the team environment and expressing confidence in their trophy prospects, acknowledging they have "some unfinished business."

Henry, who has earned eight caps for Ireland and made 109 appearances for Ulster, is determined to help the province secure silverware after defeats in the Heineken Cup and Pro12 finals in the past two seasons. He is also aiming for a spot in Joe Schmidt's Ireland squad for the 2015 World Cup. "Being at Ulster gives me the best chance to fulfil that ambition," he stated. "This squad is getting better and better, with experienced and young players proving they can perform at the highest level."

Ulster’s Director of Rugby, David Humphreys, described Henry as "a cornerstone of our success in recent years," pointing to his performance against Montpellier as a clear example of his commitment, intensity, and ferocity at the breakdown. Humphreys added, "It would be hard to find anyone more passionate about playing for Ulster than Chris Henry, and I am extremely pleased he will be part of the squad until at least 2017."

Liam McDonald, 31, has been named manager of Solihull Moors, with newly appointed head coach Keith Bertschin joining him in the coaching setup. McDonald takes over from Marcus Bignot, who left Solihull on 7 November to become manager of League Two side Grimsby Town. Since assuming charge of Hednesford Town in May, McDonald guided the team to fourth place in the Northern Premier League Premier Division. His first game in charge at Solihull will be Tuesday’s FA Cup first-round replay against Yeovil at home.

Solihull Moors, promoted last season, currently sit 16th in the National League standings. McDonald will be supported by assistant manager Nick Green and coach David Bridgwater, both of whom worked with him previously at Hednesford and Redditch.

In an interview with BBC WM’s Rob Gurney, McDonald said, “With my ambitions as a football manager, the opportunity to come to Solihull was just too good to turn down. Part of the decision was to aid my development. Keith has a wealth of experience that will help. But I’m in charge. I have my management team with me, and I want to put my stamp on things and continue the good work Marcus has done in transforming this club.”

He added, “It was a tough decision and Saturday was an emotional day for me, but the people at Hednesford understand why I’ve made it.”

Oyster beds were set up off Porlock Bay in 2013 as part of a scheme to increase employment and enhance the area's image. Since then, shellfish farming has grown steadily, earning the highest quality rating and gearing up for local sales. Roger Hall, from the Porlock Futures Community Interest Company, called the initiative a "brilliantly successful trial."

The trials used oysters sourced from Morecambe Bay in Lancashire to test their viability in Porlock’s waters. "We've proved the oysters not only grow but have the best Class A classification for cleanliness you can get," Hall said. He added, "It's the realization of an interesting idea, and now we have 70 trestles with thousands of oysters ready for restaurant consumption."

Following the trial’s success, the project secured £75,000 from the Power To Change fund and raised over £65,000 from the local community. David Salter, also from the Community Interest Company, acknowledged that while their site "hasn't got the fastest-growing site in the South West," they expect to sell about 30,000 oysters this year. He projected, "Next year, we'll reach 80,000, and in four to five years, we'll have 500,000." Salter added, "It's really growing, and in a few years, we'll have 500 trestles."

Gorka Marquez required dental surgery after two of his lower front teeth were severely chipped in Blackpool. According to the BBC, the 26-year-old Spaniard was attacked by a group of youths while reportedly walking to a nightclub with colleagues on Saturday. A spokesperson for Strictly confirmed that Marquez "doesn't wish to make a formal complaint" and "just wants to move on."

Marquez was in Blackpool to participate in a live edition of the show at Blackpool Tower Ballroom when he became the victim of an "unprovoked incident." The spokesperson added that he was getting out of a car when a "random group of lads" ran past and assaulted him.

A Lancashire Police representative said, "We have checked CCTV and spoken to the club and inquiries continue. We have had no formal complaint from Mr. Marquez."

In a tweet following the attack, Marquez wrote: "Thanks for all your kind messages and support about Blackpool. It was a bad experience but I'm feeling better and just want to look forward to the show on Saturday!"

Marquez made his debut on Strictly Come Dancing this year, partnered with EastEnders actress Tameka Empson, who portrays Kim Fox in the BBC soap. Although they were eliminated in the second round, Marquez has remained involved in the programme through the weekly group routines.

During a Friday assembly at Newington Church of England Primary School in Sittingbourne, children aged four to 11 were presented with a scenario related to refugees. The school admitted that the exercise had not been discussed with parents or senior staff beforehand. It was part of a week focused on learning about refugees.

In a statement, the school explained, "We intended to provide a scenario that would enable the children to empathise with those we were raising money for." It added that future activities of this kind will require approval from a member of the senior leadership team before being carried out. The school emphasized that only activities fostering empathy and understanding without causing undue stress or anxiety will be permitted.

Acknowledging that the message could have been delivered in "a more appropriate manner," the school apologized to parents and children. The exercise formed part of the school’s participation in Christian Aid's refugee week.

Christian Aid, the charity benefiting from the school’s fundraising, said, "We have very little information about what pupils were actually told in the assembly, but we would never recommend any teaching approaches that put undue stress on children."

The French flag has been raised above the City Chambers in George Square as a gesture of solidarity with the people of France. On Wednesday, 12 people were killed by suspected Islamists at the office of the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo. In a similar show of support last month, Glasgow flew the Pakistan flag following the Peshawar school massacre.

Council leader Gordon Matheson called the Charlie Hebdo attack "a brutal attack on democracy and freedom of expression." He stated, "Glasgow unites in unequivocal condemnation. Our thoughts and prayers are with the victims and their loved ones." Matheson highlighted that "the murderous actions of perverse and unrepresentative extremists will never overcome a free press, which is so fundamental to the values of a democratic society."

He added, "We are flying the flag of France at half-mast from the City Chambers today as a mark of respect for those who have died and to show our solidarity with the people of France and journalists everywhere." Matheson and Lord Provost Sadie Docherty intend to send a joint letter of condolence to the mayor of Paris and the French consulate in Edinburgh on behalf of Glasgow.

Jamie Peacock, Kevin Sinfield, and Kylie Leuluai concluded their careers with Leeds Rhinos after the team’s victory over Wigan Warriors at Old Trafford on Saturday. The win completed a domestic treble, adding to earlier successes in the League Leaders' Shield and Challenge Cup. The three were honored during a special event at the First Direct Arena.

Following the Grand Final, former England captain Jamie Peacock commented, "It's a bit difficult to sum up. I'm lost for words. I just feel fortunate to be in a great team. It's a team sport and that's why rugby league is such a great sport."

Judith Blake, leader of Leeds City Council, said, "It has been another amazing season for the Leeds Rhinos, and this event gives supporters the chance to congratulate the team and thank legends Kevin Sinfield, Jamie Peacock, and Kylie Leuluai. We are extremely proud of the Rhinos, whose commitment and achievements on the field, as well as their work in our communities, are simply fantastic. They truly deserve an event like this."

Leeds Rhinos chief executive Gary Hetherington described the celebration as a "spectacular live show," with performances by The Pigeon Detectives in tribute to the three retiring players.

England lost both of their home one-day series this summer, falling to Sri Lanka and India, and have claimed just seven wins in 18 one-day internationals this year. They are currently touring Sri Lanka as part of their World Cup preparations ahead of the tournament in Australia and New Zealand, beginning in February.

Speaking to BBC Sport, 25-year-old Finn expressed confidence, saying, "If we stick together, I think we're capable of upsetting people at the World Cup." England kicked off their winter campaign on Friday with a 56-run victory over Sri Lanka A, secured via the Duckworth-Lewis method. They are set to face the same side again on Sunday before commencing a seven-match one-day international series against Sri Lanka’s full team.

While England are not considered tournament favorites, Middlesex right-arm fast bowler Finn believes their underdog status could work in their favor. "It suits us to go over there as underdogs, and if we can slip under the radar having had a good month of preparation under our belt here in Sri Lanka," he said. "In the last few games of the season, we put in some good performances against India, who are arguably the best one-day team in the world. If we can get some belief and team ethics in place to go forward into the World Cup, that should stand us in good stead."
