A missed green along the cushion by Liang gave Higgins—who had already recorded three century breaks of 119, 104, and 133—the chance to clinch the victory.

Neil Robertson, the UK Championship titleholder, secured a commanding 6-0 win over Marco Fu, who had been unwell with a virus on Tuesday and nearly withdrew from the contest.

Media playback is not supported on this device. Robertson is set to meet world number five Judd Trump in the quarter-final on Friday at 13:00 GMT. Later that evening at 19:00 GMT, Higgins will face world champion Stuart Bingham.

Commenting on his win over Liang, Higgins said, "Many players might have seen the green shot as easy, but I knew it was difficult. It was great to come through. We all know he is a great player. He played very well today, stayed focused, and potted some incredible balls." He added, "If I play like that, I have a chance against anyone."

On Friday morning, Tomasz Procko, 22, and Karol Szymanski, 29, were delivering sofas to a Knightsbridge property when the balcony gave way. Mr. Procko, from Greenford in west London, died at the scene, while Mr. Szymanski, from Wembley in north-west London, later died in hospital. Both men, originally from Poland, had their next of kin notified.

The London Ambulance Service reported that eight others received treatment for injuries. A neighbour, speaking anonymously to BBC News, said the workers were trying to lift a couch to the first-floor apartment using ropes, but the couch was reportedly too heavy, causing the fence to break off and fall onto them.

Sinclair Johnston, an engineer with experience on another property in the square, stated the decorative railings could not be trusted to bear weight. The wrought-iron railing appeared to have fallen about 3.6 meters (12 feet) to the ground, while the stone base of the balcony remained intact.

The hotel chain has revealed that its investment programme will generate 150 jobs and 10 apprenticeships. Two new hotels located off the Royal Mile on New Market Street are scheduled to open by the end of this month, while a third hotel in York Place, New Town, is planned for late spring. These openings will increase the total number of Premier Inn hotels in the city to 14, providing more than 1,500 rooms.

Among the two hotels near the Royal Mile, one will introduce a hi-tech "hub by Premier Inn," marking the chain’s first such facility in Scotland. This hub will enable guests to control their room settings using an Apple Watch. Additional investments include a £1.8 million extension at Premier Inn Newcraighall and a £1.2 million refurbishment at Edinburgh Central.

Simon Ewins, chief operating officer for Premier Inn and hub, said: "We are absolutely delighted to be opening three new fantastic hotels in Edinburgh and it is great that we are able to bring so many jobs and apprenticeships to the city. Hub is a new concept for us which we are really excited about, especially as this is the first one in Scotland and outside of London. We are confident our guests visiting the beautiful city of Edinburgh will enjoy this new digital experience and we will look to open more in Scotland in the future."

Courts in Stirling, Kilmarnock, and Dundee sentenced nearly 20% of women appearing before them to imprisonment, in contrast to 7% in Edinburgh and 5% in Airdrie. The judiciary deemed it inappropriate to interview a serving sheriff for the programme, but retired sheriff Peter Gillam offered his perspective. Gillam, who served from 1991 to 2013, attributed these differences to judicial independence.

He stated, "There is now, as I understand it, a board advising the judiciary on sentencing. But every judge is their own person, with different approaches and views, and all are independent."

Gillam added, "There must be some uniformity, which is ensured by the Appeal Court, correcting any particularly outrageous decisions. However, variety is the spice of life, and it would be wrong to force judges to act against their own judgment."

He concluded, "Judges have local knowledge, know the person, have full information, and make decisions to the best of their ability. You have to trust them to handle cases accordingly."

Nineteen children were released after mediation by the South Sudanese government, marking the first group freed since roughly 125 children were abducted in a cross-border raid. The attack, conducted by members of the Murle community, has drawn accusations of livestock theft and abducting children to raise as their own. On 15 April, the raid resulted in the deaths of over 200 people from the rival Nuer community in Ethiopia's western Gambella region.

In response, Ethiopian forces crossed into South Sudan and surrounded villages where the children were held. The Ethiopian News Agency reports the children were released without violence following negotiations between South Sudanese officials and the abductors. Talks are expected to continue to secure the release of all the abducted children.

James Pitia Morgan, South Sudan’s ambassador to Ethiopia, emphasized the need to rescue the children, reunite them with their families, and return stolen cattle to their rightful owners. Ethiopia and South Sudan share a long border, and cross-border raids involving the Murle and Nuer communities occur frequently. Still, the scale of the 15 April raid shocked many in both countries and led to protests in Ethiopia’s Gambella region, where parents called for stronger protection of their children.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn condemned the raid, describing it as the work of “primitive and destructive forces.”

A 17-year-old fell approximately 40 meters (130 feet) into a dry riverbed while participating in "puenting," a type of bungee jumping where jumpers dive with two cords attached and swing beneath a bridge or viaduct. The teenager was part of a group from the Netherlands and Belgium staying at a nearby surf camp.

The jump took place from a bridge over the A8 road at Cabezon de la Sal in Cantabria. Local police chief Joaquin Gonzalez said he was unaware puenting occurred on the bridge and described the activity as "extremely risky." A police spokesman told Dutch media that the recent "ghastly accident" may have resulted from carelessness, though the exact cause remains unknown.

In a separate incident last month, British tourist Kleyo De Abreu died during a bungee jump off a bridge near Granada, southern Spain, after hitting the bridge wall below and sustaining fatal injuries.

Bungee jumping has become increasingly popular in Spain among locals and tourists alike. Scenic rural areas in Andalusia, Cantabria, and the Pyrenees attract both seasoned jumpers and beginners. Operators offer both traditional bungee jumping and puenting.

Since the 1980s, around 10 deaths in Spain have been linked to bungee jumping. Prior to the two fatalities this summer, the most recent was in 2013, when a 48-year-old man died at Robledo de Chavela near Madrid.

Mayor Isabel Fernandez called the incident an enormous tragedy, highlighting the victim’s youth. She added, "We're ready to help her family as much as we can."

James, a 23-year-old from Colwyn Bay, who is 3ft 7in tall and was born with diastrophic dysplasia, a type of dwarfism, has a compelling story. After a major neck operation at age three and another surgery at seven—during which he began using lizeroth frames to straighten his legs—he now lives a life considered normal. He has been selected to carry the Olympic torch in Rhos-on-Sea as it travels through Wales from 25 to 30 May.

His nomination was made by a friend he met at the 2008 Beijing Paralympics through the British Council’s Young Advocate Programme. James expressed his excitement about the honor, stating, "I'm really excited about it and looking forward to the day." He reflected on the significance of the nomination, noting, "The guy who nominated me I met in Beijing at the Paralympic Games. He's in London, I am in north Wales." He added that his friend often describes him as an inspiration, which encourages him to persevere.

James emphasized his acceptance of his condition, saying, "I've always accepted the way I am and I strongly believe God made me the way I am." This perspective fuels his resilience and determination to pursue his goals.

As a member of the Dwarf Sports Association, James has achieved notable success, winning the Junior Sports Personality award three times and holding the British Class 1 badminton championship within the DSA for nine years. His friend Russell Swannack praised his efforts, stating, "James has worked extremely hard to encourage others to become involved in disability sport and particularly dwarf sport." Swannack, who met James at the 2008 Beijing Paralympics, described him as an incredible individual who has inspired him and whom he now considers a friend. For James, carrying the Olympic torch would be a dream fulfilled.

Official data reveal that from January to March, Scotland’s sales value edged up by 0.1%, trailing the UK’s 0.3% growth. During the same timeframe, sales volumes in Scotland increased by 0.7%, slightly less than the UK’s 0.8%. Over the past year, the Scottish Retail Sales Index recorded a 2.7% rise in sales volumes, while sales value saw a minimal 0.1% gain.

David Lonsdale, director of the Scottish Retail Consortium, welcomed the return to growth but highlighted persistent "fragility" in consumer confidence impacting retailers. He urged the incoming Scottish government to focus on policies that foster investment and expansion in the retail sector. Lonsdale emphasized that retailers’ prospects hinge on economic conditions and their adaptability, calling on new MSPs to help bolster Scotland’s largest private-sector employer.

Euan Murray from Barclays Corporate Banking in Scotland attributed the "measured increase" in first-quarter sales volume mainly to food sales, marking a shift from the previous quarter. He noted that non-food retailers continue to benefit from a strong online presence, with consumers increasingly comparing prices online to find better deals. Murray anticipates that online retail will grow in importance going forward.

March’s industry figures painted a mixed picture for Scottish retailers. The SRC-KPMG monitor showed total sales for the five weeks ending 2 April fell 1.3% compared to the same period last year. Within non-food, household goods like furniture and flooring performed well, but fashion and footwear suffered their steepest decline since May last year. The report partly attributed this drop to the timing of the early Easter holiday.

Ogbonna, the younger brother of the former Arsenal striker, told BBC Sport that his brother is recovering well following surgery. The decision to operate was made during the player’s annual medical examination. "We give thanks to God that everything went well and he's in perfect condition," Ogbonna stated.

The family expressed gratitude to Nigerians and Nwankwo Kanu's supporters worldwide for their prayers and well wishes. Kanu first underwent heart surgery in November 1996 to correct a faulty aortic valve. After a year away from the game, he returned to play for Inter Milan before joining Premier League side Arsenal in February 1999.

Motivated by his experience, Kanu established a charity aimed at building five hospitals across Africa to diagnose and treat heart disease and provide surgical care. Recently, the Nigerian government honored him as one of the 100 most distinguished Nigerians during a ceremony commemorating the centenary of the unification of northern and southern Nigeria.

Kanu retired from international football at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa. His international accomplishments include winning the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in 1993 and securing the Olympic football gold medal in 1996. He also received the African Footballer of the Year awards in 1996 and 1999.

The 27-year-old midfielder has been met with a wave of congratulatory messages on social media following the birth of his daughter Raine on Friday night. AFC Bournemouth chairman Jeff Mostyn was among the first to extend his congratulations, tweeting to Arter and his partner Rachel: "Thrilled with the incredible news." The couple had previously suffered the stillbirth of their daughter Renee in December 2015. Bournemouth also shared their well wishes on Twitter, posting: "From one family to another, congratulations." Arter replied with thanks, writing, "Thank you to everyone for all of your kind messages," accompanied by a rainbow and heart emoji. The phrase "rainbow baby" is used to describe a child born after a miscarriage or stillbirth, symbolizing hope following loss. Following Bournemouth’s match against Manchester City on Monday, TV cameras captured an emotional moment as City manager Pep Guardiola embraced Arter and offered his best wishes for the forthcoming birth. Arter spoke highly of Guardiola, saying, "He's someone I have massive respect for. I watched his Barcelona teams and he is, without doubt, the best manager in the world." Additional messages have arrived from other clubs and fans, including Leeds United’s Liam Cooper, who tweeted, "Congrats mate," while some Leeds supporters commented, "Lovely to see the football world come together to congratulate you - congrats Harry." Stourbridge Wolves also tweeted: "Fantastic news, congratulations from all Stourbridge FC fans."

On 30 September 2013 in Anfield, 19-year-old Sean McHugh was fatally stabbed with a "sword stick" by a group that Judge Clement Goldstone described as a "truly wicked, marauding mob." Reese O'Shaughnessy, also 19, was convicted alongside four others and sentenced to a minimum of 18 years in prison. The other defendants—Andrew Hewitt, 15; Keyfer Dykstra, 14; Corey Hewitt, 14; and Joseph McGill, 14—were also sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court. Dykstra received at least 12 years, Andrew Hewitt and McGill were each sentenced to a minimum of nine years, and Corey Hewitt was given at least six years.

During sentencing, Justice Goldstone stated, "Each of you has been convicted of the murder of Sean McHugh—a truly wicked attack in which each of you played different roles." A victim impact statement from McHugh’s mother, Lorraine, read in court conveyed her sorrow: "They might as well have killed me."

The teenagers belonged to the Lane Heads gang, rivals of the Walton Village Heads, with whom McHugh was associated. The court heard that months earlier, Dykstra had been stabbed in the chest by a Walton Village Heads member and sought to "avenge that stabbing." Justice Goldstone observed, "The stabbing was avenged not by attacking the person responsible, but by attacking someone... by virtue of his affiliation to the Walton Village Heads."

Following a minor dispute, the gang located McHugh around 19:00 BST at the Priory Road launderette, where he had left his washing. Armed with knives and a makeshift sword stick—described as resembling a broom handle with a blade attached—they forced open the back door of the room where McHugh was hiding. After beating and stabbing him, the group fled. McHugh managed to escape but was later found in an alleyway with a stab wound to the groin. He died several days later in hospital due to blood loss.

Around 06:25 BST, two people were found injured at a residence on Elmshurst Crescent, East Finchley. The Metropolitan Police have identified the victims as 52-year-old Anny Ekofo and her 21-year-old nephew, Bervil Ekofo, both reportedly relocated from Congo in central Africa. Both were pronounced dead at the scene.

Maymie Botamba, mother of Bervil Ekofo, shared her sorrow, saying she had lost her "life" and "best friend." She added, "He was my life, they have taken my life away. He was my best friend. He was so lovely and kind to everyone, always surrounded by girls. He had never been in trouble before, he had never been in a fight in his life."

The Metropolitan Police’s homicide and major crime command is leading the investigation. Fifi Selo, cousin to Anny Ekofo, said the family remains in shock and cannot explain what happened. She described them as "an amazing family" and said, "Anny was the kind of person who was a mum to everybody. She always brought everybody together."

Local resident Lizzy Holsgrove recalled the response: "About 20 police cars and four or five paramedic cars, and three ambulances sped past my window. They cordoned off the street quickly, and police were sprinting from the top of the road where they'd stopped. There had been screaming before the police arrived."

Typhoon Phanfone has resulted in at least one fatality: a US airman on Okinawa who was swept away by high waves. Three US military personnel were caught in the waves off southern Okinawa, where a large US base is located; one died, while two remain missing. A police spokesman said the group had been taking photographs of the sea.

The typhoon made landfall Monday morning near Hamamatsu in central Japan, bringing winds up to 180 km/h (112 mph). Though downgraded from super typhoon status, the Japan Meteorological Agency cautioned that Phanfone remained dangerous. Japan experiences an average of 11 typhoons annually.

At least 9,500 homes have lost power, and 10 people have been injured. NHK reported a university student missing after surfing off Kanagawa Prefecture, south of Tokyo. The Transport Ministry predicted about 100mm of rain in Tokyo over 24 hours.

In response, many schools closed Monday, and two Japanese carmakers suspended production at some plants. Japan’s two largest airlines canceled numerous flights, with NHK reporting over 174 domestic flights disrupted nationwide by Sunday.

Search operations for those missing after last week’s volcanic eruption were halted due to the storm. On Sunday, heavy rain delayed the Japanese Formula One Grand Prix in Suzuka. French driver Jules Bianchi crashed in wet conditions, sustaining a severe head injury.

The storm-tracking website Tropical Storm Risk forecasts that Phanfone will rapidly weaken as it moves further into the Pacific over the next few hours.

On Tuesday evening, students and staff at the INTO language skills centre in Haymarket were evacuated from the building. Early the next morning, a bomb disposal team conducted a controlled explosion on the Town Moor. An 18-year-old man was arrested in London in connection with the incident. Newcastle University confirmed that the campus has since reopened, with no injuries reported and police affirming there was no risk to the public.

A university spokesperson said, "The INTO building is now open for staff and students following last night's evacuation, and we are working closely with Northumbria Police on their ongoing investigations." Roads in the area reopened before 01:00 BST.

Northumbria Police added, "Residents near Newcastle Town Moor may have heard a slight bang, which was related to the university incident and was planned. Inquiries are in the early stages, and we are cooperating closely with Newcastle University. There is currently no cause for concern among students or the wider community."

Newcastle University educates over 22,000 UK and international students and employs 1,200 academic staff. The INTO Centre, which covers four floors, provides facilities for more than 700 mainly international students.

Jamaica’s relay team set a new world record of 36.84 seconds, surpassing the previous mark by two-tenths of a second to claim gold ahead of the United States, who took silver. Nesta Carter and Michael Frater delivered strong performances in the first two legs, while 100m and 200m silver medallist Yohan Blake’s explosive third leg secured a decisive lead. Usain Bolt sealed the victory with a commanding final leg, pulling away from Ryan Bailey as the crowd erupted in applause.

Canada was initially awarded the bronze medal but was later disqualified after third-leg runner Jared Connaughton stepped outside his lane, promoting Trinidad and Tobago to third place. Bolt, who previously won the 100m and 200m titles in Beijing 2008 and London 2012 along with the 4x100m relay, now holds six Olympic gold medals before his 26th birthday.

Describing the atmosphere, Bolt called it "electric," highlighting Blake’s impressive bend while competing against Tyson Gay. He added, "Usain Bolt was watching that clock all the way down the home straight." The race provided a fitting conclusion to a memorable nine days of athletics at the Olympic Stadium.

Reflecting on the London 2012 Games, Bolt described the experience as "amazing" and said, "It's a wonderful feeling to end on a high note. It was a great championships, I’m happy, the team came out and gave it their all. I wish we could have gone faster but we leave room for improvement." When asked about the possibility of a third treble gold haul in Rio 2016, he acknowledged the challenge, saying, "It’s going to be hard. Yohan is running hard and I’m sure there’s going to be more young cats coming up."

Crossing the finish line, Bolt celebrated with a "Mobot," paying tribute to Britain’s Mo Farah, the double Olympic champion in the 5,000m and 10,000m events.

Els Borst, 81, a medical academic and minister from 1994 to 2002, was instrumental in the 2001 legislation that made the Netherlands the first country to legalize euthanasia. Her body was discovered Monday evening near her home close to Utrecht, leading police to seal off the area. Although initial investigations were inconclusive, officials ruled out natural causes by Tuesday.

Forensic experts have been unable to determine the cause of death, with police indicating it could have been either an accident or a crime. A full post-mortem examination is scheduled at the Netherlands Forensic Institute. A police spokesperson told Dutch media, "She may have had an accident after feeling unwell, but that cannot yet be confirmed. We cannot say whether a crime was involved." Earlier, another spokesperson told Dutch radio there were no signs of foul play.

Borst had attended a conference of her liberal D66 party on Saturday. Her passing came as a shock to political colleagues in The Hague. She led the party for a period in the 1990s. Prime Minister Mark Rutte described her death as a great loss for Dutch politics. Health Minister Edith Schippers said, "She ensured a breakthrough in euthanasia for which many remain grateful." Borst also sponsored legislation regulating the use of tissue from aborted fetuses for medical research.

Steve Bannon, the former head of the populist right-wing Breitbart News website, will join senior-level national security discussions following an order signed on Saturday. Unlike previous administrations, the director of national intelligence and the joint chiefs will attend these meetings only when the agenda pertains to their specific areas, rather than participating in all sessions of the National Security Council’s (NSC) core group, known as the principals' committee.

The NSC, which advises the president on national security and foreign affairs, is chaired by retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, a close adviser and staunch supporter of Mr. Trump during the campaign. In the executive order, Mr. Trump stated, "The security threats facing the United States in the 21st century transcend international boundaries. Accordingly, the United States Government's decision-making structures and processes to address these challenges must remain equally adaptive and transformative."

Last week, Mr. Bannon described the US mainstream media as "the opposition party," asserting it should "keep its mouth shut." Breitbart News, which he formerly led, advances an anti-establishment agenda that critics accuse of xenophobia and misogyny. Under Bannon’s leadership, it became one of the most widely read conservative news and opinion outlets in the US.

In addition, Mr. Trump has directed a reorganization of the Homeland Security Council through two separate executive actions.

Jean Jeanie, an eight-year-old Dexter cow, was "adopted" by Derbyshire resident Trisha Boyko, who became fond of her after passing by her field. Facing financial challenges in caring for the cow, Ms Boyko raised £3,500 through online donations and affectionately referred to Jean Jeanie as "the people's cow."

Martin Sands, an accountant from Cornwall who came across the story, agreed to contribute £65 monthly toward the cow’s ongoing care. Although he admitted sponsoring a cow was "not a normal thing" for him due to a lack of particular interest in animals, he described Jean Jeanie as "a really beautiful cow" and was touched by her story. He also mentioned that some previous sponsors had promised 12 months of support but later withdrew, leading him to commit to funding her for at least a year, with the possibility of extending that.

Ms Boyko first noticed Jean Jeanie alone in a field and, after learning she might be sold at market, purchased her. The 52-year-old then created a Facebook page for Jean, whose registered name is Mooridge Jeanie, which drew donations. Ms Boyko said, "She lit my days up and I'd like to think I cheered her up. She's got a lovely character, she's really gentle, she's lovely." She added, "She is the people's cow."

On Facebook, Ms Boyko reported that Jean Jeanie and her Cornish sponsor got along well: "I am pleased to say he was most impressed to meet the beautiful Jean and she was on her best behaviour." She also observed that the cow was "so much better than this time last year—what a difference a year makes."

The CIES Football Observatory has released a ranking of players based on league appearances by birth year. Leading those born in 1996 or later is 19-year-old Dele Alli, who has made 98 appearances for Tottenham Hotspur and MK Dons. The list is largely dominated by Premier League players, who outnumber their counterparts in Spain, Germany, Italy, and France.

England international Alli has one more league appearance than 19-year-old Alen Halilovic, a Croatia Under-21 international currently on loan at Sporting Gijon from Barcelona. Villarreal’s Spain Under-21 winger Matias Nahuel, also 19, holds third place.

Among players born in 1985 or later, Bournemouth defender Simon Francis leads with 460 appearances, exceeding those of Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney. For players born after 1993, Everton’s Romelu Lukaku, 22, tops the list with 210 games played for the Toffees, Anderlecht, Chelsea, and West Brom.

Chelsea’s Eden Hazard leads players born after 1991 with 277 appearances, just ahead of Liverpool’s Nathaniel Clyne.

Chelsea manager Guus Hiddink has called on medical teams at the Football Association and Premier League clubs to urge authorities to reduce fixture congestion for English sides. With Chelsea set to play four matches in 12 days across three competitions, Hiddink stressed the importance of safeguarding player welfare.

Former Chelsea doctor Ralph Rogers, speaking on BBC Radio 5 live on Monday, dismissed the idea as unrealistic. “I appreciate his concern but it’s all market-driven. People want football,” Rogers said.

The search giant has launched multiple lawsuits against the London-based company in California, accusing it of infringing four patents, and has also filed a separate case in the UK. BT had expected such legal action after initiating its own lawsuit against Google in 2011, a dispute that remains unresolved.

A Google spokeswoman stated, "We have always viewed litigation as a last resort and strive to avoid lawsuits. However, BT has brought several meritless patent claims against Google and our customers—and they have also been supporting patent trolls." The term "patent troll" describes entities that acquire patents primarily to seek settlements over infringement claims.

In 2012, Suffolk Technologies, a New Jersey-based intellectual property owner, sued Google and US internet service provider AOL over two patents it had acquired from BT. Additionally, Steelhead Licensing—another patent-holding firm that does not manufacture products—filed suit against 14 handset makers and mobile networks, including Google’s Motorola division, alleging infringement of a wireless technology once owned by BT.

A BT spokesman declined to comment on the ongoing litigation. Google has responded with claims that BT infringed a patent originally filed by Fujitsu, covering a method that enables PCs to use an internet-based telephone system. Google also alleges BT failed to license a data prioritization system for computer servers, an IBM invention now owned by the search firm.

Patent consultant Florian Mueller observed this is the first clear instance of Google suing another company over its patents, noting that earlier cases involving Motorola were filed before Google acquired the Razr handset maker. BT and Google are set to meet in Delaware in July for a mediation hearing concerning the 2011 case.

At 15:25 BST on Saturday, 2 April, a collision between a black Vauxhall Astra and a red Ford Fiesta took place on Eastfield Road in Bordesley Green, Birmingham. The driver of the Vauxhall Astra left the scene following the crash. PC John Slater from West Midland Police’s traffic collision investigation unit reported that the Fiesta’s driver, who was eight weeks pregnant, suffered a miscarriage due to the collision. A two-year-old boy was seriously injured with head trauma, while a four-year-old boy sustained minor injuries. PC Slater has called on any witnesses to contact police on 101 and urged the Astra driver to come forward.

Kromtech, the Germany-based developer of MacKeeper, has confirmed that customer data—including names, internet addresses, and login credentials—was exposed. The company stressed that payment information was "never at risk" and believes only the security researcher who reported the vulnerability accessed the data.

In a statement, Kromtech said, "The privacy and security of our clients' information remains our top priority, and from the moment we were aware of the access, we immediately took several proactive steps to identify and correct the issue." The firm also expressed gratitude to security researcher Chris Vickery for uncovering the breach attempt, which allowed them to prevent any harm.

Vickery told security blogger Brian Krebs that he discovered 21 gigabytes of MacKeeper user data "after spending a few bored moments searching for database servers" without password protection, using Shodan, a search engine for internet-connected devices.

Krebs initially reported that Kromtech had acknowledged exposure of 13 million customers' details, but that figure was later removed from the company's statement. A Kromtech spokesperson told the BBC the number included both "active and non-active" users.

MacKeeper is widely advertised online, including on Ookla’s Speedtest site, as software designed to "clean" and "protect" Macintosh computers for improved performance. However, critics argue that the software can slow down, crash, and be difficult to uninstall. Addressing these concerns, a Kromtech spokesperson said, "There are no ways that the program itself can harm or de-stabilise the system as described by some sources."

Andrew Ridgeley took to social media on Thursday to condemn Channel 5’s documentary, The Last Days of George Michael. The former Wham! member described the decision to air the programme as "insensitive, contemptuous and reprehensible," arguing it should have been postponed until after his friend’s funeral. Channel 5 defended the documentary as "a measured account" of Michael’s life and death.

In a statement, the broadcaster said, "George Michael was a high-profile public figure and there has been legitimate public interest in the circumstances surrounding his death." The documentary, which aired at 21:00 GMT on Thursday, drew on contributions from those who knew and reported on Michael over many decades.

Ridgeley, who delivered an emotional tribute to Michael at last month’s Brit Awards, called the programme "a piece of voyeurism" that should have been broadcast only after "a respectful period." Earlier this month, it was confirmed that Michael—born Georgios Kyriacos Panayiotou—died on Christmas Day from heart and liver disease.

Fans of the late singer expressed their disapproval on Twitter, describing Channel 5’s programme as "pathetic," "disrespectful," and "utter trash." One viewer who submitted a complaint received a response from the broadcaster stating the show was not intended "to upset or cause any offence."

Dover District Councillor Bob Frost faced criticism after making remarks about black people during an online discussion about recent riots. The comments were made while Mr. Frost, who is also a teacher, was on holiday and engaged in a social media conversation referencing the London riots. He posted on his status, "I'm missing the vibrant and multi-cultural society which I normally celebrate here in Sicily! Not!" When another user suggested he visit north London, he responded, "All the bunnies here are of the woodland variety rather than the jungle."

In response to the backlash, Mr. Frost issued an unreserved apology and removed the posts. Deputy Council Leader Sue Chandler condemned the remarks, stating, "There is no place in our society for this kind of language," and confirmed that Councillor Frost has been suspended from the Conservative Group pending an investigation.

Sola Afuape, chair of the equality charity Afiya Trust, criticized the comments, saying, "You don't expect somebody in a position of power, in a leadership position, to make comments like this. They're clearly offensive—racist in fact."

Mr. Frost released a statement saying, "What I said was wrong and I apologise unreservedly. I am mortified by the offence that I have caused and have deleted these comments. I am very sorry."

Officials have confirmed that the move is part of the Sustainability and Transformation Plan covering Buckinghamshire, Berkshire, and Oxfordshire. The Oxfordshire Clinical Commissioning Group (CCG) said community services are currently "under review" and that further work is required to evaluate the impact on community hospitals.

The Green Party, in a motion to Oxford City Council, proposed replacing community hospitals with four hubs, including one at the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford. Larry Sanders, the party’s health spokesperson, stated, "This is not a decision, this is part of the process, but it does look like they may be in for the chop." He also raised concerns about the limited information from Oxfordshire CCG, saying, "One of the problems is they [Oxfordshire CCG] are not giving us a lot of information. We do fear that it's going to happen because the size of the cuts are enormous."

It was disclosed in November that details of the Sustainability and Transformation Plan related to community hospitals will be released after next May. Oxfordshire CCG added, "We will be engaging clinicians, patients, and the public as we develop these plans and proposed changes to services will be subject to consultation." The CCG has forecast a £200 million funding shortfall in 2020 unless measures are taken.

Mark Dayan of the Nuffield Trust observed that financial pressures across the NHS mean "very tough decisions are going to have to be made in nearly every area of the country."

Lille’s first-choice goalkeeper since 2013, he has made 130 appearances for the club in all competitions. The 33-year-old, whose previous contract was due to expire next year, said he feels settled at Stade Pierre-Mauroy.

“I am very happy to extend my contract with Lille, a club I call home,” Enyeama told BBC Sport. “I appreciate the family atmosphere here and thank the club for the confidence they have shown me since I joined five years ago. Although I received offers from other clubs, I never considered putting money before happiness, which is why I decided to stay. I will continue to give my best with my teammates to bring joy and success to our supporters who have always supported us.”

During the 2015-2016 season, Lille finished fifth, surpassing Saint-Etienne to earn a spot in next season’s Europa League, despite losing the Coupe de la Ligue final to Paris Saint-Germain. Enyeama kept 17 clean sheets in 35 league games this season.

Lille official Jean-Michel Van Damme expressed his satisfaction at securing a new contract with the Nigerian goalkeeper. “Vincent is exceptional both on and off the pitch,” Van Damme said. “Having a player of his calibre and character is fantastic for the club. He once again demonstrated his immense qualities this season. He is happy here and feels at home. His talent, mentality, and leadership inspire the squad, so we could not pass up the opportunity to extend his contract.”

Van Damme also pointed to Enyeama’s role in mentoring young understudy Mike Maignan, saying, “We are pleased that Enyeama can finish his career at Lille.”

First Minister Arlene Foster stated that the terms for an independent inquiry were drafted in collaboration with the attorney general and forwarded to Sinn Féin, who have yet to respond. Sinn Féin MLA Conor Murphy described the terms as "insufficient," pointing out that "there has been no agreement with the DUP on the terms of reference of an independent investigation." He stressed the necessity of a robust, transparent, and time-bound inquiry led by a senior judicial figure from outside the jurisdiction, empowered to compel witnesses and subpoena documents, to rebuild public trust in political institutions. Murphy also called on Foster to step aside to enable the investigation to move forward pending a preliminary report.

Launched in November 2012 by the Northern Ireland Executive, the Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme aimed to increase the use of heat from renewable sources. However, it has become heavily oversubscribed and is roughly £490 million over budget, as businesses received subsidies that exceeded the cost of the renewable fuel they consumed.

Daniel Ricciardo remains under contract with the team through the end of 2018, while Daniil Kvyat’s future is uncertain after a mixed first season. Team principal Christian Horner stated, "Ricciardo's contract is fixed and all the options are on our side with Kvyat. He's doing great. So long as we're here, he'll be in the car next year." These comments appear to dismiss rumors of Toro Rosso’s Max Verstappen being promoted to the senior team following his impressive debut as an 18-year-old Dutch driver.

Red Bull’s status for the 2016 season remains unsettled due to the lack of a confirmed engine supplier. The team nearly terminated its contract with Renault a year early last month amid rising tensions, but negotiations ceased when it became clear Mercedes would not supply Red Bull and Ferrari confirmed they could not provide their 2016 engine.

Insiders indicate Red Bull is likely to continue using Renault engines, rebranded to obscure the ongoing partnership from casual fans. Renault is also close to acquiring the Lotus team, marking its return as a constructor and team owner. Nevertheless, Horner suggested other options might exist, saying, "There may be something else. We'll see."

Red Bull has engaged in talks with Honda regarding an engine supply, but McLaren chairman Ron Dennis, a works partner, has exercised his contractual veto to block Honda from supplying Red Bull. Meanwhile, Toro Rosso is expected to run 2015 Ferrari engines next season.

The Coast Guard is urging people to continue calling emergency phone numbers despite concerns about low mobile phone batteries. Many individuals have tweeted their addresses seeking rescue, though not all messages may be seen or verified. An expert highlighted the difficulty in authenticating social media posts. Euan Semple, an advisor on social media’s impact on businesses and society, described the internet as "messy and unpredictable," stressing the importance of distinguishing meaningful information from noise. He also noted the challenge of persuading people to follow the Coast Guard’s guidance, particularly when official channels are unavailable and alternative sources of help appear more accessible. In a related case, residents of a care home were rescued after a photo showing them waist-deep in floodwater went viral on Twitter. Meanwhile, Facebook has activated its safety check-in feature in Texas, enabling users affected by the floods to mark themselves as safe.

Bow Street station, situated on the Cambrian line north of Aberystwyth, was closed in 1965 as part of the Beeching cuts. The Welsh Government is now seeking £6.8 million from the UK government to cover 75% of the cost to build a new station. Eluned Morgan, Assembly Member for Mid and West Wales, described the proposal as having a "very strong" economic case, highlighting the nearby opening of a new university campus.

Ms. Morgan emphasized the role of rail infrastructure in enhancing connections to Aberystwyth and beyond. She pointed to growing economic activity in the area, including the new Aberystwyth University campus. The planned station aims to reduce traffic, boost local business, cut pollution, and provide essential transport for commuters and the elderly.

The Welsh Government has applied for a £6.8 million grant from the UK government to help fund the project, which would include a new train station, interchange, car parking, and bus stops. Economy Secretary Ken Skates confirmed a "strong" application was submitted for 75% of the total cost—the maximum contribution available from the UK government—with the Welsh Government covering the remaining £1.7 million.

Plans for the new Bow Street station have been showcased at a public event. If approved, the station is expected to open in 2019, located a short distance south of the original site, now occupied by a builders' merchants. A spokesperson for Ceredigion Council said there was "considerable support" following public consultation. The council anticipates a funding decision in early 2017.

Ms. Morgan also expressed hope that Welsh ministers will consider reopening Carno station in Powys, also on the Cambrian line, which closed in 1963.

AMC chief executive Adam Aron suggested permitting mobile phone use during films as a way to draw so-called millennials to cinemas. The proposal met with significant backlash on social media, where moviegoers expressed strong opposition. In response, AMC stated, "We have heard loud and clear that this is a concept our audience does not want."

The company operates nearly 400 cinemas across the United States, with more than 5,000 screens, and also manages a multi-screen complex in Manchester, UK. While cinemas generally ask patrons to turn off mobile devices before screenings, Aron told Variety magazine that allowing phone use might appeal to younger audiences. He remarked, "When you tell a 22-year-old to turn off the phone, don't ruin the movie, they hear please cut off your left arm above the elbow."

After receiving widespread negative feedback, AMC acknowledged the idea’s unpopularity. "In this age of social media, we get feedback from you almost instantaneously," the company said. "This is an idea we have relegated to the cutting room floor... there will be no texting allowed in any of the auditoriums at AMC Theatres."

The announcement was met with approval from many film fans online. Twitter user Kristin commented, "Bravo for making the right decision," while Shavonne added, "Thank you so much. I love you guys for this." Nonetheless, some critics remained dissatisfied. Geoff tweeted, "The idea shouldn't have been floated publicly in the first place, though. It was a horrible idea from the beginning."

The social media giant has faced criticism for not doing enough to tackle cyberbullying and extremism. In a blog post, the company highlighted its updated policy, which firmly rejects behaviour intended to harass or intimidate. It also clarified its definitions of "abusive behaviour and hateful conduct," covering harassment and hate speech, and committed to suspending or closing accounts that "cross the line into abuse."

Pressure is growing on social media platforms to address online extremism and cyberbullying, issues said to affect millions of young people in Britain each year. Last week, The Times reported that Home Secretary Theresa May suggested using new surveillance powers under the Investigatory Powers Bill to help police identify anonymous cyberbullies. In a letter to MP James Cartlidge, May wrote that "Internet connection records would update the capability of law enforcement in a criminal investigation to determine the sender and recipient of a communication," which could include "a malicious message such as those exchanged in cyberbullying."

Twitter has been criticised for its inadequate response to online abuse. In February, former CEO Dick Costolo admitted the company "sucks" at handling trolling. Yet, in its latest update, Twitter said it introduced several protections in 2015, including enhanced tools for reporting abusive behaviour and a ban on the "promotion of terrorism."

A spokesperson for the NSPCC, a child protection charity, described Twitter’s new rules as "a long overdue but very welcome step." They added, "We have been urging social media companies to take decisive action to curb cyberbullying, which damages the lives of many children who tell us it is almost impossible to find a safe haven from it." The spokesperson said the industry is starting to acknowledge the seriousness of this harmful behaviour and welcomed the more proactive measures some companies are now taking.

The event Shifting the Curve - Sharing the Challenge seeks to tackle Scotland’s stagnant breastfeeding rates over the past decade. In 2013/14, 48.4% of babies were breastfed at around ten days old, compared to 44.4% in 2004/05. The data also indicate an increase in mixed feeding with breast and formula milk, alongside a decline in breastfeeding by six to eight weeks.

Specialists will convene to discuss the latest research on breastfeeding benefits, evaluate effective approaches, and identify ways to raise rates. A key focus is on increasing breastfeeding in the most deprived areas to help reduce health inequalities. Mothers in the wealthiest areas are nearly three times more likely to exclusively breastfeed at six to eight weeks than those in the most deprived areas.

Public Health Minister Maureen Watt stated: "Breastfeeding has major health benefits, in the short and longer term, for both mother and baby. That is why the Scottish Government continues to promote it as the best source of nutrition for babies." She added, "It is important to understand the factors influencing a mother's feeding decisions and develop effective strategies to encourage more women to breastfeed. Research shows women who know the health benefits are more likely to start, so discussing these benefits during the antenatal period is essential."

Earlier this month, a Unicef study found that extending breastfeeding could save the NHS millions by improving the health of both mother and baby. The summit is scheduled for 24 February at Murrayfield Stadium in Edinburgh.

Several female athletes have drawn attention to challenges related to the menstrual cycle, including tennis player Heather Watson, who cited "girl things" as a reason for her 2015 Australian Open exit. In January, Dr. Richard Burden, senior physiologist at the English Institute of Sport, told the BBC that research into the menstrual cycle’s impact on sport remains "limited."

A recent study conducted by two London universities involved the Female Athlete Health Group, a partnership between St Mary's University and University College London. The group carried out two surveys, one of which included participants in the London Marathon. Of the 1,862 women surveyed, including 90 elite athletes, 41.7% said their menstrual cycle affected their performance. Nearly 44% met the criteria for heavy menstrual bleeding, yet only 22.3% had sought medical help for related issues.

PhD student Georgie Bruinvels, who is leading the study, told BBC Sport that many questions about periods in sport remain unanswered. "As a female athlete myself, I can see how much it impacts. So many elite coaches are male and it's hard for them to understand," she said. Bruinvels described menstruation as "this big taboo," highlighting widespread lack of awareness and understanding. "By doing this research, we hope to raise more awareness and encourage further study," she added.

Bruinvels is currently crowdfunding to fund the next stage of her research, which will focus on heavy menstrual bleeding and its possible connection to increased iron deficiency.

On Thursday, Brent crude rose 0.4%, closing at $49.94 a barrel. Prices dipped initially but rebounded after data revealed a decline in US crude inventories over the past week. Opec reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining a "stable and balanced oil market." Following the meeting, Saudi Arabia pledged to avoid flooding the market with increased production. Saudi Energy Minister Khalid Al-Falih stated, "We will be very gentle in our approach and make sure we don't shock the market in any way."

Opec members account for 40% of global crude oil production. A previous meeting in Qatar in April, which included most Opec members and other exporters such as Russia, also failed to reach a consensus on output limits. John Hall, an oil analyst at alfaenergy, observed, "Now that there is a realisation that Opec will not be restricting output, traders are caught long with too much oil in a falling market and so once $50 had been reached, there was a general mood to sell off rapidly."

Oil prices peaked near $115 a barrel in summer 2014 before steadily falling to around $27 in January this year, driven by weaker demand and increased supply. Opec Secretary-General Abdulla al-Badri rejected suggestions that the failure to cap output meant the cartel’s demise, saying, "Opec will be powerful, will be strong. Opec is alive." Bob Minter, an analyst at Aberdeen Asset Management Investment, commented, "This should have been an easy meeting to re-establish Opec relevance, but they missed the opportunity."

The ministers agreed to appoint Nigeria’s Mohammed Sanusi Barkindo as Opec’s new secretary-general, effective 1 August, ending a prolonged dispute between Saudi Arabia and Iran, who had each put forward their own candidates. They also approved Gabon’s admission as the 14th member of Opec starting next month.

Channel 4 has issued an undisclosed fine to Glasspool, which he will donate to a domestic violence charity. The 24-year-old actor, who joined the soap last year as student Harry Thompson and earned a nomination for best newcomer at this year's National Television Awards, has apologized for his actions. He stated, "I am truly sorry to anyone I have upset or offended. I would never condone domestic violence in any way and on reflection see that my video was insensitive and inappropriate."

In June, Glasspool shared a video on his Instagram account in which he waved a knife while portraying a woman warning her boyfriend against speaking to other girls. He said, "I would kill you if you did... With this knife I know exactly how to. Done it before and I'll do it again so don't even think about it." The clip has since been removed.

A Hollyoaks spokesperson said, "Parry Glasspool has apologised and will begin an immediate two-week suspension from Hollyoaks. He will also be donating a fee to a domestic violence charity."

Follow us on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram, or email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

Tim Robinson, 54, sustained a leg injury after slipping on rocks at the western end of the beach beneath Golden Cap, east of Lyme Regis on the Jurassic Coast, on Saturday at about 16:30 GMT. Unable to call for help, he dragged himself off the rocks onto the beach and crawled nearly three-quarters of a mile (1.2 km) in the dark toward Seatown. After around two hours, his wife, worried for his safety, went looking for him, found him, and raised the alarm.

The couple, from Derby, were holidaying in Bridport. A coastguard statement described the incident as "quite an ordeal" for Mr. Robinson. Rescue teams spotted "faint torch lights" on the beach, prompting RNLI lifeboat crew to swim ashore to reach him. Fog prevented helicopter rescue, so he was taken aboard the lifeboat and transported to Lyme Regis, where an ambulance then conveyed him to a hospital in Dorchester.

Mr. Robinson, a full-time member of the Territorial Army, said, "I just slipped on a rock and have two fractures of the right leg. Everyone who helped me was just terrific." RNLI helmsman Jon Broome said, "His military background came to the fore. He found some sticks and used them to get to the beach. He then crawled on his hands and knees for a good two hours." Broome added that the location was challenging to access but stressed the importance of providing the best care possible.

The coastguard urged anyone walking along the coast to carry a fully charged smartphone.

The 7% growth rate fell short of the previous quarter’s 7.4% but surpassed analysts’ forecast of 6.4%. Economists had anticipated a downturn following the government’s withdrawal of high-denomination banknotes as part of an anti-corruption campaign. Nonetheless, the federal statistics office upheld its 7.1% growth forecast for the year ending March 2017.

Economists were taken aback by the figures, having expected a sharper slowdown after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s November move to withdraw old 500-rupee and 1,000-rupee notes, which removed 86% of currency from circulation almost overnight. Aneesh Srivastava, chief investment officer at IDBI Federal Life Insurance, remarked, “Perhaps this data is not capturing the impact of demonetisation. I am totally surprised and stunned to see this number... I believe that, with a lag, we will see an impact on GDP numbers.”

Saugata Bhattacharya, chief economist at Axis Bank, pointed to strong growth in agriculture and manufacturing as evidence that demonetisation’s effect on the economy has been less severe than expected. Conversely, Rupa Rege Nitsure, chief economist at L&T Holdings, warned that this year’s growth “appears to be overstated as our National Accounts Statistics does not adequately capture activities from the unorganised sector.” She added, “While the numbers make sense in terms of direction of change, their actual magnitude appears to be overstated.”

The “unorganised sector,” which comprises informal workers, is estimated to account for roughly 40% of India’s economy.

George Calombaris, a judge on MasterChef Australia, has confirmed that repaying outstanding wages is the company’s "highest priority." His business, MAdE Establishment, has reimbursed 162 current employees at its Melbourne locations and is reaching out to former staff. The average amount owed to each employee exceeds A$16,000.

In a statement to staff, Calombaris expressed regret, saying, "I am sorry we have messed up and let you down on a fundamental issue, which is to ensure our people are paid their full entitlements." He added, "I am devastated by what has happened and we have been working extremely hard to fix this."

The company said the errors, which date back to 2011, were due to miscalculations of overtime pay rates. Calombaris noted the issue was initially flagged in 2015 by Australia’s Fair Work Ombudsman. "Regrettably, our attention to detail at that time wasn't at a level it should have been," he admitted.

The wage shortfalls affected staff at The Press Club, Gazi, and Hellenic Republic. Former employees have been urged to contact the company.

Macclesfield Town earned a 3-0 victory against Maidstone United, with goals from Rhys Browne, Danny Whitaker, and Jack Mackreth. This win moves the Silkmen to within six points of the top five, with five matches left in the season.

Browne struck early, scoring from the edge of the area just 58 seconds into the game. Before halftime, Whitaker, Chris Holroyd, and John McCombe each had opportunities to increase the lead.

In the second half, Macclesfield goalkeeper Craig Ross made a crucial double save from Joe Piggot and Yemi Odubade. The hosts secured the result in the final four minutes as Whitaker converted a penalty in the 86th minute, followed by Mackreth finishing a counterattack to make it 3-0.

Substitutions saw George Oakley replace Bobby-Joe Taylor for Maidstone, Luke Summerfield come on for Danny Whitehead for Macclesfield, and Maidstone introduce Jamar Loza for Alex Flisher and Yemi Odubade for Jack Paxman.

Yellow cards were issued to Maidstone’s Bobby-Joe Taylor and Tom Mills.

Match timeline:
- First half began.
- Rhys Browne’s goal gave Macclesfield a 1-0 lead at halftime.
- Second half started with the score at 1-0.
- Danny Whitaker scored a penalty in the 86th minute to make it 2-0.
- Jack Mackreth added a late third goal.
- The match ended with Macclesfield Town defeating Maidstone United 3-0.

Report supplied by the Press Association.

After spending a year in a refugee camp in France, Lawand Hamadamin and his family arrived in the UK. They fled northern Iraq after IS threatened disabled children. Their journey took them through Greece, Germany, and France before they concealed themselves in a lorry to reach the UK, ultimately settling in Derby.

Lawand now attends Derby’s Royal School for the Deaf, where he receives specialized education. In December, head teacher Helen Shepherd told the BBC that he had made "exceptional progress" and described the family as "understandably devastated" by the decision to deport them.

The family has appealed the deportation order, with their case due to be heard in the High Court, although the hearing date remains unconfirmed. According to the school, if the appeal is unsuccessful, they will be deported to Germany, which the government says is where they should have initially claimed asylum.

A Home Office spokesman said: "It is only fair that we do not shoulder the burden of asylum claims that should rightly be considered by other countries. Asylum seekers should claim in the first safe country they arrive in. Where there is evidence that an asylum seeker is the responsibility of another European country, we will seek to return them there."

Live updates and further information are available from Derbyshire.

Russian state media accused the USS Ross of acting "aggressively," while the US Department of Defense maintained the vessel stayed "well within international waters at all times, performing routine operations." On Monday, the US Navy released footage showing a Russian aircraft approaching as close as 500 meters to the USS Ross. According to a military source quoted by Russian state media, the ship's crew behaved "provocatively and aggressively," prompting concern among monitoring stations and ships of the Black Sea Fleet. The source added that a Su-24 attack aircraft demonstrated its readiness to firmly prevent border violations and protect national interests.

Pentagon spokesman Colonel Steve Warren confirmed on Monday that the Russian planes were unarmed and that the USS Ross held its course throughout the incident. The Pentagon also emphasized that the ship’s deployment to the Black Sea had been publicly announced. Russia’s Defence Ministry declined to comment.

These encounters underscore ongoing military tensions between Russia and Western countries amid the conflict in eastern Ukraine. Last month, the UK and Sweden scrambled fighter jets to intercept Russian bombers near their airspace.

Manchester City's second £18 million offer for 29-year-old Northern Irish centre-back Jonny Evans was turned down last week. Tony Pulis revealed that City have not made contact "for a couple of days" and added, "We are hoping to get this situation resolved and move on. But whether Jonny goes or not, centre-half is one of four areas we need to fill."

Last week, Pulis also stated that while West Brom "don't need or want to sell" their captain Evans, "every player is for sale at the right price." Evans, who has two years remaining on his contract, missed West Brom’s opening Premier League games against Bournemouth and Burnley with a hamstring injury and is expected to miss Saturday’s home match against Stoke.

BBC Sport football reporter Simon Stone highlighted the challenges of transfers during this period. Manchester City are keen on Evans, and West Brom are open to selling at the right price, but City must first free up space in Pep Guardiola’s squad by offloading Eliaquim Mangala.

Inter Milan have expressed interest in Mangala; however, with the French defender’s lucrative contract running until 2019, his agent Jorge Mendes has little motivation to accelerate a transfer. Consequently, Evans will have to wait longer for his move to proceed.

The Welsh government is now over halfway through a five-year, £4.6 million programme to vaccinate badgers in north Pembrokeshire. Ahead of a global tuberculosis (TB) control conference taking place in Cardiff on Monday, Christianne Glossop said that although infection rates have dropped across Wales, it is still too early to assess whether the vaccination has delivered any "additional benefit."

Speaking to BBC's Sunday Politics Wales, Dr Glossop explained, "The programme is for five years. We've completed two years and we're now well into year three, so the results are by no means available yet." She added that TB infection rates have fallen across Wales over the past year. "The reduction in north Pembrokeshire is in line with the national reduction, so right now, we have no evidence that the vaccination programme in badgers is delivering an additional benefit—and we wouldn't expect to see any evidence at this stage either."

Between 2012 and 2013, 2,776 badgers were trapped and vaccinated within the Intensive Action Area (IAA), which covers parts of Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire, at a cost exceeding £1.8 million. Dr Glossop also highlighted that the wider TB eradication programme cost £28 million last year, with most of the funding directed toward cattle testing, biosecurity measures, and compensation for farmers. "You've always got to have the balance here between all the different elements of the programme, making sure that you're tackling all sources of infection," she said.

The vaccination initiative was introduced by Labour ministers in 2012 after they abandoned the previous coalition government's plan to cull badgers in the IAA.

The club has confirmed that the 32-year-old defender intends to return north to spend more time with his daughter. Berra, who has earned 35 caps, initially moved to England in 2009 to join Wolves under manager Mick McCarthy, who later signed him for Ipswich in 2013.

McCarthy told the Ipswich website that the club had been aware of the situation for some time. Although Ipswich had the option to extend Berra's contract by 12 months, they opted not to, enabling him to move closer to home.

During his spell at Ipswich, Berra made 185 appearances and scored 14 goals. McCarthy emphasized that Berra’s decision was driven by family reasons and noted that he had been among the Championship’s top defenders over the past four years. While reluctant to lose him, McCarthy expressed understanding of Berra’s choice and wished him well.

Only four parishioners from St Peter Port have come forward to stand for election, leaving one of the five available seats vacant. Parish constable Dennis Le Moignan said this is the first time there have been too few candidates, attributing it to a "lack of interest" and limited understanding of the role. However, some believe that criticism of the Douzaine over appointing a town centre manager has discouraged volunteers from seeking the unpaid position.

Shane Langlois, chairman of the Douzaine Council, acknowledged the controversy but dismissed such suggestions as "just guesswork." He also pointed to the complexity of the parish system as a factor in low engagement, while noting a more positive situation elsewhere on the island. Mr Langlois commented, "There are far more contested elections than I've ever seen... it's very unusual and encouraging. There's normally not more than one or two."

He has called for the abolition of electors' meetings when elections are uncontested—currently, parishioners can vote to hold ballots—describing these meetings as unnecessary. Mr Le Moignan confirmed that the St Peter Port Douzaine will need to advertise the fifth vacancy again and hold a further election. He added that the election could be rejected at the electors' meeting, delaying the process until another candidate steps forward.

Paramedics outside Queen Alexandra Hospital reported waiting for hours to transfer patients, a delay they say is severely affecting staff morale. They also warned that the public is not receiving the ambulances they need and deserve. On Monday night, Portsmouth Hospitals NHS Trust experienced "extremely high demand" in its A&E department. At 16:00 GMT, 16 ambulances were lined up outside, accounting for one third of the 46 ambulances on duty across Hampshire at that time.

A South Central Ambulance Service (SCAS) paramedic described the scene as "chaos," occurring almost daily and taking a significant toll on staff morale. Another paramedic, speaking anonymously, said, "I love my job but every time I log on I know there's potential that I could be put back in that same situation where I'm stuck with a patient at their own home and I can't do anything for them and it's too much, it's too much stress."

A spokeswoman for Portsmouth Hospitals NHS Trust stated the Emergency Department has seen "15 per cent more attendances compared to this time last year" and highlighted that the hospital received 2,154 more ambulances last year than any other in the region. The trust is working with health system partners on an emergency care improvement programme.

Mark Ainsworth, SCAS director of operations, voiced increasing concern over ambulances being held at the hospital, reporting that patients have waited outside for more than two hours.

Mr. Field stated that Sir Philip introduced a "substantial" recovery plan to tackle pension deficits at Arcadia, the owner of Top Shop. However, he characterized the initial approach to the BHS pension scheme as "inadequate." Sir Philip owned BHS for 15 years before selling it in March 2015. The retailer was purchased for £1 by Dominic Chappell, a former bankrupt with limited retail experience, and entered administration a year later.

In response, the Work and Pensions Committee launched a lengthy and often contentious inquiry into the management of the BHS pension fund. Sir Philip promised to "sort" the issue and, after months of negotiations with the Pensions Regulator, agreed in February to contribute £363 million to bolster the BHS scheme.

The committee also sought details on the pension schemes of Arcadia, which controls Dorothy Perkins and Miss Selfridge and is owned by Sir Philip. Documents released over the weekend revealed that Arcadia’s pension deficit had increased to nearly £565 million by March 2016, up from about £456 million in March 2013. To address this gap, Arcadia doubled its annual contributions to the two main funds, raising them to £50 million.

Mr. Field described this as a "credible plan for tackling a giant deficit" and "great news for Arcadia pensioners who must have been concerned." He noted that the figures indicate Sir Philip prioritized Arcadia’s pension schemes over BHS’s, despite BHS having more members. In 2012, while still owning BHS, Sir Philip agreed to a 23-year plan to resolve the pension deficit, which Mr. Field called "ludicrous," contrasting it with a 13-year recovery plan for Arcadia that involved significantly larger contributions.

Mr. Field added, "I imagine Sir Philip would say that Arcadia could afford it because it was profitable, whereas BHS was not." Sir Philip has not responded to these comments.

Drug Aid Cymru links the increase in drug-related deaths to the greater potency of drugs and a large number of users unaware of available support services. Data shows that after five years of decline, drug-related deaths rose again in 2015. The Welsh Government stated it is reviewing options and stressed that lowering these figures remains a "priority."

Ifor Glyn, regional director of Drug Aid Cymru, said, "Deaths are likely to rise because there is more heroin available, its purity has increased, and many people are unaware of services." He added, "We have been unable to tackle this problem. Agencies like ours across Wales must address it."

Glyn proposed encouraging users to share information about others or creating supervised spaces where individuals can use drugs safely. The Welsh Government allocates £50 million annually to drug services and said a spokesperson they are doing "everything we can to reach those individuals not currently in contact with substance misuse services."

Mark Wylie of Calne claimed the town crier title in Bermuda, outperforming 24 competitors from across the globe. The three-day competition assessed participants on sustained volume from 20 meters (65 feet), diction, and bearing. Wylie, who nearly lost his voice during the event, said, "I decided to give it my all and my all is what it took."

Serving as Calne’s town crier since 2007, Wylie typically wears a heavy, custom-made uniform in the town’s flag colors. To cope with Bermuda’s tropical heat, his wife crafted a lightweight cotton outfit for the competition. "My normal regalia is 100% wool and I would have melted in that," he explained. "So my wife made me a new set which was the right weight and very comfortable to wear."

The contest featured a different cry each day over three days. Wylie won all three rounds, defeating the reigning world champion, Canadian Chris Whyman. Reflecting on his vocal condition, he said, "My voice is better than it was but it's still rough. Some criers seem to be able to bellow for as long as they like and it doesn't affect them at all. I'm not too bad usually but in the final round, I could feel it was already pretty hoarse."

Despite nearly losing his voice in the final stages, the Wiltshire crier secured both the championship trophy and the winner’s prize. "It was an awful lot of rum, would you believe, which I need for medicinal purposes," he added.

A survey by Global Wireless Solutions of 2,000 mobile users found that 40% experience signal blackspots at home, with Liverpool and Cardiff reporting the highest rates. In Liverpool, 60% of respondents said they had trouble making and receiving calls at home, followed by 54% in Cardiff and 53% in Bristol. The survey highlighted kitchens as the most common area for poor reception and identified Georgian-era and 2000s-built homes as particularly challenging for mobile signals.

Paul Carter, CEO of GWS, commented, "The UK is no longer a fixed-line nation. When we're at home, we don't just receive calls on our mobiles, we make them too. The best phone is the one you've got on you—not the one sitting in its dock out in the hallway."

Telecoms analyst Matthew Howett told the BBC that coverage is expected to improve as operators begin using different frequencies. He added, "I don't think the results of the survey are hugely surprising as it is the sort of common problem most of us have experienced—whether at home or increasingly in the office."

Howett also outlined current solutions from providers: EE and Three offer services allowing users to make calls and send texts via their existing broadband and equipment, though compatibility is not guaranteed across all devices. Vodafone and others have long supplied 'signal boosters'—hardware connected to home broadband that supports a wider range of devices. The benefit of EE and Three’s approach is that it eliminates the need for additional hardware.

Looking ahead, Howett pointed to O2’s regulatory commitment to deliver indoor 4G coverage to 98% of the population by 2017 and expressed confidence that mobile blackspot issues will likely be resolved by then.

At 29, Seaward shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best, finishing in 2:14.52—comfortably inside the Rio qualifying time of 2:17.00. Northern Ireland’s Paul Pollock also achieved the standard with a 2:15.38 but was only the fourth Irish runner to finish. Moldovan-born Sergiu Ciobanu recorded 2:15.14, while Raheny’s Mick Clohisey crossed the line just ahead of Pollock at 2:15.35.

With Ireland restricted to three male marathon spots for Rio, Pollock faces the challenge of improving his time next spring to secure selection. Ciobanu, a Clonliffe athlete who declared for Ireland this summer, has been a consistent figure in distance running within his adopted country for several years.

Seaward, a Loughborough-based teacher and St Malachy’s athlete, said after his performance, “I thought I’d run around 2:15 but didn’t expect to go under it, so I’m absolutely delighted.” His previous best was 2:18.46, set at last year’s Manchester Marathon.

Pollock, 28, pointed to recent injury issues as obstacles. “Three weeks ago I had an 11 centimetre tear in my quad, so I couldn’t run for about 10 days, then a week of just two or three miles a day,” he explained. His time was 52 seconds faster than his 2012 Dublin personal best. “I caught Mick with four or five miles to go, but he caught me back with 3K remaining. At the Brandenburg Gate, it came down to a sprint finish, and everything seized up—I ended up walking over the line. I’m gutted to be the fourth Irishman.”

Meanwhile, Lizzie Lee has no doubts about her Rio selection. The 35-year-old Cork mother moved to fifth on the all-time Irish list with a time of 2:32.51, more than nine minutes inside the Olympic qualifying standard. She had previously recorded 2:38.09 in Berlin two years ago.

Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) reported that a Metrolink driver notified authorities of a tram-pedestrian collision at approximately 19:45 BST on Sunday. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) confirmed that a 31-year-old woman, who is not the tram driver, is currently in custody and being questioned. GMP also confirmed that a man died at the scene.

Stephen Rhodes, Metrolink’s customer director, called the fatality "absolutely devastating" and offered his condolences to the victim’s family and friends. He added that further comments would be inappropriate due to the ongoing police investigation.

The collision caused several hours of disruption to Bury line services, affecting attendees of the Parklife festival at Heaton Park, which concluded at 23:00 Sunday. Metrolink issued a walking map, estimating the three-mile journey back to the city centre would take about an hour. Some Twitter users criticized this guidance, calling it "unbelievable" to suggest young people walk the distance in wellies and darkness, while others believed there was safety in numbers.

Metrolink also tweeted of an "ongoing medical emergency," advising passengers to avoid Manchester Victoria station. Rhodes encouraged those able to walk to do so and noted that 100 buses were deployed to support travellers, asking for patience. By Monday, Metrolink reported a "good service" on all lines, with trams running in and out of Victoria station.

Roberto Firmino’s two goals matched Fernando Llorente’s brace, but Gylfi Sigurdsson’s strike in the 74th minute secured Swansea a crucial three points. Prior to this fixture, Swansea had never recorded a win at Anfield, where John Toshack spent eight years as a player.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales, Toshack remarked, "Liverpool probably thought it was going to be a lot easier than it turned out." He hailed Swansea’s victory as "great" and highlighted the unpredictable nature of football, describing it as "full of these surprises." Toshack called the result one of the most memorable in Swansea’s history and said it should serve as a significant morale boost.

Before the match, Toshack had predicted Swansea’s relegation from the Premier League and questioned the appointment of manager Paul Clement. Nonetheless, he conceded that Swansea earned the victory and insisted it was not simply down to Liverpool’s poor display.

"In the first half, Swansea were very well focused and organized. Liverpool probably thought the game was going to be a lot easier than it turned out to be," Toshack said. He added that scoring three goals away at Anfield, or anywhere in the Premier League, is a notable accomplishment for Swansea. "As disappointing as Liverpool were, you have to look at how focused Swansea were, particularly in that first 45 minutes," he concluded.

Alex Pritchard, aged 22, is set to join West Bromwich Albion’s squad for Tuesday’s Premier League home fixture against Swansea City. A product of Tottenham Hotspur’s youth system, Pritchard made his first-team debut in 2014 following loan spells at Peterborough and Swindon. Last season, he was on loan at Brentford, where he scored 12 goals in 47 appearances, but has played only once for Tottenham this season.

The England Under-21 international signed a four-year contract extension with Tottenham last summer. Commenting on his transfer, Pritchard stated, “It’s been a hectic few hours – I was close to going elsewhere. But when this came about I didn’t hesitate to come here.”

West Bromwich Albion remained resolute in their stance not to sell Saido Berahino before the transfer deadline, despite ongoing speculation. Chairman Jeremy Peace rejected all offers from Newcastle, which lessened the chances of the club making further squad additions.

The only signing West Brom made on deadline day was the loan acquisition of midfielder Alex Pritchard from Tottenham Hotspur.

For the latest updates on football transfers, visit our dedicated page.

From a field of 91 entries, Kay's book secured the £30,000 prize, marking the first occasion the winner was determined by public vote, alongside unanimous endorsement from the judging panel. Runners-up Leila Aboulela, Stewart Conn, and Sue Peebles each received £5,000.

Kay, born in Edinburgh to a Scottish nurse and a Nigerian student, was adopted at birth by a white couple from Glasgow. Her book, Red Dust Road, chronicles her search for her birth parents. Reflecting on the award, Kay said, "I happened to write the book, but it feels like my whole family is the winner. The book doesn't just belong to me." She added, "It now seems to have a life of its own in the heart-warming and unexpected way readers connect it to their own lives."

Past winners of the prize include James Kelman and Edwin Morgan. Andrew Dixon, chief executive of Creative Scotland, commented, "With more than 40 literature and book festivals from the Borders to Ullapool, Scotland's writers continue to raise Scotland's cultural profile to an international audience. Jackie Kay is one of Scotland's national treasures."

Johnny Sexton endured several heavy tackles during France's 10-9 victory over Ireland, ultimately forcing him off the field. Following the match, France lock Yoann Maestri received a caution from the citing commissioner. Jenkins remarked, "I think these boys have to realise they're in the firing line in today's game. There's no hiding place and he's just got to get on with it and front up."

Throughout the game, Sexton came under intense pressure, with a replay showing Maestri striking the Leinster fly-half in an off-the-ball incident. Meanwhile, Biggar was forced off during Wales' 16-16 draw with Ireland in Dublin after twisting his ankle. He featured in most of Wales' 27-23 win over Scotland but was substituted in the 76th minute with his foot strapped.
