Addressing BBC Radio Wales, Jenkins said, "He (Biggar) is tough, so let's just hope he keeps going and doing what he has been doing. We need him to keep playing as well as he has. If sides target him, that is a positive for us because it shows how well he has been playing. We can't hide him. Wherever he plays, unless we get him a seat near the posts, he will be targeted, as he was against Ireland and Scotland. If they want to target him, he is good enough and strong enough to deal with that and should take it as a compliment."

Jenkins also noted that Biggar’s Ospreys half-back partner, Rhys Webb, requires more game time before a recall to Wales. Webb made his Ospreys return against Munster last Sunday after being sidelined since September with a foot injury but suffered a head knock likely to rule him out of Friday’s match against Edinburgh.

A police officer was injured in an incident on Ferry Lane in Tottenham Hale on Thursday evening. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) has launched an investigation into the death and confirmed that a firearm was recovered at the scene. An IPCC spokesperson said the officer—who was taken to hospital and later discharged—may have been shot first, although this has not been confirmed.

The IPCC stated, "It is understood that the shooting followed an MPS [Metropolitan Police Service] operation." The Metropolitan Police declined to confirm whether the deceased man was shot by a police officer. A Scotland Yard spokesperson said, "One male was pronounced dead at the scene and one officer was taken to hospital."

Local resident David Akinsanya arrived shortly after the incident and said a witness told him a police officer had shouted at the man to stop several times, but the man did not comply. The witness, who lives next to the scene, then heard four shots. Akinsanya added, "There were lots of helicopters and sirens all over the place," and noted a surveillance van was parked on the corner.

A waitress at a nearby pub, who wished to remain anonymous, said the incident occurred a few minutes’ walk from Tottenham Hale station. She reported, "One man came in and he said that he saw police trying to pull some clothes off a man who was bleeding." Another worker described seeing "lots of cars" in the area. Police have cordoned off a large section, and Ferry Lane remains closed.

David Lammy, Labour MP for Tottenham, said he was "shocked and deeply worried" by the incident. He added, "There is quite a lot of anxiety now in the community, but we should try to stay calm and not rush to judgement." Lammy called on the IPCC to act swiftly to address concerns and dispel rumours surrounding the case.

Scotland under-20 international Ali signed his first professional contract with the Warriors in December and has appeared in nine matches this season. Reflecting on his development, Price said, "The last few months have been great, as I've played regularly and feel I've made a positive impact." He also acknowledged that training and competing alongside skilled teammates at Scotstoun have helped sharpen his abilities.

Warriors head coach Gregor Townsend commended Ali’s progress as a scrum-half, stating, "It's great news that he's staying with us for the next couple of years." Townsend highlighted Ali’s dedication over the past year and observed that his confidence is now evident in both his kicking and his readiness to take on defenses with the ball. He added that Ali has consistently shown the essential scrum-half traits—quick, precise passing and strong fitness—while capitalizing on opportunities in several key fixtures this season.

Justine Henshaw-Bryan, who is expecting to give birth in November, chased Damien Doughty through Stoke Newington, north London, resulting in him being thrown into a tree. The incident took place on 10 February 2016, when Henshaw-Bryan, using her mobile phone, pulled out in front of Doughty, a cycle courier, on Stoke Newington High Street, nearly causing a collision. After Doughty confronted her about her phone use, she shouted at him. At the next traffic lights, Doughty kicked her wing mirror. Henshaw-Bryan, with her then-boyfriend in the car, then pursued Doughty down Victorian Grove and struck him with her vehicle, causing serious injuries that required three days in intensive care.

Henshaw-Bryan claimed her then-boyfriend had grabbed the steering wheel and directed the car at Doughty, also alleging she had been a victim of domestic violence during their relationship. Judge Gregory Perrins dismissed her account, stating he did not believe she was genuinely afraid of her boyfriend. He described her conduct as a "calculated attempt to run him over and use your car as a weapon," emphasizing the significant risk of injury and potential fatality. Henshaw-Bryan, from Hackney, was found guilty of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and sentenced at Wood Green Crown Court. She was also disqualified from driving for four and a half years.

Thames Valley Police are currently analyzing extensive CCTV and dash-cam footage following the abduction and rape of a 14-year-old girl on her way to school between 08:15 and 08:40 BST last Wednesday. Officers continue patrols in the Summertown area while seeking further witnesses.

Detective Superintendent Chris Ward, head of major crime, stated, "We are securing evidence, interviewing witnesses, and reviewing the substantial quantity of CCTV, dash-cam footage, and information received from the public." A dedicated team of specially trained officers is providing ongoing support to the victim.

The teenager was located at midday by a member of the public on Cavendish Drive in Marston. Police have issued descriptions of two suspects. The first is a white man in his mid-20s, balding with shaven dark blonde hair, blue eyes, medium build, and approximately 6ft (1.82m) tall. He spoke with a northern accent and wore black trousers and a hooded top featuring a single front pocket, without drawstrings or a logo.

The second suspect is a white man with brown gelled hair, clean-shaven, and brown eyes. The victim described him as late teens to early 20s and slightly smaller in build than the first suspect. Police are focusing patrols and inquiries in the nearby Marston Meadow area.

Superintendent Joe Kidman, Oxford’s local policing commander, expressed gratitude to the public for their support, saying, "I know the shock this rare incident has caused and want to add my thanks for all the support provided by the public."

New figures obtained by BBC Radio Oxford through a Freedom of Information request reveal that 411 signalling faults occurred during the 2014/15 financial year, marking a 22% rise from 337 incidents in 2012/13. This increase has sparked criticism from commuters who are also facing higher fares.

Network Rail has attributed the rise to insufficient investment in railway infrastructure. Signalling failures can stem from issues such as power outages or blown fuses, which cause signals to go black and require train drivers to stop. A spokeswoman pointed to the age of the equipment as the underlying cause, saying, "We are replacing all of the signalling equipment along the Western route as part of our £7.5bn modernisation programme."

In the 2013/14 financial year, 379 signalling faults were recorded. Sim Harris, managing editor of Railnews magazine, said the problems are causing "major disruption to thousands of people," adding, "The problem with the signalling between Oxford and Reading, which is where these problems do occur, is that it's getting on [in age]."

Commuters have voiced their frustration over the ongoing issues. Simon Stevenson, 42, a company director from North Oxford who travels to London two or three times a week, said, "There seems to be a disconnect. We have constant increases in fares, but that doesn't translate into improvements in service." Similarly, Damian Fantato, 26, a journalist who commuted daily from Oxford to London until earlier this year, stated, "Commuting to London costs an arm and a leg, so when you are delayed most mornings because you are sat somewhere just outside Reading it feels like you are being taken for a ride."

In preparation for a craft fair on Saturday, Laura Whitford decorated Royston’s town centre with vibrant nets and bunting. Alongside her friend Anne Walls, she crocheted bollard covers and a large net to cover the Royse Stone, a local landmark that once featured a cross and lent its name to the town. The decorations were put up on Sunday night, with Mrs Whitford describing the effort as carried out "under cover of darkness, like all good guerrilla knitters and yarn bombers do."

Since then, the nets have repeatedly been thrown onto a roof and into trees. On Monday morning, the decorations vanished, leading Mrs Whitford to post "missing" notices on local Facebook groups. The items reappeared that afternoon but were again found scattered on the pavement and tossed into trees by Tuesday. After being retrieved and replaced, the stone cover was spotted the following day on a bank’s roof. Staff from a nearby pub used a stepladder to assist Mrs Whitford in recovering it.

Despite these ongoing disruptions, the nets were once again discovered in the trees, where Mrs Whitford said they would stay until the fair. Sharing her experience online, she noted that the attention ensured everyone "now knows about the fair." She added, "Actually, I'd like to thank the vandals because they really have done me a huge favour, and this whole saga of missing netting has given the fair more publicity than I ever could."

Dickie Bird, 78, from Barnsley, was widely recognized as one of cricket’s most popular and dependable umpires. His final Test match, England against India at Lord’s in 1996, featured a players' guard of honour and a standing ovation from the crowd. After retiring in 1998, he founded the Dickie Bird Foundation, which offers grants to underprivileged children.

Speaking to the BBC about receiving the OBE, Bird said, "It came as quite a surprise... but I'm tremendously delighted and honoured to get this great honour." He called it "a marvellous and wonderful honour" that he had not anticipated, noting, "I got the MBE in 1986, which is a long time ago, so when this came along I was completely stunned, shocked."

Regarding his foundation, he explained, "It's for under-privileged kids whose parents cannot afford sports equipment. If we believe they are a worthy cause, we send them a grant." He added, "My aim is to get them off street corners, away from television, doing exercises and giving them a start in life."

Other South Yorkshire recipients include Med Hughes, recently retired chief constable of the county police, who was appointed CBE for services to policing; Sarah Stevenson, a world taekwondo champion from Doncaster, awarded an MBE for services to martial arts; and Christine Manby, appointed OBE for her work with South Yorkshire’s Women’s Royal Voluntary Service.

A panel of industry experts will determine the shortlist for the 2016 award, with the final winner chosen by public vote. Past winners include James McAvoy, Tom Hardy, and Jack O'Connell, who received the accolade at this year’s Baftas.

Colman said she seeks a performance "you couldn't ignore." Reflecting on her role as a juror, she noted, "I think it's important to support people who are coming into it. I would have liked someone to go 'well done, you' at the very beginning... it's nice to be able to do that for each other."

The award is open to both newcomers and actors with multiple film credits. Ross, who hosted the BBC’s film review programme for 11 years, said he looks for someone who has "already made a splash." He explained, "It's not about being just a new young face. It's about someone who can shine on screen, regardless of the film’s quality, role, or genre."

He added, "Someone who has earned the audience’s affection so that when people see their name in the cast list, they think, 'OK, I want to see that film because that person always does interesting work.'"

The jury comprises producer and chair Marc Samuelson; film critic James King; Gabrielle Tana, producer of Philomena; Lucy Bevan, casting director for Pirates of the Caribbean and Testament of Youth; Mike Newell, director of Harry Potter and Four Weddings and a Funeral; and Nina Gold, casting director for Star Wars Episode VII, The King's Speech, and The Imitation Game.

This panel will select five nominees, to be announced on 6 January 2016. The winner will be revealed at the EE British Academy Film Awards in February 2016.

Gloucester City Council has implemented new enforcement measures in response to reports of drug use and aggressive begging in the city centre. Public Space Protection Orders (PSPO) will prohibit begging and tackle public nuisance. Some individuals who beg have raised concerns about a lack of adequate support services.

Cabinet member Jennie Dallimore noted that some of those causing issues are "housed and in receipt of benefits," a situation she said "cannot be tolerated." These powers derive from the Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014. A similar PSPO was previously used in Taunton to curb the use of legal highs.

Those who violate the new regulations and refuse to engage with the council or drug charities risk fines or prosecution. During Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, councillors also endorsed a campaign to increase awareness of support available to rough sleepers.

Martin, a street beggar, told the BBC, "I want to get myself clean but there's no help. I need help now, not in a few months down the line. At the end of the day they should sit here, then they would understand. I'm not abusive, I'm polite, I'm only sat here, I'm not going out shoplifting or mugging people."

Ms. Dallimore emphasized that support is accessible for those seeking to overcome addiction. "We have been working with the police and charitable partners, including Turning Point, who assist people with substance misuse issues," she said. "It's encouraging this individual wants help, and the public should report anyone they encounter to us."

Luke Durbin, 19, from Hollesley, disappeared after a night out in Ipswich on 11 May 2006 and failed to return home. No charges have been made in connection with his disappearance, and the current reward is the first to be offered since the investigation began. His mother, Nicki Durbin, said, "My family and I desperately need answers."

On the evening of 11 May, Luke spent part of the night at Zest nightclub on Princes Street. He was last seen on CCTV near the Cattle Market bus station in the early hours of 12 May. The reward is being offered jointly by Nicki Durbin, Crimestoppers, Suffolk Police, the East Anglian Daily Times, and the Ipswich Star.

Ms. Durbin commented, "It’s more than nine years since I reported Luke as missing. We still believe someone locally knows what happened to Luke, and we hope this reward encourages them to come forward with information that will help find my son."

Detective Superintendent John Brocklebank said, "We do not offer rewards lightly because of legal implications. Previously, we had sufficient lines of inquiry without a reward. The timing is for operational reasons. We are appealing to anyone with information who may be motivated by the financial reward."

Suffolk Police are also seeking to identify the driver of a white or silver Volvo 440 seen on Orwell Place at 04:09 BST on 12 May 2006. Although CCTV captured images of the vehicle, the number plate was not visible. Police confirmed that a Volvo 440 with the registration M206 LYE was in the Ipswich area at that time but was registered under a false name and address. Authorities urge anyone who recognizes this number plate to come forward to confirm whether it matches the vehicle in the footage.

The Cube in Corby, which cost £48 million, now has its fourth-floor office space finished and available for lease. The building also houses Corby Borough Council offices, a library, a theatre, and a register office.

Tom Beattie, leader of the council’s Labour group, admitted to a cost overrun, stating, “We held our hands up and accepted responsibility.” Since its opening in November 2010, The Cube has encountered issues including a leaking roof. Inspectors described the helical staircase as “dangerous, like a helter skelter,” while David Sims, then Conservative opposition leader, criticized it as a “poorly managed, waste of taxpayers’ money.” The council has since completed repairs to rectify these problems.

Mr. Beattie added, “It’s taken a while, but the building is now functional, people have adapted to it, and it reflects Corby’s ambition. The developments around the town centre likely wouldn’t have happened without this building—it has attracted further business.”

Rob McKellar, the current Conservative opposition leader, said, “The Cube is a building Corby can be proud of and represents its ambitions. Although controversial with multi-million pound overspends, the public punished Labour at the May ballot box, and Labour has apologized. Now it’s time to look ahead, and Corby’s future is bright.”

Earlier this year, council officer Steven Redfern reached an out-of-court settlement after filing a £1 million damages claim following his whistle-blowing on the project’s escalating costs.

Drainage work between junction 12 at Tal-y-Bont and junction 13 at Abergwyngregyn is scheduled to start this autumn, subject to landowner approval. This effort addresses a stretch of the A55 that was closed following flooding on Boxing Day.

First Minister Carwyn Jones also announced a separate £1.9 million flood alleviation scheme in Tal-y-Bont, set to begin in spring and be completed before winter. He visited the village in January, shortly after Christmas flooding, a week after residents voiced frustration that he had passed through without stopping. Jones apologized, saying he was unaware they expected his visit.

At the Traffic Management Centre in Conwy on Thursday, Jones said, "When I saw the flooding on the A55 and then met residents of Tal-y-Bont who had been affected, I said that the money was available for a flood alleviation scheme to help reduce the risk of it happening again." Following discussions with Gwynedd council, construction is planned to start this April and finish ahead of next winter.

On the A55 work, he highlighted the need for extensive planning due to its scale. "The plan is not that there are perpetual road works on the A55," he said. "At the moment, we need to make sure that the tunnels are safe for the future." He added that no work is planned after Easter this year but noted the A55 was "built on the cheap, unfortunately." He explained, "If you look at some of the sections like the tunnels, it's just the old road. We would never build a road like that now; we would build a far better road. So we have to improve the road's resilience for the future."

In April, with Crotone seemingly destined for relegation after winning just three of 29 matches, Davide Nicola stepped in under a new agreement. The team then won six of their final nine games, securing survival by a two-point margin. Nine days after leaving Crotone, the 44-year-old returned to his hometown of Vigone, near Turin, on Sunday.

“Am I tired? I still do not feel any particular pain,” Nicola said. “It’s been a beautiful journey, a fairytale. From tomorrow maybe I will feel a bit tired, but what matters most is that my goal has been achieved.”

Three years earlier, Nicola’s 14-year-old son, Alessandro, was killed after being struck by a bus while cycling in Vigone. “I kept the promise and, with the help of many people, we have raised awareness about road safety,” he added. Upon returning to Turin, he said, “I was greeted with great enthusiasm. I am very excited.”

Nicola secured the deal with his players following a 2-1 victory at Chievo—Crotone’s first away win in Serie A. The club had collected just 14 points from their first 29 matches but finished with 34 points, two above the relegation zone.

Despite this late surge, Crotone entered the final day in the bottom three. Their survival was confirmed after a 3-1 win over Lazio, combined with Empoli’s defeat to Palermo, ensuring the club remained in its debut top-flight season.

Dumfries and Galloway Council and Stena Line have joined forces with the McKinney Group to advance detailed plans for the regeneration of the East Pier, which is owned by Stena Line. The proposed redevelopment includes new retail, leisure, and housing projects. Councillor Colin Smyth described the announcement as "another positive step forward" for the town, pointing out that the council has already invested approximately £4 million in Agnew Park, the West Pier, and sailing facilities as part of its overall waterfront strategy. He stated that private sector investment in redeveloping the East Pier is a crucial next phase for Stranraer and confirmed that discussions with the Scottish government are ongoing to secure support for the initiative.

Les Stracey, representing Stena Line Ports Ltd, referred to the agreement as a "significant milestone." Billy McKinney of the McKinney Group also welcomed the partnership, emphasizing the project's potential to transform Stranraer and the southwest of Scotland. He committed to working with Stena Line and the council to develop proposals that reflect the aspirations of the local community and create new opportunities for growth in Stranraer.

Sixteen two-man teams representing different nations will compete at the Centurion Club in St Albans on 6-7 May for a prize pool of one million euros (£852,000). The event will feature amphitheatre-style seating around the tees, along with music and pyrotechnics. Players will wear microphones and are encouraged to interact with the audience.

Keith Pelley, chief executive of the Tour, said the aim is to "emulate" the Ryder Cup atmosphere. He stated, "Golf needs to modernise, and introducing innovative new formats is key. We want to broaden the sport’s appeal to millennials, and this format will help achieve that."

On the first day, teams will be divided into four groups of four, with the top two from each group progressing to the knockout rounds. The second day will host the quarter-finals, semi-finals, final, and a third-place play-off.

Matches will be played in a greensomes, match-play format: both players tee off, select the best shot, then alternate shots until the hole is completed. One point is awarded for each hole won, with the team holding the most points after six holes declared the winner.

Each nation’s team will be led by its highest-ranked and available European Tour member as of 13 March, who will then choose a teammate.

The Hampshire County Men's Final between Southsea Waverley and Boscombe Cliff was held in Southampton on Sunday. According to the Bournemouth Echo, a Boscombe player confronted an opponent over a dispute regarding "bowls etiquette." Following this, other Boscombe players conceded the match, allowing Waverley to retain the men's county champions title.

Peter Aldridge, secretary of Southsea Waverley, said both clubs were "mortified by the behaviour." He was told by members present that the player involved, who is in his 30s, was injured after the disagreement escalated during the final and that a headbutt was attempted. Aldridge added, "Bowls has changed over the years—people do get excited but this was not acceptable. It doesn't represent the attitude of Boscombe Cliff and is not representative of the game."

Boscombe Cliff Bowls Club declined to comment on the incident.

Bowls Hampshire, the county’s governing body, confirmed that a Boscombe player was "asked to leave the green," leading the team to concede the match. Secretary Spencer Kerley said he is awaiting statements from both clubs and county officers before deciding on any further action.

A spokeswoman for Hampshire Constabulary confirmed the incident was not reported to the police.

A 36-year-old is scheduled to appear at Edinburgh Sheriff Court following the discharge of a firearm in Dalkeith early Sunday morning. Police reported no injuries and no visible damage to the property on Woodburn Road. Searches connected to the investigation were conducted on Monday at Meadowfield Terrace in Edinburgh and Kippielaw Steading in Dalkeith, where a firearm was recovered.

Chief Inspector Kenny Simpson of Police Scotland stated, "This was an isolated incident, and we are not seeking anyone else in connection with it." He added, "We recognize the impact on the local community and have launched extensive inquiries alongside high-visibility patrols. A swift arrest has been made, and I thank residents for their support. Firearm offences will not be tolerated, and we will use all available resources to bring those responsible to justice."

Christie, 20, who transferred from Inverness Caledonian Thistle in September, appeared as a substitute against his former team on Saturday. He acknowledged the challenges of competing within a large squad, stating, "Because it's such a big squad, there's so much competition, it's going to be frustrating at times. But I think over a long period, the players that keep working hard will eventually get success in the team."

His role at the new club differs from his position in the Highlands, where he was a key figure under manager John Hughes. Speaking to BBC Scotland, Christie noted, "I wasn't going to be straight into the starting 11; I had to almost start from scratch again. But I'm delighted I've eventually started making appearances on the park."

Celtic overcame a difficult first half at Parkhead to secure a 3-0 victory over Caley Thistle in the second half. Reflecting on playing against his former teammates, Christie described the experience as "very strange," adding, "Nice to see them again and I wish them all the best in the future. I spent many good years at Inverness, but it's time to move on now."

Regarding the match, he said, "First half, fair credit to Inverness, I think they passed the ball excellently and shocked us a bit. We regrouped at half-time and showed we were definitely the better team. I think in front of goal we were more clinical, which can prove vital in these games."

Journals penned by sailors aboard HMS Trincomalee, currently moored in Hartlepool, have been preserved in the Royal Navy archives in Portsmouth for 150 years. The ship, built in India in 1817 for the Admiralty in Bombay, served in the West Indies and the Pacific before being used as a training vessel in West Hartlepool from 1862 to 1877. Relocated to Hartlepool in 1987, it underwent restoration lasting over a decade. Today, HMS Trincomalee serves as the centerpiece of Hartlepool's Maritime Experience, attracting 54,000 visitors each year.

The vessel is now being integrated into the new National Museum of the Royal Navy (NMRN). Bryn Hughes, general manager of the HMS Trincomalee Trust, said, "The positive links with the NMRN in Portsmouth will heighten public awareness of HMS Trincomalee. It is a wonderful long-term scheme following hard on the profile of the recent Tall Ships Races so successfully staged in Hartlepool." The seldom-seen journals will be exhibited in the static Trincomalee display in Hartlepool. Among them is a journal from 1852, kept by midshipman William Dawson, featuring a detailed log and tracking maps of the ship’s voyages during that time.

Dr. Dominic Tweddle, director general of the NMRN, commented, "Welcoming HMS Trincomalee as part of the museum allows the story of the Royal Navy, its ships, and its people to be told on a national scale."

A group of boys and girls aged 11 to 14 was reported missing after they failed to return to the Carrbridge area. The scouts, undertaking a practice hike for an award, had adult supervisors waiting for their return. After becoming lost, they made their way to a remote bothy on the River Dulnain, located seven miles from their original camp at Sluggan Bridge. As night fell and temperatures dropped, they lit a fire inside the bothy to keep warm.

A Coastguard helicopter later located the group, who were waving and flashing lights at the bothy. When the crew approached, one scout asked, "Are we in trouble?" Aircraft captain Simon Hammock said, "They had travelled a significant distance across uneven ground, and as the weather deteriorated had elected to seek shelter in a bothy. Their scouting training had been put to good use and had ultimately ensured their safety." He added, "When we returned them to their camp they were met with open arms by the other cubs and scouts. A great result." The scouts were then airlifted back to Sluggan Bridge.

The rest of the group raised the alarm at around 18:45 when the scouts did not return, and the missing children were found at approximately 20:40. Inspector Mike Middlehurst of Police Scotland said, "This was a very well co-ordinated operation and we are very grateful to our partners, especially Cairngorm Mountain Rescue Team and the local estate staff, whose local knowledge and expertise helped locate the children quickly and safely." He also noted the group was well equipped with maps, food, and water, and that their choice to seek shelter in the bothy contributed to their safe rescue.

UK-based lorries will be subject to a new fee, offset by a matching reduction in vehicle excise duty. The government intends to establish a "level playing field" for British drivers, who currently pay tolls when using European roads. However, the AA has expressed concern that this could eventually lead to a universal road charging scheme for all motorists.

Ministers revealed that draft legislation will be published next month, with the charge expected to come into effect by the end of the current parliament. The fee, which will vary depending on vehicle size, is forecast to generate around £20 million annually.

Transport Secretary Patrick McLoughlin said, "These proposals will deliver a vital shot in the arm to the UK haulage industry. It is simply not right that foreign lorries do not pay to use our roads, when our trucks invariably have to fork out when travelling to the continent. By introducing charges we will create a level playing field, increasing UK competitiveness and boosting growth."

At present, British hauliers operating in Europe face various road tolls, while continental lorries can use UK roads without charge. Geoff Dunning, chief executive of the Road Haulage Association, called the announcement a "happy day" for the industry. He added, "We have been campaigning for years to see a system introduced which will lessen the financial advantage currently enjoyed by our European neighbours. UK hauliers travelling to mainland Europe have to pay road charges but foreign-registered vehicles travelling to the UK pay nothing."

Mr. Gill voiced his support for devolution but acknowledged he is "not enthusiastic" about Wales receiving additional powers. Speaking on BBC's The Wales Report, he criticized the assembly's current powers as being "badly used" and emphasized that local parties will determine UKIP's candidates for the Welsh assembly election in May.

Addressing reports that former Tory MPs Neil Hamilton and Mark Reckless might be centrally imposed as candidates, Mr. Gill stated, "As a principle, I think that it's madness to have people standing who the local party don't want to stand for them. Which is why the local party will now decide who represents them."

On the forthcoming elections, he said they present an opportunity for the party to show discipline and deliver "good things for the people of Wales." He added, "We want to be a constructive part of the assembly. We want to be there to get the voices and the views of those people who vote for us heard and we need to make sure that people start to believe in this institution for the right reasons."

The seventh-seeded duo overcame Koreans Kim Gi Jung and Shin Seung Chan 21-12, 21-16 at the Barclaycard Arena. In Friday’s quarter-finals, the Adcocks are set to meet Indonesia’s Tontowi Ahmad and Liliyana Natsir, who ousted them at the same stage last year. The husband-and-wife pair have yet to advance to the Championships’ semi-finals.

Reflecting on their progress, Gabby Adcock said, "It's another quarter-final here and that's an amazing feeling, but we do want to go that step further." She added, "We know it's tough. We had a close match last year but we are going to go out there and give our everything." In 2015, Gabby and Chris Adcock lost the final set 21-19 to Ahmad and Natsir.

In the men’s doubles, Britons Marcus Ellis and Chris Langridge secured a quarter-final spot after defeating Korean seventh seeds Kim Gi Jung and Kim Sa Rang 14-21, 21-15, 21-16. Ellis and Langridge will now face top seeds Lee Yong Dae and Yoo Seong of Korea, with a place in the semi-finals on the line.

The United Nations has documented incidents of looting, property destruction, abductions, and killings in territories retaken from the Islamic State (IS) group. It highlighted that Sunni Arabs are facing discrimination from Iraqi authorities and other groups who accuse them of supporting IS. In October, Amnesty International voiced concerns over "war crimes" committed by Kurdish fighters in northern Syria.

The UN expressed particular alarm over roughly 1,300 Sunnis stranded in a "no-man's-land" near Sinjar, caught between Kurdish security forces and IS. UN spokeswoman Cecile Pouilly stated, "Reports indicate that Iraqi security forces, Kurdish security forces, and their affiliated militias have been responsible for looting, property destruction, forced evictions, abductions, illegal detention, and in some cases, extrajudicial killings" targeting Sunni Arab communities.

Pouilly also reported that these communities have limited access to essential services and supplies such as water, food, shelter, and medical care. Additionally, the UN has received information about 16 mass graves containing bodies of IS victims, though the precise number of bodies is unknown. The UN has urged the Iraqi government to conduct thorough investigations.

Sinjar, located in northern Iraq, was freed from IS control in mid-November. The militant group had seized the town in 2014, killing and capturing thousands of Yazidis. The UN noted that Sunni Arab communities left behind now face accusations of IS sympathy.

Metropolitan Police Assistant Commissioner Mark Rowley confirmed that Portuguese police would lead the operation, with British officers also involved. Madeleine McCann was three years old when she vanished from a holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, Portugal, in May 2007. Scotland Yard reopened the investigation in July last year. Although Mr. Rowley did not disclose specific details about the next phase, he stressed that officers were following every credible lead as part of the "slog of a major investigation." He stated, "It's something that you would expect in any major inquiry. A thorough serious crime investigation works systematically through all the credible possibilities, and often in an investigation you will have more than one credible possibility." He added that the forthcoming work might not immediately produce answers that clarify everything. Mr. Rowley also highlighted that collaboration between the Metropolitan Police and Portuguese officers was effective. Scotland Yard’s inquiry, dubbed Operation Grange, began two years after a case review commenced. In March, British authorities announced they were searching for an intruder who sexually abused five girls in Portugal between 2004 and 2006. Detectives said these assaults took place in holiday villas in the Algarve region occupied by UK families.

The Very Rev Dr Houston McKelvey is set to lead the Canons of St Anne's Cathedral onto Donegall Street for this year's Black Santa sit-out, which will be his final participation before retiring in April 2011.  

Dean McKelvey remarked, "This is likely to be the most challenging sit-out yet, both economically and weather-wise." He continued, "As usual, we will be on the street each day from Thursday through Christmas Eve, from nine in the morning until five in the evening, depending on the remarkable generosity of local people, schools, and businesses."  

The annual fundraising appeal supports various charities across Northern Ireland, as well as Christian Aid. Since its inception in 1976, when Dean Sammy Crooks launched the collection, the vigil has raised millions of pounds. Dean McKelvey began participating five years ago, following in the footsteps of his predecessor, Dean Jack Shearer, who passed away in January 2001. Dean Shearer was popularly known as Black Santa, a nickname given by the media due to his distinctive attire, which was embraced by the public.  

Maintaining a 30-year tradition, Dean McKelvey plans to stay outside St Anne's Cathedral until Christmas Eve. He extended an invitation for the community to visit or join him on "our day off," Sunday, 19 December, when "Carols for the City" will be held to celebrate the Christmas message of God's generosity.  

Expressing appreciation, Dean McKelvey said, "I sincerely thank everyone who has already responded to our Postal appeal. It’s encouraging to know that £90,000 has been raised so far for this year's campaign."

The bank's Credit Conditions Survey reveals that lenders have experienced a third straight quarter of declining demand. Mortgages for high-value properties saw the sharpest drop, the largest since the third quarter of 2008. Despite this, demand is projected to rebound in the second quarter. Several lenders linked the recent downturn to a mix of regulatory changes, housing affordability concerns, and uncertainty about the housing market’s outlook.

This expected recovery may be tied to the general election campaign’s influence on the UK housing market. Jonathan Samuels, chief executive of Dragonfly Property Finance, pointed out that the significant decline in demand at the upper end of the market underscores this group’s sensitivity to political uncertainty. He explained that many prime and super-prime buyers are delaying purchases until the election outcome is clear. Samuels added that this election, described as the most uncertain in decades, has prompted increased caution within this segment.

Additionally, the survey indicated that lenders have become more willing to offer mortgages to borrowers with deposits under 10% of the property value so far this year, a group that includes many first-time buyers.

As of 23 October, approximately 3,740 people have died attempting to cross the Mediterranean, with the death toll expected to rise as the two deadliest months approach. Last year’s total was 3,771. This increase comes despite a sharp decline in crossings this year. William Spindler, spokesman for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, said smugglers are taking more hazardous routes, leading to one death for every 47 migrants or refugees traveling between Libya and Italy.

Speaking in Geneva, Spindler called the situation "by far the worst we have ever seen in the Mediterranean," noting that the death rate has tripled. UN figures show 327,800 crossings this year, compared to over one million in 2015. The UN reports that smugglers are organizing crossings during severe weather and coordinating mass departures, with thousands setting off at once in fragile boats. This overwhelms rescue services, making it impossible to save everyone if problems arise.

Spindler added that smuggling has become an industrial-scale operation. "They now send several boats at the same time, which puts rescue services in difficulty because they need to rescue several thousand people from hundreds of boats," he said.

An agreement between Turkey and the European Union to block migrants from reaching Greek islands has sharply reduced arrivals there. However, traffic has increased on the dangerous route between North Africa and Italy. On Monday, the Italian coastguard recovered 16 bodies during 21 rescue missions and saved about 2,200 migrants from 18 rubber boats.

The Consumer Electronics Show (CES), the largest annual consumer technology trade event worldwide, is hosting more than 3,500 companies this year. Starting Tuesday, leading technology firms will reveal their newest gadgets.

Among the featured devices is the Zano, a small quadcopter that fits in the palm of a hand and records HD-quality video. The latest 3D printers will also be on display, highlighting innovations in food printing and machines capable of producing detailed, multicolored 3D objects using paper and ink.

The show will showcase a variety of self-driving cars, including one with seating arranged so passengers face each other and another that can be parked via a smartwatch app. New quantum dot TV technology, which utilizes crystals 50,000 times smaller than a human hair to improve color quality, will be demonstrated. Additionally, TVs with higher brightness levels, measured in nits (not related to head lice), will provide enhanced picture clarity even in well-lit environments.

Unconventional gadgets at the event include a toothbrush that plays video games, an internet-connected baby’s dummy, a ring that displays the number of unread emails, and a dog collar that enables communication between owners and their pets.

CES runs from January 6 to January 9.

Northern Lights will present the work of designers who have chosen to stay in Scotland to grow their careers, showcasing items from hand-crafted wooden furniture to ceramic jewellery. Organisers say the event reflects the "increasing confidence" among designers in establishing their businesses within Scotland.

Scott Jarvie, a product and furniture designer, commented, "London Design Festival will be the centre of the design universe in September, so I'm thrilled to be part of the V&A Dundee show, exhibiting alongside leading lights in contemporary Scottish design." He also noted that the V&A in London has inspired his work since childhood.

Launched in 2003, the London Design Festival features more than 400 events and exhibitions. Philip Long, director of V&A Dundee, said, "We are delighted with the calibre, ambition and volume of submissions we received to exhibit as part of Northern Lights." He added that the festival provides both established and emerging designers a platform to showcase their creativity and elevate their international profiles.

The complete list of Northern Lights participants has yet to be announced. The exhibition runs from 17 to 25 September at the Victoria and Albert Museum in South Kensington.

Ars Technica reports that a settlement was reached in the early hours on the day the US trial was scheduled to start, despite the jury already being selected. Unwired Planet had sought $33 million (£25.7 million) plus a share of iPhone and iPad sales, alleging these devices used its technology. The settlement terms have not been disclosed.

Apple previously described the lawsuit, which involved inventions related to voice recognition and data transmission, as "frivolous." Nevada-based Unwired Planet, formerly Openwave Systems, once developed mobile software but no longer produces its own products. The company acquired the patents in question from Ericsson through a controversial deal that involved sharing future patent revenues with the Swedish telecom equipment maker rather than an outright purchase.

Unwired has been called a "patent troll," a label its legal team rejects as "hackneyed." A spokeswoman for PanOptis Patent Management, which recently acquired Unwired’s licensing business, told the BBC the company seeks to promote efficiency and fairness in patent licensing and to create a marketplace where manufacturers and innovators can access high-quality technology at reasonable prices.

She added that since acquiring the Unwired Planet patent portfolio nine months ago, PanOptis has resolved most of the litigation initiated by Unwired, including cases involving Samsung, LG, and Apple.

Earlier this month, Unwired secured a court victory against Huawei in London, with the Chinese firm ordered to pay a global fee for using Unwired’s 4G patents or face a UK sales ban. Unwired had previously won a case against Samsung concerning 2G technologies and remains involved in disputes with Google and HTC.

Prior to officially commencing his duties, he laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier in Canberra and presented a letter from the Queen. In the letter, she expressed that her grandson would "benefit greatly" from spending time with Australian troops. Serving as Captain Wales in his military role, the prince is set to leave the British army in June after a decade of service.

During his assignment in Australia, he will patrol alongside Aboriginal soldiers and train with the special forces. Following the wreath-laying and the placement of a poppy at the Australian War Memorial, he formally reported for duty to Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin, Chief of the Defence Force.

The Queen’s letter emphasized the longstanding relationship between the Australian and British armies, noting that the prince’s secondment would strengthen their shared values and professional ties. She wrote: "I am delighted that the long and enduring association between the Australian and British armies will be joined by the military secondment of my grandson, Prince Harry... I know that Captain Wales will benefit greatly from spending time with the Australian Diggers [soldiers] and I thank you for welcoming him into your ranks."

Describing the assignment as "challenging and hectic," the Australian military noted the demanding nature of the placement, while the prince said he is "tremendously looking forward" to it. His deployment will be briefly paused later this month when he travels to Turkey for commemorations marking the 1915 Allied campaign at Gallipoli, where thousands of Australian and New Zealand soldiers lost their lives.

Later this year, the prince is expected to undertake voluntary work for charities as he considers his future plans.

Eifion Gwynne, 41, who passed away last month, had expressed a wish to be buried at Plascrug Cemetery in Aberystwyth. Although only plots with exclusive burial rights remained, Ceredigion Council confirmed that a plot has been transferred to his family, enabling his funeral to take place there on Saturday.

Wayne Thomas, a family friend, told BBC Wales that Mr. Gwynne had shared his burial wishes with his wife, Nia. "He always said he wanted to be buried in this cemetery; it’s close to the rugby club and near his home," Thomas said.

A memorial fund set up in Mr. Gwynne’s memory has raised almost £12,000.

Ceredigion Council leader Ellen ap Gwynn said a family who had reserved a plot offered it to Mr. Gwynne’s family. "We were very pleased the council could assist. We offer our deepest sympathy to the family at this difficult time," she added.

Mr. Gwynne was a father of three and a former rugby player for Aberystwyth and Llandovery.

In Kampala, the capital of Uganda, crowds gathered to dance, sing, and wave rainbow flags, marking the end of a week-long series of events. One participant described the occasion as a possible "step forward" for the nation. Despite this, many Ugandans remain opposed to gay rights, and homosexuality is still punishable by imprisonment. Last year, Uganda’s supreme court invalidated laws that imposed life sentences for "aggravated homosexuality" and banned the "promotion of homosexuality."

Moses Kimbugwe, who took part in the march, said, "It is about trying to show the wider community that violence, discrimination, harassment, stigma against LGBT (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender) people is bad. So we are here to send a message to the wider population that we do exist, and we want rights like any other Ugandan." Richard Lusimbo, one of the event’s organizers, told AFP, "For us, this is a celebration of who we are."

Earlier in the week, events included a transgender awareness day and a "Mr and Miss Pride" beauty pageant. During his recent visit to Africa, US President Barack Obama voiced support for gay rights, although some African leaders maintain that homosexuality is not part of African cultural traditions.

On Friday night, Mohanna Abdhou, also known as Montana, was shot and killed on Malvern Road in Kilburn. Two males on bicycles approached her group and opened fire. A post-mortem examination on Saturday confirmed that she died from a single gunshot wound.

In a statement, her family expressed they were "heartbroken at the loss" of their "loving daughter," adding, "We are truly saddened, heartbroken and still in complete shock that we have lost a beautiful and caring soul. No words can truly express our feelings towards this situation. She was a loving daughter, sister and friend. She was loved by everyone and her warmth and kindness will be remembered fondly."

Detective Chief Inspector Andy Partridge said police found no evidence indicating Ms. Abdhou was specifically targeted. The suspects are described as medium build, wearing all dark clothing with their faces covered—a detail police noted "would have made them stand out on such a warm evening."

Festival-goers on Anglesey were instructed on Monday to use shuttle buses from the Anglesey Showground at Mona to access the Bodedern Maes. Some attendees reported waiting up to two hours for a bus. Elfed Roberts, chief executive of the Eisteddfod, urged patience, describing the shuttle arrangement as a "temporary measure" to protect the site.

Roberts attributed the delays to the "horrendous" rain the previous day, noting, "There are people complaining that there is some mud on the Maes, I don't think that any field anywhere would have coped with what we got last night." He encouraged visitors to stay calm, adding, "We all need to be patient, we need to calm down and not panic."

The shuttle service will continue on Tuesday. Blue badge holders are advised to park at Ysgol Uwchradd Bodedern, where transport to and from the Maes is provided.

Mansfield 103.2 has experienced eight disruptions in the past month, with outside broadcasts hijacked and replaced by The Winker's Song, performed by comedy band Ivor Biggun. The station reported that attempts to identify the perpetrator have so far been unsuccessful, while some listeners have expressed concern that "their children have started humming the song."

Station manager Tony Delahunty recounted the most recent incident on Sunday during a live interview at the town's Party in the Market event, when a male voice interrupted the broadcast before the song began. Delahunty said, "We have had calls from people who have found it hilarious, while some have raised their concerns, including our competitors, and many in the industry are aghast at how difficult it is to stop these people."

He added, "For listeners under the age of 11 travelling to school, it can be a very offensive thing to hear, so I just want it to stop. But I would also love to see who it is and have them caught." Delahunty explained, "There's absolutely nothing we can do. The first time we reported it to the police, but they said they would have to catch him in the act. Our transmitter team can't intervene because the person is using a mobile transmitter."

Ivor Biggun, led by Robert "Doc" Cox—known for his appearances on BBC TV's That's Life—has released four albums featuring songs filled with double entendres.

Delahunty also noted that communications regulator Ofcom has made three attempts to track the offender but has been unsuccessful. An Ofcom spokesperson said, "Ofcom takes malicious radio interference extremely seriously. Our Spectrum Engineering Officers are working closely with Mansfield 103.2 to trace and identify those responsible for these criminal activities." They added that malicious interference is a criminal offense punishable by up to two years in prison and an unlimited fine.

The 32-year-old former Warwickshire seamer made his final first-team appearance for Sussex in June 2014. Over his tenure with the Hove-based club, the right-arm bowler took 199 wickets in 63 first-class matches, with an average of 32.38.

Anyon joined Sussex ahead of the 2010 season and established himself as a regular in their Championship side. He claimed 55 first-class wickets at an average of 32.45 in 2011, followed by 50 wickets at 28.64 in 2013. In addition, he scored 1,086 first-class runs during his time at the club.

Reflecting on his retirement, Anyon stated, "It's been a frustrating 18 months. On the advice of the club's medical staff, I have decided not to pursue my first-class cricketing career." He added, "I'm very fortunate to have played my best cricket at Sussex. I'd like to make a special thank you to the medical staff and the Professional Cricketers' Association for all their help over the past 12 months. I wish the club success going forward."

Flooding in November and December submerged the main line at Cowley Bridge near Exeter, resulting in an 11-day closure. In response, business leaders and the councils of Devon and Cornwall jointly wrote to the Environment Agency and Network Rail. Their letter acknowledged the "severe impact" the closure had on the regional economies but highlighted the absence of a "firm, positive and long-term solution."

Network Rail confirmed ongoing efforts and said it has submitted a £30 million bid to the government to enhance flood and landslip resilience at 10 sites across the South West. However, the letter noted that while work is scheduled to begin in January, Cowley Bridge is not among the planned locations.

The correspondence ended by requesting confirmation from Network Rail and the Environment Agency that a solution "acceptable to the region as a whole" to prevent flooding at Cowley Bridge will be identified promptly.

Mike Gallop, Network Rail’s route asset management director, told BBC News that a detailed study had been conducted after the flooding. He explained, "We're not proposing to stop the flooding at Cowley Bridge. What we are proposing is to improve the resilience of the railway—to recover the service and recover the track and signalling much more effectively than we did last year."

Gallop also stressed Network Rail’s awareness of the vital role rail services play in the South West economy and said finding a solution remains a priority. "The railway to the South West is a priority—not only Cowley Bridge," he added.

When Vicky Harrison was assigned to develop a community project supporting the restoration of Ashton Gatehouse, she was surprised to discover it was absent from all maps. Collaborating with volunteers aged 15 to 70, she helped create an embroidered map that took 600 hours to complete. This piece will be exhibited at the gatehouse starting Wednesday. Ashton Gatehouse, the original entrance to Ashton Court Estate, is currently undergoing renovation funded by a £550,000 grant from the Heritage Lottery Fund.

Artist Ms. Harrison explained, "After searching for it online, I quickly realised that it was not on Google maps and so the idea to put it back on the map was born." The embroidered map depicts local areas including Long Ashton, Bower Ashton, Ashton Vale, Southville, and Bedminster. It features key roads alongside landmarks such as peregrine falcons in the gorge, deer in the park, and hot air balloons above Ashton Court. The artwork was crafted using hundreds of stitches, including cretan stitch, woven wheel stitch, zigzag chain stitch, and Roumanian couching.

Following a club-record run of 10 consecutive league wins, the team has drawn their last two matches. "We're in a fantastic position – but anything can happen in a week of football, there's nine points to play for," Wilder said. He added, "Other teams have got to go on great runs to catch us and we've got to have a dip, but I don't see it."

In an interview with BBC Radio Northampton, Wilder remarked, "I'm not seeing any nervousness or apprehension in our play – we're going for it and enjoying this situation." When discussing the prospect of winning the next 12 games, he acknowledged the difficulty: "I think it's going to be a real difficult task because to win three games on the bounce is tough. When you're talking about the exposure we get, we should do, because it's a special run, breaking club records."

The Cobblers are set to travel to face play-off hopefuls Carlisle on Saturday, following draws against Hartlepool and AFC Wimbledon. Wilder pointed out that with teams below them facing each other, it will be challenging for any side to sustain a winning streak. "Look at some of the games coming up – Accrington are going to Wimbledon on Saturday, Portsmouth play Accrington next week, Oxford v Plymouth – they're all going to cut their own throats," he explained.

He concluded, "I don't see a team sticking 10 wins on the bounce again between now and the end of the season. We've got Cambridge coming up who fancy getting into the play-offs, Carlisle on Saturday, and even down to the likes of Luton – there are tough games ahead for everyone."

During the 1960s and 70s, Nick Hedges traveled across the UK for the housing charity Shelter, documenting families living in dilapidated homes. He described being "shocked to the core" by the conditions he witnessed. Reflecting on those families, Hedges said, "I often wonder what happened to them, if they went on to lead happy and healthy lives." He added, "It's heart-breaking to know that the conditions some people have to live in today aren't a million miles away from the photos I took all those years ago." He stressed that "a home should be a place of safety and security, but too many families are having to live without."

Shelter’s chief executive, Campbell Robb, acknowledged that while slums have disappeared, the UK is now facing "another housing crisis." He called on the government to boost support for vulnerable families, warning that "the double blow of sky-high house prices along with cuts to welfare support means just one thing like an illness or cut in hours can leave a family hurtling towards homelessness."

The photographs are available online and are currently exhibited for free at the Custard Factory in Digbeth, Birmingham, until Friday. Vicky Hines, manager of Shelter’s Birmingham services, described the images as "an incredibly important part of this city's history." She said they demonstrate "how far we've come in the past 50 years," while also underscoring the ongoing need to help the tens of thousands still desperate for safe and secure homes.

A spokesman for the Department of Communities and Local Government, which oversees housing, said building more homes remains "an absolute priority" and called the current plans "the most ambitious housing programme in a generation."

The exhibition has previously been shown in Sheffield and is scheduled to open in Manchester later this month.

The American began the day tied for the lead with three others and bounced back from a bogey on the first hole by making his fifth birdie on the 10th. Spieth followed that with three consecutive birdies starting at the 14th, finishing at 12 under par, three shots clear of Dustin Johnson.

"I've been striking the ball well this year," said the 24-year-old, a three-time major champion. Although Spieth executed an impressive eight-foot shot, he three-putted the ninth hole. He maintained a four-shot lead until world number one Johnson birdied the 18th, carding a 67 and moving two strokes ahead of Paul Casey, Jon Rahm, Patrick Reed, and Matt Kuchar.

Spieth, who has won every one of the five times he has held a lead of two or more shots after 54 holes on the PGA Tour, attributed his success to a "heated putter." "Today was about the most committed I've been finishing a round—Michael [Greller, his caddie] said ever—and I agreed with him," he added. "[We] committed to targets away from holes, knowing I'm in the lead and the putter was getting hotter with each putt. That last six-hole stretch, I played beautiful golf."

Out of 16 applications, three projects have been chosen, with plans to establish 10 campuses over the next five years. The successful initiatives include Moy Primary School and St John's Catholic Primary in Moy; St Mary's High in Limavady; and Limavady High School, Ballycastle High, and Cross and Passion College.

The Shared Education Campuses Programme, launched by Education Minister John O'Dowd in January 2014, set a 31 March deadline for expressions of interest. Speaking on Tuesday, the minister said, "I believe shared education has the potential to deliver real educational benefits, to ensure best use of resources and to further community cohesion."

This programme enables schools to expand on existing sharing arrangements and access funding to develop or improve shared facilities. Mr. O'Dowd remarked, "We received a significant level of interest in this programme with 16 applications. I am pleased to be in a position to announce the first three projects to be supported."

He added, "The three projects selected will build on well-established sharing arrangements between the schools involved and will help embed and enhance those sharing arrangements." Noting the tight timeframe, the minister acknowledged this was the first call for projects and that some schools were unable to submit proposals by the deadline.

While approving the three projects to advance to the detailed business case stage, Mr. O'Dowd also announced a second call for projects opening in September. Unsuccessful applicants will receive feedback and may resubmit their proposals if appropriate.

The selected projects will now move forward to the planning phase.

Leicester City striker Jamie Vardy, 29, is serving a three-match suspension after being sent off at Stoke on 17 December for a two-footed tackle on Mame Biram Diouf. Following the Football Association’s rejection of his appeal, the club produced 30,000 masks, one of which Vardy wore while watching from the stands.

Vardy will miss league fixtures against West Ham and Middlesbrough but is expected to return for the FA Cup third-round tie against Everton at Goodison Park on 7 January. Leicester manager Claudio Ranieri said he did not see the masks, as he had not yet emerged from the tunnel at the King Power Stadium. “I’m sorry, I didn’t see when I came out. I don’t know, it’s not my matter. I didn’t see. I’m sorry,” he stated. On Vardy’s absence, Ranieri added, “It’s difficult to say how much we missed Vardy. I didn’t see the masks.”

Foxes owner Vichai Srivaddhanaprabha called the suspension “unfair” in an Instagram post. Meanwhile, Ranieri left Riyad Mahrez on the bench against Everton, urging more from the Algerian winger. “He’s not in good form now and I wanted to stimulate him,” Ranieri said. “I didn’t see him do well during the training sessions and he must give more for the team. I want more.”

Leicester, the reigning Premier League champions, have won only four of their first 18 league games this season and sit three points above the relegation zone. Reflecting on the team’s struggles, Ranieri commented, “This season is this way—nothing is right, nothing is easy. We wanted to give a good present on Boxing Day, but it was not possible. Here everything was right in first six months and now everything is wrong.”

Since Jose Mourinho took over as Manchester United manager this summer, 32-year-old midfielder Bastian Schweinsteiger has been training either alone or with the club’s under-23 squad. The former Germany captain last appeared for the Red Devils in March under Louis van Gaal. In August, Schweinsteiger stated he had "no personal problems" with Mourinho and that United would be his final European club.

United left-back Luke Shaw welcomed Schweinsteiger’s return, commenting, "It's great to see him back. We found out the news a couple of days ago." Shaw emphasized Schweinsteiger’s strong influence both in the dressing room and on the pitch, particularly for younger players like himself.

It remains unclear whether Mourinho will now consider Schweinsteiger for first-team duties. Although named in United’s Premier League squad this season, he was omitted from their Europa League roster. Since his £14.4 million transfer from Bayern Munich in July 2015, Schweinsteiger has made 31 appearances for the club.

Simon Stone of BBC Sport notes that before Schweinsteiger can think about a comeback—something he hoped for during his time training alone—he needs clarity on Mourinho’s reasons for reintegrating him. Schweinsteiger is ineligible to play against Fenerbahce on Thursday, as he is not registered in the Europa League squad.

With Ander Herrera suspended, Schweinsteiger could be considered for United’s Premier League trip to Swansea. However, given his lack of recent match fitness, it remains uncertain whether this is a genuine option or simply Mourinho’s way of signaling to potential January suitors that the 32-year-old midfielder is still available.

The 34-year-old defender, born in Brazil but representing Portugal, has been linked with Paris St-Germain and AC Milan, and reportedly received "proposals from England." Over his Real Madrid career, Pepe made 334 appearances and secured three La Liga titles alongside three Champions League trophies. He missed Saturday’s win over Juventus, stating, "I didn't say goodbye because they knew before I did."

In an interview with radio station COPE, Pepe confirmed his departure and disclosed he had not spoken with manager Zinedine Zidane since Real Madrid’s Champions League final victory in Cardiff. "What he has done for Real Madrid is spectacular, but there are things I still do not understand," he remarked.

The centre-back, who endured a hamstring injury during the season and broke two ribs in April, lost his place to Raphael Varane and Nacho in the battle to partner captain Sergio Ramos in defense. Reflecting on his time at the club, Pepe said, "I've had years of great pride in which I have given my body and soul. But I took the decision in January when it was clear which way it was going. I'm happy for the love of the people, and that's worth more than everything."

Biffa has revealed that its crews found 93 people sleeping in rubbish bins over the past year. To tackle this issue, the company has fitted cameras to 140 of its 800 trucks to prompt staff to check bins before emptying them. Tragically, four people sheltering in bins died last year after being tipped into the backs of trucks.

Tim Standring, Biffa’s divisional health, safety, environment, and quality coach, told BBC Radio 4’s You and Yours that the cameras offer drivers additional "peace of mind." He noted that some vehicles also capture footage inside the hoppers. Standring stressed that the company is not monitoring staff but aims to protect workers from the "anguish" of unknowingly compacting a person inside a bin.

He said, "If it's the only place you've got to stay and it's the most secure place, I can kind of see the appeal, but the downside is if we don't find you, you're not going to survive." He added, "Once you're in the hopper, the blade comes down and it crushes and breaks the waste and takes it into the body [of the vehicle] where it's compacted again. These machines won't differentiate between cardboard, wood and unfortunately people as well."

Biffa intends to have all its refuse lorries equipped with this technology by the end of the year. The company has also partnered with the Chartered Institute of Waste Management and homelessness service StreetLink to raise awareness of the problem. Research conducted last year by these organizations found that 28 of 176 waste management companies surveyed had found people sheltering in bins within the previous 12 months.

South Sudan secured an important point through disciplined defensive play in their latest match. After a 2-0 victory over Djibouti in their opening Group C fixture on Monday, South Sudan is well placed to advance to the tournament quarter-finals. "We are happy that we have picked a point against a strong Sudan side," South Sudan goalkeeper Juma Ginaro said after the game. "We now wait to face Malawi in our last group game."

The draw leaves Sudan in third place, behind their neighbors, with only one point following a 2-1 defeat to Malawi in their opening match. Visiting team Malawi tops the group and has already clinched a quarter-final berth after a 3-0 win over Djibouti. In that match, Yaboh Idriss Moussa missed several chances for Djibouti before Gerald Phiri converted a penalty, with John Banda and Chiukepo Msowoya adding goals to secure the victory.

On Wednesday, defending champions Kenya and Burundi played to a 1-1 draw. Meanwhile, hosts Ethiopia recovered from an opening loss to Rwanda by beating Somalia 2-0 in front of a capacity crowd.

The Direct Energie rider took advantage of a brief lapse in concentration by Team Sky’s Nicolas Roche to secure victory in the sprint finish. Roche finished second in the stage and held second overall, six seconds behind Voeckler. Britain’s leading rider, Adam Yates from Bury, claimed third place in the stage and fourth in the general classification. The final stage covered 198 kilometers from Middlesbrough to Scarborough and included six categorized climbs.

In wet and demanding conditions, Team Sky set a relentless pace after launching an attack at the halfway mark, with 44 kilometers remaining. At that point, five of their riders were at the front of the main group. Roche attacked on the Harwood Dale ascent, joined by Voeckler, Yates, Anthony Turgis (Cofidis), and Steven Kruijswijk (LottoNL). Voeckler stayed close as Roche increased the pace on the descent into Scarborough.

Having finished third the previous year after narrowly missing out in a sprint, Voeckler exercised tactical patience, shadowing Roche along the seafront before large crowds gathered on the town’s grass banks. When Roche briefly looked away, Voeckler surged past him near the finish line.

Speaking to ITV4, Voeckler said, “It wasn’t just with the strength in my legs that I used, but also my head. It was difficult to follow Team Sky’s attack on the climbs, so I chose patience. Then I launched the sprint at 300 meters. Although early, with the wind at my back, it was not so bad.”

He also praised the Yorkshire crowd despite the persistent drizzle, adding, “I feel like this is home because the crowd were shouting my name.” The Tour de Yorkshire was established as a legacy of the county’s hosting of the 2014 Tour de France Grand Départ, drawing an estimated two million spectators along the three-day route.

In Nottinghamshire's Championship victory over Warwickshire, 37-year-old Read increased his dismissal tally to 998 by taking five catches. He is on track to become the first player since Jack Russell in 1997 to reach 1,000 dismissals.

Reflecting on the approaching milestone, Read said, "I’m thinking about it more now and willing people to find the edge." Speaking to BBC Radio Nottingham, he added, "I probably won't do a lot. I’ll likely throw the ball up a bit higher than usual. But I’m excited by this group of bowlers. Jake Ball bowled brilliantly against Warwickshire. If he keeps that up, I’m sure more edges will come my way."

The former England wicketkeeper is set to become the 26th player in history to reach 1,000 dismissals when Nottinghamshire face Durham at Trent Bridge on 9 September. Despite missing part of the season with a hamstring injury, Read currently leads Nottinghamshire’s batting averages with 762 runs from 16 innings at 63.50.

This week, he also passed a batting milestone by surpassing 15,000 first-class runs with a score of 69 against Warwickshire. Read, who has three centuries this season, said, "I didn’t feel it was a big thing, but everyone said, ‘yeah, that’s a lot of runs.’ For me, we talk about landmarks, but that wasn’t one I was aiming for."

He added, "I’m in good form right now, and I’ve always said when you’re in form, you need to make it count. There are times in your career when you have lows and don’t know where your next run is coming from, so you really need to make those times pay."

Jeremy Vine, Radio 2 presenter and the first contestant confirmed on Monday, will be joined by Harriott and Bright in the 13th series of BBC One’s Strictly, which begins in September. Harriott, who hosted BBC One’s Ready Steady Cook for 16 years, and Bright, best known for her role as Linda Carter on the BBC One soap, complete the initial lineup.

At 58, Harriott said, “I do love to dance, but doing it in front of the nation is a whole different matter. In my day job, the only salsa I know is the one in my recipes, so I’m looking forward to the challenge. Bring it on!” He also commended Vine’s “wonderful discipline,” adding, “Dancing is about discipline and effort. If you put the time in, you can be more expressive.”

Bright shared her reasons for joining the show: “I’m turning 40 next year and wanted to be the fittest I’ve ever been or at least give it a good try. It will be challenging, and I want to see what my body can still do before it all goes kaput.”

Further contestants will be revealed in the coming weeks. Last year’s series was won by X Factor presenter Caroline Flack.

France will fully reimburse Russia for two helicopter carriers in a €1.2 billion (£838 million; $1.3 billion) deal, with Russia having already paid around €840 million upfront. The Kremlin has announced that the dispute is resolved. French President François Hollande’s office confirmed Russia will be "fully reimbursed," while France will retain ownership of the vessels.

The sale was suspended by France following the outbreak of conflict in eastern Ukraine. The Kremlin stated that France agreed to refund the payments made under the contract, adding, "France has already transferred these funds and, after the return of equipment, will acquire ownership and be able to take charge of both ships." The Élysée Palace said all Russian equipment installed on the ships will be removed and returned to Russia.

Last year, the deal was described as the largest arms sale by a NATO country to Russia. The Mistral-class vessels can carry about 700 troops, 16 helicopter gunships, and up to 50 armored vehicles. President Hollande denied reports of a finalized agreement last month. At that time, compensation was reported at €1.16 billion, covering Russia’s expenses for training 400 sailors, port infrastructure in Vladivostok, and the development of four prototype Ka-52K helicopters.

Since March 2014, following Russia’s annexation of Crimea, Western sanctions against Russia have intensified. Russia denies supporting pro-Russian separatist rebels fighting in eastern Ukraine.

Eubank, 27, is set to defend his IBO world title against a 37-year-old German challenger at Wembley Arena on 15 July. The Super Series tournament features eight super-middleweights, including WBA champion George Groves and fellow Britons Callum Smith and Jamie Cox. Smith notably relinquished a WBC world title shot against Anthony Dirrell to take part in the event.

The knockout competition awards the winner a share of $50 million (£38 million) and the Muhammad Ali trophy. Fighters must advance through quarter-finals in September, semi-finals in January, and the final in May. Organizers say the tournament will "change the world of boxing." Additionally, if a competitor faces a current world title holder during the event, those belts will also be on the line.

Eubank stated, "It would be great to fight George Groves and to take his title away from him but let’s see what the draw in Monaco brings." Concurrently, a cruiserweight tournament will run alongside the super-middleweight bracket. With all four cruiserweight world champions competing, that division is expected to crown an undisputed champion by May.

Abraham, a former two-weight world champion with 46 wins from 51 fights, described the Super Series as "the Champions League of boxing." Eubank has lost only once in 24 bouts. Both fighters will learn their potential Super Series quarter-final opponents on Saturday, when the draw takes place in Monte Carlo.

Chipolopolo caused a significant upset by beating Ivory Coast on penalties in Gabon but failed to advance past the group stage in the following two tournaments. The team’s 47-year-old coach told BBC Sport that "some of the players thought they were untouchable," adding, "Our players were big-headed, that's no secret. Club coaches meant little to most of the players who won that cup."

He clarified that these comments would not damage his relationship with the current squad, which still includes some players from the 2012 team. "Not all of them were so big-headed, and it is all about recent performance and discipline. The process is still ongoing, and we are moving in the right direction," he said.

Niyrenda stressed that attitude is now central to the team’s success. "It all comes down to attitude—the hard work was no longer there," he remarked. Citing Egypt’s back-to-back title wins, he attributed their success to discipline. "Our biggest issue is satisfaction—most of our players win four games in a row and become content; they are too easily satisfied with very little. This is where we need to start managing our players."

After missing out on qualification for the 2017 Nations Cup finals in Gabon, Zambia currently competes in a group with Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, and Namibia for a place in the 2019 tournament in Cameroon. In 2018 World Cup qualifying, Zambia sits third in their group with one point from two matches. Nigeria tops Group B with six points, Cameroon follows with two, and Algeria is level with Zambia. Only the group winner will qualify for the World Cup in Russia.

Malcolm Beer, speaking in advance of a Windsor council aviation forum, warned that constructing a third runway northwest of Heathrow Airport could mean greenbelt land would be needed for housing. A Heathrow spokesperson responded, saying, "There will be little or no need for additional house-building over and above current local authority plans."

This issue was raised following a recent Airport Commission report, which forecast that Heathrow’s expansion would generate between 47,400 and 112,400 jobs by 2030. Such job growth is expected to require 29,800 to 70,800 new homes in local areas including Windsor, Slough, and several London boroughs.

Mr. Beer, who is on the Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead Borough aviation forum committee, said "anxious" Windsor residents’ associations are planning a public meeting within the next 10 days, ahead of the commission’s public consultation deadline on 3 February. He commented, "We have an enormous housing problem in the area. We are having a real problem considering if we have to release greenbelt land for housing, which is an unpopular suggestion."

He also pointed out that, besides concerns about noise, urbanisation would become a significant issue, which many people may not fully recognise. "The impact will be felt across the Thames Valley—it’s commercial greed gone mad." After a Heathrow report indicated most residents are in favour of expansion, the borough council forum is planning its own residents’ poll.

The Heathrow spokesperson further stated that the expansion would benefit 700,000 local residents "who are unemployed, under-employed or are commuting out of the area at present." The aviation forum is scheduled for 19:00 GMT at The Guildhall Chamber in Windsor.
