NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde, NHS Lanarkshire, and Health Protection Scotland are investigating two suspected cases of wound botulism—one in Greater Glasgow and Clyde and the other in Lanarkshire. The investigation is focused on individuals who inject heroin.

Dr. Gillian Penrice, a public health medicine consultant with NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde, urged heroin injectors to remain vigilant. She advised anyone experiencing early symptoms such as blurred or double vision, difficulty swallowing or speaking, or inflammation at the injection site to seek immediate treatment at accident and emergency departments.

While underscoring the importance of addiction support services, Dr. Penrice stressed that those who continue injecting heroin must seek urgent medical care if symptoms arise. She also recommended avoiding intramuscular injections, noting that injecting into a vein or smoking heroin can lower the risk of botulism. Nonetheless, she emphasized that complete abstinence from heroin remains the safest option.

At 28, Carroll last featured for England in October 2012 but has found the net in each of his last four appearances for West Ham. Manager Bilic praised the striker, stating, "Every manager would like to have him in his team or squad. Andy would help any team. Andy would help the German team, the Croatian team, the Spanish team, because he is a top player."

Carroll has scored twice for England, including a memorable header in Euro 2012 against Sweden. Since initially joining West Ham on loan in 2012, he has encountered multiple injury problems. He has started 68 of a possible 176 Premier League matches for the club and is currently doubtful for this weekend’s clash with West Brom due to a groin injury.

Bilic added, "He is a top player. He brings you everything, everything that you could ask from a centre-forward. We didn't want to take any risk with him; we will see on Friday if he will be available for Saturday. It is not something major. If it was bigger, we would rule him out."

England is set to face Germany in a friendly on 22 March, followed by a home game against Lithuania four days later.

Shortly after 19:00 local time, emergency services arrived at Poddle Park in Kimmage following a stabbing. A boy was discovered with a knife wound to his upper chest and was pronounced dead at the scene. His mother, a woman in her 40s originally from the Middle East, also sustained knife injuries and remains hospitalized with non-life-threatening wounds.

Irish national broadcaster RTE reported that the Garda (Irish police) are treating the incident as a personal tragedy and have appealed for witnesses to come forward. BBC News NI Ireland correspondent Shane Harrison told Good Morning Ulster that local residents raised the alarm after hearing a distressed woman. Authorities found no visible signs of a break-in at the apartment.

The mother, described as a medic of Iranian descent and believed to be in her 40s, is separated from her husband, who is also thought to be Iranian. Police are currently interviewing family members, neighbours, and friends as part of their ongoing investigation.

The Ospreys recorded a 39-22 win, marking their third consecutive Pro12 victory, with Wales and British and Irish Lions flanker Justin Tipuric scoring a try in each half. As captain, Tipuric also played a significant role in two other tries, delivering a commanding performance.

"Justin is a class act. When he plays like that, he can be nearly unplayable," Tandy remarked. "He leads from the front, and although he rarely speaks, when he does, everyone listens."

Just two minutes after setting up Eli Walker’s try with a precise pass, Tipuric took advantage of a defensive error by Zebre wing Kayle van Zyl to score his first try. In the second half, he covered 40 metres with a dummy and side-step to score, then broke through once more to assist Jonathan Spratt’s try.

Following a slow start with only one win in their first six Pro12 matches this season, the Swansea-based side has now secured three consecutive league victories. The Ospreys also top their European Champions Cup qualifying pool after a win over Exeter and earning two bonus points in a defeat to Clermont Auvergne.

Looking ahead to their fixture against Bordeaux-Begles in Swansea on 12 December, Tandy expressed confidence in the team’s condition. "It’s a six-day turnaround, but we rested some players who featured in the World Cup, so we should be in good shape for that," he added.

Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn is speaking at the Scottish Trades Union Congress in Aviemore. Currently, Labour holds only one parliamentary seat in Scotland after losing 40 seats to the SNP in the last general election. A recent poll indicates Labour trails the Conservatives by 20 percentage points and is further behind the SNP in Scotland.

Corbyn affirmed, "Labour will never, ever apologise for the closeness of our relationship with the trade union movement, you are our family." He committed to making the repeal of the Tory Trade Union Act an immediate priority for a Labour government, aiming to restore workers' rights to organise collectively and improve conditions.

The Trade Union Act, introduced by former Prime Minister David Cameron, requires a voting threshold for strike ballots to be legally valid. The government defends the law, saying it "protects millions of people from the effects of undemocratic strike action."

SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon is also set to address the congress, where she is expected to describe the general election as "a two-horse race between the SNP and hard-line Tories." A Panelbase poll for the Sunday Times in Scotland shows Labour at 13%, the Conservatives at 33%, and the SNP at 44%.

Scottish Conservative deputy leader Jackson Carlaw described Corbyn as a "clear and present danger to the Union." He accused Sturgeon of using the election to push for a second independence referendum and claimed that under Corbyn’s leadership, Labour would "simply roll over and let her do so."

Steve Stannard, 37, died from stab wounds at his flat on Bowers Avenue in Norwich on 5 November 2016. At Norwich Crown Court, it was revealed that a knife found nearby bore Stannard’s blood. Hassiem Baqir, 19, of Howberry Road, Thornton Heath, south London, denies murder.

Prosecutor Andrew Shaw told the court that DNA from the knife’s handle matched Baqir. He said Stannard, a drug user and low-level dealer, had permitted Baqir to use his home as a base for selling drugs in Norwich. Another drug user who visited the property saw Baqir carrying the knife and asked why; Baqir responded, "It's not a game, it's just in case."

The court heard that Stannard suffered five stab wounds—two to the back and three to the front—that pierced his lung and heart. Stannard’s border collie, Trixy, was also stabbed, likely while defending her owner, Shaw said.

Baqir has admitted supplying heroin and cocaine. He is on trial with two others: Veron Antonio, 24, of Green Lane, Morden, south London, who denies supplying heroin and cocaine and denies assisting an offender by refusing to provide his phone PIN to police; and Jamil Theo Carrol, 28, of no fixed address, who denies assisting an offender. The trial is ongoing.

York City maintained control throughout the match at Bootham Crescent, with Jon Parkin and Rhys Murphy frequently testing visiting goalkeeper Brendan Moore. In the first half, Parkin lobbed the ball over Moore and the crossbar before missing a close-range shot, while Murphy’s best opportunity came in the 78th minute with a near-post effort. Torquay United’s primary chance occurred early in the third minute when goalkeeper Kyle Letheren made a sharp one-handed save to deny Ben Gerring at close range.

The game finished in a 0-0 draw between York City and Torquay United.

Yellow cards were issued to Sean Newton, Rhys Murphy, and Jon Parkin of York City, as well as Courtney Richards and Ben Gerring of Torquay United, all for fouls. Substitutions included Paul Rooney replacing David Fitzpatrick and Brett Williams coming on for Jamie Reid for Torquay, while Callum Rzonca replaced Daniel Nti for York City.

The first half ended goalless, with the second half starting with the score still level. Prior to kickoff, team lineups were announced and players completed their warm-ups.

The company reported that its retail division generated an operating profit of £456.8 million for the 12 months ending in March, driven by a 50% increase in retail energy supply profits. Average profit per dual fuel customer reached £69, restoring profit levels to those last seen in 2012-13.

Energy supply profit margins rose to 4.6% in 2014-15, up from 2.9% in 2013-14 and 4.2% in 2012-13. The average margin over the past three and five years stood at 3.9%. SSE has kept gas and electricity prices frozen for customers through 2016 and has reduced prices twice recently.

Despite this price freeze, customer numbers declined to 8.5 million accounts, a drop the company attributed to "increasingly challenging and highly competitive market conditions" and growing competition from smaller providers taking on the UK's big six energy firms.

At the group level, SSE posted an adjusted pre-tax profit of £1.56 billion for the year to March, slightly up from £1.55 billion the previous year. The company also announced plans to close the Ferrybridge power station on the West and North Yorkshire border by March 2016, with intentions to redeploy the plant’s 172 employees "where possible." SSE added it would consider extending the price freeze or further reducing prices if additional cost savings can be found in energy supply and pledged to work with the new UK government or other stakeholders to explore such options.

Timothy Storey, 35, formerly of Peckham, south London, was convicted at Woolwich Crown Court of grooming girls while employed at a religious summer camp. He was found guilty on three counts of rape and one count of assault by penetration. The former trainee vicar remains in custody and is scheduled to be sentenced on 15 April.

Storey had a previous conviction in 2014 for grooming girls aged 10 to 16. The offences for which he was recently convicted occurred in 2008 and 2009 and involved two women who are now in their twenties. The court heard that Storey befriended the victims "from an early age" and sent them sexual texts and messages via social media. He sexually assaulted one girl twice during 2008 and 2009 and assaulted the other at his home after taking her to a concert.

Following Storey’s 2014 conviction, which led to a three-year prison sentence, the victims came forward to police. A spokeswoman for the Diocese of London said: "Timothy Storey has today been convicted of a series of appalling crimes and we are profoundly sorry for what his victims endured." She added that the diocese first received complaints in early 2009, cooperated with police, and removed Storey from ordination training.

Detective Constable Paul Hill, speaking after the trial, said: "In his role as a youth leader, he manipulated the victims and forced them to engage in sexual acts against their will. Storey believed he had escaped justice, but the victims were determined to see him held accountable." Police have encouraged any other victims to come forward.

In the 2015 election, the party came third in nine out of 11 constituencies across Bristol and South Gloucestershire. A recent development could boost the Conservative vote in key marginal seats such as Thornbury and Yate, where Conservative Luke Hall is defending a 1,500-vote majority. In that constituency, UKIP previously secured over 5,000 votes.

Russ Martin, UKIP’s candidate for Thornbury and Yate in 2015, has been re-elected as the prospective parliamentary candidate. He described the decision as a "tactical strategic decision" aimed at protecting the broader Brexit goal.

Before the Conservatives captured the seat in 2015, Thornbury and Yate was held by Liberal Democrat pensions minister Steve Webb. Liberal Democrat candidate Claire Young said, "Two years of Conservative government has shown people what we actually did in coalition because they've seen, without us as a restraining influence, what they are doing."

Conservative Luke Hall stressed the seat’s national significance, stating, "This is a vital seat for the Conservatives nationally. There has never been a Conservative majority government without this seat." Other candidates standing in Thornbury and Yate include Green Party’s Iain Hamilton and Labour’s Brian Peter Mead.

Hamilton described UKIP’s move as "not surprising," noting the party has "completely collapsed." He added, "I know a lot of people say where will UKIP's votes go, but there are a lot of people who don't like either of the main parties, and they're happy I'm standing, as it gives them other options."

Labour’s Mead said, "I'm standing to give people the opportunity to vote in favour of Labour policies of investment in public services run for the many and not the few and against the austerity agenda."

At approximately 21:15 BST on Thursday, police responded to an incident at Glanmor Crescent in Barry, where they discovered a 54-year-old woman with burns. She was transported to hospital and remains in serious condition. South Wales Police confirmed the arrest of a man from Penarth, who is believed to be known to the victim. "A crime scene is being preserved at the address and a police cordon has been established," a spokesperson said. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities have called for witnesses to come forward. Fire crews from Barry and ambulance teams also attended the scene. According to a Welsh Ambulance Service spokesperson, emergency services were dispatched around 21:35 BST on Thursday, 4 August, after reports of a fire. The woman was initially taken to the University Hospital of Wales before being transferred to Morrison Hospital.

On Monday, Trina Hibberd of Mission Beach, Queensland, woke to find a 5.2-meter scrub python named Monty stretched from her lounge room to her bedroom. Before snake-catcher Dave Goodwin arrived, Monty had turned on a light and knocked over a lamp.

Mr. Goodwin coaxed the 40kg snake to coil around his forearm before capturing it inside a plastic home-brewing jug. He told the BBC the snake was "choking [his] arm to death" prior to being placed in the container.

Explaining the snake’s behavior, he said, "When you go near them, they have this deep gurgle in their throat, which basically means don't come near me." To encourage Monty to grip his arm, Mr. Goodwin first used tongs to grab near the snake’s head. "The tongs won’t hold it—it’s too big—so I use them to divert its attention and then grab it by the scruff of the neck," he said. "That makes the snake let go of everything else and wrap around my arm."

Ms. Hibberd told the BBC that a friend staying at her home was the first to spot the large reptile. "I guess he came in to have a bit of a feed or say hello, or he's gone a bit senile. I've no idea," she said. She also believes Monty has lived in her roof for many years.

Monty has since been relocated to a sewage pond within the Cassowary Coast Regional Council area, where he is expected to help control a rat infestation. "I guess Monty has gone to snake heaven and he's going to be this big fatso," Ms. Hibberd remarked.

Stephen Archer, 50, of Openshaw, Manchester, is wanted as a suspect in an attack at his 49-year-old sister’s home, where she sustained burns over 70% of her body. Detectives report that petrol was poured on the victim before she was set on fire.

Greater Manchester Police have called on petrol station workers to stay alert and report any sightings of Archer. Superintendent Arif Nawaz described him as typically wearing a baseball cap, carrying a large rucksack, and traveling by bicycle. Nawaz added that Archer may be carrying multiple bottles of petrol in his backpack, and a man fitting his description was seen cycling away from the scene. Despite following several leads and receiving valuable information, police have yet to locate him.

The victim remains critically ill in hospital and is fighting for her life. A police spokesperson said specialist officers are supporting the family during this difficult time and reassured the public that efforts to find the suspect and bring him to justice are ongoing.

In addition, a 19-year-old woman escaped unharmed by climbing out of an upstairs window with assistance from neighbours.

Paul Drinkwater, 52, from Maidenhead, Berkshire, conducted a three-week crime spree in Berkhamsted during November and December 1984. At St Albans Crown Court, he was convicted on seven charges he had denied, including rape and possession of a knife. The conviction was obtained through new DNA evidence. Judge Marie Catterson ordered that Drinkwater remain in custody, with sentencing scheduled for 30 January.

He was found guilty of raping and robbing a 15-year-old girl on 25 November in Durrants Lane, as well as possessing a knife. Additionally, Drinkwater was convicted of raping an 18-year-old woman and indecently assaulting another 18-year-old woman on 16 December in Bullbeggers Lane. During the attacks, he wore a woollen mask and repeatedly stated, "I hate slags, tarts and lesbians," the court was told.

Prosecutor Ann Evans described the case as "every woman’s worst nightmare," emphasizing that the assaults involved knife-point rapes by a masked assailant targeting young girls late at night. On 14 January, Drinkwater’s DNA profile was submitted to a forensic scientist. A swab from the 15-year-old victim was found to be "seven million times more likely to come from Paul Drinkwater than from an unrelated person," Evans said. DNA recovered from the trousers of the 18-year-old victim also matched Drinkwater, with the odds of it belonging to someone else estimated at 1 in 43 million.

At the time of the offenses, Drinkwater lived with his girlfriend in Berkhamsted and had been linked to the crimes since 1984. Evans noted that advances in DNA technology allowed forensic experts to definitively connect the DNA from these attacks to Drinkwater.

Brian Matthew had been the presenter of Sounds of the 60s since April 1990. Although his last full episode was broadcast in November 2016, he returned in February to present a final compilation programme. He also hosted the ITV show Thank Your Lucky Stars, which featured bands such as The Beatles and the Rolling Stones.

Matthew passed away on Saturday at the age of 88. BBC Director General Tony Hall described him as "an outstanding broadcaster who entertained and engaged millions over generations," adding, "He had a wonderful style of delivery and a real connection with his listeners. Brian was a true broadcasting great. We will all miss him and, of course, that voice."

Lewis Carnie, Head of Radio 2, said Matthew would be "sadly missed by us all" and called him "a much loved and valued presenter on Radio 2—by both the audience and his colleagues." Carnie noted Matthew hosted Sounds of the Sixties for 27 years and expressed regret that plans for a new series for him to share his career memories did not materialize.

Former Radio 2 Controller Bob Shennan paid tribute to Matthew’s "wit and warmth," calling him "a radio legend" whose voice defined Saturday mornings for decades. Referencing his on-air sign-off, the station tweeted, "Farewell to your old mate and ours, Brian Matthew."

Born in Coventry to a singer mother and conductor father, Matthew began his broadcasting career at the British Forces Network before moving to Radio Netherlands Worldwide. He joined the BBC in 1954 and became known as the voice of the pop music explosion.

Earlier this week, it was revealed Matthew was critically ill, following an initial mistaken announcement of his death by Radio 2. His passing on Saturday morning was later confirmed by both Radio 2 and his god-daughter.

B2Space and Snowdonia Aerospace Centre intend to create 93 specialist jobs at Llanbedr airfield in Gwynedd, driven by plans to launch 30 satellites annually by 2020 to monitor environmental and coastline changes. The former military airfield is among eight sites shortlisted by the UK government for commercial space flight launches.

Valentin Canales of B2Space noted that approximately 3,000 microsatellites will need to be launched over the next five years as space usage evolves. His company, together with the aerospace centre, has applied for £10 million in grants to develop the airfield near Harlech into a major UK satellite launch site. These satellites could also support communications in remote areas and assist natural disaster response efforts.

Mr. Canales highlighted Wales’ strong aerospace manufacturing reputation and its infrastructure to support the growing space sector. If the project succeeds, B2Space plans to relocate from Bristol to Llanbedr to facilitate access to small satellites for individuals, businesses, and organisations.

A spokesperson for Snowdonia Aerospace Centre said establishing a low-cost satellite launch operation will encourage innovation and job growth. John Idris Jones, chairman of Snowdonia Enterprise Zone, added that the project could attract global technology, research, and investment, offering significant opportunities for the North Wales supply chain and the wider Welsh space industry.

Additionally, Llanbedr submitted £10 million funding bids to the UK Space Agency in April to become the UK’s first commercial passenger spaceport.

Commemorating the first International Dylan Thomas Day in Swansea, an exhibition will feature a long-forgotten exercise book that Swansea University purchased last December for £104,500. The notebook will be available for viewing by up to 200 visitors on Thursday.

Prof John Goodby of Swansea University described the notebook as the "holy grail" for Dylan Thomas scholars and the most significant discovery related to the poet since his death in 1953. Thought to have been left at Thomas’s mother-in-law’s home in the 1930s, the notebook was later forgotten. It is one of five notebooks used by Thomas, with the remaining four held by the State University of New York at Buffalo.

Displayed under protective glass, the notebook’s full contents will be shown on plasma screens. Hannah Ellis, Thomas’s granddaughter, noted that the crossings-out and rewritings reveal the teenage poet’s meticulous work and experimentation with language. Speaking to BBC Wales, she said, "It was so important this notebook would be seen by scholars, fans and the general public." Ellis also mentioned that the other notebooks remained boxed away until they were brought to Wales and made accessible during the centenary year.

The exhibition will be held in the university’s council chamber, coinciding with the anniversary of Under Milk Wood’s first New York performance in 1953.

Following Derry City’s 2-1 loss to Dundalk in the FAI Cup semi-final replay at Brandywell Stadium, reports surfaced that a Dundalk supporters’ bus was vandalised outside the venue. Neither police nor Derry City have confirmed or commented on the incident.

Derry councillors have condemned the attack. Councillor Gary Donnelly said a gang of youths cornered Dundalk fans outside a pub on Lecky Road. “When I arrived, the crowd had dispersed, and the Dundalk fans’ mini-bus, which had been attacked, had been repaired and they were about to leave but were visibly shaken,” he told BBC Radio Foyle.

Donnelly added that the bus had slashed tyres and graffiti on its windows. Residents informed him that after the match, several supporters were returning to the bus when one young fan was assaulted. “A young boy of about 14 years old was hit on the back of the head with a bottle before locals intervened and the four attackers ran off,” he said.

Local Sinn Féin councillor Patricia Logue warned that additional security may now be necessary on match nights. “This is criminal behaviour by youths who are causing mayhem in our community,” she said. “The people of the Brandywell, the visiting fans, and Derry City Football Club do not want this happening in the area.” Logue noted that residents are distressed and said she will raise the issue of enhanced security with relevant agencies today.

Jessica Wren, 46, of Camden, London, discovered a handwritten letter on her doorstep earlier this week. The letter, adorned with dolphin stickers and a cut-out image of kittens, was addressed to Alex, Irene, and Anya, and signed by a child named Tabby. As a psychologist, Mrs. Wren is determined to get the letter to its intended recipients. She said, "There's no surname for these people or for the girl writing the letters, but this time she even decorated the paper with finger painting, so I really want it to reach the people it's meant for." The letter reads: "To Alex, Irene and Anya, Happy New Year! Thank you very much for the lovely Frozen nightdress you gave me for Christmas - it's my first ever nightdress as I usually wear pyjamas and I love it! Lots of love from Tabby xxx."

Having lived on Mansfield Road for ten years, Mrs. Wren does not know who Alex, Irene, or Anya are. Without surnames, her Google searches have come up empty. With assistance from her children, Eliza, 17, and Tash, 15, she has posted a message on Facebook in an effort to find the recipients. She added, "It could be a godparent or maybe a relation, and the sad thing is the receiver has no idea the child is writing to them because they have the wrong address."

Following US President Donald Trump's address to Congress last night, the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 303.31 points to close at 21,115.55. The S&P 500 gained 32.32 points, reaching 2,395.96, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 78.59 points to finish at 5,904.03.

Since Trump's election victory, investor optimism about deregulation has pushed share prices higher. He has also committed to cutting taxes and boosting infrastructure spending. Financial firms led the Dow’s advances, with JP Morgan Chase and American Express each climbing more than 2.3%.

Tom Stevenson from Fidelity International observed that the Dow only surpassed 20,000 points three weeks ago, marking the fastest rise between 1,000-point milestones since 1999. Sentiment received an additional lift from comments hinting that the US central bank may raise interest rates sooner rather than later.

Although a rate hike in March would increase borrowing costs for stock purchases, it would also reflect the Federal Reserve’s confidence in economic growth following a period of stagnation. Warren West, principal at Greentree Brokerage Services in Philadelphia, said, "It's not necessarily the rate increase that matters. It's that they're seeing things improving. If the Fed feels more confident, maybe we should too."

Jack Hobbs, the 10-11 favorite and runner-up to stablemate Golden Horn in the Derby at Epsom, secured a five-length victory over Storm The Stars, with Giovanni Canaletto taking third. This win marks the first British-trained success in the race since Commander In Chief, trained by Henry Cecil, in 1993.

Storm The Stars, who started at 10-1 and led early, was overtaken by Jack Hobbs, who then pulled away to claim the win. Newmarket trainer John Gosden commented, "It was genuine good to firm ground and it's nice to see the form from Epsom working out so solidly. He travelled really well and William just waited after he came at the head of the straight and I loved the way he finished off his race."

Gosden added, "The second horse has run a blinder and he was third at Epsom." He also confirmed that Jack Hobbs will be rested before running in the Prix Niel in September and the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe the following month.

Following the race, bookmakers cut Jack Hobbs’s odds for the Arc to around 7-1 from 14-1, placing him behind 3-1 favorite Treve and 4-1 contender Golden Horn.

After finishing second to Golden Horn in the Dante Stakes at York in May, Sheikh Mohammed’s Godolphin racing team bought a majority stake in Jack Hobbs. Jockey William Buick said, "I had a lot of belief in him before Epsom and he was even better today. He's a horse that's improving all the time."

Daniel Pelka, a Coventry resident, died in March 2012 after suffering starvation and abuse at the hands of his mother and her boyfriend. Following a four-week Ofsted inspection, Brian Walsh of the city council voiced concerns about the forthcoming report, which is due to be published later this month.

A serious case review in September revealed that Daniel was at times "invisible" to police, NHS, and social care agencies. Since his death, referrals to child protection services have risen from 3,085 in March 2013 to 4,529 in March 2014.

Mr. Walsh, who took over the department in September, said, "I am very concerned about what Ofsted are going to say. The rise in referrals has overwhelmed our social care services." He highlighted that Coventry’s child protection services differ markedly from those in Birmingham, which Ofsted’s chief inspector, Sir Michael Wilshaw, labeled a "national disgrace" in October.

Birmingham’s children’s services have been rated inadequate by Ofsted since 2009, with the latest inspection canceled to allow a government review of the authority’s improvement plans. Mr. Walsh added, "We are in a very different position from Birmingham. We are a much smaller authority and aware of the challenges. We will seek external support if necessary."

Roberto Pannunzi, 65, was apprehended on Friday at a shopping centre in Bogota during a coordinated operation involving Colombian authorities and US anti-drug agents. The Colombian defence ministry named him as an alleged leader of the 'Ndrangheta crime syndicate, based in Calabria, southern Italy, and accused him of importing up to two tonnes of cocaine into Europe every month.

The ministry confirmed that the US Drug Enforcement Administration played a role in the arrest. At the time of his capture, Pannunzi presented a counterfeit Venezuelan ID card with the name Silvano Martino, according to a post on Colombia’s defence ministry Twitter account. Within 24 hours, he was flown out of Bogota.

Italian police detained Pannunzi upon his arrival at Rome’s Fiumicino airport on Saturday evening. Authorities believe he coordinated large shipments of cocaine from South America to Europe, handled payments from multiple criminal groups, and managed lucrative drug trafficking operations.

Italian investigative journalist Roberto Saviano told AFP that Pannunzi is “not a mafioso, not a killer, he is a broker.” Pannunzi was initially detained in Colombia in 1994 and extradited to Italy but released after his detention order expired. He was re-arrested in 2004 and convicted, but in 2010 escaped dramatically from a private hospital in Rome while undergoing treatment for heart disease.

Italian officials regard the 'Ndrangheta as the country’s most dangerous and wealthiest criminal organisation, surpassing even the Sicilian Mafia. Nicola Gratteri, deputy chief prosecutor in Reggio Calabria province, described Pannunzi as “the biggest cocaine importer in the world.”

BBC Sport reports that the Rio 2016 organising committee is two weeks overdue in paying $3.7 million (£2.9 million) in travel grants owed to national Paralympic committees. Several smaller nations financed their teams’ trips to Brazil through loans, with the International Paralympic Committee (IPC) providing emergency funding to cover these costs. The IPC is reportedly considering legal action against the Rio organisers.

Despite budget cuts to venues, staff, and transport linked to the recession and additional Olympic expenses, the Rio Paralympics proceeded in September. Although an initial instalment of the delayed grants for athletes and officials was paid, the second payment remains outstanding, threatening the legacy of South America’s first Games.

IPC spokesman Craig Spence expressed disappointment over the delay, stating, “We’re hugely disappointed that the second instalment of the travel grants, just like the first set, have not been paid on time by Rio 2016 and are urgently seeking a resolution from all parties concerned.” He added that the IPC has intervened to support smaller national Paralympic committees (NPCs) and warned that continued delays could prompt more financial aid requests.

Rio 2016 officials have told the IPC they cannot make payments as they await funds from city authorities. Their accounts have also been frozen by a court following lawsuits from two suppliers over unpaid invoices. In response, the IPC has sent a letter to Rio mayor Eduardo Paes requesting his intervention.

In August, Paes secured an additional £36 million in funding and £24 million in sponsorship from state-run companies after an injunction blocking further state aid for the Paralympics was lifted. Spence said, “Overnight we have sent a letter to Rio mayor Paes, who was hugely supportive of the Paralympic Games, asking him to step in and intervene.”

The East of England Agricultural Society has confirmed that this year’s East of England Show, planned for July in Peterborough, has been cancelled. Last year’s event attracted just 10,000 visitors—half of the expected turnout. The society acknowledged that the show "became disconnected from its agricultural roots," with a spokesman noting that local people had "voted with their feet." Jeremy Staples, the society’s chief executive, described the decision to cancel as "very difficult."

Staples explained that while the show had been operating at a loss for several years, the more significant concern was a steep decline in attendance over the past 20 years. At its peak, the event drew around 100,000 visitors. He added that last year’s show required four months of preparation but, with fewer than 10,000 attendees, it no longer appealed to the local community. Staples also conceded that wet weather during the 2012 show may have contributed to the drop in numbers.

He pointed to a wider trend away from traditional agricultural shows that showcase new materials and techniques, leading to diminished interest among farming audiences and a loss of focus for events like the East of England Show. Participants were notified of the cancellation before Christmas, and Staples confirmed that no jobs would be affected.

The society plans to return to its core mission of educating the public about farming and rural life. As part of this renewed focus, 4,000 children are expected to attend on 5 July, supported by a comprehensive children’s programme being developed throughout the year. Staples called this strategic shift "a very positive step."

At a rally on Tuesday that concluded the second day of his campaign tour in Wales, the left-wing MP received strong applause for his calls to protect benefits, end austerity, raise taxes on the wealthiest, and abolish university tuition fees.

Competing for the Labour leadership against Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall, Mr. Corbyn earlier addressed supporters near the memorial stones in Tredegar honoring Welsh Labour hero and NHS founder Aneurin Bevan. There, he commended the Welsh Labour government in Cardiff Bay for its initiatives.

“I’ve been reviewing their economic plans and efforts to promote industrial development in Wales,” he said. “They need greater powers and more resources, particularly for infrastructure improvements. Building a stronger industrial economy requires upgrading basic infrastructure—mainly rail and some roads.”

Mr. Corbyn also expressed a desire to strengthen ties between the Labour parties in Wales and Westminster, noting his familiarity with former First Minister Rhodri Morgan. He praised Morgan’s efforts to create “clear red water” between the former UK Labour government’s policies and a more traditionally socialist approach in Wales, adding, “Perhaps we can narrow that red water and cross it.”

Confirming he was “absolutely” willing to meet First Minister Carwyn Jones, as the other leadership contenders have done, Mr. Corbyn said he would do so when their schedules permit.

Ballot papers will be sent to Labour members and registered supporters on Friday, with the result announced on 12 September.

Just before midnight on Tuesday, a collision took place on the A90 Aberdeen to Peterhead road at Auchiries, Longhaven, near Peterhead. Emergency services freed both drivers from their vehicles and transported them to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary. The 46-year-old police officer remains in critical condition, while the 58-year-old male driver is stable. Police Scotland confirmed that two police dogs inside the van survived; one was uninjured, and the other is being assessed. The officer’s family has been notified. Inspector Jon Barron said, "Our inquiries into the circumstances of this crash are obviously still at an early stage. I would be very keen to speak with anyone who may have seen either vehicle shortly beforehand, or anyone who witnessed the collision and who hasn't yet been spoken to by police. Please contact us on 101." The A90 was closed for several hours while investigators examined the scene and vehicles but has since reopened.

England is scheduled to face Lithuania in a European Championship qualifier at Wembley on 27 March. Ahead of the match, manager Roy Hodgson and the squad will convene at the national football centre at St George's Park. Speaking to the FA website, Hodgson said, "We've all agreed we're going to get together. Unfortunately, my time with them won't really begin again until March."

Since the World Cup, England has maintained a perfect record, winning all six matches. This includes friendly victories over Norway and Scotland, which frame four Euro 2016 qualifying wins. After four games in Euro 2016 qualification group E, England sits six points clear at the top.

Securing a place in the finals in France would allow Hodgson to make amends for England's disappointing World Cup campaign in Brazil, where the team failed to win any games and was eliminated at the group stage for the first time. Looking ahead to the New Year, Hodgson added, "I am looking forward to seeing the team qualify for France in 2016. Most importantly, I am looking for constant progression. I am looking for us to be a better team at the end of 2015 than we are at the start of it. Hopefully we will be a serious competitor when we get to France."

Network Rail’s £50 million Great Western Electrification Programme is set to reduce journey times between London Paddington and Swansea, though passengers should anticipate substantial disruption this summer. To accommodate overhead power lines, 10 km of track east of the city and within Box tunnel will be lowered, and several bridges will be altered.

The track lowering will occur at Dundas Aqueduct, Box tunnel, Middle Hill tunnel, and Sydney Gardens to preserve historic structures. The project also involves installing eleven new sets of points. Replacement bus services will run throughout the duration of the work.

Andy Haynes, Network Rail’s project director for the west of England, said, “The preparation work we are doing in Bath is essential to make the line ready for electrification.” He apologized to passengers and added, “Bath remains open for business during this time, although journeys may take longer than usual.”

The line between Chippenham and Bath will be closed from 18 to 31 July, with services continuing via Melksham. In August, all lines east of Bath will shut for a month, halting train services between Westbury, Freshford, Avoncliff, and Bath Spa. Passengers traveling toward London from Bath Spa will be diverted via Bristol Temple Meads and Parkway.

At 33, Adams captured the world title on Friday by defeating Thailand’s Peamwilai Laopeam, adding to her Olympic, Commonwealth, and European accolades. The English boxer secured the 51kg final in Astana by split decision. Having already qualified for the Rio Olympics, Adams had previously earned three silver medals at the World Championships.

After a cautious opening round, Adams asserted control with increased aggression. In the second round, she landed a straight right that visibly stunned Laopeam. Although Laopeam responded with a combination in the third round, Adams closed the contest strongly in the fourth.

“I’ve finally done it,” Adams said. “And what better year to do it than in the year of the [Olympic] Games? I’ve cemented my place in history. The champ is here!” While one judge scored the bout in favor of Laopeam, Adams credited her win to meticulous preparation and determination. “I stuck to the tactics, listened to the coaches, did all the training and left nothing to chance,” she explained. “It was a touch-and-go fight. She’s a really good opponent and deserved to be in the final, but I just gave a little bit more and wanted it that much more.”

A special guide is available for those interested in starting boxing.

For the 2016-17 season, sixteen clubs with Category One academies are taking part, while League One and League Two sides must field a set number of first-team players. Robinson criticized this arrangement, asking, "How can we have a development trophy for Premier League teams who can do what they want, yet we can't develop our own players in it?"

The EFL responded that it will "continue to assess the format." An EFL spokesperson said the revised Checkatrade Trophy format, introduced as a one-year pilot, aligns with the league’s long-term aim of producing more and better homegrown talent. The changes also seek to revitalize the competition for League One and Two clubs amid concerns that it had lost its purpose in previous seasons.

Robinson’s Dons are scheduled to face Peterborough in the group stage on Tuesday. Their starting lineup must include either the five players with the most appearances, five who played in the previous match, or five listed for the next league fixture. Clubs with Category One academies, such as Leicester and Chelsea, are required to start at least six players under 21 but may fill the remainder of their squad with first-team players.

Speaking to BBC Three Counties Radio, Robinson said, "I think the rules need to change drastically, or don't have the competition. I don't think it is conducive to development anymore. I think it's rubbish." He added, "If they made this an open competition where we could all play our under-21s, play players to get fit, close half the stands, and make it more of a competition for development. Don't make it just a development competition for Premier League teams when clubs like us work so hard to develop our own players."

Webb closed her round with a birdie on the 18th, carding a 69 to join world number 11 Kim at six under par. At 42, Webb is chasing her eighth major title, her last coming in 2006, while 24-year-old Kim aims for her first. Overnight leader Christie Kerr slipped to third place, two shots behind, after a 73.

England’s Georgia Hall is the leading British player at level par, six shots off the pace. English golfer Bronte Law and Scot Carly Booth are tied at four over, 10 shots back. Charley Hull dropped to 12 over following an 80 in the third round.

Booth, one of three Scots to make the cut, posted a 75, adding to earlier rounds of 75 and 70 despite a costly triple bogey on the 15th hole. Reflecting on her round, the 2012 champion said, “The weather was pretty brutal to be honest. I played OK today apart from my four-putt from five feet. I had a triple on the 15th which was just stupid but apart from that it was good golf. I rushed the putt and my head went a little. It’s just one of those; you have to forget about it now. I’ll kick myself for a little bit, but tomorrow is a new day.”

Catriona Matthew, seeking her third Scottish Open title, shot a 76 to finish on eight over, while Sally Watson posted a 77 to end on 10 over.

Great Britain will be represented by 20 riders at the World Championships in Hong Kong from 12-16 April, including ten riders making their debut, such as Scot Neah Evans and Welshman Lewis Oliva. Head coach Iain Dyer praised the squad as "a good mix of experienced and developing riders," highlighting the selection of Evans and Oliva for their dedication and the support from Scottish and Welsh Cycling.

Dyer also noted that several Olympians are part of the team and that this year's championships provide an opportunity for them to compete in events previously unavailable due to Olympic commitments. Four-time Olympic gold medallist Laura Kenny, 24, will miss the competition after announcing in February that she and her husband Jason Kenny are expecting their first child.

The Great Britain Cycling Team lineup is as follows:

Women's Endurance: Katie Archibald, Elinor Barker, Ellie Dickinson, Neah Evans, Emily Kay, Manon Lloyd, Emily Nelson.

Men's Endurance: Matt Bostock, Steven Burke, Kian Emadi, Chris Latham, Mark Stewart, Andy Tennant, Oliver Wood.

Sprint: Jack Carlin, Katy Marchant, Lewis Oliva, Ryan Owens, Callum Skinner, Joe Truman.

A judicial officer determined that a tackle in the first half of a European Champions Cup match on 16 January warranted a red card. Saracens contested the 10-week suspension, arguing it was overly harsh. Chris Ashton described the ruling as "incredibly disappointing."

In a statement on the Saracens website, Ashton said he intends to focus on the remainder of the season and work hard throughout his ban. He maintained, "I vehemently maintain that I have never made an attempt to intentionally make contact with the eye area of any other player." While calling it "extremely disappointing" to miss the chance to represent both his country and Saracens, he added he will respect and accept the decision.

Former England teammate Toby Flood criticized the ruling on Twitter, calling the original decision "horrible" and labeling the appeal process "incompetence," asserting that Ashton was treated unfairly.

England will open their Six Nations campaign against Scotland on Saturday, with Anthony Watson and Jack Nowell starting on the wings at Murrayfield as the team aims for a strong start under coach Eddie Jones. Ashton will be eligible to return on 28 March.

Around 360 kg (793 lbs) of cocaine washed up on Hopton Beach near Great Yarmouth, as well as on a nearby beach close to Caister. A member of the public alerted Norfolk Police after discovering several holdalls on Hopton Beach. The National Crime Agency (NCA) has taken over the seizure, and officers continue to search the area.

Matthew Rivers of the NCA’s border investigation team said, “We are collaborating with Border Force, the Coastguard Agency, and Norfolk Police to establish how the bags ended up at these locations; however, it is highly unlikely this was their intended destination.” He added, “This is a significant seizure of class A drugs and a major setback for the organised criminals involved.”

Superintendent Dave Buckley of Norfolk Constabulary stated, “While we believe all packages have been recovered, anyone who finds one should contact Norfolk Constabulary immediately. Additional officers will be deployed to monitor the area.”

Further information on this and other stories is available at BBC Local Live: Norfolk.

Wasps have appointed 32-year-old Lee Blackett, former Rotherham captain from Chester, as their backs coach for the 2015-16 season. He succeeds former Wales international fly-half Stephen Jones, who is returning to Scarlets. Blackett will be part of a four-man coaching team led by director of rugby and head coach Dai Young, alongside defence coach Brad Davis and part-time assistant coach Andy Titterrell.

Blackett became the youngest coach in the Championship in 2013 when, at age 30, he was named head coach of Titans, guiding them to a fourth-place finish. Young hailed him as “one of the brightest young coaches in Britain” and commended his success in transforming Rotherham into one of the strongest sides outside the Premiership.

Speaking on Jones’s departure, Young said, “We always knew the time would come when Stephen would want to return to Wales with his young family. He’s done a great job for us, moving straight from player to backs coach after Shane Howarth left.”

Regarding Blackett’s appointment, Young explained, “We had two options: recruit a vastly experienced backs coach or select the best up-and-coming coach. The experienced option was not feasible, as no suitable candidate was available, so we focused on promising young coaches.”

He added, “Lee has impressed experts with his attention to detail, enthusiasm, professionalism, and his ability to get the best from his players.”

A bystander’s mobile phone video documented Michael Slager shooting Walter Scott, 50, as Scott fled a traffic stop in North Charleston on April 4. On Monday morning, a grand jury issued a murder indictment, moving the case closer to trial. Officer Slager, 33, who has been in jail since charges were filed in April, faces up to 30 years in prison. He has asserted that he feared for his safety because Scott tried to grab his stun gun.

During a press conference on Monday, Rodney Scott, Walter Scott’s brother, said the family is "very happy and pleased" with the indictment but acknowledged it is only the initial step. In addition to the criminal case, Scott’s family plans to file a civil lawsuit in the coming months.

Scarlett Wilson, solicitor for the North Charleston court, warned that despite the video evidence, the murder charge must still be proven in court. “Just because you have video in this case, it doesn’t mean it’s the be-all and end-all,” Wilson said, emphasizing that the case will depend on testimony from witnesses who were present. No trial date has been scheduled.

Nico Rosberg, who retired after clinching the world championship, warned that the cars will push drivers to their physical limits. He called the vehicles "absolute monsters" and "such an awesome hype," adding, "We might even see drivers losing race wins because of just being physically knackered, and that is the direction the sport should be in."

This season, Formula 1 rolled out new regulations aimed at making the cars faster, more demanding, and visually striking. Tyre supplier Pirelli was tasked with creating tyres that enable drivers to sustain flat-out pace over multiple consecutive laps—a capability missing for the past six years.

Reflecting on his retirement, Rosberg said he has no regrets. During the first pre-season test at Spain’s Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, he remarked, "There was not one moment when I thought it should be me sitting in that car. It was interesting to realise that. And perfect."

Rosberg also engaged with his Mercedes successor, Valtteri Bottas, who posted the fastest time so far on the third morning of the four-day test. When asked about Bottas’s prospects of challenging Lewis Hamilton in his first season with Mercedes after moving from Williams, Rosberg responded, "He is a good driver so you'd expect him to be challenging Lewis. It is difficult to predict exactly how they compare. We all know that Lewis is a massive benchmark, so it is not going to be easy. I'd assume that sure there is going to be a good battle."

At the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) in Slimbridge, Gloucestershire, two female spoon-billed sandpipers have laid a total of seven eggs. This critically endangered species has an estimated 200 breeding pairs remaining in the wild. Nigel Jarrett, the trust’s head of conservation, said staff "almost couldn't believe it" when the first egg was found last week.

To encourage breeding, the WWT team installed special lightbulbs, timer switches, and added sand and netting to simulate the birds’ migration from tropical Asia to the Russian Arctic. "For the last two years—ever since all the spoonies came into maturity—we've been doing everything to get these birds in the mood for love," Mr. Jarrett said. "For two years, we’ve been scratching our heads and feeling a bit deflated. Now, with two mums laying eggs, the significance is only just starting to sink in."

Since 2011, the trust has been working to establish a flock at Slimbridge as a safeguard for the wild population, which has declined by up to 25% annually. The species’ demanding 10,000-mile migration between breeding grounds in the Russian Arctic and wintering sites in Southeast Asia has so far prevented successful captive breeding.

In the wild, spoon-billed sandpipers face threats from habitat loss in East Asia and trapping by villagers in Bangladesh and Burma. Mr. Jarrett stressed that the trust is now making progress toward captive breeding, describing it as "the ultimate insurance policy for the species in the wild."

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) have confirmed that the man previously associated with the case has been "eliminated" from their investigation. The victim, found with a head injury on Thursday in a play area in Rochdale, has not yet been formally identified. On Friday, Jalalia Jaamé Mosque shared on Facebook that Koran reader Jalal Uddin "passed away last night." Mr. Uddin, believed to be a qari (Koran reader) at the mosque, is thought to have been assaulted between 20:40 and 20:55 GMT while returning home from a friend's house.

Detective Chief Inspector Terry Crompton of GMP said officers remain focused on determining the precise circumstances surrounding how Jalal Uddin sustained his injuries and are keeping an open mind regarding the motive, with multiple lines of inquiry underway. He noted the incident has raised concern within the community, leading to increased patrols to offer reassurance. Crompton also urged the public to refrain from speculation on social media and encouraged anyone with information to come forward.

In the first half, the Saddlers looked more likely to score, with Albion goalkeeper Jon McLaughlin making important saves to deny Paul Downing and Romaine Sawyers. Burton came close when Stuart Beavon skillfully entered Walsall’s penalty area but his shot struck the side-netting. Following Wigan’s victory over Bury, Albion’s lead at the top has been cut to two points, while Walsall remains in fourth place.

Burton Albion manager Nigel Clough told BBC Radio Derby, "There was nothing in it at all. It was never going to be an open, free-flowing classic, I don't think. Chances were few and far between, but we got a clean sheet and another point on the board. We played better on Monday night in terms of ball control, without doubt. But we returned to what the team has been about for the last season or two—being solid and not giving anything away."

Walsall head coach Sean O'Driscoll told BBC WM 95.6, "I think we were organised, disciplined, and professional. I've seen many games here where teams fall into the trap of trying to play where there's no space. They play in a defensive shape and do it very well, so I thought we created the better chances. It was a different kind of performance compared to previous ones. Hopefully, the chances we created today will lead to goals in upcoming matches."

Imrich Joni, 19, stands accused of murdering 68-year-old Gordon Bolam in Glasgow’s Pollokshields area, with the alleged offence occurring between 29 June and 14 July 2016. Prosecutors allege that Joni killed Bolam using a knife and a ligature, then attempted to obstruct justice by concealing the body. Joni denies all charges.

The trial date was set for April by Judge Lady Scott at the High Court in Glasgow. According to prosecutors, Bolam suffered injuries to his head, neck, and body inflicted by a knife and a mug or similar object. Joni is also alleged to have caused blunt force trauma by unknown means and to have placed a ligature around Bolam’s neck.

Additional allegations claim Joni hid Bolam’s remains in a wardrobe, covering the body with clothes and bags. He is further accused of cleaning the flat to remove blood and disposing of clothing, trainers, and a knife.

Joni also faces a charge of breaching a bail condition imposed by a sheriff on 20 June, which prohibited him from entering Glasgow except for court appearances. Prosecutors further accuse him of breaking into Edinburgh’s Festival Theatre on 30 or 31 July and possessing bladed items in a public place.

The trial is set to begin at the High Court in Edinburgh on 11 April.

The Academy issued its ruling following an agreement with Nate D. Sanders, an auction house specializing in movie memorabilia. The Oscar statuette at the center of the dispute was awarded in 1942 to Joseph C. Wright for his color art direction on My Gal Sal. Wright’s heirs sold the statuette in June 2014, prompting the Academy to attempt to block the sale by citing a 1951 rule that requires Oscar winners and their heirs to first offer statuettes to the Academy for $10 before selling them elsewhere.

Academy lawyers maintained that Nate D. Sanders was aware of this rule when it purchased the Oscar at a sale organized by Rhode Island-based Briarbrook Auctions. In 2012, Nate D. Sanders had handled the auction of 15 Oscar statues, which collectively sold for more than $3 million (£1.9 million). Gary E. Gans, the Academy’s attorney involved in the prolonged litigation, stated, “The Oscar is perhaps the world's most distinctive and prestigious award for achievement in the arts. This case established that the Academy can maintain the dignity and value of such an award by keeping it from becoming a commodity.”

In a related case last year, the Academy filed legal action against the heirs of cinematographer Robert Surtees after they allegedly sold one of his Oscars on eBay.

The Scottish SPCA suspects that the puppies discovered on 18 November in a field beside a layby on the A77, between Cairnryan and Ballantrae, were victims of the puppy farming industry. An undercover officer from the charity estimated the animals were between six and 12 weeks old and possibly of a Spaniel breed.

Please note: A photograph of the deceased puppies appears later in this article and may be distressing to some readers.

According to the officer, "The A77 is the main route between Scotland and Northern Ireland, where most puppy farm suppliers are based." They further highlighted that Scotland’s central belt contains the majority of potential buyers. A BBC Scotland investigation earlier this year brought this illegal trade to light.

The officer stated, "We believe these puppies were part of a shipment from Northern Ireland and tragically died during the ferry crossing before being callously abandoned." The charity is currently awaiting post-mortem results to establish the cause of death. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Animal Helpline at 03000 999 999.

The Scottish SPCA is urging buyers to exercise caution when purchasing puppies this Christmas. The officer described the trade in farmed puppies as a "reprehensible practice" that disregards animal welfare, expressing concern that many buyers may inadvertently support the industry by purchasing from unscrupulous breeders and sellers.

Puppies bred in these conditions are often kept poorly, leading to disease and infection, the officer explained. Even if a puppy appears healthy at the time of sale, health problems often develop soon after, by which point the buyer has already paid and the seller cannot be traced.

The charity has provided the following advice for those considering buying a new dog:

Parag Sawant, 36, was hospitalized while his wife was pregnant with their daughter. On 11 July 2006, during the evening rush hour, one of seven bombs exploded in his train carriage. PTI reported that the bombs, concealed in seven pressure cookers inside bags, killed at least 187 people and injured over 800.

Following the blast, Sawant remained in a deep coma for nearly two years before gradually improving to a semi-conscious state, able to follow simple commands, neurosurgeon BK Misra told PTI. In 2010, after emerging from the coma, Sawant’s wife Preeti told The Hindu, "He recognised me, our daughter. I am very happy." The newspaper also noted that Preeti secured a job with Western Railway and that officials covered Sawant’s medical expenses.

Despite this improvement, Sawant eventually died when his lungs and heart ceased functioning and resuscitation efforts failed. He was visited by Sushma Swaraj, then leader of the opposition in parliament, who condemned the government for not prosecuting those responsible. Indian militants were held accountable for the attack. NDTV reports that the trial of 13 accused has concluded, but a Mumbai court has yet to deliver its verdict.

The Bahraini state news agency BNA reported that the group had planned attacks targeting "policemen... vital sites and security locations, including an embassy." Human rights organizations in Bahrain condemned the trial as "unfair" and criticized the sentences imposed. Since the large-scale Shia-led protests were suppressed in 2011, the country has experienced sporadic unrest. In the most recent case, defendants received prison terms ranging from three years to life, with activists noting that some of those imprisoned were minors. Four individuals were acquitted.

The Gulf Daily News identified the targets as the Saudi embassy in Manama and the King Fahd Causeway, which links Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. The court accused the defendants of receiving funding from the main Shia opposition group, al-Wefaq, and the banned organization al-Wafa (Fidelity). Two Bahrain advocacy groups issued a joint statement noting that nine of those convicted were under 18. Husain Abdulla of Americans for Democracy and Human Rights in Bahrain said, "Bahrain's politicised courts are disenfranchising an entire generation of Bahrainis with unfair imprisonment."

The 2011 uprising saw the Shia majority demand democratic reforms from the Sunni-led government. Since then, protests have become more sporadic following a government crackdown. In January, Bahrain revoked the citizenship of 72 individuals, citing national security threats.

Kelman Edwards, 78, of Edinburgh, mistakenly pressed the accelerator instead of the brake. He had previously admitted to causing the death of Rev Thomas Sinclair, 76, through careless driving in May 2014. On 19 May, while dropping off his daughter at Waverley station, Edwards encountered a newly installed security barrier blocking the ramp. As he reversed onto the main road, his foot unintentionally hit the accelerator, causing his automatic vehicle to speed across the road. The car struck Rev Sinclair, then collided with a bus on the opposite side, and hit the minister again as Edwards moved forward.

Rev Sinclair, from East Tarbet on Lewis, was attending the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland and died at the scene. Following the incident, Edwards was banned from driving and given a six-month night-time home restriction order.

John Cunningham, Presbytery Clerk of Lewis, described the incident as "a great tragedy for all involved." He added, "As a Presbytery, our prayers are with Mrs. Pam Sinclair and her family who are now reliving the horror of 2014. Our prayers are also with Mr. Edwards and his family as he tries to come to terms with the life-changing consequences of this dreadful accident. Above all, we commit all concerned to the love and care of our sovereign God who works out all things for good for those who trust him."

Gatwick Airport has confirmed that its automated baggage system has been repaired and is collaborating with airlines to return luggage to passengers "as soon as possible." On Friday, the disruption caused long queues at check-in desks for departing flights from both the north and south terminals. The baggage system for arriving flights remained unaffected and continued operating normally.

A Gatwick Airport spokesperson stated, "Arrivals, and those travelling with carry-on baggage only, were unaffected by this issue and all bags and passengers were security screened as normal." The spokesperson added that the airport is working to clear the backlog of luggage resulting from the incident.

Amid one of the airport’s busiest weekends, passengers took to social media to express frustration over a lack of information from airlines at check-in desks. Charles Duffield tweeted, "Total shambles at Gatwick this morning." Phil Collins also posted, "Absolute chaos @Gatwick_Airport multiple gate moves, multiple flights from the same gates and staff ask us for advice and info #BankHoliday." EasyJet attributed the disruption to a failure in the baggage belt system.

President Ashraf Ghani nominated Mohammad Yaqub Haidari for a government post, but Haidari has appeared on Interpol’s most-wanted list for significant tax evasion and fraud. The presidential office told the BBC it is currently verifying the accuracy of these allegations.

Interpol’s website indicates that Estonian authorities are seeking Haidari for tax evasion and additional fraud charges related to currency conversions. Haidari told the BBC he is the target of a political conspiracy and a criminal mafia. He said, “They [Interpol] have mentioned in this document that they are pursuing me. I am not in hiding,” and expressed his intention to travel to Estonia to “defend his rights.” Estonian law enforcement officials were not immediately reachable for comment on Sunday.

According to Estonian media, Haidari was investigated for embezzlement and tax evasion while serving as director of Rapla Dairy, which went bankrupt in 2003. Legal proceedings were initiated against him, and he subsequently fled Estonia. Reports state he was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison in 2011.

These charges represent a setback for President Ghani, who aims to reform Afghanistan’s political culture by appointing qualified and unblemished officials, according to BBC’s David Loyn in Kabul. Nearly four months after the new government assumed office, no ministers have been confirmed, raising concerns about the administration’s stability, our correspondent adds. Ghani announced his cabinet nominees on Monday, roughly three months after his inauguration, following extensive negotiations with former rival and current chief executive Abdullah Abdullah.

South Africa-born back-rower Strauss, who became eligible to play for Scotland ahead of last year’s World Cup, is preparing for his first Six Nations start against France. Emphasizing the importance of the match, he said, "Every game is a must-win game. Pride-wise, though, this is a must-win game." He described the fixture as crucial and expressed confidence in the team’s readiness.

Following Scotland’s recent win over Italy in Rome, which ended a nine-match losing streak in the Six Nations, Strauss aims to build on the team’s momentum. "We feel there has been a constant improvement in the team," he said. "That’s a very important factor at this level, trying to build on the positives and eliminate the negatives." Reflecting on that performance, he added, "Two weeks ago against Italy, things came together nicely. We’ve got to build on what we did well."

Though Strauss played a limited role in Scotland’s World Cup campaign—partly due to David Denton’s form—he now seeks to claim the number eight jersey in Vern Cotter’s squad. Stepping in for Glasgow Warriors teammate Ryan Wilson in the starting lineup, he described it as "a very big opportunity for myself." He characterized his recent experience as "a bit of a topsy-turvy experience with the World Cup and coming straight back into the Pro12," noting it was his first time facing such circumstances. Strauss also acknowledged injuries before the Six Nations affected his form but expressed satisfaction at rejoining the squad and being ready to contribute.

Having trained with the team from the outset, Strauss is eager to make an impact after regaining match fitness with the Warriors. "I’ve been in since the start, but I’ve been biding my time just training with the team, trying to get my fitness back to where it needs to be to play," he explained. "I’ve played a few games for the Warriors, and I feel my fitness is where it should be." He concluded by recognizing the strong competition for starting spots, saying, "Everyone wants to start. Everyone wants that jersey."

Over 1,000 individuals invested in the Ingenious film financing schemes in pursuit of tax relief. Ingenious, a producer of films including Avatar, qualified for tax breaks designed to support the UK film sector. HMRC contended that the company claimed relief based on artificial losses, classifying the schemes as tax avoidance rather than legitimate investments.

On Wednesday, a tax tribunal confirmed the 2016 decision to recover the avoided tax, ruling that the incentives were "not allowable deductions." As a result, 1,400 investors—including celebrities Gary Lineker, Bob Geldof, and Ant and Dec—face substantial tax liabilities. While £420 million in tax was initially avoided, interest will bring the total amount owed to nearly £700 million.

An HMRC spokesperson stated, "We are pleased that the tribunal has agreed with us that the vast majority of what was claimed in tax relief by Ingenious investors was simply not due." Ingenious intends to appeal the ruling, with a company representative describing it as "wholly unsatisfactory" and noting it was reached with "misgivings and reluctance."

Investors were required to invest a minimum of £100,000 and were promised generous tax breaks on any losses. Many later reported they had been poorly advised and unaware of the risks.

HMRC previously secured victories against another film tax avoidance scheme, Icebreaker. In August 2016, the Tax Tribunal found that members claimed tax relief on losses significantly exceeding their actual investments, with £134 million in tax at stake.

Strong winds and heavy rain struck boats crossing Lake Togo, located about 40 km (25 miles) east of the capital, Lome. Police reported that the passengers were returning from a funeral on the opposite side of the lake. Local official Akouete Edan confirmed 21 survivors and stated that most of the deceased were students. The total number of passengers remains unknown, and the search for additional bodies is ongoing.

A survivor, who spoke to a local radio station and was cited by Reuters, said the largest boat, carrying men and drums, capsized first when the winds hit. He added that two or three smaller boats carrying women and children also overturned, and he lost three of his children in the incident.

Women’s Minister Henriette Amedjogbe, accompanied by the prime minister, visited the village of Agbodankope, where many victims originated. In remarks to AFP, she described the event as "a real tragedy" and said, "We came to bring you the support of the government and the Togolese people."

Following Richard Cockerill’s dismissal in January, the 36-year-old former All Black stepped in as head coach. Mauger will oversee his final match against Northampton Saints on Saturday before being succeeded by former Tigers coach Matt O’Connor.

“I definitely wanted to stay and see it through for the rest of the season,” Mauger told BBC Leicester Sport. “I was kept informed throughout, but I’m clearly disappointed and devastated by the outcome. The club made this decision based on what they believe is best for the future, so I have to respect that and move on.”

O’Connor’s return was announced on Monday, coming just one day after Mauger led the Tigers to victory over Exeter in the Anglo-Welsh Cup final, securing the club’s first trophy in four years.

After Cockerill’s departure, Leicester lost their first three games under Mauger but then won three of the next eight across all competitions. They currently sit fifth in the Premiership, one point behind Bath, with five matches remaining.

“Where the group is at the moment is pretty exciting,” Mauger added. “We’ve turned things around over the past eight or nine weeks. There’s a real positive energy reflected in some strong performances. Unfortunately, that wasn’t enough. We have a big game on Saturday against Saints and look forward to starting a home run for the play-offs.”

An unannounced inspection conducted in October and November 2016 found widespread deterioration at Swinfen Hall prison near Lichfield, Staffordshire, which holds 600 male inmates aged 18 to 25, and judged the facility "not safe enough." The HM Inspectorate of Prisons report revealed that prisoners at both the main prison and the young offenders institution were not receiving daily showers. Nonetheless, inspectors recognized significant efforts to tackle offending behavior and described the prison’s resettlement work as "reasonably good."

Peter Clarke, Chief Inspector of Prisons, stated that "basic standards need to improve." Frances Crook, Chief Executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, expressed alarm, saying, "For the second time in as many weeks, we read of a prison where men are so frightened for their safety because of rising violence that they are refusing to come out of their cells." She pointed out that Swinfen Hall is not overcrowded, unlike many other prisons, making the findings particularly concerning.

In response, Michael Spurr, Chief Executive of the National Offender Management Service, announced plans to recruit additional prison officers at Swinfen Hall and introduce an action plan to address the problems. A prison spokesperson attributed the issues to "operational pressures."

The prison has previously experienced security challenges, including a lockdown in August 2015 and an incident in December 2015 when several staff members were hospitalized following attacks by inmates.

A recently released photograph of Prince George, taken at Kensington Palace ahead of his birthday on Saturday, features the young royal smiling. Kensington Palace confirmed that royal photographer Chris Jackson captured the image and said the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge were "delighted" to share it. The palace added, "The Duke and Duchess are very pleased to share this lovely picture as they celebrate Prince George's fourth birthday, and would like to thank everyone for all of the kind messages they have received."

Born on 22 July 2013, Prince George Alexander Louis holds the formal title His Royal Highness Prince George of Cambridge. In the days leading up to his birthday, he traveled with his parents on a tour of Poland and Germany. On the tour's final day, the Duke of Cambridge took Prince George and Princess Charlotte to the Airbus factory in Hamburg for a guided helicopter tour. During the visit, Prince George tried on a pilot's helmet while Princess Charlotte explored the cockpit buttons.

Chris Jackson, the Getty Images royal photographer who took the portrait at the end of June, said, "I'm thrilled and honoured that the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge have chosen to release this portrait to celebrate Prince George's fourth birthday. He is such a happy little boy and certainly injects some fun into a photoshoot."

Prince George is scheduled to start school in September at Thomas's Battersea, a private preparatory school located a few miles from the family's residence at Kensington Palace in London, where they will be based.

Last Sunday, referee Jon Moss stirred controversy by awarding West Ham a penalty against league leaders Leicester after Foxes defender Wes Morgan tangled with Winston Reid, sparking widespread debate about grappling during set-pieces. On Thursday, Koeman commented, "I think if you start to give penalties for that then it stops." When Tottenham defeated Stoke 4-0 on Monday, cutting Leicester's lead at the top to five points, the clear lack of contact during corner setups stood out. Koeman called on referees to maintain consistent standards in penalty decisions at corners. Following Morgan’s penalty for holding Reid, Leicester's appeals were rejected after a similar 90th-minute incident involving Angelo Ogbonna and Robert Huth. The Dutchman added, "Everybody knows if you take somebody in his shirt or like a rugby player, you take your man in the box, it's a penalty. If one day it's a penalty and even in the same game next time it's not, that doesn't help or make it clear for everybody."

Building on their 1-0 first-leg lead, Barcelona increased their advantage as Luis Suarez scored with a low finish, followed by a Lionel Messi penalty that made it 3-0 on aggregate. Juanmi pulled a goal back, but Suarez quickly restored a 4-1 lead. Willian Jose’s header narrowed the margin again before Suarez netted his second goal of the match.

Barcelona, who hold a record 28 titles in the competition, have advanced to the semi-finals for the seventh consecutive season. They will be joined in Friday’s draw by 10-time champions Atletico Madrid, Celta Vigo—who eliminated Real Madrid—and Alaves.

Denis Suarez, the 23-year-old Spanish midfielder, has featured more often as a substitute than a starter in La Liga this season. Still, he impressed with two notable finishes indicating a promising future. His first goal came after Samuel Umtiti intercepted Xabi Prieto deep in Sociedad’s half, sparking a move involving Neymar, Messi, and Luis Suarez that set up Denis Suarez for a first-time strike into the far corner. By the time he scored his second goal—the fifth of the night for Barcelona—the tie was effectively settled; the former Villarreal player beat two defenders, rounded the goalkeeper, and calmly slotted the ball home.

Barcelona have now won their last five matches across all competitions. Reflecting on the game, Denis Suarez said, “I came with a desire to be a part of this team and I am feeling better and better. We started the game by dominating, and once it was 1-0 they left us plenty of space. Everything is easier when you have the three forwards we have. We weren’t nervous at all, we just wanted to dominate the game and continue on this great run that we’re on.”

Veterans, most over the age of 90, were honored as VIP guests at a civic lunch in Belfast City Hall. The gathering marked the anniversary of Japan’s formal surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945, which ended World War II. Each veteran was presented with a commemorative medallion in recognition of their service.

Among the attendees was 95-year-old Alfie Martin, a recipient of the Distinguished Flying Cross for bravery. He described the event as "a very nice gesture by Belfast City Council, and one which is very much appreciated," adding, "It was a very nostalgic event for all of us."

Belfast’s Deputy Lord Mayor, Guy Spence, remarked, "It was a real honour to host this commemorative luncheon and to recognize the extraordinary contributions of these veterans. Given their ages, this anniversary holds special significance, and we are grateful to have them with us for such an important occasion. We owe them a great deal." He added, "Paying tribute to those who made tremendous sacrifices and demonstrated remarkable bravery to defend our freedom is a privilege."

Shortly after 2:30 a.m. on Thursday, a woman arrived at the Garthdee branch of a supermarket in Aberdeen. She later posted on social media that she had sleepwalked 1.5 miles from her home to Asda to buy a watermelon and was found by a police officer in the fruit and vegetable aisle. Police Scotland confirmed that officers safely escorted her home.

The woman described feeling confused, barefoot, dressed only in her nightdress, and cold. She expressed gratitude to the Asda staff for providing shoes, socks, a cup of tea, and helping her warm up, and thanked the police officers who took her home.
