A Police Scotland spokesperson said, "Police in Aberdeen were called to reports of concern for a 23-year-old woman at Asda at Garthdee. Officers attended and assisted the woman home safely."

Robert Wallace, deputy store manager at the Garthdee branch, added, "We do our level best to create a relaxing shopping environment, so we're flattered that she chose our store to visit on her trip out. Our colleagues were quick to make sure that she was well looked after and we are glad that she got home safely for a good night's sleep."

Glasgow Warriors' Mark Bennett, 23, has been named inside centre for Scotland, replacing Huw Jones, who was injured while setting up Sean Maitland’s try in the 19-16 victory over Argentina. Captain Greig Laidlaw sealed the win with a late penalty. Ross Ford returns to the hooker role, with Richie Gray rejoining to partner his brother Jonny Gray in the second row. In the back row, Rob Harley starts at blindside flanker and Ryan Wilson at number 8, pushing John Barclay to the bench, while Magnus Bradbury misses out after his debut against Argentina.

To make room for Richie Gray’s return, Fraser Brown steps aside for Ford, and Grant Gilchrist joins Brown on the bench. This win came after a narrow 23-22 loss to Australia, with both opening Tests held at Murrayfield.

Scotland will face Georgia at Kilmarnock FC’s Rugby Park, an artificial 3G pitch that also hosted Scotland’s 2014 victory over Tonga. Head coach Vern Cotter expressed enthusiasm about returning to Kilmarnock and highlighted the vital role of crowd support in motivating the players.

Georgia, aiming to break into the world’s top 10 rankings, are expected to rely on a physical, forward-oriented style while continuing to develop their backline.

Scotland’s starting XV: Hogg, Maitland, Bennett, Dunbar, Seymour, Russell, Laidlaw (capt); Dell, Ford, Fagerson, R Gray, J Gray, Harley, Watson, Wilson. Replacements: Brown, Allan, Low, Gilchrist, Barclay, Price, Horne, Hughes.

Barnardo’s Cymru cautions that sexual stereotyping often leads to boys’ abuse being overlooked, even as professionals frequently recognize signs of harm in girls. Negative behaviors in boys tend to be accepted without deeper investigation, whereas similar actions in girls are more likely to trigger trauma assessments. The charity is urging increased focus on this disparity.

Menna Thomas, senior policy research officer and co-author of the report *I Never Spoke About It*, explains that boys encounter “additional barriers which prevent them from being identified and, more importantly, from being able to speak up about their abuse.” She observes that boys’ problematic or criminal behavior is often viewed without acknowledgment of their exploitation or victim status. Thomas points to a widespread lack of awareness regarding boys’ vulnerability to sexual exploitation and insufficient communication assuring them they will be believed and supported.

The report further reveals that vulnerable boys entering adolescence face heightened risks of mental health issues, substance misuse, homelessness, and offending behavior. It highlights that isolation, more common among these boys, raises their risk of sexual exploitation. Moreover, many professionals surveyed reported cases of boys running away or being forced to live on the streets, where they engage in “survival sex”—exchanging sex for food or shelter.

During the January transfer window, Ayew was frequently linked with a move to Sunderland, with additional reports indicating summer interest from West Ham. However, the Ghana international said he is content at Swansea after finishing as the club’s top scorer with 12 goals. "I'm happy here. If I have to stay, fine. If I have to leave, I have to leave," he stated.

Ayew scored Swansea’s final goal of the Premier League season, securing a 1-1 home draw against Manchester City on Sunday. When questioned about his future, he responded, "I think you should ask the chairman." He joined Swansea on a free transfer from Marseille and signed a four-year deal. "What is important for me is that I keep doing my work, and in football the truth of today is not the truth of tomorrow. We'll see what's going to happen, we'll have a discussion and see the way forward," he added.

Expressing a wish to remain in English football, Ayew said, "I've enjoyed the Premier League, I think it's the best league in the world. The intensity, the determination from every team. It's a league where you enjoy every game. Every game is difficult, you can never say you've won it before you've played it. I hope to stay in the Premier League if I leave, but I'm here at the moment at Swansea."

The 26-year-old also believes Swansea, who finished 12th after a strong end to the season, will continue to improve next term under manager Francesco Guidolin, who recently signed a two-year contract extension. "I think everyone has learned a lot from the season. We've had three managers, which is not easy to deal with, but we managed to cope with all the changes and stayed up. We now have a coach with a lot of experience who knows what he wants to do. I've had friends from the national team who have been coached by him, and I know what he can do," Ayew said.

After successfully completing her jump, the Olympic gymnast struck a barrier. Within two weeks of the Channel 4 show’s debut, several celebrities have been hospitalized, leading some viewers to call for the program’s cancellation amid the rising injury count.

The gymnast fractured two bones in her neck and has undergone surgery. Her parents say early medical reports are positive, noting she can "move her hands and feet." She is the third contestant to withdraw due to injury.

Olympic swimmer Rebecca Adlington was the first to leave after dislocating her shoulder. Actress Tina Hobley followed, exiting after injuring her elbow and fracturing her arm.

A Channel 4 spokesperson told Newsround: "The Jump is now in its third series, and since its inception, 46 celebrities have successfully taken part. Although the course is new, the events are designed to be no more challenging than in previous years, and all participants have undergone rigorous training to prepare. All winter sports carry some risk, but in light of this year’s injuries, Channel 4 has requested that producers review safety procedures once again to further reduce the likelihood of accidents."

Images provided by Channel 4.

Army bomb disposal teams were called on Thursday to investigate suspicious items in Derry's Waterside area. Around 10:25 GMT, police discovered a pipe bomb in the front garden of a property on Trafalgar Court. A second device was later found on Jeffrey Avenue, also within Waterside. Both sites were attended by army bomb experts. Chief Inspector Tony Callaghan, Area Commander for Derry, confirmed that "Two viable devices have now been recovered for forensic examination and all cordons have been lifted." Residents who had been evacuated earlier have since returned home, and he expressed gratitude for their cooperation. DUP councillor Drew Thompson stated that up to 20 homes were evacuated on Trafalgar Court, with community centres opened to assist those affected.

Bury St Edmunds councillor Paul Hopfensberger has proposed installing fences around two football pitches, with £19,855 allocated for the work later this month. The fencing will be added to pitches at Oakes Road and Tollgate Recreation Ground, both located within his ward. At present, local teams are required to clear dog mess from the fields before their matches.

On the possibility of using DNA testing to identify dog waste offenders, Mr. Hopfensberger told the BBC, "I'm not saying we're going to do it, we have to look at it." He noted that a national company experienced in implementing DNA testing in other UK counties has been consulted. "We have to get the facts, get the details, to see if it will work in Suffolk," he said.

Mr. Hopfensberger described the fencing initiative as "democracy in action," emphasizing community involvement. CFC Bury coach Mark Stiff expressed support for the plan, pointing out that teams frequently have to clean up before matches. "It's not all the dog owners; some are fantastic and engage with us during games. But the irresponsible ones have made it a big problem. I would love all soccer pitches, especially youth pitches, to be fenced off," he said.

Funding for the project comes from the Premier League, the FA Facilities Fund, St Edmundsbury Borough Council, and several individual councillors' locality grants.

The Cochrane Collaboration analyzed eight exercise trials involving more than 300 patients living at home or in care facilities. Their findings showed that while exercise had little impact on patients' moods, it did improve daily activities such as standing from a chair and enhanced cognitive function. Although it remains uncertain whether these benefits translate into an improved quality of life, the researchers view the results as promising.

Dementia currently affects around 800,000 people in the UK, with numbers rising due to increased life expectancy. By 2021, this number is projected to reach approximately one million. With no cure available, efforts to improve the lives of those affected remain crucial.

Dorothy Forbes, a researcher at the University of Alberta and co-author of the review, emphasized the need for further study: "Further research is needed to develop best practice guidelines to help healthcare providers advise people with dementia living at home or in institutions. We also need to determine the appropriate level and intensity of exercise for these individuals."

Dr. Laura Phipps of Alzheimer's Research UK added, "Exercise is important for overall health. While it may not prevent dementia, evidence suggests it can help reduce the risk as part of a healthy lifestyle."

Corie Adams, formerly of Maltby, Rotherham, has admitted to 11 sexual offences involving two girls aged 13 and two aged 14 at Sheffield Crown Court. The 18-year-old had earlier pleaded guilty to six additional offences against three girls aged between 12 and 14. These crimes occurred between January 2015 and early 2016. Adams is due to be sentenced on 2 December.

His arrest and charges resulted from a joint investigation by South Yorkshire Police and Rotherham Council. Detective Inspector John Fitzgibbons described the offences as "prolific and incredibly shocking," adding that although several victims have been identified, others may still come forward. He stressed that Adams’ admissions do not reduce the serious impact his actions have had on the victims.

Det Insp Fitzgibbons further stated that Adams exploited the girls’ youth and vulnerability for his own gratification, calling the offences "truly despicable." Adams confessed to six counts of sexual activity with a child, one count of rape, three counts of causing a child to engage in sexual activity, four counts of inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, two counts of causing a child to watch a sexual act, and one count of grooming.

Highland Council is facing a budget shortfall of £17-18 million, caused by rising costs and reduced funding from the Scottish government, budget leader Bill Fernie said. To tackle this, the council has introduced a simulator that presents options for cuts, including possible reductions in spending on schools and public toilets.

The simulator, which remains open until 5 February, encourages residents of the Highlands to share their views on council services. Mr. Fernie stated, "We have done our best to look at how we can make savings whilst causing the least impact on essential services and jobs." He added that although a variety of savings have been identified to help close the gap, the council seeks to understand what priorities matter most to locals before finalising proposals.

He also explained, "The council cannot spend more than it has, and some budget areas have fixed costs that cannot be cut. For this reason, the simulator does not cover the entire budget but challenges residents to tackle the difficult task of cutting £14 million from the budget."

He endorses manager Chris Coleman's decision to use the upcoming matches against Ukraine and Northern Ireland to "try out" new tactics ahead of the tournament. Coleman is "99% certain" that Wales will also play Sweden before their first major tournament finals in 58 years.

Crystal Palace goalkeeper Wayne Hennessey expressed surprise at the scheduling of two fixtures, particularly the one in Ukraine. "We're quite surprised with two games, especially out in Ukraine," he said. "But obviously the gaffer has got something up his sleeve he wants to try out and, probably look at a few players. So it's always good, those little warm-up games to go into a big tournament."

Hennessey featured on Saturday as Crystal Palace drew 1-1 at Swansea. Wales will host fellow qualifiers Northern Ireland at Cardiff City Stadium on Thursday, 24 March. "They've done really well themselves, so it's always good to play against good competition and they'll be a good team to play against," he added.

Four days later, Wales will travel to Kiev to face Ukraine at NSK Olympiyskiy Stadium. Their Euro 2016 campaign begins on 11 June in Bordeaux, where they will face Slovakia in Group B alongside England and Russia.

In the early hours of Friday, Tanvally and Corbet halls near Banbridge, situated about five miles apart, were defaced with graffiti and paint. These incidents follow an attempted arson at Muckery Orange Hall in County Armagh last weekend. The Orange Order has reported that 12 of its halls have been targeted so far this year. A spokesman for the group described the attacks as "clearly coordinated and deliberate criminal acts" that do not reflect the area's "excellent community relations." He added, "The mindless morons responsible for such callous sectarianism ought to be ashamed of their actions and must be held accountable." The spokesman also called the double attack "particularly sickening," noting it occurred on the centenary of the Battle of the Somme and stood in stark contrast to the bravery of those who made the supreme sacrifice 100 years ago.

Conservative MP Mr Javid took to Twitter to voice his frustration, tweeting, "No signal @O2. Please sort it out," as reports emerged of service disruptions in Manchester, Bristol, Birmingham, Glasgow, and parts of Northern Ireland. O2 acknowledged awareness of "isolated instances" of intermittent service affecting customers across the UK and confirmed it is investigating the issue.

Responding to complaints on Twitter, O2 advised users to reset their devices and directed them to its support page if problems continued. Its online network status checker showed phone masts were down in multiple locations, including London. Numerous customers reported difficulties with making and receiving calls and texts, along with issues affecting 3G internet connectivity.

Craig Newrick from Lowestoft, Suffolk, expressed his dissatisfaction: "I have contacted O2 and got told to switch my device on and off again. It is really not good enough. What am I paying for?" Others criticized O2’s customer service. Aaron Nelson tweeted, "The impersonal, predictable and robotic style of responses from @O2's Twitter is an embarrassment. Still learning the internet?"

An O2 spokesperson said, "We are aware of isolated instances across the UK where some O2 customers are currently experiencing intermittent service. We are investigating the situation and will update as soon as possible."

Rafael Guillen Vicente, better known as Subcomandante Marcos, announced on a Zapatista website that he no longer speaks for the movement. He stated, "The one known as Insurgent Subcomandante Marcos no longer exists," adding that "the voice of the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN) will no longer come from my voice." Citing "internal changes" within the 20-year-old far-left guerrilla group as his reason for stepping down, he denied rumours about his health, calling them unfounded and spread by the rebel army for their own purposes.

The announcement came shortly after Marcos’s first public appearance in months, when he attended a memorial for another prominent Zapatista leader in Chiapas, one of Mexico’s poorest states. BBC correspondent Will Grant in Mexico City noted there were few signs that Marcos was preparing to withdraw from public life.

Marcos has previously reshaped his public image, including launching an alternative presidential campaign. However, the correspondent suggests his leadership of the organisation, which once challenged the Mexican political establishment, now appears to have ended.

Under Marcos’s leadership, the Zapatista movement has long sought greater recognition of indigenous peoples' rights in Chiapas. On New Year’s Day 1994, he led an armed uprising in the state, triggering several days of intense clashes with the federal government that left dozens dead. Although a peace agreement was signed, the Zapatistas’ demands were never fully met, leading them to establish autonomous justice, health, and education systems in several communities.

The British Ironwork Centre in Oswestry, Shropshire, has been commissioned to craft a 12ft (3.6m) primate sculpture for Geller’s garden in Sonning-on-Thames, Berkshire, where he also owns a Cadillac decorated with spoons. Mr. Geller revealed plans to transport the sculpture to his home suspended in a large cage beneath a helicopter.

To support the project, the centre is appealing to the public for spoon donations. Managing director Clive Knowles emphasized the importance of community involvement, saying, "It will make it even more special to have the community involved." He acknowledged the difficulty in sourcing enough spoons, noting they are not readily available, and stressed the need for a variety of spoon types to ensure the sculpture’s aesthetic appeal. "A sculpture made from one type of spoon would be very mundane," he added.

Geller, who opens his gardens to charity five times annually, selected a gorilla for the sculpture because he owns five paintings by a chimpanzee. He pointed out that the statue will be visible from the nearby river. Reflecting on his garden, he said, "My garden already has many interesting features, and you cannot saturate the place with sculptures made from spoons. But this will be amazing and unusual."

In 1996, the body of 20-year-old Janet Murgatroyd was recovered from the River Ribble in Preston after a night out. A man previously convicted of her manslaughter had his conviction overturned on appeal in 2004. Detective Chief Inspector Gary Brooks of Lancashire Police said, "Twenty-one years on from Janet's brutal murder, we remain committed to finding her killer." He highlighted that Janet, a student at the University of Central Lancashire and part-time staff member with Lancashire Police, had her whole life ahead of her.

Brooks characterized the attack as vicious and opportunistic, believed to be sexually motivated, and committed by a dangerous individual who must still be brought to justice despite the time that has passed.

On 15 June 1996, Janet had been shopping with a friend in Preston before visiting several pubs. She was seen leaving The Adelphi pub with a man but later separated from him and was subsequently spotted sleeping on Fishergate near Preston Railway Station. Early on 16 June, a taxi driver witnessed Janet fleeing from a man across Penwortham Bridge. Two witnesses reported hearing a female moaning and saw a man crouched on the bank of the River Ribble—an incident detectives believe involved Janet and her attacker. Her body was later found floating in the river. A post-mortem examination determined the cause of death as drowning and head injuries.

After losing all their league and cup matches this season, New Mills, competing in the eighth-tier Northern Premier League Division One North, secured their first point of the campaign with a 2-2 draw against Witton Albion on Tuesday evening. Manager Garry Brown said he hopes the result marks a turning point for the season.

The match, held at Witton Albion’s Wincham Park in Northwich before 218 spectators, saw New Mills take the lead twice through goals by Darryl Mason. However, Witton Albion fought back with strikes from Danny Andrews and Rob Hopley to earn a draw. This was New Mills’ first point since 11 April 2015.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Brown, the club’s fourth manager since June, said, “We have got rid of that duck.” He added, “The ‘worst team in England’ tag had driven me. I know we are not, and I think we can still surprise a few people this season. New Mills is no longer a place to get easy points. It was a fantastic performance and just what the lads deserve.”

The redevelopment plan for Botley’s West Way shopping area would have required demolishing the existing precinct. Developer Doric Properties proposed constructing a supermarket, a 100-bed hotel, a six-screen cinema, 525 student residences, and a Baptist church. The company has not yet decided whether to appeal the council’s ruling. Simon Hillcox of Doric Properties said, "We're obviously disappointed with the outcome. We are now going to take some time to review and understand the decision before we decide on our next steps."

Caroline Potter, speaking on behalf of West Way Community Concern, which opposed the plan, welcomed the decision by Vale of White Horse District Council. She said, "We are delighted. Common sense, democracy and justice have won out." The group reported that 2,200 people signed a petition against the redevelopment. In October, hundreds of protesters formed a human chain around the site to express their opposition.

The 49-year-old singer told Today FM that he recently completed a two-week course of radiation and chemotherapy. In conversation with presenter Matt Cooper, he said, "I have just started a journey with cancer." While the diagnosis came as a "huge shock," he noted that he had "caught it really early" and felt "incredibly lucky."

Earlier this year, the singer—known for hits such as "A Better Man" and "Life Love and Happiness"—received a clean bill of health from his GP. However, sensing that "something was out of kilter," he pursued further testing. A colonoscopy led to a diagnosis of a rectal tumour. He encouraged anyone with even a "grain of doubt" about their health to seek medical evaluation.

Kennedy also shared that he recently reconnected with his brother, fellow musician Bap Kennedy, after a prolonged estrangement. Bap is currently receiving palliative care following a pancreatic cancer diagnosis. Reflecting on their separation, Brian said, "Estrangement becomes like a very bad habit. It just becomes the norm. We just got used to not hearing or seeing from each other." He added, "I got to see him again and give him a hug, and if anything good has come out of this, it was the chance to see him again." He concluded, "I think that cancer puts manners on the best of people, the best of situations and the worst."

Last year, 38-year-old English golfer Paul Casey relinquished his European Tour membership to focus on the PGA Tour, improving his world ranking from 75th to 24th. Casey described staying in the United States as the "right decision for my family," though he admitted feeling "very sad" about missing the opportunity to qualify for Europe’s Ryder Cup team.

Europe captain Darren Clarke expressed disappointment, emphasizing that only European Tour members are eligible for selection. Having teamed up with Casey at Oakland Hills in 2004 and the K Club in 2006, Clarke said, "It is obvious that representing Europe in the Ryder Cup is not on Paul's priority list, which is disappointing, but I wish him all the best for the future." He added, "The focus is firmly on the players committed to the European cause as we approach Hazeltine, and I look forward to working with them over the next 10 months."

A former world number three, Casey contributed to Europe’s nine-point victories in 2004 and 2006 and also competed in their 2008 defeat at Valhalla. Despite being ranked seventh globally in 2010, he was left in tears when Colin Montgomerie omitted him from a wildcard selection.

Reflecting on his choice, Casey said, "With my wife and young son as my priority, I have decided to continue to concentrate on the PGA Tour, which has worked well for us this past year. I believe this decision will help me to be the best I can be both on and off the course."

The 2016 Ryder Cup is scheduled to begin on 27 September.

Five works by Irish-born British artist Francis Bacon, valued at over €25 million (£22 million; $29 million), were stolen from the Madrid residence of José Capelo, a friend and owner of the paintings. Authorities have arrested ten suspects in what is considered Spain’s largest theft of contemporary art.

Born in Dublin in 1909, Bacon had no formal artistic training but rose to prominence as one of the leading artists of his generation. He died of a heart attack in Madrid in 1992 at age 82. During the burglary, thieves also took a safe containing jewels and other valuables from Capelo’s home while he was in London. The investigation remains ongoing.

Spanish police reported that three of the stolen works were recovered after a tip-off from a London-based art recovery team. The team was contacted by an individual in Sitges, near Barcelona, seeking to authenticate one of the stolen paintings. The person sent photos by email showing Bacon’s signature on the back, suggesting the images were taken after the theft.

By tracing the camera used to capture the photos, police identified professional photographers and arrested a suspected thief along with several accomplices. Seven arrests were made in Madrid in May 2016, with three more following in January of this year.

Bacon frequently visited Madrid and maintained many friendships there. In 2015, two of his self-portraits, long hidden in a private collection, sold for a combined £30 million at Sotheby’s in London. In 2013, a Bacon painting featuring his friend and fellow artist Lucian Freud set a record as the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction, fetching $142 million (£89 million) in New York.

Singapore Airlines, the inaugural launch customer of the two-deck A380 jet in 2007, has confirmed it will not renew its contract for the aircraft when the current ten-year lease expires next year. The airline’s first A380, one of five leased with options to extend, will reach the end of its lease in October 2017, and Singapore Airlines has decided against extending it. Decisions regarding the remaining four aircraft will be made later.

Nonetheless, Singapore Airlines has placed an order for five new A380s from Airbus, with deliveries expected to begin in the second half of 2017. This announcement follows Airbus’s decision to more than halve its delivery target for the A380, stirring concerns that the manufacturer could return to losses on the program, which only broke even last year.

In July, Airbus indicated it could still avoid losses on the A380 in 2017 with as few as 20 deliveries but offered no further details. Analysts note that large aircraft such as the A380 and Boeing’s 747 series have fallen out of favor, as smaller jets generally prove more profitable due to higher passenger load factors and lower operating costs.

In November 2014, 14-year-old Matthew Collett-Leslie from Hastings was referred to Sussex Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (Camhs) for the first time. A psychologist identified signs of autism in May but recommended a full assessment, which was scheduled for 26 November. The NHS trust has reported a significant increase in referrals.

The referral was made by Matthew’s school, Hailsham Community College. Since then, he has started a petition on change.org and written to the prime minister, expressing that the diagnosis delay has affected both his school and home life. "Children do pick on me sometimes because they don't feel the way I am feeling," he said. "There is not much support at school because I am not officially diagnosed."

His father, Joe, stressed the importance of support at school, especially from a teaching assistant. "At home I need the support for myself to deal with the situation," he added.

Tom Purser of the National Autistic Society explained that a diagnosis can help young people better understand their behavior and access support both at home and at school.

The Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust noted that autism assessments involve several stages and multiple professionals due to the complex symptoms, which can be mistaken for other conditions. The trust acknowledged that the rise in referrals has increased pressure on services. "It is a key national priority to reduce the wait, and we are working with other NHS professionals to review delays and explore what more can be done," they said.

Phil Matthews, principal of Hailsham Community College, confirmed that the school refers students to Camhs when appropriate.

The single-deck bus will primarily run along the Lime 2 route, which serves Burghfield Common—the village near Reading where Mears resides—but it will also operate on other routes throughout the town. This follows the installation of a fake golden postbox in his village last August. Mears and his diving partner, Jack Laugher, won gold in the men's synchronised 3m springboard event. Describing seeing his image on the bus as "surreal," Mears said, "My old friendship group use this service, so it's going to be weird for them getting on the bus and seeing me on the side of it." He added that he hopes his Rio success will inspire local youth and encourage interest in diving.

Jake Osman of Reading Buses explained, "After the achievements at London 2012, gold medal-winning athletes were honoured with gold post boxes in their hometowns, but this was limited to those Olympics." He continued, "Since Chris will not receive a golden post box in Burghfield Common, we decided to provide him with something that shows the people of Burghfield and Reading are proud of his accomplishments." The bus was unveiled at the Pride of Reading Awards on Friday.

Paul Jones has voiced frustration with David Cameron, accusing the former Prime Minister of failing to follow through on his threats last year to impose strict laws on internet giants if they did not act. Speaking to Channel 5 News, Jones said progress on the issue has been insufficient. A Downing Street spokesperson acknowledged that “there is always more to do.”

Following the conviction of Mark Bridger, 47, for abducting and murdering their daughter, Coral and Paul Jones from Machynlleth, Powys, launched a high-profile campaign. Their five-year-old daughter, April, disappeared outside her home on 1 October 2012, and her body remains missing.

Jones criticized Cameron, stating, “I think he's hoodwinked us a little bit by coming out banging the drums, but hasn't actually put any money in place – he's left it to the internet [companies].” He added, “When I last met David Cameron I said 'aim high' – but he's fallen well short of the mark.”

In July last year, Cameron warned he would impose tough new laws on internet giants if they failed to blacklist key search terms linked to abuse images. By November, Google and Microsoft had pledged to implement software that would automatically block 100,000 “unambiguous” search terms associated with illegal content.

The Bridger trial focused attention on internet abuse after it emerged he had accessed child abuse images online just hours before abducting April. Following this, Cameron met with April’s parents to discuss the issue and potential solutions.

A Downing Street spokesperson said, “The Prime Minister has personally led efforts to eradicate child abuse imagery from the web, including establishing a new National Crime Agency, nationwide child-safe internet filters, and the first-ever agreement from major search engines to block illegal images in the past year. Of course, there is always more to do, and we continue to work with other countries, industry, and groups to explore further action.”

Piers Linney, the 43-year-old digital entrepreneur, has confirmed he will leave Dragons' Den after the 12th series to "pursue other interests." Alongside Linney, Kelly Hoppen and Duncan Bannatyne will also depart, leaving Peter Jones as the sole original investor remaining. Deborah Meaden will continue her role on the show.

Reflecting on his tenure, Linney said, "After hearing over 200 pitches and making nine deals, I have had a fantastic experience." He added, "I feel honoured to have contributed to such an iconic, long-running TV show and to have been the first Dragon with Afro-Caribbean heritage." Linney described his time on the programme as "a great experience and a pleasure to share with millions of viewers the growing importance of digital innovation."

While he believes the timing is right to move on, Linney intends to keep supporting entrepreneurship and diversity, causes close to his heart. "I've got many more things I want to do in life – and I've got family as well, so time is at a premium," he said.

The married father of two joined Dragons' Den in 2013 alongside Kelly Hoppen. He plans to remain engaged with the companies he has backed, including digital picture book publisher Lost My Name. Other investments include self-tanning brand Skinny Tan, festival and clubbing holiday operator Mainstage Travel, and customised trainers company Skribbies.

Linney has not ruled out a future return to television, stating, "I might do TV again. I'm good at being me and if something reflects my interests, it might be something I'm interested in doing." He previously appeared on Channel 4’s The Secret Millionaire in 2011.

Dragons' Den continues to air on BBC Two on Sundays at 21:00 GMT. Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

Two men wearing lifejackets were thrown into the water between Fortrose and Avoch and remained there for about 35 minutes before the alarm was raised. The Kessock Lifeboat launched at 12:30 and arrived on scene seven minutes later. Upon arrival, the North Kessock crew found the men had climbed back into their waterlogged boat but were suffering from hypothermia.

Volunteer helmsman Stan MacRae explained that the dinghy took on water due to the conditions, and the men were unable to bail it out quickly enough, leading to the capsize. After assessing their condition, the crew brought the men aboard the lifeboat and arranged for them to be winched into a coastguard rescue helicopter.

By 12:56, the men were aboard the helicopter and flown to Raigmore Hospital in Inverness. The Inverness Coastguard Team also assisted in the rescue. Meanwhile, the Kessock Lifeboat crew recovered the sailing boat and towed it back to Fortrose.

Following a recent update that disrupted users' access to internal company networks, Russian cybersecurity firm Kaspersky Labs advised disabling its anti-virus software or rolling back the update. Two hours later, the company issued a fix; however, because affected PCs could not automatically install the new code, users needed to complete several steps first. Kaspersky directed customers to disable the web anti-virus component in their managed computers' protection policy, download the update from the repositories section, and then re-enable protection. The company apologized for the inconvenience caused by the database update error and stated that measures have been implemented to prevent similar incidents in the future.

On Twitter, Dorset-based IT consultant Graham Lord criticized the update, saying, "Bravo on breaking the internet on all your XP clients. Your update just set back one of my repair jobs by a day's work." In contrast, Spain-based security blogger David Barroso acknowledged the error but commended Kaspersky’s prompt response, tweeting, "So Kaspersky QA [quality assurance] team failed with this update but they quickly released a fix, which it is something good."

Private Matthew Boyd of the Royal Gibraltar Regiment was discovered injured and unconscious in Brecon early Sunday morning and later died. Two men have been arrested in connection with his death.

Elaine Mawhirk said Matthew had long aspired to be a soldier, joining the Army at 16 with his parents' consent. He was nearing the renewal of his four-year contract and was making good progress in his military career.

Though Boyd and his family lived in Gibraltar, he was originally from Northern Ireland, where some relatives still live in Carrickfergus, County Antrim. Mrs. Mawhirk explained that he volunteered for a training exercise in Brecon to fill a shortage of personnel, stepping forward to assist in training new recruits. She highlighted his close friendships and strong support within his regiment.

Tributes from his regiment in Gibraltar have been described as deeply moving. Boyd’s aunt said the family is devastated by his death, remembering him as fun-loving and full of life, with many achievements by age 21. She also recalled family holidays in Spain, noting that future trips will never be the same without him.

Welsh police have arrested a 23-year-old man on suspicion of murder and detained a 22-year-old man in connection with the case. Both remain in custody. Dyfed-Powys Police confirmed Boyd was found wearing civilian clothes and that the 23-year-old arrested is not an active soldier.

The 27-year-old athlete from Norwich, named among BBC Sport's Paralympic Ones to Watch for 2015, has suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament. This injury will rule him out of this week’s International Blind Sports Federation World Games in Korea, where Great Britain is sending a four-member judo team.

Drane, who earned bronze at last year’s World Championships, addressed the emotional challenges that come with injury. He started judo as a teenager but transitioned to visually impaired judo at 22 after his eyesight worsened due to corneal dystrophy. Despite this setback, he remains determined to secure a place on Great Britain’s squad for the 2016 Paralympics in Rio. “My intentions remain the same as when I first started this journey—to do everything in my power to shape my best performance to Rio 2016. The rest is just uncontrollable,” he said.

With Drane sidelined, Great Britain’s medal hopes in judo rest on London 2012 silver medallist Sam Ingram (-90kg). Alongside Ingram, Chris Skelley (-100kg), Jack Hodgson (+100kg), and Natalie Greenhough (-70kg) are working to earn qualification points for Rio. Great Britain will also compete in the women’s goalball and men’s football events in Korea.

For the next three days, bus replacements will run on rail routes between Great Yarmouth and Norwich, Marks Tey and Sudbury, and Ipswich and Felixstowe. The company attributed these cancellations to necessary repairs on trains with damaged wheels.

A spokesman for the train operator explained that Abellio’s diesel trains have sustained wheel damage caused by poor rail conditions, leading to excessive wear that must be repaired before the trains can return to service. On average, two trains per day are affected, more than double the rate seen in previous autumn periods.

Great Yarmouth MP Brandon Lewis described the situation as "unacceptable," emphasizing the importance of this period for the high street, particularly with new shops opening. He criticized Abellio for poor stock management, stating, "At a time when we are trying to encourage people into the centre of Great Yarmouth, this is just not good enough."

Ian Edwards, chairman of the Marks Tey and Colchester Rail Users Group, also expressed concerns, saying Abellio has not invested sufficiently and appears focused solely on cost savings, which he called inadequate.

An Abellio spokesman apologized for the ongoing cancellations affecting local routes and confirmed the company is working to repair the trains as quickly as possible. The operator is also cooperating with Network Rail to improve rail conditions and prevent further damage.

A Network Rail spokesman said additional rail cleaning trains and extra staff have been deployed to help maintain services. He assured that all efforts are being made to minimize disruption and that Network Rail will continue collaborating with Abellio.

In the wake of the Grenfell Tower fire that resulted in 79 fatalities, housing association Gentoo removed certain materials as a precaution. So far, 60 buildings across 25 council areas have failed combustibility tests. In Sunderland, cladding was taken down from five blocks: Zetland, Church North, Dock, Dame Dorothy, and the Victor block of flats.

Gentoo confirmed none of its properties featured the same cladding as Grenfell Tower but moved ahead with the removal to reassure residents. The company said, "We took the precautionary measure to remove a small amount of decorative panelling from five of our blocks in the St Peter's area. We are also carrying out face-to-face reassurance meetings with our residents as part of this exercise to ensure the ongoing safety of our customers."

An elderly resident on the 13th floor of the Victor building, who wished to remain anonymous, expressed no concern, citing Gentoo's regular fire safety checks. He added, "Gentoo is always doing things to keep the residents happy."

Meanwhile, a petition has been launched calling on the owners of another student accommodation block to notify residents if their building is affected. St James Point, owned by Brookfield Student Real Estate, accommodates 80 Newcastle University students and more than 200 others. A company spokesperson stated the building was designed to the highest fire safety standards.

Steph Mosley of Acorn, a renters’ rights group, commented, "We don't know what is in the cladding. We've been told that it follows regulations. But people at Grenfell were told that regulations had been followed. We are after specifics—is the cladding the same? What is it made of? Is it flammable? The residents really need to know."

Gentoo confirmed it does not intend to remove any further cladding from its properties.

Controlled explosions will bring down the towers at East Lothian power station at noon on Saturday, 26 September, followed shortly by a second blast to demolish the turbine hall. For safety, an exclusion zone will be established from 09:00, covering Greenhills, parts of Edinburgh Road, the John Muir Way, and extending into the Firth of Forth. Traffic restrictions around the power station will begin earlier, at 07:00.

Scottish Power has cautioned that viewing opportunities close to the site will be very limited. Police Scotland and East Lothian Council have encouraged spectators to plan their viewing locations in advance. Insp Andy Harborow said: "The iconic Cockenzie chimneys have stood within the local community for nearly fifty years, and we expect many people to attend their demolition. To keep everyone safe, we have worked with East Lothian Council and Scottish Power to establish a suitable exclusion zone. No vantage points or parking spaces have been allocated for viewing, so visitors are asked to respect the local community and minimise disruption."

Each of the twin chimneys stands 149 meters tall and was constructed for the coal station’s opening in 1967. The turbine hall is mainly made of steel. The demolition will be initiated by a "button press" performed by East Lothian resident Donald McCulloch, who won the honor in a charity raffle.

Lisa Foster, 36, from Derbyshire, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer—the most advanced stage—three weeks ago. Since then, she has launched a fundraising campaign to cover the cost of a caregiver for her three children—Ruby, seven; Zach, four; and Scarlett, seven and a half months—while she receives treatment. The funds will also support her husband if her condition worsens.

Foster’s primary motivation is to live long enough for Scarlett to remember her. She hopes to witness Scarlett’s first steps and words, see Zach start school, and watch Ruby begin secondary education. To capture these moments, she is recording videos for her children to view at milestones such as their 18th birthdays.

Her online fundraiser has exceeded its £50,000 goal, attracting donations from over a thousand supporters. Foster expressed her gratitude, saying, "I just can't believe the generosity of this world and I will be forever grateful to all of those hundreds who have donated. They really have helped me." She added, "I want to enjoy every single minute, of every single day, of every single month now of what I've got left."

Reflecting on the support she has received, Foster said, "A lot of people have said they feel for me because they're a similar age and they have three children." She concluded, "If I can get a year that means I can see Zach's first day at school, I can see Scarlett maybe start walking or saying her first word, and that's what's going to keep me going."

A survey by Dogs Trust Bridgend found that 52% of Cardiff residents consider dog poo their top frustration in public spaces, ranking it above smoking and littering. The survey also showed that 40% encounter dog poo more than once a week, while 57% said they feel "too polite" to confront dog owners.

The Big Scoop campaign reminds pet owners that failing to clean up after their dogs can result in fines. Alex Jackson, head of campaigns at Dogs Trust, said, "Dog poo is among the top complaints local authorities receive each year. It’s vital that everyone understands how easy it is to properly dispose of dog mess."

A spokesperson for Cardiff council noted that dog fouling has "fallen significantly" since 2015, when a city-wide survey ranked it as the third most pressing concern for residents, behind litter and fast food-related rubbish. The council is updating its street management by "bringing different service areas together to improve the cleanliness of all council land in neighbourhoods across the city."

He added, "Dog owners must take responsibility by clearing up after their pets. The same applies to those who litter; such behavior is unacceptable and will not be tolerated. Our combined efforts are essential to keeping Cardiff clean and tidy."

The Ospreys’ quarter-final fixture has been relocated to Cardiff, coinciding with Swansea City’s Premier League match against Middlesbrough at their home ground. Broadcasters moved Swansea’s game to Sunday, with Paul Clement’s side kicking off at 13:30 GMT. Later that day, the Ospreys will take on Stade at 17:45 GMT.

After earning top seed status for the knockout stages of European club rugby’s second-tier competition, the Ospreys’ quarter-final venue was initially undecided. European Professional Club Rugby, the tournament organizer, confirmed the dates and times for all eight quarter-finals across both the Champions Cup and Challenge Cup.

With Swansea’s potentially televised match against relegation-threatened Middlesbrough rescheduled to Sunday, the Ospreys examined alternative venues beyond the Liberty Stadium. Options included the Principality Stadium and Cardiff City Stadium, although the team reportedly preferred not to move the game to the closer Parc y Scarlets in Llanelli.

Speaking to BBC Wales Sport, Ospreys commercial manager Huw Warren said, “It’s a positive move. It’s our first home European quarter-final and a huge match. We looked at all the options on the table. Clearly it’s the best option both for on the field with Steve [Tandy, head coach] and the team but it’s also a commercial opportunity for us in Cardiff for what is a massive game. Ultimately it’s a massive opportunity for us as a brand to take the game there and hopefully our supporters understand and come and support us.”

UK house prices rose by 1.1% in June, rebounding from a 0.2% decline in May. The average price increased by £2,590 to £211,301, while annual growth picked up to 3.1% from 2.1% in May. Meanwhile, London recorded its slowest annual price rise since 2012, with a 1.2% year-on-year increase.

Nationwide economist Robert Gardner warned that "monthly growth rates can be volatile, even after accounting for seasonal effects." He highlighted a regional shift, noting that slower price growth in the south of England is now more in line with trends elsewhere in the country. In the second quarter, the gap between the strongest growth region, East Anglia at 5%, and the weakest, the North of England at 1%, narrowed to its smallest on record. However, Gardner emphasized that significant price disparities between regions remain.

Gardner also pointed to London’s "particularly marked slowdown," with its 1.2% annual growth ranking as the second slowest among the UK’s 13 regions. Industry experts described these regional shifts as significant. Jonathan Hopper, managing director of Garrington Property Finders, remarked, "For London's house prices to be growing at the second slowest rate in the country would have been unthinkable for much of the past decade." He added that growth is now more evenly distributed across the UK, creating a fragmented market of smaller hotspots and coldspots.

Nationwide further cautioned that rising living costs are expected to dampen household spending, creating a "drag" on housing market activity. Despite this, the building society forecasts house prices to rise by 2% this year, supported by a shortage of new homes and limited properties coming onto the market.

The 33-year-old sustained an injury in February while playing for Western Australia, which worsened just before a planned return in March. As a result, he is expected to miss the start of the upcoming season. Toby Radford, coach of Glamorgan’s County Championship Division Two side, said, "It could be a couple of weeks, it could be longer. As soon as we can get the proper scan done, we'll know where we stand."

Glamorgan’s Division Two campaign kicks off on 12 April with an away fixture against Leicestershire, followed by a home match against Surrey a week later. Hogan has been a key strike bowler over the past two seasons, taking 98 wickets last season across all competitions despite missing three weeks on paternity leave.

Speaking to BBC Wales Sport, Radford said, "He was running around [at Swalec Stadium] and looking in good shape in some ways, [but] we just don't know how bad the injury is. He only experiences pain when he bowls, so we'll have a scan next week, see where he's at, and then we can make a real plan for when he returns."

Although several players lack experience, Radford is weighing the option of signing a loan player or facing Leicestershire with his current bowling options. He added, "It is [inexperienced], but Ruaidhri Smith didn't do himself any harm [against Cardiff MCCU], David Lloyd batted and bowled well, and Craig Meschede bowled very well."

Other seam bowlers available include Will Owen and Dewi Penrhyn-Jones. Jack Murphy, also part of the county squad, took two wickets playing for Cardiff universities against Glamorgan in the final warm-up match. The game ended in a draw, with Glamorgan scoring 434-7 and Cardiff MCCU finishing on 110-8.

Following the inspection, Leodegar Tenga, head of Caf's delegation, affirmed that Cameroon is ready to "organise a good competition." He highlighted progress at hotels and stadiums, stating, "The competition is not tomorrow but in November, and we believe that everything will be perfect by then." Tenga also commended the pitch, calling the grass "good, exactly what is needed - the best in the continent."

He acknowledged that visa and transportation issues may still require resolution before the tournament but expressed confidence in Cameroon’s ability to host a successful event. The inspection team visited Yaounde, Buea, and Limbe, and thanked the organising committee for their warm reception, which Tenga said "facilitated our work."

Recognising the challenges of organising the competition, Tenga conveyed Caf President Issa Hayatou’s gratitude to the Cameroon government for agreeing to host the tournament. Scheduled from 19 November to 3 December, the African competition will feature eight teams: holders Nigeria, hosts Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Ghana, Kenya, Egypt, Zimbabwe, and South Africa.

In a recent interview on Howard Stern's radio show, actor Jamie Foxx revealed that Oprah Winfrey had criticized his "gallivanting" and warned him he was "blowing it." Foxx, 49, said Winfrey arranged a meeting with Sidney Poitier to help him grasp the significance of his Academy Award nomination.

The meeting took place one week before the 2005 Oscars, where Foxx won Best Actor for his portrayal of Ray Charles in Ray. That same year, he was also nominated for Best Supporting Actor. Foxx later appeared in Quentin Tarantino's western Django Unchained.

Looking back, Foxx admitted he was "going hard," drinking and engaging in reckless behavior without realizing he was "messing up." An unexpected call from Winfrey led him to Quincy Jones’s home, where the producer encouraged him: "You're doing good, man, we just don't want you to blow it, baby."

At the gathering, Foxx met veteran Black actors from the 1960s and 1970s who offered their support. Sidney Poitier, present on his birthday, February 20, told Foxx that his portrayal of Charles in Taylor Hackford’s film had made him "grow two inches." Foxx said the meeting helped him understand the true importance of his nomination.

Describing the experience as "the most significant time in my life" and "a chance to grow up," Foxx recently appeared in the crime thriller Sleepless and will soon portray a volatile bank robber in the action comedy Baby Driver.

For more entertainment news, follow BBC News Entertainment on Facebook, Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or Instagram at bbcnewsents. Story suggestions can be emailed to entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

The Australia international was forced to leave the field after being struck on the head by a throw from the boundary. Carberry scored 107 and, alongside an unbeaten Liam Dawson (87*), added exactly 100 runs before Carberry was caught off James Harris’s bowling. In the final 10 overs, Harris, Toby Roland-Jones (3-87), and Tim Murtagh took wickets as Hampshire concluded their innings at 315-7.

Hampshire lost opener Jimmy Adams early, with captain James Vince, an England Test hopeful, following for 25 when he was caught by Voges off Roland-Jones. Shortly after surpassing his half-century, Carberry was dropped at second slip off Murtagh’s bowling. Having previously failed to convert a fifty into a century on 10 occasions in 2015, Carberry seized the opportunity to reach three figures.

After Carberry’s dismissal, Middlesex claimed the wickets of Adam Wheater, Ryan McLaren, and Chris Wood, raising hopes of restricting Hampshire’s total. Should Voges be diagnosed with concussion, he will be sidelined for a minimum of six days under England & Wales Cricket Board protocols.

Speaking to BBC Radio London, Middlesex managing director of cricket Angus Fraser said, “The feeling from the physio is that Adam has got concussion. It was a freak injury. It’s sad for Adam and disappointing for us, as we are not going to have any more use of him in this game. He wasn’t feeling very well in the dressing room, so we decided to get him taken to hospital. He feels a lot better now and seems to be coming around. He wants to remain here and be part of what is taking place, even if he can’t do anything on the field.”

Two of the three girls involved said they acted as anyone else would under similar circumstances. They feared the victim might drown during a violent attack by two men who were under the influence of alcohol and drugs, and hoped others would do the same in their position. Their actions in Wrexham were acknowledged by a crown court judge.

Natasha Bostock and Tia Platt, who were 13 at the time and are now 14, said they did not consider themselves heroes. "I could not believe it," Natasha said. "They were punching, kicking and stamping on him, and holding his head under the water." Despite the risk to their own safety, the girls went to the River Gwenfro and shouted at the attackers to stop.

As the girls approached, Paul Loose, 24, and Ryan Roberts, 18, both from Wrexham, fled the scene. The girls then assisted the victim, Jason Mee, 26, from the river, took him to nearby steps, gave him jumpers to keep him warm, and stayed with him until police and ambulance arrived.

Both Loose and Roberts pleaded guilty to wounding. Loose received a sentence of 28 months in prison, while Roberts was given 20 months in youth custody.

Since taking over this summer, McClaren has overseen United's drop to 19th place in the Premier League and their League Cup exit to an under-strength Sheffield Wednesday. Speaking to BBC Sport, Howey dismissed calls for a managerial change as "a knee-jerk reaction" and "ridiculous at this point," adding, "We have to wait until at least Christmas."

Howey, who contributed to Newcastle’s second-tier title win and was part of Magpies squads that finished as Premier League runners-up twice in the 1990s, urged the current players to "take a long hard look at themselves." He acknowledged, "Everyone can get beaten and we have already seen that this season, but it is the way, attitude and sometimes how easily they go down."

Reflecting on his playing career, Howey said, "When I was playing, and even afterwards, teams didn't like coming to St James' Park because it was hostile and it was difficult to win there." He described Newcastle’s current form as "basically there for the taking," calling it "horrifically disappointing," and stressed, "the fans expect better."

Newcastle will host reigning champions Chelsea on Saturday, with only local rivals Sunderland below them in the Premier League standings. On the club’s struggles, Howey said, "It wouldn't be the same in the North East if there wasn't all this turmoil. Every year they say it's going to be different, but it ends up being the same. The football at the moment is not even good."

He warned that unless Newcastle and Sunderland improve, "you can see them both going down and Middlesbrough coming up." He concluded, "This area is a hotbed of football. It's a pity the teams aren't as good as the fans are."

While Arsène Wenger was in Rome for a charity match, the 23-year-old completed a £16 million transfer from his boyhood club Manchester United to Arsenal. Wenger remarked, "If I'd stayed at home he wouldn't be here now," but declined to provide further details. Though he initially aimed to sign Welbeck on loan with an option to buy, Wenger was ultimately "happy" to make the deal permanent. He did not confirm whether Welbeck would start against Manchester City on Saturday.

On Welbeck’s potential starting role, Wenger said, "I cannot tell you if Welbeck will start but it's a possibility. I have to assess the squad." Welbeck, who scored both goals in England’s 2-0 victory over Switzerland on Monday, expressed confidence in his ability to score regularly if given consistent opportunities as a striker. He stated, "Once I get into the box and get the opportunities I have got faith in my ability. Before I wasn't getting into the box because I wasn't playing too much as a striker and I had to worry about my defensive work. Once I get the opportunity and a run of games up front I will do my best."

Midfielder Aaron Ramsey could also be fit to start against the Premier League champions at the Emirates Stadium. Ramsey twisted his ankle earlier this week during Wales’ 2-1 win over Andorra on a 3G pitch. Wenger said, "His ankle injury will be assessed today, he has a little chance of playing on Saturday." He added he was "relieved" the injury was not serious, recalling Ramsey’s muscular injury last year that sidelined him for three months. Ramsey had previously expressed confidence he would be ready for Saturday’s match.

Uber and Lyft contested city council regulations mandating fingerprint-based background checks for drivers before they could operate. These rules, which were introduced in December 2015, were upheld by a public vote. Both companies expressed disappointment with the result. The regulations were designed to bring Lyft and Uber under the same standards as traditional taxi services.

According to US broadcaster NPR, Uber invested $8 million (£5.5 million) in a campaign supporting self-regulation through Proposition One. Nonetheless, 55% of the 87,212 votes cast opposed the measure.

Chris Nakutis, General Manager of Uber Austin, stated, "Disappointment does not begin to describe how we feel about shutting down operations in Austin. We hope the city council will reconsider their ordinance so we can work together to make the streets of Austin a safer place for everyone." At the time of reporting, Uber continued to display fare estimates for rides within the city.

Lyft criticized the regulations, saying they "don't allow true ride-sharing to operate," and added that the rules "make it harder for part-time drivers, the heart of Lyft's peer-to-peer model, to get on the road and harder for passengers to get a ride."

During early discussions on the regulations, Austin Mayor Steve Adler told the Texas Tribune, "Ultimately our goal is to not keep any particular company here or not here." Despite this, many social media users pointed out that it was the companies' decision to withdraw. Burnie Burns, founder of the comedy and gaming community Rooster Teeth, tweeted, "Not happy that Prop 1 in Austin failed, but less happy that Uber & Lyft put so many drivers out of work with less than 48 hours notice." Ben Wear, transport reporter at the American-Statesman, added on Twitter, "Prop 1's defeat wouldn't mandate that Uber or Lyft stop operating in Austin. That is entirely up to the companies."

Police report that Sean Cleathero, 28, is believed to have ingested 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP), a substance reportedly obtained from a local gym. The father of one became unwell and died at a hospital in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, on Wednesday. The coroner has been informed, and an investigation is ongoing.

In a statement, Cleathero’s family described him as "very loved and popular," expressing that his death was a "complete shock" to friends and relatives. They added, "He was a fun, loving, caring son, grandson, brother, and nephew. As a father, he leaves behind a three-year-old daughter who will carry on his infectious personality, which made him popular to all who knew him."

A police spokesperson confirmed that the coroner’s office referred the case to Thames Valley Police on Wednesday. The spokesperson said, "It is believed he may have taken 2,4-Dinitrophenol, a performance-enhancing drug obtained from a local gym."

The post-mortem examination was inconclusive. The spokesperson added, "The investigation into the cause of death continues, and further tests are required." Police are investigating any possible link between the drug and Cleathero’s death and have cautioned against using DNP tablets purchased from unofficial sources.

DNP is used to aid fat burning but carries serious risks, including dangerously high body temperatures that can cause brain damage and blindness.

The £49 million Pontio project, which was originally scheduled to premiere its first productions in September 2014, faced delays due to construction. Its opening will commence in October with a phased rollout, followed by the full programme launching in December. The new venue will house the Bryn Terfel Theatre, research facilities, and the students' union. Earlier this year, a construction worker described the project as "chaotic." Construction firm Galliford Try acknowledged encountering several challenges but maintained these were typical for a project of this scale. The centre’s artistic director, Elen ap Robert, said, "We will be gradually trialling small scale shows, artistic events and screenings." The Arts Council of Wales welcomed the announcement, stating, "As people have watched this remarkable building take shape, they will have been intrigued by what might be available inside. Now local residents, artists and students will be able to see for themselves, touring the building and experiencing firsthand this unique and innovative facility."

In 2015, HMP Woodhill in Milton Keynes recorded five suicides, the highest number among prisons in England and Wales that year. One of those who died was Kevin Scarlett, a 29-year-old from Milton Keynes who took his own life on 22 May 2013. Scarlett had been remanded at Woodhill in January 2013 after being charged with armed robbery. His family insists that missed opportunities to prevent his death remain unaddressed and claims that "nothing has changed" since.

Scarlett’s step-brother, Lee Jarman, said Kevin had mental health issues and that prison staff failed to recognize key warning signs, including self-harming and previous suicide attempts. Jarman expressed frustration that, three years after Scarlett’s death, no lessons have been learned.

Following the death, HMP Woodhill reviewed its procedures for supporting at-risk prisoners. Prison Minister Andrew Selous MP confirmed the review and said the prison introduced enhanced staff training and established a new task force aimed at reducing self-inflicted deaths. Selous stated, "We make every effort to learn from each death."

A report from the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman into Scarlett’s death also highlighted concerns about conditions at Woodhill. Ministry of Justice data shows that 89 people died by suicide in prisons across England and Wales in 2015, with Woodhill reporting the highest number at five. Exeter, Ranby, and Winchester each recorded four suicides.

The Howard League for Penal Reform called for increased use of non-custodial sentences for non-violent offenders. Its director, Frances Crook, warned of the dangers of imprisoning vulnerable individuals with mental health problems, saying, "We are locking up a lot of fragile people who have mental health problems alone for hours and it is very dangerous." Crook also cited overcrowding, noting that staff often lack time to build relationships with prisoners.

Authorities reported that an express train’s engine and three coaches derailed in Gaibandha district, trapping dozens of passengers. Gaibandha police chief Sajid Hossain told AFP that three trapped passengers—two men and one woman—have died. He added that five passengers rescued from one carriage remain in serious condition, while others suffered minor injuries. Private broadcaster Somoy estimated at least 40 people were injured.

Mahbubul Alam Bakshi, head of Bangladesh Railway’s northern region, called the derailment “an act of sabotage,” accusing protesters of deliberately removing “fishplates,” the metal bars that connect rails. Police said two members of the Islamist Jamaat-e-Islami party, allied with the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and barred from contesting the election, were detained at the scene.

The derailment happened amid rising political tensions over the planned 5 January elections. The opposition has rejected the date, demanded a transport blockade, and called for Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to hand over power to a neutral caretaker government to oversee the polls, a practice used in previous elections. Wednesday marked the fifth day of a nationwide blockade of rail, road, and waterway transport led by the BNP and 17 other opposition parties. The opposition has yet to respond to the derailment.

Ospreys head coach Steve Tandy is optimistic that the 30-year-old will extend his contract, which is due to expire at the end of this season. Meanwhile, former Ospreys coach Sean Holley anticipates interest from clubs in England and France in signing Jones.

Jones, who has earned 94 caps for Wales and appeared in six Tests for the British and Irish Lions, made his Ospreys debut in 2005. In March 2015, he agreed to a dual contract with the Welsh Rugby Union, with funding split 60% from the Union and 40% from the regional side.

“I have several factors to consider before making a final decision,” Jones said. “Everything is connected, and credit to the Ospreys and the [Welsh Rugby] Union for that. Ultimately, I will have to decide sooner or later.”

Discussing his future, Jones added, “I have a family now, so I need to make the choice that’s right for me. I’m not going to say culture is the biggest draw. In the end, I’ll have a job wherever I go or whatever I do. Even if I stay, I’ll still have a job. Financially, if that were my only motivation, I would have made different decisions during my previous two contract negotiations.”

Steven Jackson, 40, fatally stabbed his former partner, Kimberley MacKenzie, at a Montrose flat before dismembering her body in a bathtub. Michelle Higgins, 29, was sentenced to eight years in prison for assisting in the disposal of Ms. MacKenzie's remains. Following a five-week trial, both were convicted, although a High Court jury in Glasgow returned a not proven verdict on the murder charge against Higgins.

Judge Lady Rae condemned their conduct as "despicable and callous," calling the killing "a wholly motiveless and brutal murder of a defenceless woman." She further criticized their handling of the victim’s body, stating it exhibited "a level of depravity, thankfully, not often seen in these courts."

Evidence at trial showed that Ms. MacKenzie, 37, suffered at least 11 blows to the head and was stabbed more than 40 times. Both defendants blamed each other for the murder. Higgins testified that she was terrified of Jackson and only assisted in disposing of the body after he had killed Ms. MacKenzie.

While assisting his friend with a tyre change near Newmarket, Suffolk, 24-year-old Whiter was struck by a car. Jan Adamec, 40, has pleaded guilty to two counts of causing injury by dangerous driving and is due to be sentenced in September. Speaking to BBC Look East, Whiter said, "People have been in touch from the Paralympic side, I'd love to get involved. I can only dream and hope that one day I could be there. If I can focus with sport, it is going to help me progress more within myself and get me through these times."

The incident also left Whiter’s friend, Joey Abbs, a Soham Town Rangers player, with serious leg injuries. While Whiter showed interest in disability sport, he did not specify which sport he might pursue. At a fundraising event in Exning, Suffolk, supporting his rehabilitation, Whiter remarked, "You've got to have a dream, you've got to start somewhere. I know how hard it is to win a medal at the Paralympics, I'm not saying I am going to turn up and do it, but I would love to go."

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has refused the request to rest 30-year-old Stuart Broad. In Nottinghamshire’s opening match, Broad made a significant impact by bowling 21 overs and claiming four wickets in their 10-wicket victory over Leicestershire. Both Broad and fellow fast bowler James Anderson, who is currently unavailable for Lancashire, are expected to return for the third round of fixtures.

According to ECB director of cricket Andrew Strauss, “Both Stuart and Jimmy are committed to their counties and eager to play as much as possible. However, they also understand the challenges and demands ahead this summer. Counties were informed of the likely schedule back in January.”

While Nottinghamshire will be without their centrally contracted player Broad for the time being, another England pace bowler, Jake Ball, will be available after the ECB rested him for the opening game. England’s next Test is scheduled for 6 July, followed by seven Tests over just more than two months against South Africa and the West Indies, and then another seven Tests during the winter in Australia and New Zealand.

At 25, Duquemin holds the games records in both shot put and discus, having claimed gold in these events at the 2015 competition on home soil. However, the Gotland Games overlap with the British Championships, which also act as trials for the World Championships.

"I've got to put myself first," Duquemin told BBC Radio Jersey. "The main priority is the World Championships, and I have to do everything possible to qualify." He added that with the dates only recently announced, it seems unlikely he will be able to compete in the Island Games despite attempts to arrange flying into Gotland on the day to compete and then returning.

Among those confirmed to miss the Gotland Games are Jersey’s top-ranked tennis player Scott Clayton, international archer Lucy O'Sullivan, and cycling gold-medallist Kim Ashton. The biennial event is scheduled from 24 to 30 June 2017, while the British Athletics Team Trials will be held in Birmingham from 30 June to 2 July.

Following the Australian driver's victory, a group of men exposed swimwear displaying the Malaysian flag. Dubbed the "Budgie Nine," they have appeared in a Malaysian court and are expected to face charges. If found guilty of intentional insult and public indecency, they could face up to two years in prison.

The men have been held in Kuala Lumpur since their arrest on Sunday. Malaysian law allows detention for up to four days, after which the attorney-general's office may seek to extend their detention, press charges, or release them. The country enforces strict laws against public indecency, typically fining and deporting foreign offenders.

Photos taken Sunday at the Sepang track show the men standing before crowds wearing swimwear known in Australia as budgie smugglers. Abdul Aziz Ali, Sepang assistant police commissioner, said they were "caught in the act" and believes there is sufficient evidence to charge them. The group includes the son of Australia’s trade commissioner in Fukuoka, Japan, and an adviser to cabinet minister Christopher Pyne.

Officials from the Australian high commission and a local lawyer have visited the men. Australian driver Daniel Ricciardo told the Herald Sun, "It sounds like they have learned their lesson and I don't think they will be doing that again any time soon in Malaysia." He added, "I see it as pretty harmless. I respect the laws in Malaysia but beyond that I don't think they deserve any further punishment."

Foreign Minister Julie Bishop told the Nine Network that what might be seen as a foolish prank in Australia could be interpreted very differently overseas. "I don't know that it will be seen as a lapse of judgment," she said. "It was clearly premeditated. They were wearing the budgie smugglers and had bought them in Australia."

Corrie Mckeague, 23, from Fife, disappeared following a night out in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, on 24 September. His Nokia phone was tracked moving from Bury to Barton Mills but was never recovered. Suffolk Police stated that a phone discovered in Mildenhall, near Barton Mills, could not be linked to his disappearance. They added that the recovered device was missing key components, which led to the decision to cease further investigations into it.

On Monday, it emerged that Mr. Mckeague was expecting a child. Forbes McKenzie of McKenzie Intelligence Services, who supported the search, described the phone’s location as "key," saying, "Where the phone finished is indicative of where Corrie last was." He also expressed interest in identifying other phones found alongside Mr. Mckeague’s device.

The Nokia Lumia 435 is believed to have been housed in a black PVC case that was frayed and worn around the edges. Live updates on this case and other Suffolk news continue to be available.

Nearly all parents who applied for funded nursery places for their children—99.9%—have been successful, with only 16 applicants remaining on the waiting list. In April, the BBC reported that close to 800 applicants were still awaiting placement decisions. Education Minister Peter Weir welcomed the update, stating, "The department and the Education Authority have worked hard to meet demand for pre-school places, including approving or funding additional spots across both voluntary and statutory settings." He added that pre-school places remain available across Northern Ireland and that the Education Authority will continue to assist parents who have yet to secure a place.

On Friday, letters informing parents of the outcomes from the second stage of the application process were sent. Demand for funded pre-school places has risen in recent years, with schools applying several criteria to determine admissions. Legislation requires providers to prioritize children from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, particularly those whose parents receive Income Support or Jobseeker's Allowance. Additional considerations include whether a child has a sibling attending the school and the distance from home to school.

The Vulcan Hotel, which originally opened in 1853, was dismantled brick by brick last year and is currently kept in storage. St Fagans plans to rebuild the pub as it stood in 1915, with groundwork possibly beginning this year, subject to approval. Museum officials are inviting anyone with early photographs of the building to come forward.

Gerallt Nash, senior curator of historic buildings, confirmed that plans were submitted to Cardiff council last week. He stated, "We don’t have many early pictures. If anyone recalls visiting or has period photographs of the Vulcan, we would like to see them."

The museum has designated 1915 as the period for reconstruction. Nash explained, "Although the pub dates back to 1853, its substantial alterations in 1914 are our focus." The museum possesses copies of the architectural drawings from 1914.

The project will incorporate the hotel’s original exterior tiles showing its name and retain interior features such as a set of gentlemen’s ceramic urinals dating from 1914 or earlier. Nash added that running the pub as a working exhibit is still being considered.

Once located in Cardiff’s Newtown district, the Vulcan was a popular spot for the Irish community until the area was cleared during post-war redevelopment. The museum hopes the restored pub will help illustrate Cardiff’s growth and transformation at the turn of the 20th century.

The building was acquired through a compulsory purchase order five years ago, with final orders called in May 2012 as part of broader redevelopment plans.

A report from Germany-based analysts reveals that Germany has slipped below Japan to hold the lowest birth rate both in Europe and worldwide. Conducted by auditing firm BDO in collaboration with the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), the study found that over the past five years, Germany averaged 8.2 births per 1,000 inhabitants, slightly lower than Japan’s 8.4 per 1,000.

In Europe, Portugal and Italy followed in second and third place, with birth rates of 9.0 and 9.3 per 1,000, respectively. France and the UK each reported 12.7 births per 1,000 inhabitants. Globally, Africa recorded the highest birth rates, led by Niger at 50 births per 1,000 people.

Henning Voepel, director of HWWI, cautioned that Germany’s declining birth rate will reduce the working-age population (ages 20 to 65) from 61% to 54% by 2030. Arno Probst, a BDO board member, highlighted rising wage costs for employers and warned, “Without strong labour markets, Germany cannot maintain its economic edge in the long run.”

Experts remain divided over the causes of Germany’s low birth rate and the best ways to address it. Probst stressed the importance of young immigrant workers to fill a significant skills gap and increasing female workforce participation to avoid economic difficulties.
