Despite Germany’s high migration rate, support for the anti-immigration party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has grown.

These birth rate figures come despite Chancellor Angela Merkel’s government investing in childcare support.

Eyewitnesses reported that approximately 50 fans were inside the Bar BQ cafe in Brussels on Wednesday evening when up to 100 individuals attempted to force their way in. Marie Elizabeth, a bar employee, told BBC Radio London that Tottenham supporters were present as attackers arrived from outside and began striking patrons with chairs, tables, and glasses. One person sustained serious injuries during the assault.

Ms. Elizabeth described the atmosphere inside the bar as "very good" before the incident and stressed that Spurs fans "did not do anything to cause problems." She added, "It was very scary because it is the first time something like this has happened in the area. It wasn't expected and we didn't know what to do." She also said someone near the door managed to close it, preventing the attackers from entering fully, noting, "If they had come inside I don't know what was going to happen."

Several English fans were injured in the attack. Police and ambulance services were called and arrived to provide first aid. Tottenham supporter Sion Roberts shared photos on Twitter showing damage outside the bar, including displaced tables and chairs and damage to the frontage.

Supporters of the north London club have faced similar attacks abroad before, with incidents in Rome in 2012 and Lyon in 2013. Tottenham are scheduled to play Anderlecht on Thursday night.

Kevin Balmer, 52, and Brendan Cantwell, 44, provided bribes to council employees Charles Owenson, 62, and James Costello, 44, in order to secure contracts for Edinburgh Action Building Contracts Ltd (ABC Ltd) related to maintenance work on council buildings between 2006 and 2010.

All four men, who had earlier admitted guilt, were remanded in custody on Tuesday at Edinburgh Sheriff Court, with sentencing scheduled for Friday. Sheriff Michael O’Grady QC remarked, “Given the seriousness of the offences, it is clear the sentences will be custodial and substantial.”

In court, Balmer and Cantwell were identified as former directors of ABC Ltd, which went into liquidation in 2010. The proceedings also revealed that Cantwell now operates Action Scaffolding, a company that continues to legitimately serve Edinburgh City Council.

Court evidence indicated that Owenson and Costello received hospitality including corporate seats at Hibs and Hearts football matches, meals, bar outings, and cash payments. To cover the cost of these bribes, contractors submitted inflated invoices to the council. Fiscal Keith O’Mahony noted, “Essentially, the council was being charged for the cost of bribing its own officials.” The inflated invoices amounted to over £67,000.

The prosecutor described the hospitality as “extensive,” mentioning that drinks and lap dances were purchased for Owenson and Costello. The council employees also owned luxury cars, including an Audi TT Quattro and a Mercedes ML320. In total, they assigned work orders to ABC Ltd valued at nearly £1.5 million.

Ruth Pfau spent more than fifty years in Pakistan, during which she established 150 leprosy clinics across the country. Her work was pivotal in bringing leprosy under control by 1996. Yasmeen Morris, a staff member at Dr. Pfau’s national leprosy centre, called her passing "a big loss to humanity," and added, "It is very hard to find a person like her in today's era. Today, everyone thinks about themselves, but she never thought about herself. She led a very simple life and she loved humanity."

After a funeral service at St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Karachi, Dr. Pfau was laid to rest, her coffin draped with the Pakistani flag and adorned with rose petals. Prime Minister Shahid Khaqan Abbasi paid tribute, saying that although Dr. Pfau was born in Germany, "her heart was always in Pakistan." He remarked, "Dr Ruth came to Pakistan here at the dawn of a young nation, looking to make lives better for those afflicted by disease, and in doing so, found herself a home."

Dr. Pfau first encountered leprosy in Pakistan during the 1960s while serving as a medical missionary. Over her lifetime, she founded 150 clinics that treated tens of thousands of patients. Her dedication earned her several honors, including the Hilal-e-Imtiaz, Hilal-e-Pakistan, and the German Staufer Medal.

Coleman, who has previously managed Fulham, Coventry, and Real Sociedad, is considered by Ratcliffe a sensible choice to maintain continuity following Speed’s departure. Speaking to BBC Sport, Ratcliffe said, "I think we need a Welshman in charge and I do not think there were too many other candidates around who could come in." He noted that the FAW’s last managerial appointment was a close contest between Gary and Chris, making this decision a continuation of that process.

Ratcliffe also emphasized the financial advantage, pointing out that no compensation is required. He praised Coleman’s solid track record and reputation, stating, "Chris goes in there with a good track record and he's got a good reputation in the game." Describing Coleman as "a good man and a proud Welshman," Ratcliffe expressed confidence in his passion and commitment to advancing Gary’s work.

Coleman earned 32 caps for Wales and was an international teammate of Speed. Ratcliffe, who won 59 caps, commented, "He did very well for a long spell at Fulham. I know things didn't work out for him at Coventry City but financially things were tough and no one else has been able to do too well there."

Reflecting on recent events, Ratcliffe added, "Obviously there have been a lot of emotions after what happened with Gary but I think Chris is a good choice and deserves support. He has some very good, maturing young players to work with as well."

If the Moomins unsettle you, it might be wise to avoid Helsinki in March, when the Finnish National Ballet will stage a production featuring these characters. This marks the first dance adaptation of Tove Jansson’s creations. The production’s website notes that “the body of the Moomins isn’t the most flexible,” while other characters will “take care of the classical ballet part” in the show, which presents the story of Comet Moominland.

According to the synopsis, “When everything is not well in the Moominvalley, Moomintroll and his friends head to the Observatory on the Lonely Mountains.” There, they learn a comet is expected to hit Earth within days, posing the question: “Will the Moominvalley survive?”

Adult tickets are priced at 42 euros (£32.50). The show is recommended for children aged four and over, though older viewers who find the Moomins frightening may prefer to attend with an adult.

For the latest updates, follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

Five days after A-level results were published, Ucas announced that more than 463,000 university places have been confirmed, marking a 3% rise from the same period last year. Admissions increased by 4% among women and 2% among men, with 57,000 more women than men securing places so far this year.

The total includes nearly 35,000 students accepted through clearing, a 6% increase compared to last year. Alongside those who have accepted offers, about 63,000 applicants currently hold offers, while 144,000 remain without a confirmed place.

This trend points to a potential record number of students beginning full-time undergraduate courses this autumn. The data also reveal a widening gender gap: 34% of UK 18-year-old women and 25.1% of men have accepted places.

Compared with four years ago, nearly 6,000 more male students and over 13,000 more female students have accepted places. Of all accepted places, fewer than one quarter are held by 18-year-old UK men; the rest are taken by 18-year-old women, gap year students, mature students, and international students.

Regionally, Northern Ireland has the highest proportion of 18-year-olds attending university, with women there the most likely to secure a place. Within this group, 36.9% of women in Northern Ireland have gained university places, compared to 22% of 18-year-old men in Wales.

United have stretched their unbeaten run to six matches, with manager McKinnon urging his players to keep up their momentum. The Tannadice side, who finished 14 points behind Championship winners Hibs, are aiming for a swift return to the Scottish Premiership.

McKinnon described United as "the form side heading into these play-offs." The club secured third place in the second tier, concluding the regular season with a 1-1 draw away at Morton on Saturday.

Reflecting on recent performances, McKinnon said, "We should have won the last six games; we created enough chances to win all six, which is encouraging. On Saturday, we hit the woodwork five or six times." He underlined the team's strong form, stating, "We haven’t had the just rewards in these six games, but we approach the upcoming matches with the right mindset."

Last season, McKinnon’s Raith Rovers were eliminated from the play-off quarter-finals after a 2-1 aggregate loss to Hibernian. He has warned his current squad that they must perform at their best to progress and meet Championship runners-up Falkirk in the semi-final.

“If we’re at our best, we’ll be tough to beat,” McKinnon said. “That’s our focus going into these games—making sure we are at our best. We played extremely well there on Saturday and need to do the same again.” He also highlighted the importance of discipline, saying, “It’s not win or bust; it’s about controlling your game and your emotions. We’ve discussed this, and the players fully understand.”

The wave design artwork formed part of a £720,000 project to create a plaza outside the station. Along with this, a new statue of the Jolly Fisherman, the resort’s mascot, is being installed. The sculpture was fenced off in February 2012 after an accident. To deter people from using it as a "playground," Lincolnshire County Council plans to add metal studs to the artwork.

John Byford of East Lindsey District Council criticized the prolonged delay, saying, "Tens of thousands of people still arrived by train to Skegness and that first impression counts. We have to have it right for them and it’s not been right for nearly two years."

Colin Davie from Lincolnshire County Council described the situation as "health and safety gone mad," but added, "This should have been sorted out a long time ago, but I’m pleased we’ve now got a solution." The council has apologized for the delay and is coordinating the work with the installation of the new Jolly Fisherman statue. The mascot originally appeared on a 1908 railway poster promoting the Lincolnshire coastal resort.

Residents of Stanford near Folkestone have been informed after eggs of the Asian tiger mosquito were discovered in the area. Public Health England (PHE) has confirmed no further sightings of the insect and stressed that there is "currently no risk to public health in the UK." Jolyon Medlock, head of medical entomology at PHE, noted, "We regularly monitor mosquito species and look for any which are new to the UK." Following the initial finding, intensified surveillance was carried out but revealed no additional mosquitoes. As a precaution, PHE recommended insecticide spraying, which has now been completed by the local authority. The agency will maintain close monitoring of the situation. Two years ago, amid concerns that the mosquito might arrive in the UK via lorries from Europe, PHE set traps at motorway service stations, but no specimens were detected. The Asian tiger mosquito is associated with the Zika virus, which has been linked to thousands of babies born with underdeveloped brains.

At 24, Walkden secured a 7-1 victory over Morocco’s Wiam Dislam in the +67kg taekwondo event by landing two precise head shots. This win gave Team GB its third taekwondo medal at Rio, following gold from Jade Jones and silver from Lutalo Muhammad.

In the men’s +80kg division, 27-year-old Cho narrowly lost 5-4 to Brazil’s Maicon Siqueira. Cho had earlier defeated Iran’s Sajjad Mardani 4-3 in the quarter-finals but was eliminated by a last-second head kick from Azerbaijan’s Radik Isaev. Reflecting on his performance, Cho said, “I gave it my absolute everything but it’s disappointing not to come away with something after all the hard work from me and my team. One of us had to lose, and unfortunately, that was me.”

Walkden had previously beaten Serbia’s 2012 London champion Milica Mandic 5-0 but was edged out 4-1 by China’s Zheng Shuyin in a golden-point semi-final. Walkden commented, “I came here for gold, but my coach told me to fight for it. It’s still an Olympic medal. In Tokyo, I’ll aim to go further and win gold. It’s only four years away.”

Zheng went on to claim gold with a 5-1 victory over Mexico’s Maria Espinoza, while Isaev defeated Abdoulrazak Issoufou 6-2. Issoufou’s silver medal made Niger the 87th nation to win a medal at Rio, setting a new Games record.

For information on how to start taekwondo, see our special guide. Subscribe to the BBC Sport newsletter for news, features, and videos delivered directly to your inbox.

Following a suspected heart attack on a bus after the match against Fiji at Twickenham last Friday, 69-year-old Phil Nunnerley was saved by CPR performed by Richard Loach. Afterward, Mr Nunnerley launched a social media campaign to identify his rescuer, knowing only that he was wearing a Gloucester Rugby shirt. The two have since connected.

Dr Loach, a GP based on the Isle of Wight and formerly from Gloucester, reached out after reading the account on the BBC News website. He said, "Phil's a very lucky man. It was great to see him looking so well in the short video [in the BBC story]. I've spoken to him, and he sounds great. My wife and I were both involved and thrilled to see him doing well."

While traveling on the bus, Dr Loach and his wife noticed Mr Nunnerley appeared unwell. "We were minding our own business when we heard someone say 'stop the bus,'" he recalled. "He didn't look well. I had seen this before and thought we should help."

Dr Loach said Mr Nunnerley, from West Harptree, North Somerset, had no pulse when they began mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and chest compressions. Four paramedics continued treatment once the bus reached the park and ride. Dr Loach added, "Normally the outcome is not so good. I'm sure anyone else would have done the same."

Mr Nunnerley plans to meet Dr Loach soon to thank him in person.

David Cottrell, 90, from Redland, was honoured for his role in rescuing more than 70 Norwegians in June 1944. At 19, he served as an Able Seaman Gunner on HMS Swift, whose crew defied orders to save men after the Norwegian destroyer Svenner was torpedoed.

On 6 June 1944, near Sword Beach, Normandy, HMS Swift narrowly avoided torpedoes that struck and sank the Svenner. Cottrell recalled, "The ship broke in half and sank almost immediately. People were jumping over the sides." Despite instructions to leave survivors, Captain John Gower chose to rescue those in the water. Of the 219 crew on the Svenner, 32 Norwegians and one Briton died.

In 2001, Cottrell met two former Svenner crew members. One told him and Captain Gower, "What you've done, myself, my children, my grandchildren owe you a debt of gratitude that can never be repaid." Cottrell described the recognition as "a proud moment" in an interview with BBC Points West.

Nigel Fletcher, Norwegian consul for the South West, said Cottrell was nominated for the Commemorative Medal after meeting a Svenner survivor at a 2014 memorial in Norway marking the 70th anniversary. Fletcher added, "It's a great recognition and also allows him to reflect on his old shipmates and others with him that day."

David’s son, Richard Cottrell, expressed pride in his father’s actions, stating, "It's one story among thousands and they are all remarkable."

Ivor Bell, 79, from Ramoan Gardens in west Belfast, faces two charges related to the murder of a mother of ten, both of which he denies. Mrs. McConville was abducted from her Divis flats home by the IRA in 1972. She became one of the "disappeared," a term for individuals kidnapped, killed, and secretly buried by republicans during the Northern Ireland Troubles.

Bell was absent from the pre-trial hearing at Belfast Crown Court on Monday. His barrister informed the judge that Bell suffers from dementia associated with cardiovascular problems, preventing him from following the legal proceedings. The prosecution requested a psychiatric evaluation as well as full access to Bell’s medical records. The case was adjourned until 16 December.

Bell denies both counts of soliciting the murder of Mrs. McConville. Her remains were discovered by a member of the public in August 2003 on Shelling Hill beach in County Louth. No convictions have been made regarding her death. The prosecution’s case is built on tapes obtained from an oral history archive assembled by Boston College in the United States.

Delano Sam-Yorke gave the home side a strong start, scoring his fourth goal in three matches with a powerful header that left Sutton goalkeeper Will Puddy unable to respond. As Sutton gained momentum, Jamie Collins’ header struck the post. The visitors then levelled in an unusual manner when Terell Thomas’ clearance deflected off Sutton winger Kieron Cadogan. However, with seven minutes remaining, Gozie Ugwu seized on the rebound from his own shot to score the winning goal, lifting Woking out of the National League relegation zone.

This match report was provided by the Press Association.

Final score: Woking 2, Sutton United 1.

Second half highlights:
- Gozie Ugwu scored the decisive goal for Woking, putting them ahead 2-1.
- Woking made three substitutions: Jake Caprice replaced Joey Jones; Gozie Ugwu came on for Jamie Lucas; Connor Hall replaced Charlie Carter.
- Earlier, Kieron Cadogan equalised for Sutton to make it 1-1.
- Nathan Ralph (Woking) received a yellow card.

First half highlights:
- Woking led 1-0 at halftime.
- Sutton United brought on Gomis for Adam Coombes.
- Yellow cards were issued to Ismail Yakubu (Woking) and Ben Jefford (Sutton United).
- Delano Sam-Yorke opened the scoring.

The first half kicked off after lineups were announced and players completed their warm-ups.

In Luton, police spotted a car heavily loaded with sacks of grain and advised the driver to lighten the load. Despite the warning, he was seen again later and fined £300. Authorities reported that the driver had purchased 40 bags of rice, each weighing 20kg (44lb) and costing £15.49 from a cash and carry, totaling 800kg (1,764lb). With the fine included, the total cost amounted to £920.

On Friday night, officers from the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, and Hertfordshire road policing units stopped the vehicle on Dunstable Road. The driver was told to remove the basmati rice sacks and either redistribute the load or switch to a more suitable vehicle. He disregarded the advice and continued transporting the rice.

The vehicle was stopped again and taken to a weighbridge, where the driver was fined once more. He then arranged for a friend to assist in moving the sacks safely. Police later tweeted: "If you need to carry 800kg of rice, choose a suitable vehicle. This isn't it. Dangerously overweight."

William Friedkin, who directed the film adaptation of William Peter Blatty's novel, announced Blatty's death on Twitter, writing, "William Peter Blatty, dear friend and brother who created The Exorcist passed away yesterday."

Blatty published The Exorcist in 1971, and two years later, the film adaptation—also penned by him—was released. Although the production faced challenges and the initial reception was modest, the movie went on to become one of the highest-grossing films ever and is widely recognized as a horror classic.

Blatty’s widow, Julie Alicia Blatty, told the Associated Press that he died on Thursday at a hospital in Bethesda, Maryland, from multiple myeloma, a form of blood cancer.

On Twitter, horror author Stephen King paid tribute, saying, "RIP William Peter Blatty, who wrote the great horror novel of our time. So long, Old Bill."

Blatty earned an Oscar for best adapted screenplay for The Exorcist and later wrote and directed its second sequel, The Exorcist III. His other novels include Elsewhere, Dimiter, The Ninth Configuration, and Demons Five, Exorcist Nothing: A Fable. His film credits include A Shot in the Dark, The Great Bank Robbery, and Promise Her Anything.

For updates, follow us on Facebook, Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or Instagram at bbcnewsents. To suggest a story, email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

Ray Cope, a Royal Mail employee for 17 years, was initially expected to leave Lympstone, with a longer-serving colleague set to take over his role. However, after residents organized a campaign recognizing Mr. Cope as "part of the village," Royal Mail announced that "more changes have been made locally" and confirmed that "Ray will remain on his normal duty." Support for Mr. Cope appeared across the village in the form of posters, and several residents sent letters to Royal Mail following the announcement. Jennifer and Frederick Mather, who were involved in the campaign, described the news as "great" but said they plan to continue their online petition. Ms. Mather noted, "He will be with us for six months, at the end of which there will be another review." She added that Mr. Cope is "so grateful" and "doesn't know how he can thank the village enough," but they "will do our best" to support him. The Mathers also expressed their commitment to "not give up on wanting Ray to be here for the foreseeable future." Royal Mail spokesperson Mike Norman stated, "We are pleased that our customers in Lympstone have had such excellent service from one of our postmen." He added, "It is always gratifying when our customers recognise the hard work of their postman or woman," and confirmed that "as part of our ongoing reviews, more changes have been made locally," ensuring that "Ray will remain on his normal duty."

Mr. Reid, 75, is concluding nearly three decades in the Senate, where he has served as both majority and minority leader. In a video message, the Nevada senator announced his retirement, stressing it was neither a result of his recent exercise accident nor the Democrats’ loss of Senate control. “I want to be able to go out at the top of my game,” he told the New York Times.

Among those poised to step into the leadership role are Senators Dick Durbin of Illinois and Chuck Schumer of New York. Reid—a former amateur boxer—entered Congress as a Representative in 1983 and became Senate majority leader when Democrats reclaimed the chamber in 2007.

On January 1, Reid injured his eye and ribs in a fall during exercise. He said the recovery period gave him time “to ponder and to think” about his future, and that he had been weighing retirement for several months.

In his announcement, Reid vowed to press on for the Democratic Party over his remaining 22 months in office. “We have to make sure that the Democrats take control of the Senate again,” he said, adding that it would be “inappropriate for me to soak up all those resources” when they could better support other races.

After a hard-fought re-election in 2010, Reid could have faced another tough contest in 2016. He also cautioned Republicans, warning Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, “don’t be too elated,” since 22 months still remain in the term.

Andrew Griffiths credited NHS Wales’s integrated structure and an £11 million investment in computer infrastructure with reducing vulnerabilities. His department oversees systems across seven health boards. Although a cyber attack on Friday impacted health organizations in England and Scotland, Mr. Griffiths, director of NHS Wales Informatics Service (NWIS), told BBC Wales that maintaining vigilance and ongoing cybersecurity investments are vital amid increasing threats.

He stated, “We weren’t lucky; we were prepared, and that preparedness stood us in good stead.” He added, “No system is completely secure, but we had the systems, processes, and personnel in place to prevent the attacks from penetrating.” Griffiths explained that a common infrastructure across Wales allowed for easier patching and updates, while reduced fragmentation helped eliminate many vulnerabilities.

The director also praised staff dedication during the incident response. “I’m immensely proud of the on-call colleagues who came in. They contacted others who weren’t on call to join them. There was no hesitation… everyone worked superbly across the NHS. It was an excellent demonstration of cooperation.”

He cautioned against complacency and highlighted the importance of learning from the event. “We don’t want cyber attacks, and we cannot afford to be complacent. We must stay vigilant, continue investing wisely, and ensure our processes are effective. There will be lessons to learn from this experience. But it’s a good moment to recognize that planning, preparedness, and investment in common systems have truly paid off.”

WHAT HAPPENED IN WALES?

Following their 15-10 loss to Scarlets on New Year's Day, the Welsh capital region finds itself five points behind sixth-placed Ulster. Meanwhile, the Warriors, sitting fifth, hold a nine-point advantage over the Blues.

Warburton emphasized the importance of securing an away victory, stating, "We have to get a win up there. If we don't, then that top six is slowly slipping away." He continued, "There will be a big emphasis on going up there, putting a lot of pressure on ourselves to produce a big performance. Otherwise, it is going to be extremely difficult and we will be playing catch-up again."

The Pro12 season concludes with the top four teams advancing to the championship play-offs. Additionally, finishing in the top six would likely guarantee a place in the 2017-18 European Champions Cup. At present, Scarlets remain the only Welsh region to have qualified for this season's tournament.

Blues head coach Danny Wilson said his team missed an opportunity to secure a win at Parc y Scarlets, while Scarlets coach Wayne Pivac admitted his side was "hanging on a bit" late in the match. Despite earning a losing bonus point, Warburton—who captained the team in the absence of injured prop Gethin Jenkins—found little comfort in the result.

As the Blues prepare to take on Glasgow, who completed a European Champions Cup double over Racing 92 in December, the drive for a top-four finish remains a strong motivator. Warburton remarked, "It is extra motivation because we know if we lose any more than two or three more games, we are going to find it extremely difficult to get into that top six." He added, "There is pressure on all our games now. We have been decent at home, but away is where we have to improve."

Looking back on the season, Warburton noted, "We had a good win away at Munster at the start of the season, but if we want to be top six, then you have to go to a quality team like Glasgow and pick up wins." He also pointed to progress made recently: "We have made good signings, from a playing and coaching perspective, and we really need to kick on to that next level and get in that top six. It is a huge motivation for the players."

A survey by Public Health England of 731 women over 40 in England found that fewer than half of those over 70 could identify a breast cancer symptom other than a lump. The agency also reported that older women are more likely to delay visiting their GP. Each year, roughly one in three women diagnosed with breast cancer are aged 70 or older.

Public Health England’s Be Clear on Cancer campaign encourages older women to consult a doctor if they notice breast changes such as lumps or alterations to the nipple, skin, or breast shape. Jenny Harries of Public Health England said, “We want women 70 and over to be aware of their breasts and to recognise any changes, report any new symptoms and just remember that you’re not past it when it comes to breast cancer.”

About 9,500 women die from breast cancer annually, with over half (5,400) of these deaths occurring in women over 70. Sara Hiom, director of early diagnosis at Cancer Research, emphasized two key points from the campaign: breast cancer symptoms are not limited to lumps, and older women face the highest risk. She added, “We hope these latest Be Clear on Cancer adverts will encourage women, especially older ones, to tell their GP about any unusual or persistent changes to their breasts, be that a lump, or something else like discharge, or a change to the skin or nipple.” Hiom also noted that early diagnosis generally improves treatment outcomes regardless of age.

The survey showed only 48% of women over 70 could name a symptom other than a lump. Currently, women under 50 and over 70 are excluded from the national breast screening program, though a trial is underway to assess the benefits of extending screening to women aged 47-49 and 71-73. Breast cancer remains the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women in England, with approximately 41,000 new cases each year.

Only one Briton, Scot Alain Baxter, has achieved a higher World Cup slalom finish, coming fourth in Åre, Sweden, in 2001. The leading British result in alpine skiing remains Konrad Bartelski’s second place in the downhill at Val Gardena, Italy, 35 years ago.

Ryding, from Lancashire, had never previously reached the top 10. He told BBC Sport, "I am delighted. I am sure no one expected a Brit in the top six! I have been skiing well and performing in training, but this was better than I would have expected. I really had to focus before the second run and give it everything to stay up the rankings. I was aiming for a solid top 15, so sixth is amazing."

Now 29 years old and preparing for his third Winter Olympics in 2018, Ryding continues to compete without UK Sport funding. In Finland, he was fourth after the first run on a foggy Levi course, but a few mistakes cost him a podium spot.

Austrian world number one Marcel Hirscher claimed his 40th World Cup win, finishing ahead of compatriot Michael Matt, while Italy’s Manfred Molgg took third place.

Ryding’s performance capped a successful weekend for British winter sports, with snowboarders Aimee Fuller and Billy Morgan finishing fourth and seventh respectively at a World Cup big air event in Milan. The big air discipline is set to make its Olympic debut at the Pyeongchang Games in February 2018.

On Friday, Emirates airline announced a £3.5 million sponsorship deal for the Spinnaker Tower. Nearly 10,000 people signed an online petition over the weekend opposing plans to repaint the currently white tower in red and white—the colors of Southampton's football club and Portsmouth’s main rivals.

Council leader Donna Jones described the strong public backlash as "extremely worried and concerned." She said, "I am passionate about this city. I was born here and have lived here all my life... Likewise I love Portsmouth Football Club, the Royal Navy and our heritage. I fully understand people's feelings about blue being the city's colour and the city emblem."

Following discussions with Emirates, Portsmouth FC chief executive Mark Catlin, and other stakeholders, Jones confirmed that a new design is being developed to better reflect the city’s heritage.

The tower will be renamed the Emirates Spinnaker Tower, with the revised design set to be unveiled soon. The branding is planned to be installed before the America's Cup World Series sailing event in July and will remain for five years.

The petition opposing the changes read, "To allow the colours of Southampton to stand tall on one of our city's most prominent landmarks shows an incredible lack of empathy for the residents. It must be stopped." Southampton FC supporter Paul Andrews tweeted, "All it needs now is the #SaintsFC badge at the top."

Portsmouth Football Club’s colors are blue and white. The 560-foot (170-meter) tower, opened in 2005, is owned by the council and operated by a private company.

Following earlier alerts of severe gale-force winds from Tuesday afternoon, a heavy rain warning has now been issued. The wind advisory begins at 15:00 on Tuesday and remains in effect through Wednesday. Persistent heavy rain is forecast for Wednesday, with the greatest amounts expected over south-facing hills.

An amber warning covers Strathclyde; Central, Tayside and Fife; and Dumfries, Galloway, Lothian and Borders. The Met Office explained, "A waving cold front is expected to become slow moving over western Britain during Tuesday night and much of Wednesday, associated with a strong, moist southwesterly airflow." Rainfall totals are predicted between 2cm and 4cm, with some higher ground receiving up to 8cm. Exposed areas in southwest Scotland may see 10cm to 15cm (4 to 6 inches) of rain.

Wind gusts of 50-60 mph are expected across many areas, with some exposed locations reaching up to 70 mph. Jim Fraser, emergency planning officer for Scottish Borders Council, noted, "The risk depends heavily on the amount and location of rainfall, and there is still some uncertainty about these details and the timing." He urged residents to remain vigilant and regularly consult the Met Office and SEPA websites for updates on weather and flood warnings. Fraser added, "People should start preparing for this heavy rain now to help reduce its impact when it arrives."

The United Reformed Church (URC) has voted to permit same-sex weddings, following a decision by its ruling general assembly at a meeting in Merseyside. Individual congregations will not be required to participate. With around 60,000 members, the URC—a Protestant denomination with Presbyterian roots—becomes the largest Christian organization in Britain to allow same-sex marriages in its churches.

During its session in Southport, the assembly approved a motion enabling churches to register immediately as venues for same-sex marriage ceremonies if they wish. Church officials anticipate that the first weddings under this policy could take place from autumn.

Rev John Proctor, general secretary of the URC, said, "Today the URC has made an important decision—at which some will rejoice and with which others will be uncomfortable." He stressed that congregations opposed to conducting same-sex marriages will not be compelled to do so, describing the issue as sensitive for many in the church and emphasizing the importance of careful deliberation and listening throughout the process.

Quakers, Unitarians, and several smaller denominations have already performed same-sex marriage ceremonies. The Scottish Episcopal Church’s general synod is scheduled to hold a final vote next summer on permitting same-sex couples to marry in churches, following a large majority vote in favor earlier this year.

Village Bakery’s shops in Wrexham, Rhos, Llangollen, Ruthin, and Holywell will now be overseen by Nantwich-based Chatwins, as Village Bakery shifts its focus to its rapidly growing wholesale business.

Robin Jones, managing director of Village Bakery, explained that the decision was made to sell all five shops as a group rather than individually. “While selling separately might have been commercially sensible, we accepted the best offer instead of the highest to ensure the shops remain a going concern and to safeguard the future of our valued staff,” he said.

Retail manager Sharon Cooper said that after an initial surprise, she and her colleagues feel positive about the transition. “Village Bakery has looked after us well and made sure we joined a similar, family-run craft bakery,” she added.

The acquisition increases Chatwins’ total number of shops to 26, including locations across Cheshire and Staffordshire. Edward Chatwin, managing director and fourth-generation family member of the firm founded by his great-grandfather John Chatwin in 1913, remarked, “We have long-standing ties with the Jones family, and both bakeries share a similar ethos and passion for their products, making this a natural fit.”

In a personal letter to staff, Jones reassured employees that “like Village Bakery, Chatwins is a family-run craft bakery, and all current staff will be retained with pay and conditions protected. There will be no job losses.” He also highlighted Village Bakery’s rapid recent growth, driven by the expansion of its wholesale market.

Peter Clarke, chief inspector of prisons, has pointed to "chronic" staff shortages as a key cause of many poor outcomes at HMP Bristol. A report based on an unannounced inspection in March found that one in seven inmates developed a drug problem, a rate significantly higher than at the previous inspection. The report highlighted widespread use of the new psychoactive substance spice and described the positive rate from random, mandatory drug tests as "exceptionally high."

The report also cited a "history of underinvestment" at the prison. Clarke observed that this underinvestment coincided with a rise in illicit drug use, which has fueled violence, debt, self-harm, and physical and mental health issues among prisoners. He added that staffing shortages and poor conditions on the wings further aggravated these problems.

Despite these challenges, inspectors noted "some grounds for cautious optimism," pointing to reasonably good relationships between staff and prisoners and ongoing efforts to support inmates preparing for release.

Responding to the findings, Michael Spurr, chief executive of HM Prison and Probation Service, described the situation as unacceptable. He confirmed that funding has increased and recruitment is underway, including for 29 additional prison officers. Spurr said priorities include improving safety, reducing violence, and enhancing first-night arrangements.

Mark Fairhurst, acting chairman of the Prison Officers Association, called for staffing levels to be doubled. He argued this would allow daily searches, wall patrols to prevent drugs being thrown over prison walls, and the operation of a full regime to engage prisoners in purposeful activities.

Katie Cutler, 22, from Gateshead, has been honored with a British Empire Medal for her fundraising efforts on behalf of Alan Barnes. In January, Barnes, 67, also a Gateshead resident, was mugged outside his home, sparking a global wave of donations. In response, Cutler founded the Katie Cutler Foundation to sustain her charitable work.

Among those she has supported is two-year-old Kacie Martin, who suffers from spinal muscular atrophy. Cutler, a beautician, said, "It was horrible, what happened to Alan. I think it touched and affected everyone and I just wanted to help him. But receiving an award is surreal, I cried for three days when I found out."

She added, "Since I began fundraising for Alan, people have reached out for help and businesses have offered support. I’ve had to reduce my business hours, and it’s been financially challenging, but it’s worth it for the opportunities I’ve had and the people I’ve been able to assist."

Reflecting on her growing recognition, Cutler said, "Many have told me I’m a role model. I’ve never been good at accepting compliments, but I think I’m starting to embrace it now."

Barnes, whose disabilities originate from his mother contracting German measles during pregnancy, described the award as "more than an award; it’s an honour and something to live up to once the publicity fades. But I’m confident Katie will manage, and I’m happy for her."

Also acknowledged on the honours list were other recipients from the North East, including former Sunderland goalkeeper Jim Montgomery, who received a British Empire Medal for services to football.

After departing Nottingham Forest, 32-year-old Scotland international Chris Burke trained with Kilmarnock. The club confirmed his signing through Staggies manager Jim McIntyre on their website, stating, "We are delighted to announce the signing of Chris. He will provide much-needed competition on the flanks and brings a wealth of top-level experience."

Burke initially made his mark at Rangers by scoring on his debut during a 5-0 victory over Kilmarnock in 2002. With limited first-team opportunities at Ibrox, he transferred to Cardiff on a free in January 2009. He went on to make more than 100 league appearances for the Bluebirds before joining Birmingham, where he scored 28 goals in 155 matches over three seasons.

In the previous two seasons, Burke featured in 50 league games for Nottingham Forest, including a loan period at Rotherham, before becoming a free agent in the summer.

The 20-year-old swimmer from County Down set a new record of 1:04.05, improving on her earlier heats time of 1:04.53. She successfully defended her London 2012 title by finishing 2.28 seconds ahead of Dutch competitor Marlou Van der Kulk, with Northern Irish teammate Jessica-Jane Applegate securing the bronze medal.

Following her victory, Firth said, "It feels amazing. I'm just so happy," and discussed overcoming challenges over the past four years, including a broken wrist. She added, "I'm so glad to have retained my title."

Firth is scheduled to compete again on Sunday in the 200m freestyle, one of her strongest events, and will also swim in the 100m breaststroke and 200m individual medley later in the Games.

At 16, Firth won gold for Ireland at the London Games and went on to claim three silver medals at the IPC World Championships in Montreal the following year before switching allegiance to Great Britain. A wrist injury prevented her from competing in the 2015 World Championships.

Competing in the S14 classification for athletes with intellectual disabilities, the Northern Irish swimmer took part in eight events at the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. In June, she set a new world record in the S14 200m freestyle at the Scottish National Championships, also held in Glasgow.

Police discovered graffiti referencing the 1916 Easter Rising on an Orange hall on Main Street, County Tyrone, at approximately 02:30 GMT on Saturday. This follows two attacks earlier in the week on another Orange hall in the county. Authorities are treating the incident as a hate crime.

Drew Nelson, grand secretary of the Orange Lodge, condemned the attacks, stating, "It is very concerning that there has been three attacks on two Orange halls over the course of recent days." He added, "It is evident that there are those who display their hatred of what the Orange institution stands for by shamelessly attacking our properties."

Regarding the Easter Rising graffiti, Nelson described this as a "challenging year" and expressed hope that the upcoming centenary would not be used "as an excuse and smokescreen to attack the symbolic buildings of their Protestant neighbours." He also expressed confidence that a small group is responsible for the attacks, which do not reflect the wider community, "vehemently opposed to such criminality."

Sinn Féin MLA Daithí McKay also condemned the incident, calling it a "senseless action" that "does not represent the views of the local community in any way." He emphasized the community’s desire to move forward and urged anyone with information to report it to the PSNI.

Nelson appealed for no retaliation, expressing hope the centenary of the Easter Rebellion "passes off peacefully and without any further sectarian attacks."

Cristiano Ronaldo, the Portugal forward, joined Real Madrid in 2009 after transferring from Manchester United for a then world record fee of £80 million. Since then, he has become the Spanish club’s all-time leading scorer, though speculation remains regarding the 30-year-old’s future at Madrid.

Louis van Gaal commented, "We are looking at all players, not just Ronaldo. But these players are mostly ungettable. With Ronaldo, let's wait and hope."

Ronaldo, a three-time FIFA World Player of the Year, broke Raul’s record of 323 goals for Real Madrid this season. Over more than six years with the club, he has secured one La Liga title, one Champions League trophy, and two Spanish Cups.

Prior to his Madrid move, Ronaldo spent six seasons at Manchester United, where he won three Premier League titles, one Champions League, one FA Cup, and two League Cups. He joined United from Sporting Lisbon in 2003 for £12.24 million and scored 118 goals in 292 appearances.

Peter Beagrie, 51, a former winger for Everton, Manchester City, and Bradford City, was convicted of assaulting Zarah Blake while angry and intoxicated, according to his trial. Beagrie, who resides in Killinghall, North Yorkshire, received a 12-month community order on Tuesday and has announced plans to appeal the decision.

After the hearing at Skipton Magistrates Court, Beagrie stated, "I am innocent, something I have maintained from the outset; that is why the verdict was so devastating. I will be appealing." He also confirmed he remains in a relationship with Blake, adding, "This has been an upsetting and traumatic time for us and we both feel there is no other alternative but to appeal."

The court was told the incident took place during an argument in Harrogate in April. A spokesperson for Sky Sports said, "When we first became aware of the charge, we removed Peter from our coverage pending his case. Following the outcome, we have terminated his contract with immediate effect."

Fisheries Minister Yoshimasa Hayashi has announced that Japan will set its target catch at 210 Pacific whales, roughly half of the current quota. Despite an international ban, Japan continues its whaling activities, which have drawn criticism from environmental groups. Last month, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Japan’s Antarctic whaling is commercial rather than scientific, contradicting Tokyo’s claims.

Hayashi stated, “Our main policy remains research whaling, which gathers scientific data to find a way beyond the moratorium. Through this research, we aim to resume commercial whaling as soon as possible.”

In March, the ICJ—a United Nations judicial body—issued its ruling in favor of Australia, which filed the case against Japan in May 2010. The court urged Japan to reconsider its whaling policy, stating it had not adequately justified the large number of whales killed for research purposes.

An international moratorium on whaling has been in place since 1986, with Japan beginning what it calls scientific whaling in 1987. The whale meat from these hunts is sold commercially within Japan.

Hayashi also said Japan plans to “submit a new research programme by this autumn to the International Whaling Commission (IWC), reflecting the criteria set out in the [ICJ] verdict.”

The Local Government Association (LGA) has criticized existing laws as "confusing" and "utterly outdated," urging criminal record checks for drivers of specialty and novelty vehicles and requiring their vehicles to meet safety standards. The LGA also supports a unified licensing scheme that would give councils the authority to ban exploitative operators.

Last month, video footage showed a rickshaw driver attempting to charge tourists £206 for a one-mile ride from Oxford Circus to Marble Arch. London Mayor Boris Johnson condemned the incident, stating that pedicab drivers should not be allowed "to take advantage of" passengers, and renewed his call for stricter regulation.

Councillor Tony Page, the LGA’s licensing spokesman, pointed to the rising popularity of "party limousines, party buses and rickshaws," stressing the importance of strong oversight of drivers and vehicles. He called for a consistent and fair licensing system, acknowledging that while most companies act responsibly, a small number of rogue operators must not damage the sector.

The LGA recommended that future legislation be based on the Law Commission’s draft bill published last year, which seeks to modernize the licensing framework and make it "fit for the 21st Century." Currently, rickshaws operate legally in London but without formal regulation.

A spokesman for Mayor Johnson said the mayor is lobbying the government to grant Transport for London additional powers to regulate this sector. Although rickshaw drivers may voluntarily follow a code through the London Pedicap Operators Association (LPOA)—which works with Transport for London, the mayor’s office, and the Metropolitan Police—this does not amount to official regulation.

An LPOA representative said rickshaws have been operating in London since 1998, adding vibrancy and color to the city’s streets while offering emission-free transport.

After dropping the opening set, the second seeds bounced back to defeat top seeds Stephane Houdet and Nicolas Peifer 4-6, 6-1, 7-6 (8-6). The British duo missed two opportunities to serve out the match but ultimately prevailed in a tense third-set tie-break following two hours and 33 minutes of play.

“It wasn’t easy for us, but it’s a really special moment,” said 24-year-old Scot Reid, who will compete in the men’s wheelchair singles final on Sunday.

Reid, the Australian Open singles champion, will face Sweden’s Stefan Olsson, the number seven seed, for a chance to become Wimbledon’s first men’s wheelchair singles champion.

Eighteen-year-old Hewett secured his first Grand Slam title, admitting he felt nervous late in the match after twice breaking the Frenchman’s serve but failing to close out the third set. “I got carried away in the moment on a few points near the end,” he said.

“It was unbelievable. Seeing so many family and friends here is an amazing feeling. I can’t thank the crowd enough for their support.”

A security official told the AP that most of the escapees were facing serious charges. Another report confirmed a riot had broken out inside al-Kwafiya prison. The breakout occurred a day after protests erupted following the assassination of a prominent political activist, though any connection between the two events remains unclear. Benghazi, where the US ambassador and three other Americans were killed last year, is regarded as one of the most unstable areas in post-revolution Libya.

After the Saturday assassination of activist Abdelsalam al-Mismari, protesters targeted offices linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. Hundreds attended his funeral. A Benghazi security spokesman told the BBC that some of the escaped inmates had been recaptured but did not specify the number.

At a news conference, Libyan Prime Minister Ali Zeidan said residents in the city’s southern district stormed the prison to protest its presence. BBC reporter Rana Jawad noted that a small number of inmates are believed to support Col Muammar Gaddafi, the former leader overthrown and killed in the 2011 uprising. Our correspondent added these supporters had been charged with attacking security bases after the conflict.

AFP cited a security official who reported unrest inside the prison before the escape. "There was a riot inside al-Kwafiya prison, as well as an attack from outside," he said. "Special forces called in as reinforcements were ordered not to fire at the prisoners."

Manager Gary Locke is in England looking to sign a goalkeeper as the team awaits scan results for Jamie MacDonald, who was injured during Saturday’s 2-1 victory over St Johnstone. Locke expressed serious concern, highlighting that MacDonald’s ankle is severely swollen.

MacDonald was substituted on Saturday by Conor Brennan, who cannot play due to being cup-tied after appearing for Stranraer earlier in the competition. Additionally, loanee Oliver Davies remains sidelined with an injury, further limiting options.

On transfer deadline day, Kilmarnock loaned teenager Devlin Mackay to Derby County, with the terms of the cross-border loan preventing his recall. “We had an injury to Oliver Davies, who was the back-up keeper, so he’s had to go back to Swansea, which is a bit of a disaster for us, to be fair,” Locke told the Kilmarnock website.

Locke added, “We’re trying to work on one or two things at the moment because Devlin’s down at Derby and we’re not allowed to call him back. It’s a big problem at the minute, a big headache for myself, so we’re trying to get something sorted before Wednesday.”

Belgium’s rail infrastructure manager Infrabel reported that at around 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT), a passenger train traveling at approximately 90 km/h (55 mph) collided with the rear of a goods train. A spokesperson confirmed both trains were on the same track.

Francis Dejon, mayor of Saint-Georges-Sur-Meuse province, said the front carriage of the passenger train, which was carrying about 40 passengers between Liège and Namur, had folded back on itself. A local mayor noted the severe damage and expressed relief that casualties were not higher.

According to Infrabel and the national rail operator NMBS/SNCB, two of the six carriages derailed and remain on the tracks. Officials reported that several injured passengers were extracted from the wreckage, with some in critical condition.

Prime Minister Charles Michel offered condolences to the victims’ families and wished a speedy recovery to the injured in a Twitter message. Infrabel has launched an investigation but has yet to explain why both trains were on the same track.

Earlier on Sunday, Infrabel reported a "lightning incident" on the line. SNCB tweeted about a signaling fault at 21:30 local time, which was later resolved, allowing services to return to normal. Frederic Petit, an Infrabel spokesman, told public broadcaster VRT that the lightning strike is a possible factor under investigation but emphasized that safety systems designed to prevent such accidents should have been operational.

This incident follows previous serious rail accidents in Belgium, including a February 2010 collision near Halle, southwest of Brussels, which killed 18 people, and a May 2013 derailment near Ghent involving toxic chemicals that caused a major fire, killing two and injuring 14.

The Sochi Winter Olympics will administer over 2,450 drug tests, surpassing the 2,149 tests conducted at Vancouver in 2010. On Sunday, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced that Sochi 2014 will implement the "most stringent anti-doping programme" ever seen at a Winter Olympics, following the withdrawal of Russian biathlete Irina Starykh after a positive doping result.

Reedie, who assumed his role last month, told BBC Radio that while match-fixing and illegal betting appear limited, doping remains a significant challenge. "I think we can win battles, I question whether we can ever win the war. But the more battles we win, hopefully the more people we will discourage," he said. He stressed that athletes who are not clean will be excluded, adding, "It has to be an element of deterrence by testing. There also has to be a very significant effort of education, and philosophically we have to get all of the athletes to understand we are in business to protect the clean athletes."

He cited a broad, unannounced pre-competition testing programme that likely uncovered Starykh’s violation. Reedie also confirmed that athletes’ samples will be stored after the Games to allow for future retesting as technology advances. "Sometime over the next eight years they will be looking at selected samples as science and technology gets better, so athletes who think they can get away with it now may not get away with it in the future," he explained.

Calling doping "the biggest threat facing Olympic sport," the 72-year-old Scot reiterated the IOC’s firm stance: "If they're not clean, they're not welcome."

The Sochi 2014 opening ceremony is set for 7 February, with competitions starting the day before.

The British Airline Pilots Association (Balpa) has confirmed that talks have taken place to address the ongoing dispute. The union announced that proposals aimed at reducing pilot fatigue will be put to members in a ballot. Brian Strutton, Balpa’s general secretary, acknowledged that although the dispute is not yet resolved, "sufficient progress" has been made.

Strutton said, "We have been working hard today and over the last few days to find a solution to this dispute about pilot fatigue." He noted that EasyJet management has made a proposal which Balpa believes has significantly narrowed differences on key issues. Consequently, he added, "We therefore feel it is right and proper to consult with our members at this stage and so we are suspending serving notice of industrial action on the company."

Earlier this month, it emerged that pilots were considering strike action during the week coinciding with the half-term holiday in many schools. A letter from Balpa to pilots, leaked to The Daily Telegraph, outlined strike plans, attributing the dispute solely to pilot fatigue. The letter described the core issue as "fatigue had risen year on year, to levels pilots and Balpa find unacceptable."

EasyJet responded that the new proposal was developed following "extensive" discussions and will be presented to its UK pilots in the hope of reaching a "mutually agreeable solution." The airline added that there is currently "no threat of strike action."

Keshi has disclosed that an unnamed agent submitted his name for the Ivory Coast coaching role without his permission. At the same time, Enyeama said he believed his case was closed after apologizing for "uncomplimentary remarks" about security in Kaduna, made prior to June’s Africa Cup of Nations match against Chad. The Nigerian Football Federation (NFF) deemed these comments a violation of the code of conduct signed by all players earlier this year.

Keshi, who renewed his contract with the NFF for two years in April, was recently listed among 59 candidates by the Ivorian federation to succeed French coach Herve Renard. Senior NFF official Chris Green has suggested that officials may travel to Abidjan to "reach a reasonable conclusion" regarding the situation.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Enyeama said, "I was told to apologise for my comments, which I did immediately, and they told me that's fine. Personally, as it was resolved in-house, I thought that was the end of the matter." He added that he only received a cautionary letter advising him against repeating such remarks. The 32-year-old, the Super Eagles’ most capped player with 101 appearances, denies ignoring NFF requests for clarification. "But I only found out about a disciplinary hearing in the media; I didn't get any letter to that effect," he explained.

As captain, Enyeama said he raised concerns about the venue before the game, which displeased football authorities. The Lille goalkeeper now faces a possible lengthy ban for breaching the code of conduct and missing Tuesday’s disciplinary hearing. The NFF executive board will determine any sanctions at a later date.

It has also been confirmed that the Super Eagles will host their next 2017 Nations Cup qualifier against Egypt in Kaduna next March.

At St Albans Crown Court, 32-year-old Iram Shahzad pleaded guilty to two charges related to the death of Spencer Bell, who was fatally struck while assisting a man who had fallen from a bridge. The incident occurred in January last year when Shahzad’s vehicle hit Mr. Bell, 71, causing his immediate death.

The court heard that Shahzad, a mother of three, had accelerated toward the scene and attempted to overtake slowing traffic. Traveling between 82 and 88 mph with two young children in the back seat, she noticed at the last moment that two stationary cars blocked the road ahead. Instead of stopping like other drivers, she swerved into the second lane, where her car struck Mr. Bell, a former policeman and charity worker aiding Alan Trethewey, 67.

On Friday, Judge Martin Griffith called the case tragic for Mr. Bell’s family and friends, acknowledging that while the term "Good Samaritan" is often overused, it was fitting in this instance. He added that nothing could fill the void left by the untimely death of this "splendid man." Shahzad received a 14-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and was banned from driving for 18 months.

Speaking in court, Mr. Bell’s wife, Wendy, said, "My life has ended. Once it was full of laughter and giggles, chatting all day long and happiness. Now it is misery, sadness and tears." Shahzad’s defense lawyer, Sebastian Gardiner, described his client as deeply remorseful and said her driving that morning was uncharacteristic.

On Monday, police divers recovered the bodies of Damien Little and his two sons from Boston Bay in Port Lincoln. Local media reported that Little, believed to be in his 30s, had posted a detailed suicide note on social media, which was later deleted. In response to the incident, the close-knit Port Lincoln community arranged a memorial of flowers and toys on the wharf.

A neighbour told the Adelaide Advertiser, "I tell everyone how blessed those children were to have such wonderful parents. I could not fault them in any way. I just loved them. It breaks my heart. It is just so tragic." Brenton Dennis, president of the Lincoln South Football Club, described Little as deeply involved in the local Australian rules football community. Speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, Dennis said, "You couldn't have asked for a better bloke. I've been involved with him through football and I know both families – it's just something that you hear about elsewhere and the way it's touched our community here, it's just indescribable."

Witnesses reported to police that they saw a white Ford station wagon speed off the wharf at about 6 a.m. on Monday. Reports identified the children’s mother as Melissa Little and described the couple as "doting parents."

The 31-year-old Cornish athlete, who competes in the 800m and 1500m events, represented her country at the 2008 Olympics and the 2014 Commonwealth Games. During training, Simpson—who had previously considered retirement in 2014—ruptured her posterior tibial tendon, the tendon that supports the arch of the foot. She received treatment from specialist foot surgeon James Calder, noted for his work with footballer Jack Wilshere.

Speaking to BBC Radio Cornwall, Simpson revealed she would be unable to run until at least April, after which she must attempt to qualify for the Olympics. "It's a big ask," she said. "This was going to be my last push to make a real go at the Olympics—there was a real opportunity to go to Rio."

She expressed uncertainty about her chances of Olympic selection, stating, "I'm not confident (of selection for the Olympics). It would be a miracle to do that now because I have to run the qualifying time and be ready for the trials, which is in seven months, and I've got three months off." Recalling the injury, Simpson said, "I didn't feel any pain necessarily, but I heard something and my foot went limp—then I knew I'd done something quite major."

Reflecting on the challenge of ending her career, she added, "It's hard to take the decision in your mind to stop, without having a reason to stop. It's hard to explain but when you have something like this, it takes the decision out of your hands."

Last year, the church acknowledged that the late George Bell sexually abused a woman during her childhood in the 1940s and 1950s, issuing an apology and paying compensation to the victim. Since then, supporters of Bell have called for the case to be reopened, claiming there is "a strong case for his defence." Dr. Ruth Hildebrandt Grayson, a member of the George Bell Group, said, "A strong case for the late bishop's defence has now been assembled by several people close to him, so there is no excuse for the church to delay a fresh investigation any further."

A spokesman for Lambeth Palace stated that the Church of England "takes all safeguarding issues very seriously and is committed to listening to everyone affected." He added that the church had worked closely with the Bell Group in receiving the petition. The spokesman confirmed that an independent review of the procedures used in the George Bell case has been launched, following House of Bishops guidance on complex cases, and that the church continues to support "the survivor who brought the allegations."

The petition, organized by the George Bell Group and delivered to Lambeth Palace, urges the Church of England "to allow a fuller investigation before considering the case against Bishop Bell closed," including "re-examining the evidence" against him. It underscores the church’s "responsibility to ensure fair and just procedures are in place for the future."

George Bell served as Bishop of Chichester from 1929 until his death in October 1958.

Bristol Mediation, a charity specializing in resolving neighborhood disputes, has been awarded £10,000 in public funding to implement its Road Sharing Restorative Approach scheme, which aims to "bring road users together." The organization highlighted that Bristol’s congested streets—where cars, bicycles, buses, taxis, and lorries compete for space—often lead to road rage and conflicts.

The initiative has faced criticism from some. Cyclist Hugh Marshall described it as a "cosmetic exercise," while Bob Bull of the Alliance of British Drivers dismissed it as "a joke." Marshall, who has been cycling for 40 years, pointed to an "explosion in cycling" over the past five years and suggested introducing an adult cycling test. He said, "Quite a good percentage of these new cyclists are either contemptuous of the Highway Code, or completely ignorant of the Highway Code." Bull added, "The problem is that cyclists can do what they like, where they like, when they like and there's no repercussions. That clearly isn't the case for motorists. These are the circumstances that breed people's feelings, so you end up with the situation where motorists are seen as anti-cyclist. It's a complete waste of money."

Along with producing a short film, the scheme is among several community safety projects funded by Police and Crime Commissioner Sue Mountstevens’ office. The council, part of the Safer Bristol Partnership responsible for distributing the funds, expressed support for "any project that encourages positive relationships between all different road users" and said it looks forward to "seeing positive results." However, some road users interviewed by BBC Bristol remain skeptical about the project’s ability to address the underlying issues.

Somerset County Council’s Northern Inner Distributor Road (NIDR), originally scheduled for completion in March 2014, is now projected to open by the end of next year. The council cites a bridge redesign as the cause of the delay but has not confirmed whether costs will increase. The road is intended to link the town’s western and eastern areas.

Work on the Kingston Loop bridge over Station Road has started. A council spokesperson said, “Some progress has been visible but much of the recent work to revise the design of the bridge over Station Road has been taking place behind the scenes. This is now complete and we are entering the final phase of the project, with work on the bridge having started this week.” The BBC reports that engineering issues with the disused bridge contributed to the delay.

Independent county councillor Mike Rigby, who has been investigating the delay for the past year, stated, “Clearly something’s gone horribly wrong with the project.” He added that the council required him to sign a confidentiality agreement before sharing further details. “I’ve asked repeatedly about what’s going on, and I can only be told if I sign an agreement promising not to share the information,” Rigby explained.

The NIDR project is connected to the planned regeneration of Taunton’s Firepool area, which relies on the new road to improve access. Planning permission has been submitted for developments there, including a cinema, hotel, shops, and housing.

Deaths began last week in Punjab province following Sajjad Hussain’s purchase of 4.5kg of laddoos—ball-shaped sweets commonly served at special occasions—on 20 April to celebrate the birth of his son, police spokesman Irfan Faiz reported. Five people died immediately after consuming the sweets, and by the weekend, the death toll had risen. In total, 77 people were affected, with 12 fatalities including Hussain, one of his sisters, all seven of his brothers, two nieces, and a nephew. While most have recovered, five patients remain in serious condition at Nishtar hospital in Multan.

As investigations continue, authorities have arrested two owners of the local sweetshop and one employee. Officials suspect the laddoos were accidentally contaminated with pesticide from a neighboring store undergoing renovation. Senior police official Rameez Bukhari told AFP that the pesticide shop owner had left pesticides at the bakery for safekeeping. Laboratory tests are ongoing after police reportedly found sachets of pesticide inside the sweetshop.

The sweetshop owners face charges under food control and poisonous substances laws. BBC correspondent M Ilyas Khan in Islamabad noted that although food safety standards in Pakistan are often lax, tainted products rarely cause fatalities. However, several fatal incidents involving contaminated alcohol and cough medicine have occurred in recent years. In a similar case in India in 2013, more than 20 children died after consuming contaminated free school meals in Bihar state.

During Wednesday’s attack on Westminster Bridge, 19-year-old Travis Frain from Lancashire was struck "head-on" by a car, sustaining multiple fractures to his hand and leg. Frain, an Edge Hill University student, was crossing the bridge with 13 other students and a lecturer during a visit to the Palace of Westminster to watch Prime Minister's Questions when Khalid Masood’s vehicle hit him.

Angela Frain, from Darwen, said her son survived after being propelled over the bonnet of the car at the start of the attack. Shortly afterward, the politics student—who hopes to become an MP—called his mother to reassure her, saying, "Mum I'm safe... I know you will be worrying." Medical staff confirmed he required surgery on his leg and treated deep cuts and minor whiplash. Despite his injuries, Frain remarked, "At the end of the day, it could have been a hell of a lot worse."

Prince Charles visited Frain at King's College Hospital, where the student posted a photo on Facebook showing the prince at his bedside. When a friend joked he "could have dressed up" for the royal visitor, he responded, "I do what I can, with what I've got hahah."

Among other victims, 18-year-old Owen Lambert needed stitches for a head wound, while two other students received treatment for minor injuries. The attack resulted in four deaths and 50 injuries, with 31 hospitalized.

Khalid Masood, 52, drove onto the pavement, striking pedestrians on Westminster Bridge before crashing into railings and entering Parliament grounds. Armed with a knife, he fatally stabbed PC Keith Palmer before being shot dead by police. Authorities have made 11 arrests, with 10 individuals still under investigation.

Countries that sell goods below their production costs—often to gain market share—are subject to punitive duties. Beijing contends these duties should be reduced now that China has been a World Trade Organization (WTO) member for 15 years. The United States has indicated it will maintain its current position, while the European Commission expressed "regret" over China’s legal challenge, noting that a proposal to revise how duties on Chinese goods are calculated is awaiting approval from the EU’s 28 member states. Officials in Washington and Brussels remain committed to enforcing strict rules to prevent a surge of low-cost Chinese products into their markets.

Since joining the WTO in December 2001, China has maintained it should be recognized as a "market economy," a status that would alter the calculation of anti-dumping duties on its products. China’s Commerce Ministry stated, "Regretfully, the United States and European Union have yet to fulfil this obligation," adding that "China reserves the right under WTO rules to resolutely defend its legal rights."

In response, the US Commerce Department emphasized that China’s WTO accession agreement does not require automatic market economy status and allows the continued use of "alternative antidumping methodologies." A senior Commerce official noted, "The United States remains concerned about serious imbalances in China’s state-directed economy, including widespread production overcapacity in the steel and aluminium sectors and significant state ownership across many industries. China has not made the reforms necessary to operate on market principles."

Earlier this month, Barby Dashwood-Morris appeared before Brighton magistrates and admitted to breaching planning laws. Magistrates were told that alterations to her 600-year-old home in Hellingly—such as demolishing a wall and installing windows—were uncovered when she attempted to sell the property. At the time, she was chairman of Wealden’s planning committee.

In a statement to the court, Ms Dashwood-Morris said she and her former partner, Alan Proudfoot—who also admitted to breaching planning laws and was fined—“strongly believed” the work did not require authorization.

Bob Standley, leader of Wealden District Council, confirmed that Ms Dashwood-Morris was disqualified as a councillor after missing all council and committee meetings for six consecutive months. “The rules are quite clear—if a member does not turn up to a meeting for six months then they’re automatically disqualified,” he said. A council statement added that this absence led to a vacancy in the Chiddingly and East Hoathly Ward, citing Section 85 of the Local Government Act 1972, which mandates immediate termination of a councillor’s membership in such cases.

Mr Standley noted that despite warnings about her attendance, Ms Dashwood-Morris chose not to engage during the trial. “While that was going on she decided not to engage in activities and that was the consequence. What was in her mind I can’t speak for,” he said. He added he would have preferred her to resign after her guilty plea, but she did not.

Ms Dashwood-Morris served as chairman of the Planning Committee South from 2011 to 2013 before being elected vice-chairman of the council. She has not responded to BBC requests for comment.

Gerard Ellis crossed the try line twice, while Johnny Williams and Joe Trayfoot also contributed to London Irish’s 24-3 lead at halftime. In the second half, Alex Lewington scored two tries, and Rob McCusker and Sean Maitland added scores within three minutes. Agen’s only try after the break came from substitute Felicien Vergnon.

Speaking to BBC Radio Berkshire, London Irish assistant coach Clark Laidlaw said, "We're certainly happier than we have been for the last few weeks. The boys have been working hard for a long time now and it's been a long time between drinks for the club, so we're delighted to get the win. It's a bit better feeling than the last two or three weeks for sure."

Laidlaw added, "There are large aspects of our game that we need to improve, but we moved the ball much better. We got through more content in our attack and found more flow and rhythm. That's what we've worked on for the last few weeks—getting our attacking game flowing and building rhythm."

Reflecting on playing against French opposition the day after the Paris attacks, Laidlaw commented, "Sometimes it keeps sport in perspective. We get serious about winning rugby games, but ultimately it's just a sport, and we're lucky to work in a game we love. It reminds you that it's just a game—there are much bigger things in life than chasing a rugby ball around a field."

London Irish’s starting XV featured Sean Maitland; Alex Lewington, Napolioni Tikoirotuma, Johnny Williams, Topsy Ojo; Ross Noakes, Kieran Allinson; Tom Court, Gerard Ellis, Tevita Aulika, Jordan Sheriff, Tom Symons (captain), Rob McCusker, Joe Trayfoot, and Tom Guest. Replacements were Tom Cruse, Matt Smallbone, Opeti Halavatau, Topsy Sisi, Tom Narraway, Conor Murphy, Harry Brophy-Clews, and Charles Waldouck.

Agen’s starting lineup included Tardieu; Nakosi, Heriteau, Roux, Deschamps; Guemes, Abadie (captain); Bethune, Barthomeuf, Chocou, Roidot, Marchois, Miquel, Gal, and Baget. Their bench comprised Morlay, Afatia, Ryan, Bastien, Felicien Vergnon, Darbo, Bouvier, and Sicart.

The match was officiated by Irish referee Gary Conway.

While the party has members and registered supporters in Northern Ireland, it does not currently field candidates there. Members from the region have long advocated for a change in this policy. Speaking to BBC News NI, Mr Corbyn acknowledged this sentiment, saying, "There is a strong body of opinion in Northern Ireland that wants to be able to stand candidates." He added, "Up to now the party position has been the opposite of that. We will be discussing that."

Mr Corbyn made these comments during an interview in Liverpool, where the party held its annual conference. He acknowledged the arguments for fielding candidates, noting, "There is a democratic deficit in one sense. There is a question of a relationship with other parties in Northern Ireland as well and how that will be affected." He urged an open debate over the coming months, stating, "There has been a long-standing debate. Let us hear all sides."

In the same interview, Mr Corbyn addressed the impact of Brexit on Northern Ireland. He said a future Labour government would ensure that "EU investment money lost will be replaced," adding, "We are also doing our best to ensure that EU agreed programmes continue for the rest of the time we are members of the EU."

When questioned about his past interactions with Sinn Féin, Mr Corbyn said, "I have always reached out to everybody. Of course, I know people in Sinn Féin. I always felt there had to be talks that included Sinn Féin to bring about the Good Friday Agreement."

On Saturday, Mr Corbyn was re-elected as party leader, defeating challenger Owen Smith, who received just under 200,000 votes. The Islington North MP, first elected leader in 2015, increased his majority with over 300,000 votes.

Recent data shows UK house prices rose 5.8% in the year to February, up from 5.3% in January. However, reports from Nationwide and Halifax indicate the pace of growth is slowing. At the same time, the Council of Mortgage Lenders (CML) recorded strong borrowing in January and February.

Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures, which include cash sales, reveal the average property price reached a record £217,502. The East led regional price growth with a 10.3% increase over the year, while the North East saw the slowest rise at 2.2%.

Nationwide reported a drop in average prices during March, and Halifax noted that annual house price inflation is at its lowest level in four years. The CML emphasized that borrowing in the first two months of 2017 was the highest in a decade, with 93,200 loans issued—the largest total since the financial crisis.

Paul Smee, CML director general, said, "Seasonal factors traditionally keep the market quieter in winter months, but 2017 began relatively strong on the house purchase side. Borrowers took out more loans to purchase a home in the first two months of 2017 than any year since 2007." He added that increased activity among first-time buyers drove this growth, though fewer existing homeowners sought new mortgages to move.
