She added, "Someone just said this to me and it's true: 'Nothing is missing under my watch.'" Ryan also stressed that all unverified missing items had disappeared before her tenure.

Despite the positive development, Ryan confirmed she will proceed with her planned resignation. The Boston Public Library is the first municipally funded library in the United States and among the earliest free public libraries worldwide.

Train services at Carno, near Newtown, and Bow Street, near Aberystwyth, ended in the 1960s. Mid Wales Transportation, collaborating with the Welsh Government, has identified a strong case for reopening both stations. The Welsh Government has acknowledged receipt of the group’s report.

Campaigners in both villages have long advocated for restoring their rail links. Mid Wales Transportation, also known as Trafnidiaeth Canolbarth Cymru (TraCC), supports the Welsh Government in delivering national transport policies across the region. The group completed an appraisal evaluating the feasibility of reopening Carno and Bow Street stations.

Trevor Roberts, chairman of TraCC, said: “TraCC has responded positively to the request from the National Assembly’s Enterprise and Learning Committee and completed the WelTAG report (transport appraisal). The final report clearly demonstrates a strong case for the Welsh Government and rail industry to include these two stations in future investment programmes, and I urge them to act promptly.”

Projects such as Carno and Bow Street seeking funding undergo review through a Welsh Government–funded appraisal process, with findings submitted to officials for consideration in the national transport plan.

A Welsh Government spokeswoman said: “The Welsh Government provided assistance to develop the business case for both Carno and Bow Street stations. We have received TraCC’s business case appraisal conclusions and look forward to discussing how to prioritise this scheme within the regional transport plan.”

Supporters of the campaigns in Carno and Bow Street were unavailable for comment.

A Civil Aviation Authority report on 2016 airport and passenger activity places Belfast International Airport fourth among 47 UK airports by passenger numbers, following Heathrow, Gatwick, Edinburgh, and Glasgow. The airport experienced growth exceeding 17% last year, serving over 5.1 million passengers. Although United Airlines ended its trans-Atlantic service months after a £9 million rescue deal, passenger numbers are expected to rise further in 2017.

Managing Director Graham Keddie called the results "an outstanding result," observing that "Passengers are voting with their wallets. They want value for money and frequent services at the best times of the day." He also pointed to the expansion of small to medium-sized businesses in Great Britain, noting that the airport provides competitive access to target markets via airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair.

Keddie emphasized that with the right support, the airport could achieve "much more," highlighting air passenger duty as a significant hurdle for both the airport and Northern Ireland. "If it disappeared, we could transform inbound tourism, leading to significant investment and the creation of thousands of jobs. Getting rid of this impediment is, in my view, a no-brainer," he said.

On United Airlines’ withdrawal, Keddie added, "We're working closely with government to deliver a major long-haul project that would open up attractive additional and badly-needed connections."

After opening an envelope in his office, Lord Ahmed of Rotherham was told to stay put as authorities treated the incident as a potential chemical or biological threat. The independent House of Lords member said the powder inside was later confirmed to be harmless. Police received a call at 12:30 GMT reporting a suspicious package, with a spokesman stating, "We are examining the contents."

In an interview with the BBC, Lord Ahmed described how white powder spilled onto his clothes when he opened the envelope, which also contained a note reading "paki filth." He recalled, "The powder went all over my clothes and I immediately shook it off. I realised this powder could be anything." He called the incident frightening and said it was an even greater shock for those nearby, as security personnel urged calm and instructed everyone to remain seated while armed police were present.

Lord Ahmed added that medics checked his face every five minutes to "see if it had turned blue." Reflecting on the recent killing of MP Jo Cox in her Birstall, West Yorkshire constituency, he said, "I immediately thought that this could be more serious than just an abusive letter." He expressed concern about the incident and revealed he had been targeted by racist messages about a dozen times before, attributing these attacks to his status as the first Muslim life peer in the House of Lords.

Boyle told Radio Times that both he and screenwriter Frank Cottrell Boyce were left "in grief" by the refusal. He explained that the Steve Jobs film was intended to "fill the space in my heart left by the abandoned Bowie script," and said Bowie's decision only increased his determination to complete the project. The forthcoming film, written by Aaron Sorkin of The West Wing and starring Michael Fassbender and Kate Winslet, is widely viewed as a strong contender for awards season.

At the same time, Boyle is preparing to return to his 1996 cult classic Trainspotting, with plans to release the sequel alongside the original’s 20th anniversary next year. Speaking to Radio Times, he clarified, "It's not called Porno!"—a reference to the Irvine Welsh novel loosely inspiring the follow-up. "It's T2 for now. We've got a window for the original cast to shoot in spring 2016 and hopefully it will come out the same year, on the anniversary."

Ireland has claimed just one win from three Group A fixtures, with five teams competing for three places in the next round. On Friday in Colombo, tournament favourites India delivered a dominant performance, posting 250-2, with Thirush Kamini remaining unbeaten on 113. Ireland’s reply ended at 125 all out in 49.1 overs, Gaby Lewis leading the scoring with 33 and Isobel Joyce adding 31. Though Joyce and Kim Garth each took a wicket, Ireland’s bowlers were unable to restrain India’s batting lineup.

At the P Sara Oval, Kamini and Deepti Sharma established a robust 174-run opening partnership, presenting Ireland with a steep target. Ireland’s innings faltered early as wickets fell at 4-2 and 15-3, with only Laura Delany (21) and Amy Kenealy (20) reaching double figures. Poonam Yadav claimed 3-30 as India, now leading Group A, secured their third straight victory and progressed to the Super Six stage.

Ireland opened the tournament with a win over Zimbabwe, but on Wednesday suffered a heavy 146-run defeat to hosts Sri Lanka. Ireland coach Aaron Hamilton commented, “India are a very strong side and they played good cricket throughout. We struggled at the start of our batting, as we did against Sri Lanka. We hit the fielders a lot and I thought we could have been braver and taken on their bowling more and hit over the top.”

Elsewhere in Group A on Friday, Zimbabwe defeated Thailand by 36 runs, resulting in Sri Lanka, Zimbabwe, and Ireland all being level on four points, although Ireland has played an additional match. In Group B, Scotland faces near elimination after a seven-wicket loss to Bangladesh, while Papua New Guinea suffered a comprehensive defeat to Pakistan, being bowled out for 40.

The top four teams from the Super Six stage will qualify for the World Cup, set to be held in England this summer. All matches are played in Colombo, starting at 04:30 GMT, at venues including Colombo Cricket Club (CCC), Mercantile Cricket Association Ground (MCA), Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC), and P Sara Oval (PSS).

China recently reported that a senior military official visited the South China Sea, a region experiencing rising tensions amid its ongoing military expansion. This week, the US and the Philippines agreed to conduct joint patrols in the area. China claims sovereignty over most of the South China Sea and has strengthened these assertions.

On Friday, Ash Carter arrived aboard the USS John C. Stennis and spoke alongside Philippine Defense Secretary Voltaire Gazmin. Carter remarked, "What's new is not an American carrier in this region. What's new is the context of tension which exists, which we want to reduce." He underscored the US’s intent to cooperate with China and said the visit was intended to support allies, not to provoke Beijing.

In reaction to China’s military buildup, which includes constructing islands with airstrips, the US has stepped up support for its South Pacific allies. China has reclaimed land around reefs in the disputed sea—a move condemned by the US and others as militarization. Beijing maintains these developments serve civilian purposes.

Last week, US military officials announced $40 million (£28 million) in military aid to the Philippines to boost intelligence-sharing, surveillance, and naval patrol operations in the contested South China Sea.

Recent Rangers signing Barton, 33, claimed that Brown was "nowhere near his level." Scotland captain Brown, 30, responded with a joke: "I've not been in his league, he's in my league." He also said, "I think we'll get on really well, him being a Celtic fan, so I think we'll get on great."

Brown expressed excitement about playing under new manager Brendan Rodgers, commenting, "He's been really positive with what he's done on the pitch so far. It's exciting everybody, the way we're going to play, and we're just looking forward to every single moment of it." He added, "We're going to be a lot closer on and off the field, so it's going to be good times ahead. It's just a positive vibe throughout."

Looking ahead to Celtic’s league opener against Hearts on 6 August, Brown stated, "We've got a new manager, we've got a fresh start. We'll show what we can do."

Brown missed part of last season due to injury and sat out the final stages after Celtic secured a fifth consecutive title. Reflecting on his recovery, he said, "That's me back to normality. I've had a good four or five weeks off for the first time in 10 years, so it's been lovely." He added, "I feel fine. I feel just as fit as I was last season when I was playing injury-free."

In last Friday’s Heineken Cup match at Franklin’s Gardens, Ulster beat Northampton Saints 25-6. Following the match, Saints captain Dylan Hartley was cited and admitted guilt, leading to a suspension that will rule him out of the return fixture against Ulster on 15 December and the home Premiership game against league leaders Harlequins a week later.

The ban was confirmed at a disciplinary hearing in Dublin on Thursday. Earlier this year, Hartley served an eight-week suspension for biting Ireland flanker Stephen Ferris during a Six Nations match at Twickenham. In April 2007, he received a 26-week ban for gouging the eyes of Wasps players James Haskell and Jonny O’Connor.

According to a European Rugby Cup statement, judicial officer Roger Morris classified the incident against Ulster as a “low-end entry point” offence under law 10.4(a), which covers striking or punching an opponent. Mid-range offences carry five-week suspensions, while top-end offences can result in bans from eight to 52 weeks.

Saints director of rugby Jim Mallinder told BBC Radio Northampton, “He’s our captain and our talisman and it’s a frustration to lose him. But it’s competitive. He’s come up against an old adversary in Rory Best and although it wasn’t a massive incident, it was something. It’s playing on the edge, but not going over it, and it’s something all the players have to learn.”

Hartley will be eligible to return from Christmas Eve, although Northampton’s next match is their Premiership game against Saracens on 30 December.

Laura Matthews-James, 35, of Pen-y-groes, was seven months pregnant when her Fiat 500 collided with Robert Hitchcock’s car on 26 February 2016 along the B4300 near Carmarthen. She denies causing death by driving without due care and attention.

At Swansea Crown Court, it emerged that Matthews-James, a biomedical scientist, could not recall overtaking two vehicles simultaneously before the crash. She had been driving to her job at Glangwili Hospital in Carmarthen. Hitchcock, 54, died instantly in the collision. Matthews-James was airlifted to hospital, where doctors discovered her unborn baby had died and performed an emergency Caesarean section.

In court, she said she had no memory of the crash and no reason to rush, stating, "I wouldn't take any risks because I was pregnant. My boss was quite flexible as long as I was there around 9am." She acknowledged overtaking cars—sometimes two at once on the same road—but said no previous issues had occurred.

She told the court, "You can see quite far ahead." When asked why she overtook despite not being late, she explained, "Just because they were going slower than I wanted to go. I was going about 40 in a 60 area. I thought to myself, 'I don't want to do 40 all the way to Carmarthen.'"

The court heard that mud from nearby fields was scattered along the road after the crash, potentially creating a hazard. Defence counsel Ignatius Hughes QC said Matthews-James had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder following the accident and the loss of her unborn child. Hughes read a statement from a forensic psychiatrist describing her as "fragile and stressed," adding, "She has said she doesn't want to bring a child into the world because in her words 'I've killed my baby.'"

The trial is ongoing.

Last month, Mr. McGuigan was shot dead, with police suspecting the involvement of Provisional IRA members. On Wednesday, Bobby Storey, Eddie Copeland, and Brian Gillen were arrested in Belfast, followed by the detention of an unnamed 50-year-old woman the next day. Storey, Sinn Féin’s northern chairman and a former IRA prisoner, was released after two days in Antrim, his lawyer John Finucane confirmed. Finucane tweeted, “No evidence was put at any stage and my client will be suing for unlawful arrest.”

Last month, Chief Constable George Hamilton of the Police Service of Northern Ireland stated that detectives believe Provisional IRA members took part in Mr. McGuigan Sr.’s murder but found no evidence the killing was authorized at a senior organizational level. Sinn Féin has reiterated that the IRA ceased to exist after ordering an end to its armed campaign in 2005. To date, 17 people have been arrested in connection with Mr. McGuigan Sr.’s murder.

Sevgi Akarcesme expressed astonishment at the progress made by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and the AKP government, stating, "I would have never imagined that Erdogan and the AKP government would have come this far." When questioned about the European Union’s response to alleged democratic violations in Turkey, she observed that although some politicians remain committed to EU values, the institution overall is falling short. She added, "European leaders are giving Erdogan opportunities on golden plates."

Earlier this month, a Turkish court placed the Zaman newspaper—known for its criticism of President Erdogan—under state control without providing an explanation. The paper is closely associated with the Hizmet movement, led by US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. Turkey accuses Gulen of leading a "terrorist" group attempting to overthrow Erdogan’s government. Once an ally of Erdogan, Gulen has since become estranged from him, and numerous Hizmet supporters have been detained.

The full interview is available to watch on BBC World News and the BBC News Channel on Thursday, 17 March 2016, or via BBC iPlayer (UK only).

Kenny Everett’s programmes recorded for the early commercial station Radio Victory, once believed lost, feature his distinctive homemade sound effects and jingles. Former presenter Andy Ferris, who rediscovered the reels, described Everett as "relentless in his pursuit of entertainment." The collection includes Everett’s creations such as Sing-along-with-the-Beatles, The Backward Contest, and the sci-fi character Captain Kremmen.

Ferris uncovered the programmes in a batch of reels he purchased from the station after it lost its licence in 1986. He recalled, "At the time Everett was a household name with a very popular television show. He sent us a tape every week of one of his put-together programmes – it was great." He added, "It was Kenny being funny and taking the mick and playing the music he liked at the time – he'd be very amusing and dropping in lots of sound effects."

Everett’s wife at the time, Lee Everett Alkin, remembers him recording shows at their home in Cowfield, Sussex. Using multi-track recorders, he crafted effects that were groundbreaking for the era. She said, "I'd be having tea with someone and all of a sudden you'd hear all these sound effects – horrendous bloodcurdling screams – from down the corridor. So in the end we sound-proofed him!"

The Victory programmes, alongside remastered versions of earlier BBC Radio Solent broadcasts, are set to appear in a BBC documentary about Everett’s life. Producer Richard Latto commented, "It's remarkable how fresh the shows sound after all these years. The techniques Kenny used 45 years ago are still staggeringly impressive, but that's why he's hailed a genius by so many in the industry."

The tapes sold for £720 at Dominic Winter Auctioneers in Cirencester, Gloucestershire.

A hospital spokesman confirmed that fourteen patients were treated in a corridor within the A&E department on Sunday. The daughter of an 84-year-old patient, who wished to remain anonymous, described the conditions as "horrendous," stating her mother waited 18 hours for a bed. Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust, rated inadequate last year, reported a 20% increase in ambulance arrivals over the past year. On Sunday, up to 98 ambulances arrived at Worcester and 56 at the Alexandra Hospital.

To relieve capacity pressures, the trust opened 20 additional beds across Worcester and its Redditch hospital. The corridor used for patient care is staffed as required. A spokesman said, "Sunday in particular, we believe, was our busiest day ever. We did work with the ambulance service to look after patients for a short period. This is something we have done with the ambulance service before." He added that extra staff are being deployed to manage rising demand and expand the A&E department.

The trust acknowledged that some ambulance journeys could have been handled differently and said its main approach—admitting more patients—was "not working for our hospitals or for our patients." A new emergency department is expected to open later this year.

The elderly patient’s daughter told BBC News her mother was initially discharged with antibiotics due to lack of beds but was readmitted the next day, where she still waited several hours for a bed. She described two "banks" of mostly elderly patients along both sides of the corridor.

West Midlands Ambulance Service reported a 20% rise in 999 calls in Worcestershire on Sunday and noted that ambulance journeys to Worcester have "steadily increased" following a recent reconfiguration of services from Redditch. Further updates on this and other stories in Hereford and Worcester are expected.

As part of the Hull City of Culture celebrations, open-air events are set for 22 July at a new outdoor amphitheatre on the marina. Handel's Water Music will be performed three times at the Stage@TheDock theatre. David Pickard, director of the BBC Proms, highlighted the importance of recognising Hull as a City of Culture this year and noted that organisers aim to demonstrate the Proms’ nationwide appeal.

Pickard also outlined plans to build on last year’s effort to hold Proms concerts outside the Royal Albert Hall. He described marking the 300th anniversary of Handel's Water Music with "something special" as a long-held ambition.

Stephen Brady, leader of Hull City Council, welcomed the BBC Proms’ visit to Hull for the 2017 season. He called it a "real honour" for this prestigious event to leave London for the first time in recent history during Hull’s year as UK City of Culture and praised the Stage at the Dock as a "fantastic setting."

These Hull concerts form part of the BBC Proms' new "Proms at..." series, launched in London last year. This year’s festival at London’s Royal Albert Hall will include music from the Harry Potter films along with themes from Star Wars, Jaws, and Indiana Jones, celebrating the 85th birthday of film composer John Williams.

The full programme is available on the BBC Proms website. Live updates on this and other stories from the Humber region are also provided.

Kim maintained her two-shot lead overnight by carding six birdies to reach 17 under par, staying ahead of England’s Georgia Hall (70) and Thailand’s Moriya Jutanugarn (67). Fellow South Korean Inbee Park matched Michelle Wie’s first-round course record of 64, moving into a tie for fourth place. American Ally McDonald (70) trails by seven shots at 10 under.

Park, the 29-year-old Olympic champion pursuing her second British Open title after her 2015 victory, birdied her first two holes, added three more before the turn, and birdied the 11th, 13th, and 17th on the back nine, narrowly missing a long birdie putt on the 18th. Reflecting on her preparation, she said, “I’ve prepared myself pretty well last week at the Scottish Open, in the bad weather and the bad wind and all sorts. The expectation was pretty low, I just made the cut and I wasn’t putting well. The greens were much quicker today than the last two days which helped me a lot.”

Taking advantage of favorable conditions, 2013 champion Stacy Lewis shot seven under 65 to reach nine under, eight shots behind the leader. Kim will enter the final round on Sunday with a solid lead. She commented, “I know the expectation and I haven’t made the bogeys yet. But I think I should give myself a little bit of credit for it, and enjoy tonight. And whatever happens tomorrow happens.”

Hall, from Bournemouth, posted five birdies and an eagle on the fifth hole but slipped from second to tied third after a bogey on the 16th and a double bogey on the 17th during her last three holes. Among six players at eight under are English contenders Jodi Ewart Shadoff (71) and Mel Reid (69). Sally Watson, the only Scot remaining, dropped three shots in a 75 to finish at even par.

Subject to approval, New College Nottingham is planning a £27 million project to demolish and rebuild its Basford Hall campus, with a reopening scheduled for 2015. The redevelopment is intended to establish the campus as a regional hub for training and is expected to support local job growth. The Skills Funding Agency will provide £9 million, with the college securing loans to cover the remaining costs.

Throughout construction, students will continue their studies at Basford Hall, as the new campus will be developed around the existing buildings. Principal and CEO Dawn Whitemore stated the facility will concentrate on training in construction, science, technology, and sustainable technologies. She emphasized the college’s commitment to creating a "true 'community college'" that aligns with the ambitions of local residents and supports learners at all levels.

Built in the 1960s, Basford Hall campus narrowly escaped closure six years ago when the college considered selling the site due to the high cost of necessary upgrades.

Bernard Cribbins, 84, who was a staple on Jackanory from the 1960s through the 1990s, has voiced concerns that many modern children’s programs overuse "gratuitous" CGI, which he believes detracts from traditional storytelling. “You can’t help but notice how children’s TV has changed,” he said. Cribbins returns to the genre with the new CBeebies series Old Jack’s Boat, premiering Monday, praising the show for its balance of classic storytelling and animation.

Reflecting on today’s children’s TV, Cribbins remarked, “It’s all very fast and noisy now I think.” He recalled Jackanory’s gentle format, where a presenter would simply sit and say, “hello I’m going to tell you about Ratty and Mole and the Wind in the Willows,” before beginning the story. “Nice and gentle, and the only thing you saw, apart from the guy or lady talking to you, was a few captions and illustrations, which were stills. That was how it used to be. Pure, simple storytelling.”

He added that contemporary shows often pack every moment with CGI and animation, much of which he finds unnecessary when the story itself is strong. “I think we’ve got a very nice balance with Old Jack’s Boat of story and little bits and pieces [of animation] as well.”

Old Jack’s Boat was co-written by former Doctor Who writer Russell T Davies and stars former Doctor Who actress Freema Agyeman. Cribbins is also known for his role as Wilfred Mott in Doctor Who, along with appearances in Coronation Street, Last of the Summer Wine, and Worzel Gummidge. He holds the record for the most Jackanory appearances, totaling 111, and played station porter Albert Perks in the 1970 film The Railway Children.

Sunderland, known as the Black Cats, have struggled to retain their Premier League status over the past four seasons, finishing 17th, 14th, 16th, and 17th, frequently relying on late-season rallies to avoid relegation. This season has started with two straight league defeats. Manager David Moyes, who took over from Sam Allardyce in late July, acknowledged the ongoing difficulties, stating, "There have been managers come and gone and everything has been very close to the bottom every season." He added, "I've said I want to change that but I can't do that overnight."

The season began with a 2-1 defeat at Manchester City, followed by a 2-1 home loss to Middlesbrough on Sunday. Moyes, who has previously managed Preston, Everton, Manchester United, and Real Sociedad, said he wants to bring in "a few" more players but stressed he still has "got a lot of work to do with the players." Ahead of Sunderland’s EFL Cup match against Shrewsbury on Wednesday at 19:45 BST, he said, "I've told people that it was always going to be difficult. I think I said when we came we were always going to build. I've come in late on, it's never going to be easy." He added, "I hope I was being realistic. There was no point in me telling people untruths—I wouldn't do that. Do we want to be there? No."

Moyes also pointed out that the 2010-11 season was the last time Sunderland completed a full campaign without a managerial change. He emphasized the need for progress, stating, "The fact of the matter is we need to make improvements. We need to get more players in, we need to add to the squad."

Meanwhile, Sunderland goalkeeper Vito Mannone has been hospitalized after injuring his arm during training. The 28-year-old Italian, who has appeared in both of Sunderland’s matches this season, sustained the injury in a training session.

Bake A Cake Catering in Halesowen ceased operations on Monday and is no longer able to fulfill or refund orders, including cakes and table decorations. Complaints have been lodged with Action Fraud and Dudley Council's trading standards department. Owner Lisa Holt attributed the closure to a "hate campaign" involving burglary and arson.

A Facebook group called 'Bake A Cake Catering customers looking for replacement suppliers' has grown to over 2,500 members, with caterers, florists, and event companies offering support. Laura Nolan of the Nuthouse Bakery in Brierley Hill posted in the group, offering five brides free wedding cakes and homemade chocolates. She said, "It's heartbreaking for the brides. I just wanted to help. The brides are just flabbergasted when I tell them. One lady couldn't stop crying—you could see the relief."

Katie Battle, from Kits Green, Birmingham, is set to marry her partner of 10 years, Richard Washbourne, on 26 September. The couple paid Bake A Cake £600 for a cake, catering, a photo booth, room and table decorations, and a sweet cart. Battle said, "I was absolutely gutted. This wedding was a stretch for us anyway—we have saved for years to get married and this has now put me into debt. It's awful when this is supposed to be the happiest time of my life. This lovely lady rang me and said she could do the cake for me. There are just some amazing people out there."

West Midlands Police are investigating a burglary and arson at Bake A Cake’s headquarters on Albert Street, Halesowen. Action Fraud has forwarded reports to the National Fraud Intelligence Bureau. Dudley Council has advised those affected to contact the Citizen's Advice Bureau at 03454 040506.

Police said that on Wednesday night, a 25-year-old man drove onto railway tracks and became stuck while attempting to reverse. He exited the vehicle before a train collided with it, pushing the wreckage 15 meters along the tracks and causing significant delays for commuters. None of the 13 passengers on board were injured.

A local resident told ABC News that similar incidents have happened before, noting, "His GPS has turned him left onto the railway lines. It looks a lot like a road at night."

Australia has seen several GPS-related navigation errors over the years. In 2012, Mildura police warned drivers not to rely solely on satnavs after multiple motorists mistakenly drove into a remote national park.

Other notable GPS-related incidents include:

- In March 2015, Belgian tourists were diverted nearly 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) when their bus driver’s GPS directed them to La Plagne in the Pyrenees instead of La Plagne in the Tarentaise Valley.

- In June 2013, a woman in Belmont, US, followed her GPS into the path of an oncoming train.

- In January 2013, a Belgian woman intending to pick up a friend 144 kilometers (90 miles) away in Brussels ended up in Zagreb, Croatia, after using her GPS.

- In March 2012, Japanese tourists driving a rental car followed GPS directions toward North Stradbroke Island, Australia, and accidentally drove into the Pacific Ocean.

- In May 2008, travelers nearly drove off a cliff during a scenic drive from Bryce Canyon, Utah, to the Grand Canyon, Arizona, due to a GPS error.

- In October 2006, a man using GPS for a trip from New York to Pennsylvania mistakenly crossed the border into Canada.

Last summer, 29-year-old Mario Mandzukic moved from Bayern Munich to Atletico Madrid, where he scored 20 goals in 43 appearances. He has now signed a four-year contract with Juventus, the Champions League runners-up, who announced the transfer fee could reach £15 million. Speaking about the transfer, Mandzukic said, "I like Juventus and I like the city [Turin]. I hope I will be happy here. I will fight for my new team." This marks the third time in four years that Mandzukic has joined a club immediately after they lost the Champions League final, following his 2012 transfer to Bayern and last summer’s move to Atletico. Meanwhile, Juventus striker Carlos Tevez, the club’s top scorer last season with 20 Serie A goals, has been linked with a possible departure. Argentine football icon Diego Maradona recently hinted that Tevez may return to Boca Juniors. For more football transfer updates, visit our dedicated page.

Williams made his first appearance since last September by scoring in the 11th minute and assisting another try. He was substituted after 52 minutes to conserve energy ahead of next week’s Pro12 match against Munster. “Honestly, I didn’t expect him to perform that well. If anything, he over-achieved,” Pivac said. “He played very well in his first game back. His decision-making and timing of passes to hold defenders and create opportunities—that’s class.”

Pivac added, “I’m sure that would have pleased [Wales coach] Warren Gatland with the summer tour approaching.” Wales are set to face New Zealand in a three-test series this June.

Williams had previously suffered knee ligament damage during Wales’ 2015 World Cup pool win over England at Twickenham. The match against Dragons marked his first of the season for Scarlets, who remain in contention for a Pro12 play-off spot. Scarlets will secure fourth place if they defeat Munster at Thomond Park next week and Ulster lose to Ospreys.

Reflecting on his return, Williams said he planned to have “a good week training” before the Munster game after a satisfying comeback. “It was better than I expected,” he said. “It’s great to be back—it’s been a long time, and I’m just happy to be back with the boys. But it was tiring, and I thought I might not make it to half time.”

When asked about his Wales tour prospects, Williams said he remained focused on Scarlets’ remaining fixture, adding, “Those things are out of my hands.”

Julia Knight, 56, admits to administering insulin but denies attempting to murder her 81-year-old mother, Irene Robson, at Horton Hospital in Banbury in October 2014. Speaking at Oxford Crown Court, she told the jury that she gave the insulin to prevent being discharged from the hospital. Knight also denies causing grievous bodily harm with intent.

She explained her intention was to keep her mother in hospital care rather than send her home. "I felt terrible because I knew I was going to make mum unwell," Knight said. "It was a stupid, stupid thing to do. If I could go back and change it, I would."

Knight acknowledged lying to police during questioning in January. The court heard she forged a prescription for insulin, which she collected from a Sainsbury’s in Banbury. When defense barrister Simon Mayo QC asked why she denied injecting her mother, she replied, "I realised it was serious. I was ashamed of what I had done."

Prosecutor John Price QC alleged Knight intended to administer a lethal dose before leaving Horton Hospital. He questioned, "Why did you inject your mother with a substance which for all you knew could kill her within five minutes and do nothing for an hour and twenty minutes?" Knight responded, "I never intended my mother to die."

She also told the court she attempted suicide in 2006 by injecting herself with insulin. Although Robson died in September, the jury was previously told her death is not relevant to the case and will not affect their verdict. The trial is ongoing.

Sunday’s match between France and Switzerland at Lille’s Stade Pierre Mauroy saw the playing surface deteriorate, causing players to slip. Despite the stadium’s retractable roof, the damage is attributed to poor weather. The pitch, imported from the Netherlands, is scheduled for replacement on Friday.

To keep their hopes of reaching the last 16 alive, the Republic of Ireland must defeat Italy. After a 1-1 draw with Sweden and a 3-0 loss to Belgium, Martin O’Neill’s team sits at the bottom of their group. Neither Ireland nor Italy has been able to train on the stadium’s pitch ahead of Wednesday’s fixture.

UEFA has confirmed that the last-16 and quarter-final matches scheduled for 26 June and 1 July at the venue will proceed as planned. On the pitch condition, UEFA stated, "The extremely difficult weather conditions in the past few weeks (rain, humidity, lack of sunshine) have caused irreversible damage to the surface at the stadium."

Ireland left-back Stephen Ward said, "We saw the pitch didn’t look that great but it’s going to be the same for the Italians as it is for ourselves, so that makes it a level playing field." He added, "Myself and Wes Hoolahan have played in the League of Ireland, so we’re used to it."

Artist Chris Rutterford unveiled a large mural ahead of the 701st anniversary of the Battle of Bannockburn, a work that took more than a year to complete. Funded by crowd donations, the mural features the faces of contributors portrayed as soldiers. Among those depicted alongside Robert the Bruce are Lorraine Kelly and former Scotland rugby player Al Kellock. One warrior is shown holding a pet cat in one hand and a battle axe in the other.

Rutterford, known for murals depicting Edinburgh’s Hogmanay and Robert Burns’ poem Tam O’Shanter, said his aim was to “emphasise the heartbeat of humanity at the historic site.” He added, “As a proud Scot, the Battle of Bannockburn is something I’ve always wanted to paint. It’s a defining moment in Scottish history and such a powerful story. To have it hung on the battlefield is a huge honour.” He also highlighted the importance of diversity, stating, “Allowing people to add their character to the image is the only way to give it a ring of truth.”

Fought on 23 and 24 June 1314, the Battle of Bannockburn secured Robert the Bruce’s famous victory over King Edward II of England. The mural will be displayed in the courtyard of the Bannockburn visitor centre until 31 October.

At 20:25 GMT, Slough MP Fiona MacTaggart tweeted a message with a retweet deadline of 21:00. She expressed gratitude to the 14,268 people who retweeted her post, acknowledging their generosity and stating she had "no regrets," despite describing herself as "Twitter naive." She firmly rejected accusations that she would reclaim the donation through expenses, calling them "sad."

Ms MacTaggart said she initially expected to donate about £10,000, but the total amount exceeded her expectations. "I knew it would be a lot but it was more than I expected," she said. "There you go, it was a risk I took." Her goal was to motivate others on Twitter to support Comic Relief. She also mentioned that someone from Australia retweeted her post and donated 30 Australian dollars, which she described as "rather wonderful."

Recalling Comic Relief’s quirky spirit, Ms MacTaggart reflected on her first involvement with the charity when she was a teacher and spent a day dressed as a chicken. Despite some criticism, including a tweet from @greyfox63 accusing her of likely reclaiming the money on expenses, she responded, "So sad so many people said this. I won't."

Ms MacTaggart has represented Slough since 1997. She is the daughter of the late multimillionaire property developer Sir Ian MacTaggart, from whom she inherited a significant share of his estate. Regarding her donation, she said, "It is a pretty big chunk from my savings but I can afford it." However, she added she would not make any further donation pledges on Twitter.

New York’s attorney general has disabled over 2,100 gaming accounts as part of Operation: Game Over, a campaign made possible by legislation requiring registered sex offenders to disclose their online aliases. Major gaming companies including Blizzard, Microsoft, Sony, and NCSoft support the initiative, which aims to protect children from online predators.

Attorney General Eric Schneiderman highlighted the effort’s focus on creating safer online environments for children, stating, “The internet is the crime scene of the 21st Century, and we must ensure that online video game platforms do not become a digital playground for dangerous predators.” He added that many parents do not realize these platforms allow anonymous communication, a feature offenders have used to contact and "groom" children they later abused.

Under New York’s Electronic Securing and Targeting of Online Predators Act (e-STOP), convicted sex offenders must report their email addresses, login names, screen identities, and other online aliases to the state. These details are then shared with participating gaming and web companies, resulting in the removal of accounts on platforms such as Xbox Live, PlayStation Network, World of Warcraft, Guild Wars, and Gaia Online.

This latest phase of the e-STOP program follows an earlier effort that led to the closure of more than 3,500 online accounts linked to sex offenders.

Manchester City, the reigning English champions, announced on Wednesday that 34-year-old Carli Lloyd has signed a short-term contract with the club. City captain Steph Houghton told BBC Sport that Lloyd is "world class" and "a leader," noting her presence will particularly benefit younger players and be valuable for English players competing domestically.

Lloyd joins a Manchester City squad featuring England Under-19 midfielder Keira Walsh, 22-year-old winger Nikita Parris, 25-year-old playmaker Isobel Christiansen, and teenage England youth international forward Georgia Stanway.

Houghton explained that the club sought Lloyd’s leadership and experience to help them become not only England’s top team but also a dominant force in European football.

As Manchester City compete in their first European campaign, they will face Danish champions Fortuna Hjorring in the Champions League quarter-final this March. Houghton highlighted the importance of experience at this stage, pointing to Lloyd’s proven record in high-pressure matches.

Lloyd, who captains the United States national team, is the third American to join an English club this winter, following winger Crystal Dunn’s transfer to Chelsea Ladies and midfielder Heather O’Reilly’s move to Arsenal.

HMP Reading, a Grade-II listed prison closed in 2013, had been earmarked by Reading Borough Council for redevelopment. After a two-year delay, the Ministry of Justice informed the council that the site will be retained. In response, the Reading Labour Party launched an online petition calling on the government to reverse the decision.

Deputy council leader Tony Page described the announcement as a “bombshell” and a “major reversal” by the government. The council’s discussions on alternative uses have involved consultations with English Heritage and the Ancient Monuments Commission. One proposal suggests integrating the prison into the regeneration of the Abbey Quarter, which includes 12th-century ruins where Henry I is buried.

Mr. Page warned that “a unique opportunity is in danger of being lost due to government dithering and procrastination.” He urged Michael Gove and the government to reconsider and accelerate the disposal of the site to aid the Abbey Quarter’s redevelopment.

In a letter from Andrew Holdsworth, head of estates strategy at the Ministry of Justice, written on behalf of the Secretary of State for Justice, it was explained that contingency sites are necessary to address potential rises in the prison population. While the Reading site remains an option, there are currently no plans to reopen it. The site will not be disposed of until further notice, although potential future uses will continue to be explored.

Rhys Webb, scrum-half and Ospreys teammate of Jones, became the latest player to sign a new dual contract on Wednesday. Speaking to BBC Radio Wales, Davies stated, "I'd like to think that Alun Wyn will sign but that's not settled as yet. We'll wait and see really. Ospreys and the Welsh Rugby Union, along with Alun and his advisors, are in discussion."

Jones, the 30-year-old Wales lock whose current contract runs through the end of the season, said in November that he was "weighing up" his options. Dual contracts are funded 60% by the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) and 40% by the regions.

Davies emphasized additional benefits for players on dual contracts, saying, "It's more than just playing in Wales and playing for the national team as well. I think some of the leading players understand they are looked after pretty well by Warren Gatland and his coaching staff, in terms of the amount of games they play and the conditioning they receive. So I think there's a bigger picture than just playing for the Ospreys and just playing for Wales—there are other things to take into consideration as well."

A London arbitration hearing has upheld the International Tennis Federation’s (ITF) rule prohibiting players from representing more than one country. Aljaž Bedene, who became a British citizen in March 2015, had represented Slovenia in three Davis Cup ties before changing his nationality. The ITF introduced this rule on 1 January 2015, shortly after Bedene submitted his passport application.

Charles Hollander QC ruled that the ITF was not required to grant Bedene an exemption but expressed “greatest sympathy” for his situation. He noted the rule change came “at precisely the wrong time for him” and stressed that Bedene “cannot be characterised as one of those players who desire to adopt a ‘flag of convenience’.” Hollander also pointed to the Slovenian Tennis Association’s negative reaction to Bedene’s switch.

Now 27, Bedene has slipped to 104th in the world rankings and revealed at the Australian Open that he nearly quit tennis last year. The ITF board rejected his appeal in March but agreed to arbitration following strong lobbying by the Lawn Tennis Association.

Bedene must now decide whether to continue challenging the rule. Hollander expressed hope that “the passage of time will be sufficient to persuade the ITF that Mr Bedene is a worthy candidate for an exemption.” The ITF has said it sees “no reason in principle why a further application should not be made.”

The Twaddell Avenue protest, which has been ongoing since July 2013 following a Parades Commission ruling that blocked a return leg of an Orange parade from passing part of the Crumlin Road, remains active. On Friday evening, the Ballysillan lodge announced it will continue applying for an evening parade route past the Ardoyne shops. Although the lodge criticized some groups involved in recent efforts to break the deadlock, it said it had no choice but to suspend its protest—a suspension that does not mark the protest’s end.

Two other north Belfast lodges, Ligoniel and the Earl of Erne, which had supported a proposed agreement to resolve the Ardoyne parade dispute, will maintain their protests. The County Grand Orange Lodge of Belfast expressed respect for Ballysillan’s decision to pause its participation in protests seeking a homeward parade along the Crumlin Road.

Following a parade on Saturday, George Chiddick, County Grand Master of the Orange Order in Belfast, confirmed the protest will continue until a resolution is reached, meaning the Twaddell protest camp, established in 2013, will remain in place.

Sinn Féin MLA Gerry Kelly welcomed any progress toward ending the nightly protests, saying, "People in the area will be relieved at any such move." He added that Sinn Féin consistently supports inclusive dialogue involving local communities and parade organizers to resolve these issues.

Talks aimed at settling the dispute involving the Ligoniel and Earl of Erne lodges and the nationalist residents group, the Crumlin Ardoyne Residents Association (CARA), are expected to resume within weeks.

Among the seven members who have resigned is Frank Sweeney, former chair of the party’s constituency council, who pointed to a breakdown of trust within the SDLP in West Tyrone. The SDLP responded by emphasizing the area's "tremendous growth" and affirming that Mr. McCrossan "and his team in West Tyrone have the full support and confidence of the SDLP."

Mr. Sweeney accused party leadership of disregarding concerns raised by himself and others, stating, "We've been trying for two years to get the party centrally to intervene and to take action to remedy things. Nothing has happened and people feel like they can take no more."

These resignations come after three councillors left the party last week, including Patsy Kelly and Josephine Deehan, both planning to run against the SDLP in next month’s election. On Friday, the party said, "Josephine Deehan refused to engage in the selection process on the two occasions when the party held selection conventions—first to replace Joe Byrne in the assembly and secondly to stand for election. Daniel McCrossan was the only person to put his name forward and was therefore unanimously selected by more than 100 party members."

Other individuals who have resigned from the party include:

- Michaela Boyle, Sinn Féin  
- Allan Bresland, DUP  
- Barry Brown, Cannabis Is Safer Than Alcohol  
- Thomas Buchanan, DUP  
- Josephine Deehan, Independent  
- Stephen Donnelly, Alliance Party  
- Corey French, Independent  
- Ross Hussey, UUP  
- Patsy Kelly, Independent  
- Roger Lomas, Conservative  
- Declan McAleer, Sinn Féin  
- Laura McAnea, Animal Welfare Party  
- Sorcha McAnespy, Independent  
- Ciaran McClean, Green Party  
- Daniel McCrossan, SDLP  
- Grace McDermott, Sinn Féin  
- Barry McElduff, Sinn Féin  
- Susan-Anne White, Independent

Bloomberg reports that the agency tasked with stabilizing the market through stock purchases is seeking an additional $322 billion (£207 billion) in funding. Nearly 300 Chinese funds are reportedly ready to enter the market. The Shanghai Composite Index closed 2.3% higher at 3,744.20, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index rose 0.7% to finish at 24,552.47.

On its market debut, shares of China Railway Signal & Communication Corp (CRSCC), the world’s largest builder of rail traffic control systems, gained 0.3%. The company raised $1.4 billion (£902 million) through its flotation to support expansion.

Trading across Asia was mixed as investors remained cautious ahead of key US jobs data. The July non-farm payrolls report is expected to shed light on the timing of potential Federal Reserve interest rate hikes. The Fed’s next meeting is scheduled for mid-September, with opinions split on whether rates will rise then or be delayed until December.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 Index climbed 0.3% to close at 20,724.56 after the Bank of Japan maintained its stimulus program as expected. In Australia, shares declined amid falling commodity prices, including oil, due to oversupply concerns. The S&P/ASX 200 Index dropped 2.4% to 5,474.80. ANZ Bank shares fell more than 7% following the lender’s announcement of a $2.2 billion capital raise to meet stricter regulations, alongside third-quarter earnings that missed forecasts.

South Korea’s Kospi Index slipped 0.2% to 2,010.23, closing the week down 1% and marking its third consecutive week of losses.

If confirmed, this would be Pyongyang’s fourth nuclear test since 2006, marking a significant step in its nuclear development. However, nuclear experts remain doubtful that the blast was strong enough to confirm a hydrogen bomb detonation. South Korea condemned the test as a "grave provocation" but questioned whether such a weapon was actually used. China, North Korea’s primary ally, stated it "firmly opposes" the test, criticizing it for proceeding "irrespective of the international community’s opposition."

The test was suspected after an earthquake was detected near North Korea’s Punggye-ri nuclear site at 10:00 a.m. Pyongyang time (01:30 GMT), with tremors also felt in nearby Chinese border regions. Hours later, North Korean state television announced: "The republic's first hydrogen bomb test has been successfully performed at 10:00 am on January 6, 2016." Hydrogen bombs generate explosions through fusion, producing blasts far more powerful than atomic bombs, which rely on fission.

Bruce Bennett, an analyst at the Rand Corporation, expressed skepticism: "The bang they should have gotten would have been ten times greater than what they're claiming. So Kim Jong-un is either lying, saying they did a hydrogen test when they didn’t, they just used a slightly more efficient fission weapon—or the hydrogen part of the test didn’t work well, or the fission part didn’t work well."

Despite North Korea’s assertions, experts remain doubtful that it has developed a nuclear warhead small enough to be mounted on a missile. Observers agree a nuclear explosion occurred, somewhat larger than the 2013 test, but far from powerful enough to qualify as a full thermonuclear "H-bomb," as Pyongyang claims.

North Korea continues to pursue its nuclear program despite widespread international condemnation and strict sanctions. Meanwhile, China has shown reluctance or inability to intervene to curb these efforts.

The Grillet was one of three vessels escorting Hitler’s yacht, the Aviso Grille, which was seized by the Royal Navy after World War Two. The yacht spent time in Hartlepool before ultimately being scrapped in the United States. Owner Ron Cadman hopes a missing brass binnacle and compass remain in Hartlepool. Speaking to BBC Tees, he said, “It’s the original brass binnacle with the compass inside. It appeared in a June 2014 auction, but I only learned about it earlier this year. The auction house said the person who submitted it was from Hartlepool. Hopefully, I can recover it for the boat.”

Now based in the United Arab Emirates, Cadman is attempting to locate David Dixon, a Hartlepool resident who put the binnacle and compass up for auction in Taunton. The lot was returned to Dixon after it failed to sell. The Aviso Grille was one of the world’s largest yachts, accompanied by smaller motorboats used to ferry passengers into harbor. At 36 feet (11 meters), the Grillet was the largest of the three.

Adolf Hitler had planned to use the Grillet to travel up the Thames to Windsor Castle, which would have been his residence if the invasion had succeeded. Cadman emphasized that his interest lies in the boat’s historical value rather than its association with Hitler. “At the end of the day, it’s a historic boat, regardless of Hitler. It’s a 1934 German naval pinnace; very few survive. It’s simply an interesting vessel from that era.”

Following the war, the Grillet served for many years as a rescue launch with the Hartlepool Sailing Club before changing owners several times internationally. Although currently out of the water, Cadman hopes to restore the boat to its original condition.

Just two days after a five-wicket defeat to Worcestershire, the Bears bounced back with a 28-run victory over Leicestershire at Edgbaston on Sunday. The 21-year-old Hain scored 79 runs against the Foxes, marking his second T20 half-century.

In an interview with BBC WM 95.6, Hain reflected on the Worcestershire loss, saying the team had discussed where they had gone wrong. The Bears had suffered a major collapse at New Road on Friday, losing nine wickets for 35 runs, which contributed to their defeat by local rivals.

Having recorded his first Championship century of the season against Hampshire in the previous round, Hain highlighted the squad’s determination to recover after an honest conversation. "They were just words and we needed to put them into actions," he said. "We got a win on the board and want to take that momentum into the next game. It's nice to be among the runs – it's been lean at times this season, so to get a few is a nice feeling."

A win against Northamptonshire on Tuesday would secure the Bears’ place in the last eight of the competition for the 10th time in its 13-year history. Director of cricket Dougie Brown added, "It would be nice to get the job done there but we'll take one game at a time. We had a job to do at Leicester – there was a lot of expectation and we kept our stuff together."

With six games remaining, Palermo remains in the Serie A relegation zone after Novellino’s tenure, which yielded just one point from four matches and ended with a 3-0 defeat to Lazio. President Maurizio Zamparini, who dismissed Davide Ballardini in January, has reinstated him for a second stint this season. This is the second occasion this campaign that Zamparini has reappointed a manager he previously sacked, having also brought back Giuseppe Iachini in February after dismissing him in November.

Despite the club’s difficult position, 75-year-old Zamparini stated that Ballardini’s job is secure even if Palermo is relegated. “For the first time it’s in the contract that he’ll stay if we stay up,” Zamparini said. “And he’s prepared to remain even if we go down to Serie B, which is fine with me. I’ll fight over a lot of things with him but not football.”

Sunday’s match against Lazio was halted twice after Palermo supporters threw seats and flares onto the pitch. Visiting midfielder Antonio Candreva narrowly avoided injury from an exploding flare, with play stopped once in each half.

In its third year, the cycle race covers 304 miles (490 km) over three stages. It was launched as part of the legacy from the county hosting the 2014 Grand Depart for the Tour de France. The men’s race starts later in Bridlington, East Yorkshire, and concludes Sunday at Fox Valley in Sheffield, while the women’s race begins in Tadcaster and finishes in Harrogate on Saturday.

The event is co-organised by Welcome to Yorkshire, the region’s tourism agency, and the French company Amaury Sports Organisation (ASO), which also manages the Tour de France and other major European races. According to Welcome to Yorkshire, the 2016 race attracted about one million spectators, generated roughly £60 million for the local economy, and was viewed by 11.4 million people across 178 countries.

Many towns and villages along the route have decorated the roadsides once again this year. ASO race director Christian Prudhomme described the atmosphere as “amazing,” adding, “In every village there are blue and yellow flowers, with bikes, with bunting and huge flags and smiles on everybody’s face.”

Sir Gary Verity of Welcome to Yorkshire highlighted the event’s growing popularity. “We have 2,500 volunteers this time compared to 1,200 last year. Interest in the event is rising, and we have been receiving messages from across the UK and beyond,” he said.

Spectators will have the chance to see leading cyclists including Olympic gold medalist Owain Doull and former Women’s Tour winner Kirsten Wild. French rider Thomas Voeckler, who won the men’s race in 2016, will defend his title.

John Longworth, director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), has cautioned that "tawdry political tactics" risk diverting attention from critical challenges facing the UK economy. In a letter to Westminster leaders, he noted that such focus "has been sorely lacking in political discourse." Representing thousands of businesses, the BCC pointed out that for many companies, both large and small, domestic politics—not global markets—is a significant source of uncertainty in 2015.

He criticized politicians who "race between television studios and events to undercut their rivals' policy pronouncements, to proclaim themselves most 'in touch' with the needs of the people." Calling for a shift in priorities, Longworth urged, "You must focus on the causes, not the symptoms, of the challenges that face our United Kingdom."

With the general election approaching in May 2015, public spending and broader economic issues are expected to dominate discussions. In his letter to Prime Minister David Cameron, Deputy Prime Minister and Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg, Labour leader Ed Miliband, and other party leaders, Longworth set out several policies on the BCC’s agenda.

He stressed the importance of government support for UK companies "brave enough to sell products and services across the world," as well as initiatives to enhance training and create employment opportunities for both young and older workers. The BCC also called for greater devolution across the UK, advocating more local decision-making and an end to what it described as "crushing input taxes." Additionally, Longworth said that "maintaining corporation tax at 20% would be a sound beginning."

Charles Hendry has sounded the alarm that the UK could face a "real crisis" in energy supply without investment in innovative projects such as tidal lagoons. He pointed to strong backing from businesses and local communities for a project of this scale. The UK Government is currently reviewing its response to a year-long feasibility study on tidal lagoons, which Hendry led.

While Westminster ministers have largely remained publicly silent on the issue, Hendry emphasized that supporting these projects would be "beneficial for the nation." He said, "We must now decide how we create the energy we know we will need in the 2020s. We know we have £100 billion to invest in new energy infrastructure, and if we do not start that work, we will face a real crisis because there will be no supply."

He added, "If we want that investment and new jobs in the supply chain, we must send a clear signal to move forward. We can wait for something better, but ultimately, you have to get on the bus and say, 'I want to get there.' If you keep waiting, you will never begin."

Hendry is urging the public to write to Theresa May and other UK Government officials to express their views. He plans to meet Assembly members at the Senedd to discuss his review’s findings and will then address 80 business leaders and local council representatives at the Millennium Centre.

World number two Paxton added a second title over top seed Paul Foster after winning the men's pairs on Monday. This victory denied Foster and his Welsh partner Laura Thomas a chance at a record third consecutive title.

In a closely fought final, Paxton and his Welsh partner secured the win with set scores of 8-10, 9-7, 2-1. Echoing the men's pairs final, Paxton came back from a set down and a 1-0 deficit in the tie break to clinch the match. He admitted that a crucial fluke shot in the final end of the second set was vital in avoiding defeat.

Paxton told BBC Sport, "It's a shame for the game when that happens because it was a great game of bowls. To get into a tie break like that, no player likes to and I still feel bad about it, but it was a great match."

The English player, who partnered Simon Skelton to the men's pairs title by defeating Foster and Alex Marshall, downplayed the significance of consecutive wins over Foster. "You never get the better of Paul," Paxton said. "He's always there to knock you back – it's one game, that's all."

Purcell expressed his astonishment at the victory, saying, "I cannot believe it really – it's wonderful."

Foster, disappointed by the loss, reflected, "That's three years in a row we've been in the final and Laura's been a fantastic partner. It is part of the game and you've got to accept it, but it's hard to take. Yesterday hurt and so does today, but you have to move on. Congratulations to Robert and Marion. It was a great final."

If both players continue to advance in Norfolk, Foster and Paxton could face off again in the men's singles final.

The 32-year-old British and Irish Lion was left out of Sunday’s 23-man squad. Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster on Monday, Ferris described his former team-mate as "one of the best try-scorers about," and added, "Yes, he's coming back from a long-term injury, but to see him not even involved in such a must-win game was pretty mesmerising for me." He also noted that Les Kiss "has got to make big decisions at big times and he's doing that."

Bowe, who sustained a serious knee injury during Ireland's World Cup campaign in October 2015, has featured in 11 games for Ulster this season. He appeared as a replacement in last week’s Pro12 defeat to the Scarlets, after starting in the New Year’s Eve loss to Leinster.

Although the defeat ended Ulster’s European hopes ahead of Saturday’s final pool fixture at home against Bordeaux-Begles, Ferris praised their improved showing against Exeter. Director of Rugby Kiss expressed frustration at the team’s inconsistency and failure to convert chances, marking their eighth loss in 12 games.

Ferris said, "It's not working out at the minute, but Europe is over and in the league there's still a lot of points to play for." He added, "Let's hope we can get a lot more points and get into the top four and take the positives out of this season." Despite confidence in Ulster’s potential, he highlighted a challenging run-in, with home games against supposedly easier opponents followed by matches against Ospreys, Leinster, and Munster. "It's going to be a tough run-in but fingers crossed we can pick up a lot of points in the next five or six weeks," Ferris concluded.

The Bank of Scotland’s latest PMI for March showed "muted" demand for goods and services. Factory production continued to grow "at a pronounced rate," while the services sector saw its first decline in business activity in four months. The report also noted a "fractional" rise in employment.

The PMI, which monitors output across manufacturing and services, dropped to 50.1 in March after reaching a 19-month high of 51.7 in February. Readings above 50 indicate expansion. Manufacturing firms identified unfavorable exchange rates as a main factor behind rising input costs, with higher wages contributing further to increased operating expenses.

Companies responded to these pressures by raising their prices. Fraser Sime, regional director for Bank of Scotland Commercial Banking, remarked that the private sector’s economic upturn "lost momentum at the end of the first quarter." He explained that muted demand resulted in only a slight increase in new business inflows, leading overall activity to stagnate.

Nevertheless, Sime highlighted a more balanced perspective, citing ongoing job creation and generally positive sentiment among businesses. These factors suggest the Scottish economy is likely to resume growth as it enters the second quarter.

In July, Stoke City acquired 24-year-old Swiss midfielder Xherdan Shaqiri from Inter Milan for a then-club record £12 million. Since his arrival, Shaqiri has tallied three goals and five assists. Manager Mark Hughes told BBC Radio Stoke, "We're really pleased with how he has come into games and had a positive impact. Arguably he's been on his best run of form in terms of end product."

Shaqiri’s strong performances have helped Stoke move up to ninth place in the Premier League, just four points shy of a potential Europa League spot next season. However, he was forced off after 30 minutes during their 2-1 defeat to Southampton due to a thigh injury. Hughes does not expect him to be fit for Saturday’s match at Watford. "There looked like there was a bit of damage near the top of his thigh," Hughes said. "We don't know the extent of it and hopefully it's not bad but he's a major doubt."

Stoke captain Ryan Shawcross is also a doubt for the upcoming game at Vicarage Road. The 28-year-old, who missed six weeks with a back injury, returned against Southampton but suffered another setback late in the match. Hughes said, "He got knocked off balance and that's when all the pressure went through one side of his back. We're hopeful it's just a jarring and there's no damage. There's nothing you can do about it, it's just how Ryan's luck has gone of late."

In February 2014, 16-year-old Lucy Commins was a passenger in a Mercedes driven by 38-year-old Ross Clark of Kent when their car was struck by one of two racing vehicles on Ansty Road, Walsgrave on Sowe.

Clark was convicted in June of causing death by careless driving and failing to provide a blood specimen while intoxicated. At Warwick Crown Court, he was sentenced and banned from driving for four years.

West Midlands Police reported that Clark, who lived on London Road, Sevenoaks, had met Miss Commins and a friend at a pub before driving them to a nearby petrol station to buy cigarettes. In November, Reece Jones and Sean Sparkes, who were street racing when Clark pulled into their path, received their sentences.

The crash caused a Ford Fiesta to swerve to avoid the silver Mercedes, but a VW Golf struck its side, killing Lucy and seriously injuring her friend. Clark also suffered serious injuries.

Sean Sparkes, 33, of Nuneaton Road, Bulkington, was sentenced to six years and six months in prison, while 24-year-old Reece Jones of Attoxhall Road, Coventry, received an eight-year and nine-month sentence for their involvement in the crash.

Ms. Commins’ family issued a statement saying, "The people responsible have not only taken Lucy's life, they have taken the life from our whole family. We are left serving a life sentence."

Following sentencing, Sgt. Adam Green said, "Reece Jones, Sean Sparkes and Ross Clark will have to live with their actions, as will Lucy's family. Throughout the court proceedings, Lucy's family have been commended by the judge for the dignity they showed in such difficult circumstances."

Kris Doolan and Robbie Muirhead both scored twice, with Gary Fraser adding a goal between their strikes. Despite goals from Kilmarnock’s Josh Magennis and Mark Connolly, their efforts were not enough to secure a result.

Archibald told BBC Scotland, “Today was a chance to move above them, and that was our sole aim.” He added, “Like last week, it was an opportunity to climb out of the bottom two, and we succeeded.”

He described the victory at Rugby Park as Partick Thistle’s best performance this season. “Definitely the second half. For a period, we were unplayable. We created excellent chances and scored some very good goals. I’m absolutely delighted. Our ambitions today provided strong motivation.”

While the Jags now look higher up the table, Archibald acknowledged that a top-six finish remains some distance away. “Not right now, it’s far too early,” he said. “Seven or eight games ago, we were relegation candidates—probably even favourites—so it’s been a positive turnaround, but there’s still plenty of hard work to do.”

In contrast, Kilmarnock manager Gary Locke expressed frustration over what he termed an “embarrassing” display, especially following a credible 0-0 draw at Celtic Park last weekend.

Locke said, “I’m very angry. They earned praise last week for their game plan, and that needed to carry over. From start to finish, we were all over the place at times. It was nearly the same team that faced Celtic, and we worked on the same areas. Credit to Partick—they created good chances—but we simply didn’t do our job. Too many players failed to meet expectations. We must respond because that performance was embarrassing at times.”

Over the past year, accidents destroyed or damaged 20 large drones, with losses exceeding $2 million. Among the most affected was the Reaper, the military’s most advanced drone operated by the RAF and other forces involved in the US-led campaign against so-called Islamic State. Experts warn that drone crashes are likely to increase in both frequency and severity.

Documents obtained by The Washington Post through a Freedom of Information request revealed that investigators traced the Reaper’s issues to a faulty starter generator. Deputy Chief of Staff Lt Gen Robert P. Otto said the USAF is "looking closely to determine what is the core issue there."

Drone Wars UK, which tracks large military drone crashes, reports that since 2007 most incidents have occurred in Afghanistan, followed by the US, where drones are tested. Iraq ranks third. Since 2011, crashes have also been reported in or near seven African countries, as well as Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen.

Chris Cole of Drone Wars UK stated, "Large military drones crash so often that we can track the spreading use of these systems simply through looking at crash data." In 2007, crashes were recorded in just three countries—Afghanistan, Iraq, and the US. By the end of 2014, that number had grown to 23, representing an almost eightfold increase in deployment.

Cole added that remotely piloted drones are inherently less safe than manned aircraft, which accounts for the high crash rate. While most crashes have occurred in remote areas, the impact could be significantly greater if regulators allow large drones to operate in British and European airspace.

Jasper, a Border Collie, went missing during a walk with his owner, Adam Nolan, on Scafell Pike in the Lake District. The dog was last seen at approximately 14:00 on Sunday at Cam Spout Crag, below Scafell Pike. Mr. Nolan described the outing as routine, noting that Jasper was familiar with the fells.

Following Jasper’s disappearance, Mr. Nolan, from Cleator Moor, launched a social media campaign using the hashtag #FindJasper, which quickly gained widespread support. The search involved the local community, a mountain rescue team, a helicopter, police, and dog enthusiasts. After a possible sighting in Seascale on Wednesday, Mr. Nolan vowed to continue searching until Jasper was "home and in front of the fire."

In the early hours of Thursday, Wasdale Mountain Rescue located Jasper. Team member Geoff Horky ascended Scafell Pike after receiving information about a sighting near the summit, finding Jasper at 2:00 a.m. in very good condition. The rescue team then began the operation to bring Jasper safely down, and Mr. Nolan was reunited with his dog at Lingmell Col.

Expressing his relief on Facebook, Mr. Nolan said, "I'm over the moon to announce the safe return of my best friend Jasper," and thanked Geoff and the Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team for their efforts.

A Wasdale Mountain Rescue spokesman confirmed the rescue, stating, "The team responded and recovered Jasper back to the valley to meet Adam."

Meanwhile, a JustGiving page set up by Mr. Nolan to support the rescue team had raised more than £25,000 by 19:00 GMT.

Brighton may deploy Sean Long at right-back, but on-loan winger Joe Ward is ineligible to face his parent club. Striker Glenn Murray returns after serving a suspension, while full-back Liam Rosenior could feature following recovery from a long-term ankle injury. Left-back Gaetan Bong remains sidelined with a knee problem, and captain Bruno (groin) along with striker Sam Baldock (calf) will be rested.

England Under-20 defender Fikayo Tomori, recently loaned from Chelsea, is expected to make his debut for the Championship leaders.

Lincoln manager Danny Cowley told BBC Lincolnshire, "They are top of the Championship, and going into the Ipswich game we said we would need to climb a mountain to overcome that challenge. This is probably like getting to the moon. It will be a tough ask. It is a massive day for our players. For most, this will be the biggest game of their lives and the biggest test of their football careers."

He added, "Brighton have an unbelievable squad with incredible depth, and two teams that could compete successfully at Championship level. That is likely why they are having such a successful season."

Brighton manager Chris Hughton told BBC Sussex, "It is a big game, made even bigger by Lincoln’s exploits in the last round. We have to prepare as if it is a Championship match. We didn't do well in our last away game [losing 2-0 at Preston], so we know what can happen."

Hughton continued, "If we needed proof of how good Lincoln can be, most of our focus has been on that Ipswich game. In both matches against them, Lincoln were very good. We know how tough it can be, so we need to do our best."

On Thursday evening, the Rhinos, who occupy the bottom spot in the Super League, were heavily defeated 52-12 by the Tigers. McDermott, who led the Headingley club to a treble last season, described the scoreline as "terrible" and called the defensive performance "one of the worst" he has witnessed during his tenure.

This season, the former champions have lost 11 of their 14 league matches and currently sit six points outside the top eight. Should they fail to secure a top-eight position when the league splits after 23 matches, they will conclude the season in The Qualifiers, facing the threat of relegation.

Earlier this week, chief executive Gary Hetherington issued a statement affirming that the club is not in crisis and that the players remain positive. After their fourth consecutive loss, McDermott emphasized the importance of player accountability. "I back the players to come up with something and I don't want to be critical of them, but there still has to be some accountability," he said. He added that although the team showed moments of fight and made Castleford work hard, their effort was not sustained long enough.

The 27-year-old double European champion was involved in a cycling accident while riding from her Cardiff home to the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant, where she works as a physiotherapist. The incident occurred around 08:00 BST on Wednesday in Talbot Green, Rhondda Cynon Taff. She was taken to hospital and later tweeted, "No broken bones or head injury thank God," expressing thanks to those who sent get well soon messages.

Horne is currently recovering at home after sustaining bruises and requiring stitches for a cut lip. She was part of Team GB’s cycling Team Pursuit squad at the 2016 Rio Olympics but was not selected for the final four-woman team, which saw Laura Trott lead Great Britain to Olympic gold in a world record time. Horne also represented Wales at the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow and continues to balance full-time work with training for the 2018 Commonwealth Games in the Gold Coast.

The People's Pier project, a partnership between the universities of Bristol and Brighton, has turned its attention to Hastings Pier in East Sussex. Funded by a £48,000 grant from the Arts and Humanities Research Council, the 10-month study began this month. Clevedon Pier in North Somerset remains the UK’s only operational Grade I-listed pier.

Dr. Olu Jenzen, senior lecturer at Brighton's College of Arts and Humanities and lead researcher, stressed the importance of updating understanding of 21st-century pier culture. She explained, "Piers are more than just metal and wood, more than treasured architectural landmarks. They are lived experiences shaped by the mood of the time and the socio-cultural make-up of their location." Dr. Jenzen hopes the research will uncover new ways to repurpose piers as urban community spaces and boost local engagement.

Also contributing to the project, Dr. Nick Nourse from Bristol’s history department underscored the value of preserving Clevedon Pier’s "unique and varied" heritage. He remarked, "The people of Clevedon are right to be proud of their pier; it is a beautiful reminder of Victorian engineering and the then new concept of leisure. And although the pier itself remains largely as it was when it opened in 1869, leisure, and how the pier has accommodated leisure activities, has changed many times since."

Following a partial collapse in 1970, the Clevedon Pier and Heritage Trust raised funds between 1984 and 1998 to restore the 1869 structure. Hastings Pier, which opened in 1872, was badly damaged by fire in 2010 and is expected to reopen in 2016 after a £14 million redevelopment.

Pakistan has reported that Indian forces raided a military post in the Haji Pir sector of Pakistani-administered Kashmir, killing one soldier and wounding another. The Pakistani military characterized the incident as a "physical raid" on the Sawan Patra checkpost. The Haji Pir Pass, a strategically significant area, lies just south of the main road linking Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir to Srinagar in Indian-administered Kashmir. Pakistan stated that its troops "effectively responded to the attack" and that Indian forces left weapons behind as they retreated.

Indian army spokesman Col Jagadish Dahiya told Reuters that India responded to a "ceasefire violation" without crossing the Line of Control and confirmed no casualties or injuries. Another Indian official, Col Brijesh Pandey, told the Associated Press that Pakistani forces initiated "unprovoked firing" with mortar shells and automatic weapons against Indian posts, damaging one civilian home. He added, "We retaliated only using small arms," suggesting the attack was intended to facilitate militant infiltration.

Kashmir, claimed in full by both India and Pakistan, has remained a flashpoint for more than 60 years. Although exchanges of fire are frequent, fatalities are uncommon. A ceasefire has been in place since late 2003. India suspended peace talks following attacks by Pakistan-based militants in Mumbai in 2008 but resumed negotiations in February last year.
